title: Towards Critical IR Theories and Practices
summary: Belkin and Robertson urged us, half a century ago, to develop a theoretical foundation for understanding what constitutes societal good that can inform information retrieval (IR) research and serve as a basis for determining when we should limit our scientific inquiry in the face of demands that are contradictory to societal good. In this article, I argue that to achieve this, IR should embrace critical theories and practices in our work, and shift away from the dominant liberal frame through which much of the IR community today view societal concerns in context of our research. Unlike the liberal frame, the critical frame explicitly adopts nondomination as its stated goal which can clarify our conceptualization of societal good within the field, provide necessary theoretical underpinning that Belkin and Robertson urged the community to develop, and serve as a basis for critical appraisals of our progress in enacting desired societal change.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that IR research should adopt critical theories and practices—specifically a framework centered on nondomination—rather than the dominant liberal frame, to develop the theoretical foundation for societal good that Belkin and Robertson called for 50 years ago.
AI.motivation: Half a century ago, Belkin and Robertson urged the IR community to develop a theoretical foundation for understanding societal good, which could guide research and help determine when scientific inquiry should be limited in the face of contradictory demands. The author contends this foundation remains underdeveloped and that the current dominant liberal framework is insufficient for addressing societal concerns in IR.
AI.method: The paper is a conceptual/position paper that contrasts two normative frames: the dominant liberal frame versus the critical frame. The critical frame explicitly adopts nondomination as its central goal, providing conceptual clarity, theoretical grounding, and a basis for critical appraisal of progress toward societal change in IR.
AI.result: The critical frame, with nondomination as its stated goal, can clarify conceptualization of societal good in IR, supply the theoretical underpinning that Belkin and Robertson advocated, and enable critical evaluations of the field's progress in achieving desired societal change.
AI.conclusion: Embracing critical theories and shifting away from the liberal frame toward a nondomination-centered critical frame is essential for IR to responsibly address societal good and to fulfill the foundational imperative set forth by Belkin and Robertson.

title: GenPage: Towards End-to-End Generative Homepage Construction at Netflix
summary: We present GenPage, an end-to-end generative approach to Netflix homepage construction that replaces the traditional multi-stage recommender stack with a single transformer. GenPage treats the user and request context as a prompt, and autoregressively generates the entire structured, multi-row homepage as the response. We adapt the LLM training recipe: pretraining on production pages, followed by post-training via weighted binary classification (WBC) or reinforcement learning (RL). For industry-scale deployment, we introduce techniques addressing cold start, model freshness, business-rule enforcement, and serving efficiency. In online A/B tests against a mature, highly optimized production homepage recommender, the WBC variant of GenPage delivered a +0.24% lift on the core user engagement metric we use for launch decisions (p < 0.001), while reducing end-to-end serving latency by 20%. Offline, two findings stand out: enriching the prompt yields a larger improvement than scaling model capacity in our current regime, and RL post-training increases homepage diversity even though diversity is not part of the objective.

AI.tldr: GenPage replaces Netflix's multi-stage recommender stack with an end-to-end transformer that autoregressively generates the entire homepage. Trained via pretraining on production pages and post-trained with WBC or RL, it achieves +0.24% engagement lift and 20% latency reduction in online A/B tests.
AI.motivation: Traditional multi-stage recommender pipelines (candidate generation → ranking → page assembly) suffer from compounding errors across stages, engineering complexity, and suboptimal end-to-end optimization. The authors hypothesize that a single end-to-end generative model can directly optimize the final page layout holistically, simplifying the stack while improving quality.
AI.method: GenPage frames homepage construction as sequence generation: user context + request features form a prompt, and the model autoregressively generates a structured, multi-row page. The training follows an LLM-style recipe: (1) pretraining on historical production pages via next-token prediction, (2) post-training via either Weighted Binary Classification (WBC) on engagement labels or Reinforcement Learning (RL). Deployment innovations include cold-start handling, model freshness strategies, business-rule enforcement mechanisms, and serving efficiency optimizations.
AI.result: Online A/B: WBC variant achieves +0.24% lift on core engagement metric (p < 0.001) with 20% lower end-to-end serving latency vs. production. Offline: prompt enrichment provides larger gains than scaling model capacity; RL post-training increases homepage diversity as an emergent property despite diversity not being explicitly optimized.
AI.conclusion: A single end-to-end generative transformer can successfully replace a complex multi-stage recommender for homepage construction at Netflix scale, delivering both engagement improvements and latency reductions. The LLM training paradigm (pretrain + post-train) transfers effectively, and prompt engineering may be more impactful than model scaling at current operating points.

title: One Retrieval to Cover Them All: Co-occurrence-Aware Knowledge Base Reorganization for Session-Level RAG
comment: Accepted to the Towards Knowledgeable Foundation Models (KnowFM) Workshop at ACL 2026
summary: RAG systems retrieve documents optimized for answering one query at a time. Yet enterprise users arrive with sessions, that is, coherent episodes of related questions that span semantically distant parts of the knowledge base. We show that a single retrieval call over a standard knowledge base covers only 41% of a user's session-level information need. To close this gap, we reorganize the KB offline using co-occurrence-aware clustering and expand retrieval candidates through cluster neighborhoods at query time. On WixQA (6,221 enterprise support articles), our method raises single-query session coverage to 58% (+17% absolute; 95% CI: [14.1, 20.4]), reduces retrieval calls to 70% coverage by 34%, and compresses the KB to 20% of its original size, all consistently across four embedding models and six functional domains. We argue that session-level coverage, not single-query recall, should be the primary metric for enterprise RAG evaluation.

AI.tldr: Enterprise RAG systems suffer from poor session-level coverage (41%) when using standard single-query retrieval. The authors propose offline KB reorganization via co-occurrence-aware clustering and cluster-neighborhood query expansion, achieving 58% session coverage (+17%), 34% fewer retrieval calls, and 20× KB compression on the WixQA dataset.
AI.motivation: Enterprise users interact with RAG systems through multi-turn sessions containing semantically diverse but coherent questions. Standard single-query retrieval fails to capture this session-level information need, covering only 41% of it. The gap motivates shifting evaluation from single-query recall to session-level coverage and designing retrieval methods that anticipate cross-query relationships.
AI.method: Offline: reorganize the knowledge base using co-occurrence-aware clustering — articles frequently co-retrieved within the same sessions are grouped into clusters. Online: at query time, expand the retrieval candidate set by including documents from the cluster neighborhood (neighboring clusters) of the initially retrieved results. This avoids multiple retrieval calls while broadening coverage across semantically distant but session-related content.
AI.result: On WixQA (6,221 enterprise support articles): single-query session coverage improved from 41% to 58% (+17 percentage points; 95% CI: [14.1, 20.4]). Retrieval calls needed to reach 70% coverage reduced by 34%. KB compressed to 20% of original size. Results held consistently across four embedding models and six functional domains.
AI.conclusion: Session-level coverage should replace single-query recall as the primary evaluation metric for enterprise RAG. Co-occurrence-aware clustering with neighborhood expansion is a lightweight, model-agnostic method that significantly improves session-level retrieval effectiveness while simultaneously compressing the knowledge base and reducing query costs.

title: Unsupervised Data-Efficient Cross-Modal Retrieval with Global-Neighborhood Alignment Hashing
summary: Compared to supervised cross-modal hashing (CMH), unsupervised CMH reduces the reliance on manual labeling by learning binary codes from unlabeled image-text pairs. However, existing unsupervised CMH methods often rely on large-scale image-text pairs, which are costly to collect. To address this limitation, we propose Global-Neighborhood Alignment Hashing (GNAH), a novel approach that preserves the semantic structure of vision-language foundation models within a compact binary Hamming space using only a limited number of image-text pairs. Specifically, GNAH captures global structural information from the continuous latent space and transfers it into the binary Hamming space through a Prototype-Anchored Global Alignment module. In addition, GNAH extends conventional pairwise contrastive learning by modeling stochastic neighborhood relationships via a Contrastive Stochastic Neighborhood Alignment module, thereby alleviating overfitting to sparse pairwise correlations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GNAH consistently outperforms existing unsupervised cross-modal retrieval methods under data-constrained settings, offering a practical solution for real-world CMH applications.

AI.tldr: GNAH is an unsupervised cross-modal hashing method that learns compact binary codes from limited image-text pairs by aligning global semantic structures and stochastic neighborhood relationships from foundation model latent spaces into the Hamming space.
AI.motivation: Existing unsupervised CMH methods require large-scale image-text pairs which are expensive to collect. There is a need for an unsupervised hashing approach that works effectively under data-constrained settings while leveraging rich semantic priors from vision-language foundation models.
AI.method: GNAH employs two key modules: (1) a Prototype-Anchored Global Alignment module that captures global structural information from the continuous latent space of foundation models and transfers it to the binary Hamming space; (2) a Contrastive Stochastic Neighborhood Alignment module that models stochastic neighborhood relationships, going beyond conventional pairwise contrastive learning to mitigate overfitting to sparse pairwise correlations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show GNAH consistently outperforms existing unsupervised cross-modal retrieval methods under data-constrained settings.
AI.conclusion: GNAH offers a practical and effective solution for real-world unsupervised cross-modal hashing applications where only limited image-text pairs are available.

title: A Single Rewrite Suffices: Empirical Lessons from Production Skill Description Optimization
summary: Enterprise AI agents route user queries to specialized skills by matching queries against natural language skill descriptions. When two skills share overlapping descriptions, the routing LLM misroutes queries, a failure we term skill collision. As agents scale to dozens of skills, manually tuning descriptions to maintain routing accuracy becomes a significant engineering bottleneck. We deploy an automated description optimization pipeline on a production enterprise group chat agent (9 skills, 372 regression cases). The pipeline produces descriptions averaging 79.2% F1, matching manually tuned descriptions at 79.4% F1 (average per-skill difference -0.20%, within the 0.78% multi-seed noise floor), while reducing per-skill engineering effort from 120 minutes to 3.8 minutes (32 times speedup). We then examine which pipeline components actually drive this match. Systematic ablation on both the production system and ToolBench (16k tools) reveals that a single LLM rewrite using any available false-positive and false-negative cases captures most of the available improvement. Other design choices we tested (iteration budget, feedback signal composition, dual editing of confused pairs, and training set size) each affect final F1 by less than 0.5%. Description optimization addresses skill collisions caused by overlapping descriptions but cannot resolve cases where two skills intended scopes genuinely overlap. We identify a diagnostic (a large train-validation F1 gap) that flags the latter cases for architectural rather than text-level intervention.

AI.tldr: Enterprise AI agents suffer from "skill collision" when overlapping skill descriptions cause LLM routing failures. An automated description optimization pipeline achieves F1 scores matching manual tuning (79.2% vs 79.4%) while reducing engineering effort 32× (120 min → 3.8 min per skill). A single LLM rewrite using false-positive/negative cases captures most gains; iteration budget, feedback composition, and other design choices each affect F1 by <0.5%. A train-validation F1 gap diagnostic flags cases requiring architectural intervention when skill scopes genuinely overlap.
AI.motivation: As enterprise AI agents scale to dozens of skills, manually tuning natural language skill descriptions to prevent routing misclassifications (skill collisions) becomes a significant engineering bottleneck. The authors aim to automate this tuning process.
AI.method: Deployed an automated description optimization pipeline on a production enterprise group chat agent with 9 skills and 372 regression cases. Evaluated against manually tuned baselines using F1 score. Conducted systematic ablation studies on both the production system and ToolBench (16k tools) to isolate which pipeline components matter most — varying iteration budget, feedback signal composition, dual editing of confused pairs, and training set size.
AI.result: The automated pipeline achieved 79.2% F1, matching manually tuned descriptions at 79.4% F1 (per-skill difference -0.20%, within the 0.78% multi-seed noise floor). Per-skill engineering effort dropped from 120 to 3.8 minutes (32× speedup). Ablation revealed a single LLM rewrite with false-positive/negative cases captures most improvement; other design choices each affected F1 by <0.5%. A large train-validation F1 gap was identified as a diagnostic for genuine skill scope overlap requiring architectural changes.
AI.conclusion: Automated description optimization effectively replaces manual tuning for resolving skill collisions from overlapping descriptions, with most benefit coming from a simple single LLM rewrite. Cases where skill scopes genuinely overlap cannot be fixed textually and require architectural intervention, diagnosable via a train-validation F1 gap.

title: Governance Gaps in Agent Interoperability Protocols: What MCP, A2A, and ACP Cannot Express
summary: Agent interoperability protocols (MCP, A2A, ACP, ANP, and ERC-8004) have rapidly matured to enable identity, capability discovery, tool access, and message exchange between autonomous agents. However, as enterprises deploy heterogeneous agent fleets that must make collective decisions under governance constraints, a question arises: can these protocols support governed agent communities, or only task-oriented coordination? We present a systematic gap analysis applying a six-dimension governance requirements taxonomy (membership, deliberation, voting, dissent preservation, human escalation, and audit/replay) derived from organizational theory, multi-agent systems literature, and enterprise governance standards. We analyze each protocol's specification against this taxonomy, classifying capabilities as Supported, Partial, or Absent. The resulting gap matrix reveals that voting and dissent preservation are universally absent across all five protocols, deliberation is absent or at most partial, and no protocol encodes the full set of primitives required for governed agent communities. We distinguish extensible gaps (addressable through protocol extension mechanisms) from structural gaps (requiring a new architectural layer) and assess time-sensitivity based on observed protocol evolution velocity. The analysis establishes that agent community governance constitutes a missing architectural layer above current interoperability standards, not a missing feature within them.

AI.tldr: This paper conducts a systematic gap analysis of five agent interoperability protocols (MCP, A2A, ACP, ANP, ERC-8004) against a six-dimension governance taxonomy. It finds that voting and dissent preservation are universally absent, deliberation is at most partial, and no protocol supports the full governance primitives needed for governed agent communities. The authors conclude that agent community governance represents a missing architectural layer, not merely missing features within existing protocols.
AI.motivation: Enterprises are deploying heterogeneous agent fleets that must make collective decisions under governance constraints. Current agent interoperability protocols have matured for task-oriented coordination (identity, capability discovery, tool access, message exchange), but it is unclear whether they can support governed agent communities with formal membership, deliberation, voting, and oversight mechanisms. This motivates a systematic evaluation of protocol capabilities against governance requirements derived from organizational theory and enterprise standards.
AI.method: The authors construct a six-dimension governance requirements taxonomy — membership, deliberation, voting, dissent preservation, human escalation, and audit/replay — synthesized from organizational theory, multi-agent systems literature, and enterprise governance standards. Each of the five protocols (MCP, A2A, ACP, ANP, ERC-8004) is analyzed against this taxonomy using specification analysis, classifying each capability as Supported, Partial, or Absent. Gaps are further categorized as extensible (addressable via protocol extension mechanisms) or structural (requiring a new architectural layer), with time-sensitivity assessed based on protocol evolution velocity.
AI.result: The gap matrix reveals: (1) voting and dissent preservation are universally absent across all five protocols; (2) deliberation is absent or at most partial in all protocols; (3) no protocol encodes the full set of primitives required for governed agent communities; (4) membership and audit/replay show mixed support, with some protocols offering partial capabilities; (5) human escalation is inconsistently addressed. The analysis distinguishes extensible gaps from structural gaps, concluding that governance requires a new architectural layer above existing interoperability standards.
AI.conclusion: Agent community governance constitutes a missing architectural layer above current interoperability standards, not a missing feature within them. The structural gaps identified — particularly around voting, dissent preservation, and deliberation — cannot be adequately addressed through protocol extension alone and require a dedicated governance layer. This has implications for enterprise deployment of autonomous agent collectives that must operate under binding governance constraints.

title: What Drives Interactive Improvement from Feedback?
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures, accepted to the RLxF Workshop at ICML 2026
summary: We study when natural-language feedback produces improvement beyond the gains obtainable from repeated attempts alone. In multi-turn language agent setting, higher final accuracy can reflect useful feedback, but it can also arise from resampling, format correction, or additional test-time computation. To separate these effects, we introduce a controlled student-teacher protocol across Omni-MATH, Codeforces, BBEH Linguini, and ARC-AGI1, evaluating thirteen open-weight models in both student and teacher roles. We compare external feedback, self-feedback, and unguided self-refinement, while varying interaction history, task difficulty, and teacher access to privileged task information. Across settings, we find that multi-turn improvement is often not evidence of feedback use: self-generated feedback adds little beyond unguided self-refinement, whereas the strongest external teachers produce substantially larger feedback-specific gains, suggesting that useful feedback must provide guidance beyond generic retry. Dense student-teacher interaction matrices further show that interactive gains are driven more by the student's ability to use feedback than by the teacher's identity, although teacher choice remains important for a fixed student. These results suggest that feedback-based agents should be evaluated against repeated-attempt baselines, and that ability to act on feedback, not merely feedback availability, is a central bottleneck for interactive improvement. We release our controlled student-teacher evaluation framework at https://j-lojek.github.io/feedback-generation-is-a-bottleneck/.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether multi-turn improvement in language agents stems from genuine feedback utilization or merely from repeated attempts, finding that self-generated feedback adds little beyond unguided retries, while strong external feedback produces substantial gains, and that the student's ability to act on feedback—not feedback availability—is the central bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Multi-turn language agents often show improved final accuracy over multiple attempts, but it is unclear whether this improvement reflects useful feedback or merely secondary effects like resampling, format correction, and additional test-time computation. The paper seeks to disentangle these confounds to understand when feedback genuinely drives progress.
AI.method: A controlled student-teacher protocol is introduced across four benchmarks (Omni-MATH, Codeforces, BBEH Linguini, ARC-AGI1), evaluating thirteen open-weight models in both roles. The study compares external feedback, self-feedback, and unguided self-refinement while systematically varying interaction history, task difficulty, and teacher access to privileged information. Dense student-teacher interaction matrices are constructed to attribute gains.
AI.result: Multi-turn improvement is often not evidence of effective feedback use: self-generated feedback adds little beyond unguided self-refinement. The strongest external teachers produce substantially larger, feedback-specific gains, indicating that useful feedback must go beyond generic retry prompts. Interaction matrices reveal that gains are driven more by the student's feedback-utilization ability than by teacher identity, though teacher choice still matters for a fixed student.
AI.conclusion: Feedback-based agents should be rigorously evaluated against repeated-attempt baselines. The ability to act on feedback—not merely its availability—constitutes the central bottleneck for interactive improvement. The authors release their controlled evaluation framework to facilitate future research along these lines.

title: Joint discovery of governing partial differential equations from multi-source datasets by competitive optimization
summary: Discovering governing equations directly from observational data is a key step towards interpretable scientific machine learning. Current data-driven approaches typically operate on a single dataset, inherently limiting their performance when faced with restricted observations. In practice, multiple datasets are often available for the same physical system, distinguished only by distinct initial conditions or boundary configurations. Here, we present a competitive optimization framework designed to discover shared partial differential equations (PDEs) from multi-source datasets, termed MCO-PDE. The framework first trains independent neural surrogates for each data source, and then employs a soft-competitive weighting mechanism to dynamically assess dataset credibility and aggregate a consensus global coefficient. Integrated with a genetic algorithm for structural search, this approach simultaneously identifies the functional forms and parameters of the governing laws. We demonstrate that fusing as few as 50 observations per dataset across seven cases recovers canonical equations with high accuracy. The framework inherently handles two- and three-dimensional domains characterized by irregular boundaries and heterogeneous coefficients, and successfully extracts physically meaningful laws from real-world wave-tank experiments. Overall, this work establishes a promising route for automated scientific discovery via heterogeneous data fusion.

AI.tldr: MCO-PDE is a multi-source data fusion framework that discovers shared PDEs by training independent neural surrogates per dataset, then using a soft-competitive weighting mechanism with genetic algorithms to simultaneously identify both the functional form and coefficients of governing equations.
AI.motivation: Existing data-driven PDE discovery methods typically operate on a single dataset, limiting performance when observations are scarce. In practice, multiple datasets from the same physical system (differing only in initial/boundary conditions) are often available, motivating a framework that can fuse these heterogeneous sources to improve discovery accuracy.
AI.method: The framework first trains independent neural network surrogates for each data source. A soft-competitive weighting mechanism dynamically assesses dataset credibility and aggregates a consensus global coefficient. This is integrated with a genetic algorithm for structural search, jointly identifying both the functional forms and parameters of the governing PDEs.
AI.result: Fusing as few as 50 observations per dataset across seven test cases recovers canonical equations with high accuracy. The method handles 2D/3D domains with irregular boundaries and heterogeneous coefficients, and successfully extracts physically meaningful laws from real-world wave-tank experiments.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a promising route for automated scientific discovery via heterogeneous data fusion, demonstrating that multi-source competitive optimization significantly enhances robustness and accuracy in PDE discovery from limited, diverse observational data.

title: Information Terra: A Narrative-Anchored Semantic-First Projection of Document Embeddings
comment: 5 pages, 6 figures, accepted in IEEE VIS 2026 as a short paper
summary: We introduce Information Terra, a narrative-anchored semantic-first projection that places a document corpus on an Earth-like globe whose poles are two user-chosen endpoint documents and whose prime meridian is the great-circle geodesic between them on the embedding hypersphere -- so latitude encodes narrative progress and longitude thematic deviation. Land features are recovered from document density via kernel density estimation and labeled by theme. A narrative trail built from the underlying narrative coherence graph, and constrained to be monotone in geodesic progress, provides a readable storyline. The projection's axes are semantically grounded in the user's chosen narrative endpoints, and the globe metaphor affords rotation and antipodal reading. We demonstrate the method on a 540-article Cuban Protests corpus, showing a storyline from Obama's 2016 visit to the 2021 International Aid during the protests.

AI.tldr: Information Terra maps a document corpus onto a 3D globe metaphor where two user-selected endpoint documents define the poles, latitude encodes narrative progression along the geodesic between them, and longitude encodes thematic deviation. Document density creates terrain features, and a monotonic narrative trail provides a readable storyline through the corpus.
AI.motivation: Existing corpus visualization methods (e.g., scatter plots, topic models) often lack an intuitive, semantically grounded spatial metaphor that simultaneously conveys narrative progression and thematic structure. The authors aim to provide a browsable globe-based projection where axes have clear semantic meaning tied to user-chosen endpoints, making corpus exploration more interpretable and engaging.
AI.method: The method projects documents onto a 3D globe using a narrative-anchored semantic-first approach: (1) two user-selected endpoint documents serve as the north and south poles; (2) the prime meridian is defined as the great-circle geodesic between these poles on the embedding hypersphere; (3) latitude encodes narrative progress along this geodesic, and longitude encodes thematic deviation from it; (4) kernel density estimation over document positions generates terrain-like land features, which are labeled by theme; (5) a narrative trail is extracted from an underlying narrative coherence graph, constrained to be monotonic in geodesic progress, yielding a readable storyline; (6) the globe metaphor supports rotation and antipodal reading for exploration.
AI.result: The method is demonstrated on a 540-article corpus covering the Cuban Protests, producing a coherent storyline that spans from Obama's 2016 visit to Cuba through to the 2021 International Aid during the protests. The resulting globe visualization shows meaningful thematic clustering and a navigable narrative path.
AI.conclusion: Information Terra offers a novel, semantically interpretable corpus visualization technique by anchoring spatial axes in user-chosen narrative endpoints and leveraging a globe metaphor. The approach successfully integrates narrative structure, thematic content, and interactive exploration, as validated on a real-world news corpus.

title: An AI-Based Solution for Secure Service Provisioning in IoT
summary: As the Internet of Things (IoT) continues its rapid expansion, the attack surface grows accordingly, with emerging threats targeting smart objects and their interactions. In this evolving landscape, securing service provisioning is crucial to ensure the proper functioning, security, and reliability of the IoT ecosystem. Service provisioning encompasses key tasks such as device registration, configuration, authentication, authorization, and software deployment, all of which are essential for seamless and secure IoT operations. In this paper, we present a comprehensive framework designed to select the most suitable smart objects to deliver a target service within a given IoT environment while also monitoring the behavior of the entities involved during the service provisioning phase. To achieve this, we employ a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) approach in which an intelligent agent learns, through interaction with a complex, dynamic environment, how to adapt to changes while adhering to predefined security constraints. For behavioral monitoring, we leverage Federated Learning (FL) to develop a global Behavioral Fingerprinting (BF) model that is fully distributed and can analyze how IoT devices interact within the network. In addition, the BF is used to compute a reliability score for each service provider, reflecting its degree of compliance with the defined security constraints. This score is then incorporated into the service provisioning process, allowing smart objects to select providers not only according to functional suitability but also to their reliability level. Finally, we conduct an extensive experimental evaluation to assess the robustness and scalability of our approach. The results demonstrate that our solution can be effectively deployed even on resource-constrained IoT devices, making it a viable and scalable security-enhancing mechanism for modern IoT ecosystems.

AI.tldr: A DRL-based framework for IoT service provisioning that selects optimal smart objects while using Federated Learning to build a distributed Behavioral Fingerprinting model for reliability scoring and anomaly detection.
AI.motivation: The expanding IoT attack surface demands robust security mechanisms for service provisioning (registration, authentication, authorization, deployment). Existing solutions lack integrated approaches that simultaneously optimize provider selection and monitor behavior under security constraints.
AI.method: A two-component framework: (1) Deep Reinforcement Learning agent that learns to select suitable service providers in dynamic IoT environments under security constraints; (2) Federated Learning-based distributed Behavioral Fingerprinting model that monitors device interactions and computes reliability scores, which feed back into the provider selection process.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation shows the approach is robust, scalable, and deployable even on resource-constrained IoT devices, confirming its viability as a practical security-enhancing mechanism.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DRL+FL framework effectively integrates intelligent provider selection with behavioral monitoring, offering a scalable, distributed security solution suitable for real-world resource-constrained IoT ecosystems.

title: Citation Discipline in Spec-Driven Development: A Cross-Model Empirical Study of Output Determinism and Automated Hallucination Detection in LLM-Generated Code
summary: Spec-Driven Development (SDD) frameworks guide Large Language Model (LLM)-powered code generation through formal specifications, yet they differ fundamentally in how they enforce traceability between requirements and generated code. This paper presents two controlled empirical studies comparing three SDD frameworks: $traceSDD$, which enforces mandatory per-line requirement citations using hierarchical REQ-XXX.Y.Z identifiers; $Spec Kit$, which uses artifact-level traceability through user stories and acceptance criteria; and $OpenSpec$, which relies on post-hoc external trace maps. We measure two primary outcomes across two frontier LLMs -- Claude Sonnet 4.6 (N=20, 4 conditions, 240 implementations) and GLM-5-turbo (N=50, 4 conditions, 600 implementations): $output$ $determinism$ (lexical similarity across independent LLM sessions) and $automated$ $hallucination$ $detection$ $rate$ (TDR). Our pre-registered analysis reveals a consistent, cross-model replicated trade-off: the uncited condition produces significantly higher determinism than the cited condition (Claude: $d=-0.76$, $p=0.003$; GLM: $d=-0.72$, $p<0.001$), while only the cited condition enables automated hallucination detection (TDR: Claude 86.4%, GLM 88.0%, vs 0% for all alternatives, FPR=0% across both studies). traceSDD (cited) significantly outperforms $Spec Kit$ on determinism (Claude: $d=0.47$, $p=0.049$; GLM: $d=0.42$, $p=0.003$) but not OpenSpec (Claude: $d=0.18$, $p=0.44$; GLM: $d=0.14$, $p=0.32$). These findings establish that citation annotations trade determinism for verifiability, and that this trade-off generalizes across model architectures.

AI.tldr: A controlled empirical study comparing three SDD frameworks across two LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GLM-5-turbo) reveals a robust trade-off: mandatory per-line requirement citations (traceSDD) reduce output determinism but uniquely enable automated hallucination detection (~87% TDR), whereas uncited approaches yield higher determinism but zero verifiability.
AI.motivation: Spec-Driven Development (SDD) frameworks for LLM-powered code generation differ in how they enforce traceability between requirements and generated code, yet no prior work has empirically quantified the consequences of these differing traceability mechanisms on output quality and verifiability. The authors seek to understand whether mandatory citation annotations impose a measurable cost on generation consistency and whether they enable practical automated hallucination detection.
AI.method: Two controlled empirical studies with pre-registered analysis: Study 1 used Claude Sonnet 4.6 (N=20, 4 conditions, 240 implementations); Study 2 used GLM-5-turbo (N=50, 4 conditions, 600 implementations). Three frameworks were compared: traceSDD (mandatory per-line REQ-XXX.Y.Z citations), Spec Kit (artifact-level traceability via user stories/acceptance criteria), and OpenSpec (post-hoc external trace maps). Outcomes measured were output determinism (lexical similarity across independent LLM sessions) and automated hallucination detection rate (TDR, with false positive rate).
AI.result: A consistent cross-model trade-off emerged: uncited conditions produced significantly higher determinism than cited conditions (Claude: d=-0.76, p=0.003; GLM: d=-0.72, p<0.001). Only the cited condition enabled automated hallucination detection (Claude TDR: 86.4%, GLM TDR: 88.0%, vs 0% for all alternatives; FPR=0% across both studies). traceSDD (cited) significantly outperformed Spec Kit on determinism (Claude: d=0.47, p=0.049; GLM: d=0.42, p=0.003) but not OpenSpec (Claude: d=0.18, p=0.44; GLM: d=0.14, p=0.32).
AI.conclusion: Citation annotations in SDD frameworks create a fundamental determinism-verifiability trade-off that generalizes across model architectures. Mandatory per-line citations sacrifice some generation consistency but uniquely unlock automated hallucination detection with high sensitivity and zero false positives, representing a viable engineering compromise for safety-critical code generation contexts.

title: ShopX: A Foundation Model for Intent-to-Item Fulfillment in Agentic Shopping
summary: The wave of AI-native applications is moving shopping beyond page- and feed-based browsing toward intent-driven experiences orchestrated by LLM agents. A common design wraps an LLM around existing search and recommendation pipelines, forcing complex intents through low-bandwidth retrieval or ranking interfaces and leaving a gap between language understanding and item-space fulfillment. Generative recommendation gives LLMs a direct item-space interface through semantic IDs (SIDs), but existing models mainly generate candidates for retrieval rather than translate flexible intents into item-space outcomes. We propose ShopX to address this bottleneck by unifying intent understanding, execution planning, and flexible SID-native item-space operations into a single foundation model. We deploy ShopX in agentic shopping workflows through a model-native item-fulfillment framework with a serving harness that defines a model-facing action protocol and exposes support surfaces for context access, catalog grounding, and state management. Within this framework, ShopX plans and composes SID-based item-space operations such as SID beam-search retrieval, listwise ranking, or product bundling. This model-centric design reduces lossy hand-offs between agent orchestration and item-space execution. To build ShopX, we design semantically recoverable, LLM-operable SIDs and a training recipe that equips a general LLM for flexible multi-turn item-space fulfillment while retaining the knowledge and instruction-following abilities needed by a shopping agent. We evaluate the ShopX framework against tool-mediated agentic systems on single- and multi-turn fulfillment tasks derived from anonymized Taobao production logs, showing that model-native fulfillment improves overall framework behavior, especially on complex or ambiguous requests.

AI.tldr: ShopX is a foundation model that unifies intent understanding, execution planning, and SID-based item-space operations within a single LLM, enabling model-native item fulfillment for agentic shopping workflows without lossy hand-offs between orchestration and execution.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based shopping agents wrap LLMs around existing search/recommendation pipelines, creating a bandwidth bottleneck between language understanding and item-space execution. Generative recommendation with semantic IDs (SIDs) exists but only retrieves candidates rather than translating flexible intents into full item-space outcomes. There is a gap between flexible intent expression and direct item-space fulfillment.
AI.method: ShopX introduces: (1) semantically recoverable, LLM-operable SIDs; (2) a training recipe that equips a general LLM for multi-turn item-space fulfillment while preserving instruction-following abilities; (3) a model-native item-fulfillment framework with a serving harness defining a model-facing action protocol and support surfaces for context access, catalog grounding, and state management; (4) SID-based item-space operations (beam-search retrieval, listwise ranking, product bundling) planned and composed directly by the model.
AI.result: ShopX was evaluated against tool-mediated agentic systems on single- and multi-turn fulfillment tasks derived from anonymized Taobao production logs. Results demonstrate that model-native fulfillment improves overall framework behavior, particularly on complex or ambiguous requests.
AI.conclusion: Model-native item fulfillment via ShopX effectively bridges the gap between LLM-based intent understanding and item-space execution, reducing lossy hand-offs and outperforming tool-mediated agents on complex shopping tasks.

title: Indi-RomCoM: Code-Mixed Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Romanized Indic-English Instructions
summary: Romanized Code Mixing (RCM), where bilingual speakers fluidly blend local languages with English in Roman script, has emerged as the dominant form of communication across multilingual communities. While Large Language Models (LLMs) perform strongly on monolingual and native-script benchmarks, their ability to follow instructions and reason over RCM-based content remains largely unexplored. To this end, we introduce the Indi-RomCoM benchmark for facilitating systematic evaluation on Indic Romanized Code-Mixed instructions. Our benchmark spans seven instruction-following tasks, four widely spoken Indic languages, and three controlled code-mixing intensity levels. We extensively evaluate a suite of LLMs covering proprietary, open-weight, and Indic-focused models under zero- and few-shot settings. LLMs consistently underperform on RCM instructions, with performance degrading as code-mixing density increases. Furthermore, reasoning tasks suffer less degradation than detection tasks (e.g., Toxicity) because the generated explanations offer necessary context. We believe Indi-RomCoM helps the community in developing inclusive multilingual systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Indi-RomCoM, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on Romanized Code-Mixed (RCM) instructions across seven tasks, four Indic languages, and three code-mixing intensity levels. LLMs consistently underperform on RCM instructions, with performance degrading as code-mixing density increases, though reasoning tasks degrade less than detection tasks.
AI.motivation: While LLMs excel on monolingual and native-script benchmarks, their instruction-following and reasoning capabilities on Romanized Code-Mixed content — the dominant communication mode in multilingual communities — remain unexplored. This gap motivates a systematic evaluation framework.
AI.method: The authors construct the Indi-RomCoM benchmark covering seven instruction-following tasks (including detection and reasoning tasks), four Indic languages (Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu), and three controlled code-mixing intensity levels. They evaluate a diverse suite of LLMs — proprietary, open-weight, and Indic-focused models — under both zero-shot and few-shot settings.
AI.result: LLMs consistently underperform on RCM instructions compared to standard benchmarks. Performance predictably degrades as code-mixing density increases. Notably, reasoning tasks suffer less degradation than detection tasks (e.g., toxicity detection), attributed to the contextual scaffolding provided by generated explanations.
AI.conclusion: Indi-RomCoM serves as a valuable resource for advancing inclusive multilingual LLM systems. The findings highlight a critical weakness in current LLMs' handling of code-mixed input and underscore the need for targeted improvements in this area.

title: Holonic Active Distillation for Scalable Multi-Agent Learning in Multi-Sensor Systems
comment: 21 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables, accepted to EMAS 2025
summary:
The rapid expansion of sensor-based networks introduces major challenges in scalability, adaptability, and knowledge transfer, especially in open environments where new subsystems can dynamically join or leave. In this work, we propose a Holonic Active Distillation architecture within a Holonic Multi-Agent System (HMAS) to address these issues. Our approach integrates Clustered Stream-Based Active Distillation (CSBAD), a framework in which specialized student models collect local data, query pseudo-labels from teacher models, and cluster into groups of similar sensors.
  Results show that the holonic organization balances local specialization with global generalization, while efficiently adapting to sensor departures and re-integrations. We also analyzed trade-offs among incremental model updates, system reorganization, and scalability limits.
  Our findings highlight the advantages of holonic learning for multi-sensor systems while identifying key challenges related to model drift and long-term adaptation.

AI.tldr: Proposes a Holonic Active Distillation architecture within a Holonic Multi-Agent System (HMAS), using Clustered Stream-Based Active Distillation (CSBAD) where student models cluster by sensor similarity, query pseudo-labels from teachers, and dynamically adapt to subsystem changes in open sensor networks.
AI.motivation: Scalability, adaptability, and knowledge transfer challenges in rapidly expanding sensor-based networks operating in open environments where subsystems dynamically join or leave.
AI.method: Holonic Active Distillation architecture within HMAS, implementing CSBAD: specialized student models collect local data, request pseudo-labels from teacher models, and self-organize into clusters of similar sensors. The holonic structure balances local specialization with global generalization.
AI.result: The holonic organization effectively balances local specialization with global generalization, adapts efficiently to sensor departures and re-integrations. Trade-offs were identified among incremental model updates, system reorganization, and scalability limits.
AI.conclusion: Holonic learning offers significant advantages for multi-sensor systems, though challenges remain regarding model drift and long-term adaptation.

title: Contrastive Reflection for Iterative Prompt Optimization
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. To appear at Agent4IR @ KDD 2026 (KDD 2026 Workshop on AI Agents for Information Retrieval)
summary:
LLM agents are becoming central to information retrieval: they issue retrieval queries, synthesize answers, and increasingly serve as judges for IR evaluation. Improving the prompts that control these agents is an optimization problem, but in applied IR settings it often looks less like blind search and more like debugging. Engineers need to know which behavior failed, which nearby behavior still worked, what distinguishes the two, and whether a prompt edit improves held-out quality without introducing regressions.
  We present Contrastive Reflection, an iterative prompt-optimization framework for agentic IR workflows. The framework starts from a task-centric quality definition: QA agents expose retrieval or reasoning traces, and grading agents expose dimension-level scores and rationales. These structured traces are used to identify error-anchored behavioral slices, add nearby successful examples from the same region, and ask a Teacher LLM to propose a targeted prompt edit. Candidate edits are accepted only when validation performance improves, optionally subject to regression checks. We instantiate the framework with a tree-based slice selector, but the contribution is the contrastive reflection loop rather than the tree itself.
  On a public HotpotQA retrieval-augmented QA setup, one tree-selected contrastive repair improves held-out exact-match accuracy from 51.4% to 60.4%. Failure-only and random-evidence variants improve less and break more previously correct examples. A light instruction-only comparison places the method near modern prompt optimizers: MIPROv2 reaches 59.4% and GEPA 57.0%. The result is an interpretable optimization loop for IR agents, aimed at making prompt repair more inspectable and validation-driven.

AI.tldr: Contrastive Reflection is an iterative prompt-optimization framework for LLM-based IR agents that uses error-anchored behavioral slices and contrastive examples (nearby successes) to prompt a Teacher LLM for targeted edits, with validation-gated acceptance and optional regression checks. On HotpotQA, one repair iteration lifts exact-match accuracy from 51.4% to 60.4%, outperforming failure-only and random-evidence baselines and rivaling MIPROv2 (59.4%) and GEPA (57.0%).
AI.motivation: Prompt engineering for LLM agents in IR settings resembles debugging rather than blind search: engineers need to identify which behaviors failed, which nearby behaviors succeeded, what distinguishes them, and whether edits improve quality without regressions. Existing prompt optimizers lack this inspectable, contrastive, validation-driven workflow tailored to agentic IR.
AI.method: The Contrastive Reflection framework operates on structured agent traces (retrieval/reasoning traces from QA agents, dimension-level scores and rationales from grading agents). Steps: (1) identify error-anchored behavioral slices; (2) add nearby successful examples from the same behavioral region; (3) a Teacher LLM proposes a targeted prompt edit based on the contrastive pair; (4) candidate edits are accepted only if validation performance improves, with optional regression checks. A tree-based slice selector is used as one instantiation.
AI.result: On public HotpotQA retrieval-augmented QA: one tree-selected contrastive repair improves held-out exact-match accuracy from 51.4% to 60.4% (+9.0 points). Failure-only and random-evidence variants improve less and break more previously correct examples. Compared to modern prompt optimizers: MIPROv2 reaches 59.4%, GEPA 57.0%, placing the method competitively while offering greater interpretability.
AI.conclusion: Contrastive Reflection provides an interpretable, validation-driven optimization loop for IR agent prompts, emphasizing inspectability and targeted repair over blind search. The contrastive reflection loop — not the specific tree selector — is the core contribution.

title: Accelerometry-Derived Digital Biomarkers for Cardiometabolic Risk: A Population-Representative Tabular Benchmark with Uncertainty Quantification
comment: Accepted at the SD4H Workshop at ICML 2026
summary: Structured tabular data dominates clinical medicine, yet existing benchmarks fail to reflect real-world properties like complex survey sampling, demographic oversampling, and subgroup fairness. We introduce the NHANES Accelerometry Cardiometabolic Benchmark, derived from NHANES 2003-2006, comprising 1,381 adults with hip-worn accelerometry, fasting laboratory biomarkers, dietary intake, and anthropometrics. We evaluate three tabular learning methods -- ridge regression, XGBoost, and the foundation model TabPFN v2 -- to predict glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c), fasting triglycerides, and C-reactive protein (CRP) from activity phenotypes and lifestyle covariates. TabPFN v2 achieves the best overall performance (HbA1c R^2=0.156, CRP R^2=0.383), while triglycerides remain largely unpredictable (R^2 < 0.05), consistent with known genetic dominance. We apply split conformal prediction to generate distribution-free 90% prediction intervals and evaluate demographic coverage equity across sex and race/ethnicity subgroups. Marginal coverage aligns with the 90% target for CRP and HbA1c but falls below for triglycerides. At the subgroup level, we observe localized undercoverage (e.g., HbA1c for Mexican American participants), illustrating the gap between marginal guarantees and the conditional coverage required for clinical fairness. Code and data are at https://github.com/felizzi/nhanes-accel-cardiometabolic-benchmark.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce a clinical tabular benchmark from NHANES 2003–2006 accelerometry data, evaluate ridge regression, XGBoost, and TabPFN v2 on predicting HbA1c, triglycerides, and CRP, and assess subgroup prediction-interval coverage fairness via conformal prediction.
AI.motivation: Existing tabular benchmarks do not capture real-world clinical complexities such as complex survey sampling, demographic oversampling, and subgroup fairness. A domain-specific benchmark reflecting these properties is needed to rigorously evaluate tabular learning methods in clinical contexts.
AI.method: The benchmark uses NHANES 2003–2006 data (n=1,381 adults) with hip-worn accelerometry, fasting biomarkers, dietary intake, and anthropometrics. Three methods — ridge regression, XGBoost, and the foundation model TabPFN v2 — predict HbA1c, fasting triglycerides, and CRP from activity phenotypes and lifestyle covariates. Split conformal prediction generates distribution-free 90% prediction intervals, and demographic coverage equity is evaluated across sex and race/ethnicity subgroups.
AI.result: TabPFN v2 achieves best performance (HbA1c R²=0.156, CRP R²=0.383); triglycerides remain unpredictable (R²<0.05). Marginal coverage meets 90% for CRP and HbA1c but not triglycerides. Subgroup undercoverage appears (e.g., HbA1c for Mexican American participants), exposing a gap between marginal guarantees and conditional coverage needed for clinical fairness.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark highlights both the promise of foundation models like TabPFN v2 for clinical tabular prediction and the critical fairness limitation that marginal coverage guarantees do not ensure equitable subgroup-level prediction intervals.

title: Drawing Out Legal Risks: Co-Designing with Lawyers to Predict and Manage Legal Uncertainties of Medical AI Tools
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures; Note: This paper is formatted as a submission type called a Pictorial, used in some ACM venues (e.g. https://dis.acm.org/2026/pictorials/). Pictorials present visual components (e.g. study artifacts, diagrams) with text to convey contributions. We present co-created visualizations from our study alongside our analysis/. For more justification of the format, see page 4
summary: While there's optimism around medical AI tools due to their abilities to adapt from user-to-user and across environments, these new abilities complicate how people and organizations are able to predict and manage risk based on existing laws and regulations. Lawyers are trained to identify potential legal outcomes, but they lack technical AI knowledge, making it difficult to translate their expertise to creators and users of AI tools. We contribute insights from our co-design process with U.S. lawyers to identify and translate ways to predict and manage risks of medical AI tools. We present the visualizations we developed through two years of cross-disciplinary efforts and thereby illustrate our findings about how legal risks are determined and our strategies for people and organizations to predict and manage these risks. We offer insights about leveraging lawyers' expertise to understand, predict, and manage legal risks.

AI.tldr: This paper presents findings from a two-year co-design process with U.S. lawyers, developing visualizations to help predict and manage legal risks associated with adaptive medical AI tools, bridging the gap between legal expertise and technical AI knowledge.
AI.motivation: Medical AI tools that adapt across users and environments introduce novel challenges for legal risk prediction and management. Existing laws and regulations were not designed for such dynamic systems. Lawyers possess the expertise to identify legal outcomes but lack technical AI knowledge, creating a communication and translation gap between legal professionals and AI creators/users.
AI.method: The authors conducted a two-year co-design process with U.S. lawyers, engaging in cross-disciplinary collaboration to identify how legal risks are determined for medical AI tools and to develop strategies and visualizations that translate legal risk assessment into actionable insights for people and organizations.
AI.result: The co-design process yielded a set of visualizations that illustrate how legal risks are determined for adaptive medical AI tools, along with concrete strategies for individuals and organizations to predict and manage these risks. The work also produced insights on effectively leveraging lawyers' domain expertise in the AI risk assessment pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Bridging the gap between legal expertise and technical AI development is essential for responsible deployment of adaptive medical AI. Co-design with legal professionals produces actionable frameworks and visualizations that enable organizations to better anticipate and mitigate legal risks, and this cross-disciplinary approach offers a model for integrating legal reasoning into AI governance.

title: Understanding and Evaluating Claw-like Agent Security Through a Computer-Systems Lens
summary: Claw-like AI agents (e.g., OpenClaw) are always-on processes with persistent access to credentials, files, tools, and external services. They take on system-level responsibilities -- installing packages, maintaining state, scheduling subtasks, and mediating I/O -- making security failures far more severe than in other agents. Yet existing benchmarks focus on model responses and tool calls, leaving cross-component failure modes largely unmeasured. We adopt a computer-system analogy: treating a Claw-like agent as an agentic computer system whose gateway runtime plays an OS-like mediation role, whose Skills resemble user-installed applications, and whose Plugins resemble loadable extensions with runtime privileges. Each component has a classical counterpart whose protection mechanisms -- refined over decades of cybersecurity research -- are absent on the agent side. From this perspective, we develop SafeClawArena, a benchmark of 406 adversarial tasks across four attack surfaces (Skill Supply-Chain Integrity, Persistent State Exploitation, Cross-Boundary Data Flow, and Indirect Prompt Injection), executed in containerized replicas of real agent platforms with canary-marked credentials and evaluated via automated taint tracking across nine output channels. We evaluate three platforms (OpenClaw, NemoClaw, SeClaw) and five frontier LLMs. The highest attack success rate reaches 70%; malicious Plugins succeed in 100% of cases regardless of the LLM. SeClaw cuts GPT-5.4's attack success rate from 70% to 22%, partly through utility-security tradeoffs rather than active defenses, while Claude-Opus-4.6 already sits near a 22% floor on every platform. These results expose the inadequacy of current defenses and suggest directions for future hardening. Code and data: https://github.com/sunblaze-ucb/SafeClawArena.

AI.tldr: SafeClawArena is a benchmark of 406 adversarial tasks targeting Claw-like AI agents across four attack surfaces. Evaluating three platforms and five frontier LLMs, it finds attack success rates up to 70% (100% for malicious Plugins), with SeClaw reducing GPT-5.4's rate from 70% to 22% via utility-security tradeoffs, while Claude-Opus-4.6 maintains a ~22% floor across all platforms.
AI.motivation: Claw-like AI agents are always-on processes with persistent access to credentials, files, and system-level responsibilities. Security failures in these agents are far more severe than in typical agents, yet existing benchmarks only measure model responses and tool calls, ignoring cross-component failure modes. The paper adopts a computer-system analogy to identify absent classical protection mechanisms and expose this gap.
AI.method: The authors develop SafeClawArena, a benchmark with 406 adversarial tasks across four attack surfaces: Skill Supply-Chain Integrity, Persistent State Exploitation, Cross-Boundary Data Flow, and Indirect Prompt Injection. Tests run in containerized replicas of real agent platforms with canary-marked credentials, evaluated via automated taint tracking across nine output channels. Three platforms (OpenClaw, NemoClaw, SeClaw) and five frontier LLMs are evaluated.
AI.result: The highest attack success rate reaches 70%. Malicious Plugins achieve 100% success regardless of the underlying LLM. SeClaw reduces GPT-5.4's attack success rate from 70% to 22%, though partly through utility-security tradeoffs rather than active defenses. Claude-Opus-4.6 already sits near a 22% floor on every platform, suggesting some inherent robustness.
AI.conclusion: Current defenses for Claw-like agent systems are inadequate. Results point toward directions for future hardening, including adopting classical OS protection mechanisms into agent runtimes and improving cross-component security guarantees. The benchmark and code are publicly released.

title: Towards Knowledge Alignment in Code LLMs: Contrastive Unlearning for Evolving APIs
comment: The paper has been peer reviewed and accepted to the 42nd International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME 2026)
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently achieved strong performance in code generation. However, due to knowledge cut-off and the rapid evolution of software libraries, they often generate deprecated API usages that lead to unreliable and incompatible code. Existing fine-tuning methods lack selectivity when only a small portion of model knowledge requires modification. Recent model-level approaches, such as machine unlearning and model editing, offer a promising direction for modifying parametric knowledge. However, their use for deprecated API mitigation remains largely unexplored. Moreover, existing methods primarily suppress outdated APIs, but do not explicitly steer models toward correct replacements, often leading to mismatched or incomplete generations. To address this limitation, we developed CURE, a contrastive unlearning approach that shifts unlearning from purely suppressing outdated knowledge to explicitly promoting correct API replacements. Concretely, CURE jointly discourages deprecated APIs while encouraging their valid alternatives, enabling more reliable adaptation to evolving software libraries. The experiments on recent deprecated API benchmark dataset show that CURE not only reduces deprecated API usage but also improves correct API replacement, while preserving general code generation performance. CURE substantially outperforms two SOTA baselines with respect to different quality metrics. These findings highlight the importance of combining suppression with replacement when adapting LLMs to evolving software ecosystems.

AI.tldr: CURE is a contrastive unlearning method that adapts LLMs to evolving software libraries by jointly suppressing deprecated APIs and explicitly promoting correct replacements, outperforming SOTA baselines on deprecated API benchmarks while preserving general code generation quality.
AI.motivation: LLMs frequently generate deprecated API usages due to knowledge cut-off and rapid library evolution. Existing fine-tuning methods lack selectivity for small-scale knowledge updates, while machine unlearning and model editing approaches only suppress outdated APIs without steering models toward correct replacements, resulting in mismatched or incomplete code.
AI.method: CURE employs a contrastive unlearning framework that operates on two fronts: (1) discouraging deprecated API usage through negative gradient updates on deprecated API samples, and (2) explicitly encouraging valid alternative APIs via positive reinforcement on correct replacement samples. This dual mechanism shifts the model from purely forgetting outdated knowledge to actively learning correct substitutions.
AI.result: Experiments on a recent deprecated API benchmark dataset demonstrate that CURE reduces deprecated API usage, improves correct API replacement rates, and preserves overall code generation performance. CURE substantially outperforms two SOTA baselines across multiple quality metrics.
AI.conclusion: Combining suppression with explicit replacement guidance is crucial for adapting LLMs to evolving software ecosystems. CURE demonstrates that contrastive unlearning is an effective paradigm for targeted knowledge updates in code LLMs.

title: An Open-Source Tool for Reproducible Freeway Network Extraction from OpenStreetMap
summary:
Freeway simulation is often difficult to deploy at scale not only because of model formulation, but because preparing road network inputs remains a manual, corridor-specific, and difficult-to-reproduce task. This paper presents an open-source tool that extracts freeway networks from OpenStreetMap (OSM) and converts them into a compact, station-referenced representation suitable for downstream freeway simulation. Unlike existing tools that primarily support arterial or general network conversion tasks, the proposed workflow is designed around the specific requirements of freeway traffic studies. The tool supports not only OSM data cleaning and conversion, but also the broader workflow required in practice: corridor-specific querying, visual inspection of extracted segments, extraction validation against OSM, and source-data validation against aerial imagery. A locally hosted frontend allows users to define corridor-specific queries, select endpoints visually, and inspect extracted segments.
  The extraction logic is designed to address several recurring challenges in freeway OSM data, including inconsistent route references, ambiguous path selection through interchanges, managed-lane interference, incomplete corridor capture from naive bounding-box queries, and inconsistent ramp classifications. The workflow was first tested on two prototype corridors, where the extract-first-then-validate approach proposed here required roughly one-third the analyst effort of manual ramp encoding from scratch. It was then deployed across 359.6 miles of freeway in Orange County, California, with total processing and validation averaging about 41 seconds per mile. This deployment also suggests that, in a well-mapped region, OSM is sufficiently accurate for many freeway traffic studies. Overall, the tool provides a more scalable and reproducible foundation for freeway network preparation.

AI.tldr: An open-source tool that extracts freeway networks from OpenStreetMap, converts them into station-referenced representations for simulation, and was validated across 359.6 miles in Orange County, CA, requiring ~41 seconds/mile for processing and validation.
AI.motivation: Freeway simulation at scale is hindered not only by model formulation but by the manual, corridor-specific, and non-reproducible preparation of road network inputs. Existing tools focus on arterial or general networks, lacking the specialized requirements of freeway traffic studies.
AI.method: An open-source tool with: (1) OSM data extraction and cleaning tailored to freeway-specific challenges (inconsistent route references, ambiguous interchange path selection, managed-lane interference, incomplete bounding-box queries, inconsistent ramp classifications); (2) a locally hosted frontend for visual corridor querying, endpoint selection, and segment inspection; (3) an extract-first-then-validate workflow with validation against OSM source data and aerial imagery.
AI.result: On two prototype corridors, the approach required roughly one-third the analyst effort compared to manual ramp encoding. Deployment across 359.6 miles of freeway in Orange County averaged 41 seconds per mile for processing and validation. Results suggest OSM is sufficiently accurate for freeway traffic studies in well-mapped regions.
AI.conclusion: The tool provides a scalable, reproducible foundation for freeway network preparation, demonstrating that automated OSM-based extraction with targeted validation can significantly reduce manual effort while maintaining sufficient accuracy for traffic simulation studies.

title: Using AI Agents to Automate Black-Box Audits of Personalization Algorithms at Scale
summary: Personalization algorithms determine what content users encounter on online platforms. Auditing these systems is difficult because independent auditors have only black-box access to the algorithms, while personalization depends on users' attributes, behavior, and evolving interaction histories. Existing auditing methods face a tradeoff: studies with real users capture realistic behavior but are costly and hard to control, whereas sock-puppet audits scale more easily but often rely on scripted behavior that limits realism. Beyond this, both approaches struggle to decouple user attributes from user behavior, limiting our ability to causally understand personalization. To address this gap, we introduce a framework for black-box audits of personalization algorithms using generative AI agents as behavioral engines for synthetic accounts. Each agent is instantiated with a fixed persona, grounded in demographic and political survey data, and interacts with a platform's content by reasoning about it and choosing actions. Because behavior is fixed within each persona while platform-visible signals such as age, gender, or location can be experimentally perturbed, our design enables counterfactual auditing of how platforms respond to user attributes. As a case study, we deploy 1,120 agents on X shortly after the 2024 U.S. election, spanning 14 personas and three counterfactual conditions, collecting over 200,000 content exposures. We find that X's algorithmic feed amplifies toxic, polarizing, political, and right-leaning content relative to the chronological feed, with amplification varying sharply by user ideology. Counterfactual analyses show that demographic signals affect content delivery in persona-dependent ways: pooled effects are largely null, while subgroup-level effects vary in direction and magnitude. Our work establishes GenAI-based agents as a new tool for algorithmic auditing.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a framework for auditing personalization algorithms using generative AI agents as synthetic accounts with fixed personas. Deploying 1,120 agents on X post-2024 U.S. election, the study finds algorithmic amplification of toxic/polarizing/political/right-leaning content, with demographic signals affecting content delivery in persona-dependent ways.
AI.motivation: Auditing personalization algorithms is challenging because real-user studies are costly and hard to control, while sock-puppet audits lack behavioral realism. Both struggle to causally decouple user attributes from user behavior. A new approach is needed that combines scalability, realism, and experimental control to enable counterfactual inference about how platforms respond to user attributes.
AI.method: The authors introduce GenAI-based agents instantiated with fixed personas grounded in demographic and political survey data. Each agent interacts with platform content by reasoning and choosing actions, keeping behavior fixed within each persona while experimentally perturbing platform-visible signals (age, gender, location). They deployed 1,120 agents on X across 14 personas and three counterfactual conditions, collecting over 200,000 content exposures, and compared algorithmic feed content against the chronological feed baseline.
AI.result: X's algorithmic feed amplifies toxic, polarizing, political, and right-leaning content compared to the chronological feed, with amplification magnitude varying sharply by user ideology. Counterfactual analyses reveal that demographic signal effects are largely null in pooled analyses but show persona-dependent effects at the subgroup level, varying in both direction and magnitude.
AI.conclusion: Generative AI agents constitute a viable new tool for black-box algorithmic auditing, enabling scalable, behaviorally realistic, and causally informative studies of personalization systems that overcome key limitations of both real-user and sock-puppet approaches.

title: ForecastAgentSearch: Towards a Multi-Expert Agent Search System for Geopolitical Event Forecasting
summary: Geopolitical event forecasting is a challenging task, as it requires understanding complex regional contexts, dynamic event signals, and uncertain future outcomes. Recent advances in large language model agents provide new opportunities for building forecasting systems that can reason with diverse sources and expert perspectives. In this paper, we present \textit{ForecastAgentSearch}, a preliminary framework that formulates geopolitical event forecasting as a multi-expert agent search problem. Given a forecasting query, the system first analyzes the task context, then searches and ranks relevant expert agents based on their regional knowledge, domain expertise, reliability, and complementarity. The selected agents provide specialized analyses, which are further coordinated to generate a final forecast with explanations and uncertainty awareness. We discuss the key design challenges of agent profiling, expert retrieval, ranking, and multi-agent coordination, and outline possible evaluation protocols for future development. This work aims to provide an initial step toward searchable and reliable agent-based forecasting systems.

AI.tldr: ForecastAgentSearch frames geopolitical event forecasting as a multi-expert agent search problem, where relevant LLM-based agents are retrieved, ranked, and coordinated to generate uncertainty-aware forecasts with explanations.
AI.motivation: Geopolitical event forecasting demands understanding of complex regional contexts, dynamic signals, and uncertain outcomes. LLM agents offer new capabilities, but a systematic framework for searching, ranking, and coordinating multiple expert agents for forecasting is lacking.
AI.method: The framework first analyzes the forecasting query context, then searches and ranks expert agents based on regional knowledge, domain expertise, reliability, and complementarity. Selected agents produce specialized analyses, which are coordinated into a final forecast with explanations and uncertainty quantification.
AI.result: This is a preliminary framework paper; no empirical results are reported. The authors discuss key design challenges including agent profiling, expert retrieval, ranking mechanisms, and multi-agent coordination, along with proposed evaluation protocols for future development.
AI.conclusion: ForecastAgentSearch represents an initial step toward building searchable, reliable agent-based forecasting systems, establishing a foundation for future research in multi-expert LLM agent architectures for geopolitical prediction.

title: How Can AI Find My Model? A Model-Finding Experimental Study Considering Data Formats, Embeddings, and Retrieval Strategies
comment: Accepted for publication in Proceedings of the 2026 Winter Simulation Conference (WSC 2026). The final published version will appear in IEEE Xplore
summary: Discovering simulation models for reuse remains a fundamental challenge in Modeling and Simulation (M&S). When many models coexist, identifying those that align with a given modeling intent remains difficult. Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly retrieval-based approaches, offer a promising pathway to operate at this semantic layer. In this paper, we present an experimental study investigating the impact of data representation, transformer-based embedding models, and retrieval strategies on the discovery of simulation models using natural language queries. We evaluated performance across multiple query types using standard information retrieval metrics, including recall@5 and nDCG@5. Results show that data representation matters, open-source embedding models can achieve high performance, and reranking methods are important, especially as query complexity increases. This work provides a baseline for AI-driven model discovery and discusses its role in advancing toward AI-driven composability and interoperability.

AI.tldr: This paper experimentally investigates how data representation, transformer-based embeddings, and retrieval strategies affect the discovery of simulation models via natural language queries, establishing baselines for AI-driven model reuse and composability.
AI.motivation: Discovering reusable simulation models is a persistent challenge in M&S, especially when many heterogeneous models coexist and users struggle to identify those matching their modeling intent. Recent AI advances, particularly retrieval-based methods, offer a way to bridge this semantic gap, but systematic understanding of design choices (representation, embeddings, retrieval) is lacking.
AI.method: An experimental study evaluating combinations of data representation formats, transformer-based embedding models (including open-source options), and retrieval/reranking strategies. Performance is measured using standard IR metrics—recall@5 and nDCG@5—across multiple natural language query types of varying complexity.
AI.result: Data representation significantly impacts performance; open-source embedding models can achieve competitive results; reranking methods become increasingly important as query complexity grows.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a foundational baseline for AI-driven simulation model discovery and positions this capability as a stepping stone toward broader AI-driven composability and interoperability in M&S.

title: From Search to Synthesis: Training LLMs as Zero-Shot Workflow Generators
summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel across a wide range of tasks, yet their instance-specific solutions often lack the structural consistency needed for reliable deployment. Workflows that encode recurring algorithmic patterns at the task level provide a principled framework, offering robustness across instance variations, interpretable traces for debugging, and reusability across problem instances. However, manually designing such workflows requires significant expertise and effort, limiting their broader application. While automatic workflow generation could address this bottleneck, existing methods either produce instance-specific solutions without learning task-level patterns, or cannot generalize beyond their training configurations. We present MetaFlow, which casts workflow generation as a meta-learning problem: given a task and an operator set, the model learns to compose solution strategies. MetaFlow trains in two stages: supervised fine-tuning on synthetic workflow data, followed by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) that uses execution feedback across problem instances in the task to improve end-to-end success. The resulting model produces effective workflows for trained tasks and exhibits strong generalization to untrained tasks and novel operator sets.
