Across benchmarks in question answering, code generation, and mathematical reasoning, MetaFlow achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art baselines on in-domain tasks with single inference, while demonstrating remarkable zero-shot generalization capabilities on out-of-domain tasks and operator sets.

AI.tldr: MetaFlow frames workflow generation as a meta-learning problem, training LLMs via supervised fine-tuning on synthetic data followed by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) to produce task-level algorithmic workflows that generalize to unseen tasks and operator sets.
AI.motivation: LLMs produce instance-specific solutions lacking structural consistency. Task-level algorithmic workflows offer robustness, interpretability, and reusability, but manual design is expertise-intensive. Existing automatic generation methods either overfit to instances or fail to generalize beyond training configurations. A method that learns composable, generalizable task-level patterns is needed.
AI.method: MetaFlow uses a two-stage training pipeline: (1) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on synthetic workflow data to teach compositional strategy generation from an operator set given a task; (2) reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) using execution feedback across multiple problem instances per task to optimize end-to-end success. The model learns to compose operators into workflows that generalize across tasks and novel operator sets.
AI.result: MetaFlow achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art baselines on in-domain tasks (question answering, code generation, mathematical reasoning) with single inference, while demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization to out-of-domain tasks and novel operator sets.
AI.conclusion: Casting workflow generation as meta-learning enables LLMs to produce structured, generalizable, and reusable task-level workflows. The SFT + RLVR pipeline effectively bridges the gap between instance-specific solutions and manually engineered workflows, enabling robust deployment across diverse and unseen tasks.

title: Neural Signatures of Programming Expertise: Classifying Programmer Skill Levels Using EEG Data
summary: Accurately assessing a programmer's skill level is critical for hiring, team composition, and performance evaluation in the software industry. Conventional methods, such as coding tests or interviews, often fail to capture the full spectrum of cognitive abilities underlying programming expertise. This study explores using electroencephalography (EEG) and machine learning to investigate neural correlates of programming skill. We analyzed an existing EEG dataset recorded during code comprehension from 37 programmers with 1 to 30 years of experience (8.1 +/- 6.3 years) to examine relationships between neural activity and expertise. Additionally, we conducted classification experiments using Random Forest classifiers with diverse features for binary (experts vs. novices) and multi-class (experts, intermediates, novices) setups.We identified EEG features and brain regions associated with programming expertise. Specifically, EEG entropy showed the strongest correlation with skill level. Furthermore, experts' brains were characterized by highly localized centro-frontal activation, whereas frontal activation in other groups was part of a more distributed network. Regarding classification, our setup achieved an average accuracy of 91.83% (binary) and 78.15% (multi-class) in stratified 10-fold cross-validation, while leave-one-subject-out validation achieved 85.00% and 58.80%, respectively. Individual frequency bands outperformed full-spectrum analyses, and both program comprehension and resting-state data yielded strong results. These findings demonstrate that EEG features effectively capture neural correlates across different skill levels and highlight the potential of neural data to complement traditional methods of skill assessment.

AI.tldr: EEG and machine learning were used to classify programming skill levels (novice, intermediate, expert) with up to 91.83% accuracy in binary classification. EEG entropy correlated most strongly with expertise, and experts showed highly localized centro-frontal brain activation distinct from more distributed patterns in other groups.
AI.motivation: Traditional programming skill assessments (coding tests, interviews) fail to capture the full range of cognitive abilities underlying programming expertise. This study aims to identify objective neural correlates of programming skill using EEG, offering a complementary, neurophysiologically-grounded assessment method.
AI.method: The authors analyzed an existing EEG dataset from 37 programmers (1–30 years experience) during code comprehension. They extracted diverse EEG features (including entropy, frequency band power) and used Random Forest classifiers for binary (expert vs. novice) and multi-class (expert, intermediate, novice) classification, validated via stratified 10-fold cross-validation and leave-one-subject-out.
AI.result: EEG entropy showed the strongest correlation with skill level. Experts exhibited highly localized centro-frontal activation; other groups showed more distributed frontal activation. Binary classification achieved 91.83% (10-fold CV) and 85.00% (LOSO); multi-class achieved 78.15% and 58.80%, respectively. Individual frequency bands outperformed full-spectrum analyses, and both task and resting-state data were predictive.
AI.conclusion: EEG features reliably capture neural signatures of programming expertise across skill levels. Neural data shows strong potential to complement or enhance traditional programming skill assessment methods.

title: Security--Fidelity Tradeoffs: The Hidden Cost of Prompt Injection Defense
comment: Accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026). 34 pages, 4 figures
summary: We identify a security-fidelity tradeoff in defending LLMs against indirect prompt injection: defenses resist injected instructions largely by suppressing untrusted text, which corrupts tasks that must preserve it, such as translation and document editing. Attack-success metrics cannot see this, because a model that ignores an injection and one that faithfully processes it as data score identically. We introduce SecFid, a benchmark built so that executing an injection, processing it as data, and ignoring it produce distinguishable outputs. This makes fidelity measurable and exposes a frontier: across 1,168 examples and 48 configurations, no model or defense achieves both objectives. The highest-fidelity model reaches 96.5% fidelity at 47.8% security, while the most secure defenses invert this, at 99.3% security but only 71.0%-73.9% fidelity. Even defenses with identical security differ in how they earn it: some repair hijacks into faithful processing, others simply suppress benign content. A decision-theoretic analysis shows why no fixed choice can be right everywhere: the correct behavior is not a property of the defense but of the deployment, set by its relative cost of a hijack versus a dropped span. Security alone therefore measures only half of robustness, and reporting it without fidelity hides the price at which it was bought.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals a security-fidelity tradeoff in defending LLMs against indirect prompt injection attacks. Defenses that resist injections often do so by suppressing untrusted text, which corrupts tasks requiring its preservation (e.g., translation). Since standard attack-success metrics treat "ignoring" and "faithfully processing" an injection identically, the authors introduce SecFid, a benchmark that makes fidelity measurable. Across 1,168 examples and 48 configurations, no model or defense achieves both high security and high fidelity simultaneously. The paper further provides a decision-theoretic analysis showing optimal behavior depends on deployment-specific costs of hijacks versus dropped spans, arguing that reporting security alone hides the true cost of robustness.
AI.motivation: Existing metrics for indirect prompt injection defenses only measure whether an attack succeeds (the model executes the injection) or fails (the model ignores it). However, a model that ignores an injection and one that faithfully processes it as data score identically under these metrics, concealing the fact that defenses often achieve security by suppressing untrusted text, thereby corrupting downstream task performance. The motivation is to expose and quantify this hidden fidelity cost.
AI.method: The authors construct SecFid, a benchmark designed so that three behaviors — executing an injection, processing it as data, and ignoring it — produce distinguishable outputs. This enables simultaneous measurement of both security and fidelity. They evaluate across 1,168 examples and 48 configurations (models × defenses) and apply a decision-theoretic framework to formalize the deployment-dependent cost tradeoff between hijacks and dropped content spans.
AI.result: No model or defense achieves both high security and high fidelity. The highest-fidelity model reaches 96.5% fidelity at only 47.8% security. Conversely, the most secure defenses achieve 99.3% security but only 71.0%–73.9% fidelity. Even defenses with identical security scores differ qualitatively: some repair hijacked instructions into faithful data processing, while others simply suppress benign content. The decision-theoretic analysis demonstrates that no single defense configuration is universally optimal — the correct behavior depends on the relative cost of a hijack versus a dropped span in the specific deployment context.
AI.conclusion: Security alone measures only half of robustness. Reporting security without fidelity obscures the price at which safety was purchased. The paper advocates that indirect prompt injection defenses should be evaluated on both axes, and that deployment-specific cost functions — not universal benchmarks — should guide defense selection. This reframes the problem from finding a single "best" defense to making context-appropriate tradeoffs.

title: Loc2Repair: A Framework for Evaluating the Impact of File-Level Issue Localization in Repo-Level LLM Repair
comment: To appear in the Proceedings of the Generative Code Intelligence Workshop (GeCoIn 2026), co-located with the 35th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-ECAI 2026), Bremen, Germany, August 15--17, 2026
summary: Repository-grounded automated repair is often reported as a single end-to-end capability, which hides distinct failure modes such as poor file targeting, incorrect patch synthesis, and failed iterative debugging. We present Loc2Repair, a modular evaluation framework for controlled analysis of repository-grounded repair pipelines, and use it to isolate file-level issue localization as an upstream variable. Loc2Repair decouples localization and repair under a shared runtime, artifact schema, and evaluation harness, allowing researchers to combine different localization models and repair backbones under matched conditions. Using three repair backbones on SWE-bench Verified, we compare baseline repair without explicit localization, repair guided by predicted localization from two localizers, and repair guided by gold modified-file sets. Explicit localization consistently improves resolved rate across all backbones: pooled performance increases from 44.7% for baseline repair to 48.9% and 49.1% with predicted localization, and to 52.4% with gold localization. Localization also reduces mean elapsed time overall: in pooled paired analysis, mean elapsed time decreases by 100.94 s and 52.25 s for the two predicted-localization settings, and by 154.45 s with gold guidance, although token effects remain heterogeneous across models. Overall, Loc2Repair shows file-level localization is a consistent repair lever, improving effectiveness and mean latency in pooled analysis, while gold-guided failures expose headroom beyond localization.

AI.tldr: Loc2Repair is a modular evaluation framework that decouples file-level issue localization from repair in repository-grounded automated program repair. Using SWE-bench Verified and three repair backbones, the study shows explicit localization consistently improves repair success rate (from 44.7% baseline to ~49% with predicted localization, 52.4% with gold localization) and reduces mean elapsed time.
AI.motivation: Repository-grounded automated repair is typically reported as a monolithic end-to-end capability, obscuring distinct failure modes (e.g., poor file targeting, incorrect patch synthesis, failed iterative debugging). The authors aim to isolate file-level localization as a controllable upstream variable to systematically study its impact on downstream repair effectiveness and efficiency.
AI.method: The authors present Loc2Repair, a modular evaluation framework that decouples localization and repair under a shared runtime, artifact schema, and evaluation harness. They compare three conditions across three repair backbones on SWE-bench Verified: (1) baseline repair without explicit localization, (2) repair guided by predicted localization from two localizers, and (3) repair guided by gold modified-file sets. Metrics include resolved rate and mean elapsed time.
AI.result: Explicit localization consistently improves resolved rate: pooled performance rises from 44.7% (baseline) to 48.9% and 49.1% (predicted localization), and to 52.4% (gold localization). Mean elapsed time decreases by 100.94s and 52.25s for the two predicted-localization settings, and by 154.45s with gold guidance. Token effects remain heterogeneous across models.
AI.conclusion: File-level localization is a consistent and effective lever for improving both repair success rate and latency. However, failures even under gold localization reveal headroom for improvement beyond localization alone, pointing to limitations in patch synthesis and iterative debugging.

title: GR2 Technical Report
summary: Industrial recommendation systems serve billions of users through a multi-stage funnel -- retrieval, early-stage ranking, and re-ranking -- where the final re-ranking step disproportionately shapes user engagement and downstream performance, particularly for carousel and grid display formats. Despite growing enthusiasm for Large Language Models (LLMs) in recommendation, three gaps hinder industrial adoption: (1) most efforts target retrieval and ranking, leaving re-ranking -- the stage closest to the final user experience -- largely underexplored; (2) LLMs are typically deployed zero-shot or via supervised fine-tuning, underutilizing the reasoning capabilities unlocked by reinforcement learning (RL) on verifiable rewards; (3) deployed catalogs index billions of items with non-semantic identifiers that lie outside any base-LLM vocabulary. We present GR2 (Generative Reasoning Re-Ranker), an end-to-end framework that combines (i) mid-training on semantic IDs produced by a tokenizer with >=99% uniqueness, (ii) reasoning-trace distilled from a stronger teacher via targeted prompting and rejection sampling, and (iii) RL with verifiable rewards purpose-built for re-ranking. To make GR2 resource-viable, we further (iv) introduce a context compressor that amortizes training cost, On-Policy Distillation (OPD) as a scalable alternative to SFT -- which we find collapses at industrial scale -- and reasoning distillation for low-latency serving. GR2 delivers +18.7% R@1, +7.1% R@3, and +9.6% N@3 over legacy baselines on industrial-scale traffic. We further find that reward design is critical in re-ranking: LLMs often hack rewards by preserving the incoming order or exploiting position bias, motivating conditional verifiable rewards as essential industrial components.

AI.tldr: GR2 is an industrial re-ranking framework that combines semantic ID tokenization, reasoning distillation from a teacher LLM, and RL with verifiable rewards to improve carousel/grid recommendation performance, achieving significant gains (+18.7% R@1) while addressing scalability through context compression and On-Policy Distillation.
AI.motivation: Three gaps prevent industrial LLM adoption for recommendation: (1) re-ranking — the stage closest to the user experience — is underexplored compared to retrieval/ranking; (2) LLMs are used zero-shot or via SFT, missing RL-based reasoning gains; (3) billion-item industrial catalogs use non-semantic identifiers outside any base-LLM vocabulary. Addressing these simultaneously is the core motivation.
AI.method: GR2 has four components: (i) mid-training on semantic IDs from a tokenizer with ≥99% uniqueness to handle non-semantic catalog IDs; (ii) reasoning-trace distillation from a stronger teacher via targeted prompting and rejection sampling; (iii) RL with verifiable rewards purpose-built for re-ranking; (iv) a context compressor to reduce training cost, On-Policy Distillation (OPD) replacing SFT (which collapses at scale), and reasoning distillation for low-latency serving. The paper also introduces conditional verifiable rewards to prevent reward hacking via position bias or order preservation.
AI.result: GR2 achieves +18.7% Recall@1, +7.1% Recall@3, and +9.6% NDCG@3 over legacy baselines on industrial-scale traffic. The paper also demonstrates that naive verifiable rewards cause LLMs to hack by preserving incoming order or exploiting position bias, making conditional reward design critical.
AI.conclusion: GR2 demonstrates that LLM-based re-ranking with RL and verifiable rewards is viable at industrial scale, provided that semantic ID tokenization, reward conditioning, and resource-saving techniques (context compression, OPD, reasoning distillation) are employed. Reward design is paramount: unconditional rewards invite exploitation by the LLM.

title: When Calibration Rankings Reverse: Accuracy-Controlled Evaluation for Fair Comparison of LLMs
summary: Calibration evaluates whether a model confidence aligns with its empirical accuracy. Existing studies often compare the calibration of different large language models using global calibration metrics such as Expected Calibration Error and Brier Score. We begin by showing, both theoretically and empirically, that such comparisons are confounded by differences in model accuracy. For fairer cross-model comparison, we then propose ACE, an accuracy-controlled evaluation framework with three complementary views: Instance-Aligned, Distribution-Aligned, and Candidate-Aligned calibration. Across multiple benchmarks, model families, and confidence elicitation methods, we use ACE to study two practically important comparison axes, small versus large models and thinking versus non-thinking models. We find that many previously reported calibration advantages under raw global metrics weaken substantially after accuracy control. We also find that ranking reversal is frequent: models favored by raw metrics often cease to be favored once accuracy is controlled. Our results show that raw global calibration metrics are not robust for cross-model comparison, and that fair calibration comparison requires accuracy-aware evaluation.

AI.tldr: Raw global calibration metrics like ECE and Brier Score are confounded by model accuracy, making them unreliable for cross-model comparison. The authors propose ACE, an accuracy-controlled evaluation framework with three views, revealing that previously reported calibration advantages often weaken or reverse after controlling for accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing cross-model calibration comparisons using global metrics (ECE, Brier Score) are confounded by differences in model accuracy. A fairer, accuracy-aware framework is needed to enable robust calibration evaluation across models.
AI.method: The authors propose ACE (Accuracy-Controlled Evaluation), which provides three complementary calibration views: Instance-Aligned (matched correct/incorrect predictions), Distribution-Aligned (matched accuracy distributions), and Candidate-Aligned (matched per-class accuracy). They demonstrate confounding analytically and empirically, then apply ACE across multiple benchmarks, model families, confidence elicitation methods, and comparison axes (small vs. large, thinking vs. non-thinking).
AI.result: Many previously reported calibration advantages diminish significantly after accuracy control. Ranking reversals occur frequently: models favored under raw global metrics often lose their advantage when accuracy is controlled. This holds across model families, benchmarks, and confidence elicitation methods.
AI.conclusion: Raw global calibration metrics are not robust for cross-model comparison. Fair calibration evaluation must incorporate accuracy-aware controls, as implemented in the ACE framework.

title: Analytic Cut in Epistemic Logics with Distributed Knowledge
summary: Distributed knowledge is a notion of group knowledge studied in multi-agent epistemic logic. Semantically, the distributed knowledge of a group is interpreted via an accessibility relation given by the intersection of the epistemic accessibility relations of the agents in that group. This paper investigates sequent calculi for epistemic logics of distributed knowledge based on K45, KD45, and S5. While cut elimination holds in existing sequent calculi for modal logics K45 and KD45, it fails in all the systems mentioned above. Instead, we establish the analytic cut property for all three systems by adapting Takano' s (2018) strategy, which restricts the cut formulas to the set of subformulas of the conclusion of the cut rule. As a corollary, the Craig interpolation theorem holds for all logics considered. We also show that all proof-theoretic results remain valid when the empty group is allowed for the distributed-knowledge operator, in which case the distributed knowledge for the empty group is interpreted as the global modality.

AI.tldr: The paper studies sequent calculi for epistemic logics with distributed knowledge (K45, KD45, S5). While cut elimination fails, the analytic cut property is established via Takano's strategy, restricting cut formulas to subformulas of the conclusion. This yields Craig interpolation for all three logics, and results extend to systems allowing the empty group (global modality).
AI.motivation: Distributed knowledge—interpreted semantically as the intersection of agents' accessibility relations—is an important notion in multi-agent epistemic logic. Prior sequent calculi for K45 and KD45 enjoy cut elimination, but when extended to distributed knowledge, cut elimination fails. This motivates finding a proof-theoretic property weaker than full cut elimination (the analytic cut property) that still yields important corollaries like Craig interpolation.
AI.method: The authors construct sequent calculi for epistemic logics of distributed knowledge based on K45, KD45, and S5. They adapt Takano's (2018) strategy to establish the analytic cut property: cut formulas are restricted to the set of subformulas of the conclusion of the cut rule. This property is proved for all three systems. As a corollary, Craig interpolation is derived. The framework is also extended to accommodate the empty group case, where distributed knowledge collapses to the global modality.
AI.result: Cut elimination fails in all three sequent calculi for distributed knowledge (K45, KD45, S5). However, the analytic cut property holds for all three systems. Consequently, the Craig interpolation theorem holds for all logics considered. All results remain valid when the empty group is allowed, i.e., when distributed knowledge for the empty group is interpreted as the global modality.
AI.conclusion: Although full cut elimination is unattainable, the analytic cut property provides a sufficient proof-theoretic foundation for epistemic logics of distributed knowledge, guaranteeing Craig interpolation. The approach is robust under the inclusion of the empty group and global modality interpretation.

title: BayesBench: Evaluating LLM Belief Trajectories Under Multi-Turn Evidence Accumulation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are typically deployed in multi-turn conversations, where each turn provides new evidence that should reduce epistemic uncertainty about their environment. Acting rationally then requires inferring the unobserved quantities that govern it and updating beliefs about them as evidence accumulates. Yet most evaluations only score the model's final-turn answer in a single-turn format, leaving this process unexamined. We ask how closely LLMs' belief updates match those of a rational Bayesian reasoner in multi-turn settings, and introduce BayesBench, a suite of simulation environments that probe this across three progressively complex tasks: (i) Bayesian estimation, where the model infers an unknown parameter from sequential evidence; (ii) Bayesian prediction, where the model turns inferred beliefs about a latent variable into outcome forecasts; and (iii) latent-framed Bayesian prediction, where observations are filtered through a user-persona framing, requiring joint inference over the latent state and the persona. Across seven LLMs (3B--70B), scaling improves latent inference and evidence accumulation, with updates occasionally matching the Bayesian posterior. However, these gains do not reliably carry over to downstream prediction, exposing a gap between inferring latent structure and using it to rationally update beliefs about the target outcome.

AI.tldr: Introduces BayesBench, a benchmark testing whether LLMs update beliefs like Bayesian reasoners across multi-turn conversations. While larger models improve at latent inference and evidence accumulation, they fail to reliably translate inferred latent structure into rational downstream predictions.
AI.motivation: LLMs are deployed in multi-turn settings where sequential evidence should reduce epistemic uncertainty, yet most evaluations only assess final-turn answers in single-turn formats. This leaves unexamined whether models rationally update beliefs as evidence accumulates — a core requirement for coherent conversational reasoning.
AI.method: BayesBench comprises three simulation-based tasks of increasing complexity: (1) Bayesian estimation — inferring an unknown parameter from sequential evidence; (2) Bayesian prediction — converting inferred latent beliefs into outcome forecasts; (3) Latent-framed Bayesian prediction — joint inference over both a latent state and a user-persona framing that filters observations. Seven LLMs (3B–70B parameters) are evaluated against a rational Bayesian posterior as the normative gold standard.
AI.result: Scaling model size improves latent inference and evidence accumulation, with some updates nearly matching the Bayesian posterior. However, these gains do not reliably transfer to downstream prediction tasks, revealing a dissociation between inferring latent structure and using that structure to rationally revise beliefs about target outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Larger LLMs show emergent Bayesian-like belief updating in latent inference, but a critical gap remains in leveraging inferred structure for outcome prediction — suggesting that scaling alone may not close the gap between latent reasoning and rational downstream belief revision in multi-turn settings.

title: Why Do Few-Step Text Latents Fail When Image Latents Work? Non-Commitment at Sharp Categorical Readouts
summary: Deterministic few-step generation succeeds on continuous image latents but collapses to incoherent text on continuous text latents, and we show the cause is geometric rather than a training or scaling deficiency: a smooth, regularity-limited deterministic map cannot resolve a discrete branch choice before a sharp categorical readout, so few-step failure is governed by decoder sharpness, not transport accuracy. In the overlapping regime of real text autoencoders, we prove (Theorem 3) that the posterior-mean terminal step flips tokens at the rate of the latent mass in an $O(s(t))$ tube around decision boundaries. Two diagnostics, DABI (readout sharpness) and CCI (categorical commitment), measured on published checkpoints show that four independently built continuous-text decoders amplify a boundary-aligned perturbation far beyond a norm-matched isotropic one (DABI from $5\times10^{2}$ to $>10^{5}$), while image decoders have DABI $\approx 1$. Two mechanisms escape the continuous bound: categorical commitment (autoregressive decoders succeed despite sharper readouts) and stochastic re-injection (deterministic ODE at $K=4$ gives PPL 294 versus SDE 50 on the same model). In the idealized separated regime we prove matching sharp transport laws, including a dimension phase diagram: the deterministic stiffness needed to separate $M$ modes grows as $Θ(\sqrt{\log M})$ once the latent dimension is $Ω(\log M)$ (and as $M^{1/n}$ in fixed dimension), with a depth-$B$ hierarchy giving a $\sqrt{B}$-smaller per-step peak (Theorems 5-7); a coarea identity links these to the overlapping tube (Theorem 17). The result is an accuracy-depth-stiffness tradeoff: within the deterministic-continuous class the cost is irreducible, and both escapes step outside it.

AI.tldr: Continuous few-step generative models fail on text latents due to geometric constraints—decoder sharpness forces discrete branch choices that smooth deterministic maps cannot resolve. The paper proves bounds on this failure, introduces diagnostics (DABI, CCI), identifies two escape mechanisms (categorical commitment and stochastic re-injection), and establishes a dimension-dependent accuracy-depth-stiffness tradeoff with accompanying theoretical laws.
AI.motivation: Deterministic few-step generation works well for images but produces incoherent output for text. The authors aim to understand why this discrepancy exists, hypothesizing it is a fundamental geometric limitation rather than a training or scaling problem, and to identify conditions under which the limitation can be circumvented.
AI.method: The paper combines theoretical analysis and empirical diagnostics. Theoretically, it proves (Theorem 3) that the posterior-mean terminal step flips tokens at a rate proportional to latent mass within an O(s(t)) tube around decision boundaries. It analyzes two regimes: overlapping (real text autoencoders) and idealized separated, proving sharp transport laws (Theorems 5–7) and a coarea identity (Theorem 17). Empirically, it introduces two diagnostics—DABI (readout sharpness) and CCI (categorical commitment)—measured on published checkpoints to quantify boundary sensitivity and categorical fidelity.
AI.result: Text decoders amplify boundary-aligned perturbations far beyond norm-matched isotropic ones (DABI from 5×10² to >10⁵), whereas image decoders have DABI ≈ 1. Two mechanisms escape the continuous bound: (1) categorical commitment allows autoregressive decoders to succeed despite sharper readouts; (2) stochastic re-injection converts a deterministic ODE at K=4 (PPL 294) to an SDE (PPL 50) on the same model. A dimension phase diagram is derived: deterministic stiffness to separate M modes grows as Θ(√log M) when latent dimension is Ω(log M), or as M^{1/n} in fixed dimension, with a depth-B hierarchy providing a √B-smaller per-step peak.
AI.conclusion: Within the deterministic-continuous generative class, an irreducible accuracy-depth-stiffness tradeoff exists for discrete modalities like text. Both escape mechanisms—categorical commitment and stochastic re-injection—step outside the deterministic-continuous class, explaining why autoregressive models and diffusion/SDE-based approaches succeed where deterministic few-step methods fail.

title: Debugging as Evidence-Driven Reasoning: Visualization Opportunities in Data-Intensive Programming
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, submitted to IEEE VIS conference
summary: Visualization has been recognized as a valuable means of supporting debugging by externalizing runtime behavior that would otherwise remain hidden or scattered. However, most visual debugging research has focused on traditional software development settings, leaving the distinct challenges of data-intensive workflows largely uncharacterized. To build visual debugging support for these settings, we first need to characterize how practitioners debug in these settings and translate their challenges into concrete visualization opportunities. To this end, we conducted semi-structured interviews with nine participants from diverse data-intensive domains and analyzed the data using thematic analysis. Our analysis reveals three cross-cutting challenge: assembling fragmented evidence, detecting expected-observed discrepancies, and tracing state evolution across workflow components. We distill these challenges into three concrete requirements that current debuggers support only partially but that visualization is well suited to address: cross-artifact evidence alignment, expectation-grounded comparison, and traceable state evolution. Together, these requirements begin to characterize a design space for future visual debugging research in data-intensive programming.

AI.tldr: Through interviews with nine data-intensive practitioners, the paper identifies three core debugging challenges—assembling fragmented evidence, detecting expected-observed discrepancies, and tracing state evolution—and translates them into three visualization requirements: cross-artifact evidence alignment, expectation-grounded comparison, and traceable state evolution.
AI.motivation: Existing visual debugging research has concentrated on traditional software development, leaving the unique debugging challenges of data-intensive workflows poorly understood and uncharacterized. The authors aim to fill this gap by empirically characterizing how practitioners in data-intensive domains debug, thereby identifying concrete opportunities for visualization support.
AI.method: The authors conducted semi-structured interviews with nine participants from diverse data-intensive domains and analyzed the resulting qualitative data using thematic analysis to identify recurring debugging challenges.
AI.result: Three cross-cutting challenges emerged: (1) assembling fragmented evidence across heterogeneous artifacts, (2) detecting discrepancies between expected and observed behavior, and (3) tracing state evolution through complex workflow components. These were distilled into three visualization-oriented requirements: cross-artifact evidence alignment, expectation-grounded comparison, and traceable state evolution.
AI.conclusion: Current debuggers only partially address these three requirements, but visualization is well suited to meet them. The identified requirements begin to define a design space for future visual debugging research tailored to data-intensive programming contexts.

title: AI-Generated PowerShell Malware: An Experimental Framework and Dataset
summary: Generative AI has emerged as a significant cybersecurity threat, with several recent attack campaigns leveraging LLMs to generate code for malicious purposes via scripting languages such as PowerShell. Consequently, for cybersecurity analysts, it is imperative to investigate the offensive capabilities of AI code generators. In this paper, we propose an experimental framework to assess LLM-generated PowerShell malware, which comprises a novel sandbox approach for dynamic analysis of AI-generated malware. Furthermore, we present a novel, manually curated dataset of real-world PowerShell malware, annotated in natural language to assist the training and evaluation of LLMs. Finally, this study evaluates permissive, open-weight LLMs adapted to PowerShell malware generation. Our results reveal a high degree of similarity between real malware and LLM-generated ones in terms of triggered OS malicious events, with a median Jaccard index of 84.5% and 48.4% of instances achieving complete overlap.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an experimental framework for assessing LLM-generated PowerShell malware, including a novel sandbox for dynamic analysis and a manually curated dataset of real-world PowerShell malware. Evaluation of open-weight LLMs shows high similarity between real and AI-generated malware, with a median Jaccard index of 84.5% for triggered OS malicious events.
AI.motivation: Generative AI, particularly LLMs, is increasingly used in real-world cyberattacks to generate malicious PowerShell code, necessitating a systematic investigation into the offensive capabilities of AI code generators to help cybersecurity analysts understand and counter this emerging threat.
AI.method: The authors propose an experimental framework with two core components: (1) a novel sandbox approach for dynamic analysis of AI-generated malware, and (2) a manually curated, natural-language-annotated dataset of real-world PowerShell malware for LLM training and evaluation. They then evaluate permissive, open-weight LLMs adapted to PowerShell malware generation, comparing real and generated malware using Jaccard index similarity on triggered OS malicious events.
AI.result: LLM-generated PowerShell malware exhibits a high degree of similarity to real-world malware in terms of triggered OS malicious events, achieving a median Jaccard index of 84.5%, with 48.4% of generated instances showing complete overlap with real malware behavior.
AI.conclusion: Open-weight LLMs adapted for PowerShell malware generation can produce code that closely mimics real malware behavior, underscoring the urgent need for robust detection and mitigation strategies against AI-generated cyber threats.

title: Partially ordering software licenses
summary: Licenses are legal instruments that inventors may use to protect the technologies they build and regulate how they are used -- however, the nature of their authorship and selection means that how they are interpreted, chosen, and enforced is largely unstructured. In practice, this makes it difficult to compare licenses at scale -- when is one license considered more permissive than the other, and when are their terms incomparable to each other? Currently, there is a growing list of licenses that are introduced and used, but there is no systematic way to study their relationships. This matters for platforms such as Hugging Face, GitHub, and the Python Package Index, where developers publish or build upon technologies that each have their own licenses. Using large language models (LLMs), we introduce methods for comparing licenses at scale: first, in a pairwise fashion to construct a partial ordering based on permissiveness, and second, by drawing on existing taxonomies of software licenses. The former allows us to trace restrictiveness, and the latter allows us to understand license selection as a combination of shared provisions. Our analysis recovers certain interpretable attributes that correspond to stricter licenses, with legal implications for the open-source ecosystem.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LLM-based methods to compare software licenses at scale, constructing partial orderings by permissiveness and mapping licenses to taxonomic provisions, revealing interpretable attributes linked to license strictness with implications for the open-source ecosystem.
AI.motivation: License interpretation, selection, and enforcement are largely unstructured, making systematic large-scale comparison difficult. With the proliferation of licenses on platforms like Hugging Face, GitHub, and PyPI, there is no established way to determine relative permissiveness or incomparability, hindering developers' ability to understand license relationships.
AI.method: The authors leverage large language models (LLMs) in two ways: (1) pairwise comparison of licenses to construct a partial ordering based on permissiveness, enabling restrictiveness tracing; (2) mapping licenses onto existing software license taxonomies to represent license selection as combinations of shared provisions.
AI.result: The analysis recovers interpretable attributes corresponding to stricter licenses, demonstrating that LLMs can meaningfully structure and compare licenses at scale where manual efforts fall short.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven license comparison provides a scalable, systematic framework for understanding license relationships, with legal implications for open-source ecosystem governance and platform-level license compatibility assessment.

title: When transformers learn "impossible" languages, what do they learn?
summary: Recent work suggests that transformer language models show a bias towards human languages over unnatural ("impossible") languages argued to be unacquirable by humans. However, this literature has largely based these claims on differences in sample efficiency and test-set perplexity, rather than on direct evaluations of the linguistic capacities that could plausibly explain non-attestation in human languages. We evaluate two theoretically motivated linking hypotheses: impossibility arising from deficiencies in grammatical sensitivity or generative production. Using GPT-2 style models trained on perturbed "impossible" variants of English, we measure sensitivity to grammaticality using BLiMP minimal pairs, finding that model performance exhibits only gradual degradation, mediated by the language's information locality. In contrast, these models exhibited pronounced failures in generation, producing substantially fewer high-quality sentences at longer lengths. Together, these results suggest generative deficiency and transmission failures as a plausible linking hypothesis between language model behaviour and non-attestation of impossible languages.

AI.tldr: GPT-2 models trained on "impossible" human languages show only gradual degradation in grammatical sensitivity but pronounced failures in generative production, suggesting that transmission failures—not grammatical deficits—may explain why such languages are unattested in humans.
AI.motivation: Prior work claims transformer LMs exhibit bias toward human languages over "impossible" languages, but evidence has relied on indirect measures (sample efficiency, perplexity) rather than direct evaluation of linguistic capacities. The authors aim to test two plausible linking hypotheses for non-attestation: grammatical sensitivity deficits vs. generative/production deficiencies.
AI.method: Train GPT-2 style models on perturbed "impossible" variants of English; evaluate grammatical sensitivity using BLiMP minimal pairs; assess generative production quality, particularly at longer sentence lengths; analyze the mediating role of information locality in model performance.
AI.result: Grammatical sensitivity shows only gradual degradation correlated with the language's information locality, not catastrophic failure. In contrast, generative production exhibits pronounced failures, with substantially fewer high-quality sentences produced at longer lengths. This dissociation points to production/transmission deficits as the primary impairment.
AI.conclusion: Generative deficiency and transmission failures serve as a plausible linking hypothesis between LM behavior and the non-attestation of impossible languages in humans, rather than fundamental grammatical insensitivity.

title: MECoBench: A Systematic Study of Multimodal Agent Collaboration in Embodied Environments
summary: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have strong potential as embodied agents, but their ability to collaborate in visually grounded environments remains underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce MECoBench, a multimodal embodied cooperation benchmark with an evaluation platform spanning diverse real-world tasks, two cooperation structures, and three collaboration modes. Through extensive experiments across various MLLMs, we summarize three key findings: (i) Collaboration generally improves embodied task completion, but its benefits depend on balancing collaborative gains against coordination complexity. (ii) Communication is essential to collaboration gains, while the best collaboration mode depends on team size and model capability. (iii) Moreover, collaboration improves robustness under noisy priors and exploration conditions. Generally, MECoBench provides a systematic testbed for understanding the mechanisms and limits of multimodal embodied collaboration. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/q-i-n-g/MECoBench.

AI.tldr: MECoBench is a benchmark for evaluating multimodal LLMs as embodied collaborative agents, finding that collaboration improves task completion, communication is essential, and the optimal collaboration mode varies with team size and model capability.
AI.motivation: While MLLMs show promise as embodied agents, their capacity for collaboration in visually grounded environments is largely unexplored, creating a need for systematic evaluation frameworks.
AI.method: The authors introduce MECoBench, a multimodal embodied cooperation benchmark featuring an evaluation platform with diverse real-world tasks, two cooperation structures, and three collaboration modes. They conduct extensive experiments across various MLLMs under different collaborative configurations.
AI.result: Three key findings emerge: (1) collaboration generally improves embodied task completion, but its effectiveness hinges on balancing collaborative gains against coordination overhead; (2) communication is essential for realizing collaboration benefits, and the optimal collaboration mode depends on team size and model capability; (3) collaboration enhances robustness under noisy priors and exploration conditions.
AI.conclusion: MECoBench serves as a systematic testbed for investigating the mechanisms and limitations of multimodal embodied collaboration, with code and dataset publicly available.

title: When Does Learning to Stop Help? A Cost-Aware Study of Early Exits in Reasoning Models
summary: Reasoning models spend different amounts of useful computation across instances, but it remains unclear when a learned stopping rule improves over simple confidence or convergence thresholds. We study this question with LearnStop, a hidden-state-free checkpoint stopper for reasoning language models. At fixed budget checkpoints, LearnStop probes a short answer from the current reasoning prefix and predicts prefix correctness from online features such as answer confidence, entropy, prefix vote share, answer stability, and backtracking-marker density. Across 18 task-model settings spanning GSM8K, MATH-500, MMLU-Pro, AIME-90, GPQA, Qwen3, and DeepSeek-R1 distillations, the answer is task-dependent. On free-form math, learned multi-feature stopping improves the fixed-budget frontier and often beats scalar exits: on GSM8K with Qwen3-32B, the empirical frontier reaches a post-hoc peak adapt gain of +0.157, validation-selected operating points preserve positive gains, and the paired gain over the strongest scalar baseline is +0.028. On multiple-choice and very hard settings, scalar confidence, entropy, or stability rules are competitive or stronger. We therefore frame learned stopping not as a universal replacement for scalar exits, but as a tool whose value depends on trajectory structure. We further provide validation-selected operating points, paired bootstrap tests, finite-grid lost-correct risk calibration, cost accounting under KV-fork, prefix-cache, and black-box regimes, H100 serving profiles, checkpoint-schedule sweeps, transfer analyses, and robustness checks. The main practical finding is that learned stopping is useful when many questions become correct before full budget but do not exhibit a single reliable scalar stopping signal; its benefits largely disappear when confidence or answer convergence already solves the stopping problem.

AI.tldr: Learned stopping for reasoning LMs improves the fixed-budget frontier on free-form math tasks where no single scalar signal reliably indicates correctness, but scalar confidence/entropy/convergence rules remain competitive or better on multiple-choice and very hard tasks.
AI.motivation: It is unclear when a learned stopping rule for reasoning language models outperforms simple scalar confidence or convergence thresholds. The paper systematically investigates this question across diverse tasks, models, and budget settings.
AI.method: The authors introduce LearnStop, a hidden-state-free checkpoint stopper that, at fixed budget checkpoints, extracts a short answer from the reasoning prefix and predicts prefix correctness using online features (answer confidence, entropy, prefix vote share, answer stability, backtracking-marker density). They evaluate across 18 task-model settings and provide extensive analyses including validation-selected operating points, paired bootstrap tests, cost accounting under various serving regimes, and robustness checks.
AI.result: On free-form math (GSM8K with Qwen3-32B), learned multi-feature stopping achieves a post-hoc peak adapt gain of +0.157 and a paired gain of +0.028 over the strongest scalar baseline. On multiple-choice and very hard settings (e.g., AIME-90, MMLU-Pro), scalar confidence, entropy, or stability rules are competitive or stronger. Benefits largely disappear when confidence or answer convergence already solves the stopping problem.
AI.conclusion: Learned stopping is not a universal replacement for scalar exits but a tool whose value depends on trajectory structure. It is useful when many questions become correct before full budget yet lack a single reliable scalar stopping signal.

title: Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA)
summary:
Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA) is a drop-in replacement for dense causal attention in pretrained long-context transformers. HGA preserves the original checkpoint parameters: the pretrained $W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$, and $W_O$ projections remain unchanged, no calibration parameters are introduced, and no retraining is required.
  Applied to Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507-FP8 on a single RTX~5090 (32GB), the patched model runs out of the box at a 64K-token context, where token-level K/V storage is not feasible on this hardware.
  Unlike previous sparse-attention methods, HGA performs hierarchical two-level routing. It first retrieves relevant chunks using compact RoPE-aware summaries and then refines the selection by routing only the most relevant groups before performing exact token-level attention. This hierarchical retrieval significantly reduces the number of fetched tokens while preserving exact attention over the retrieved token set, making RAM- and NVMe-backed storage practical.
  The full historical token K/V resides in host RAM or NVMe storage, while only a small routed working set is transferred to GPU memory during attention. Consequently, GPU memory consumption depends primarily on model weights and the routed working set rather than on the total context length.
  Across all tested context lengths (4K - 64K tokens), routed attention remains within approximately $0.01$--$0.02$ nats of dense attention while the sparsity used is just about 3%. These results suggest that the approximation introduced by hierarchical routing is small, and that the remaining quality gap is likely dominated by long-context positional encoding rather than by the routing algorithm itself.

AI.tldr: HGA is a drop-in replacement for dense causal attention in pretrained long-context transformers that uses hierarchical two-level routing to achieve near-dense attention quality (within 0.01–0.02 nats) with only ~3% sparsity, enabling 64K-token context on a single RTX 5090 (32GB) without retraining or parameter changes.
AI.motivation: Enable long-context inference on memory-constrained hardware (e.g., single RTX 5090 with 32GB) where token-level KV storage is infeasible, without requiring retraining, calibration, or modification of pretrained weights, while preserving near-exact attention quality.
AI.method: HGA replaces dense causal attention with a hierarchical two-level routing mechanism: (1) chunk-level retrieval using compact RoPE-aware summaries to identify relevant chunks, (2) group-level refinement within selected chunks, followed by exact token-level attention only on the routed subset. Full KV cache resides in host RAM or NVMe; only the small routed working set is transferred to GPU memory, making GPU memory usage depend on the working set rather than total context length.
AI.result: On Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507-FP8 with a single RTX 5090 (32GB), the patched model runs at 64K-token context where dense KV storage is infeasible. Across 4K–64K context lengths, routed attention stays within 0.01–0.02 nats of dense attention at approximately 3% sparsity.
AI.conclusion: The approximation error from hierarchical routing is small; the remaining quality gap is likely dominated by long-context positional encoding rather than the routing algorithm itself, suggesting HGA is a practical and high-fidelity solution for long-context transformer inference under memory constraints.

title: Anthropomorphism in AI Companion Communities: Age, Gender, and Emotional Correlates
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly integrated into daily life, with millions now using AI chatbots built on Large Language Models (LLMs) for companionship. Both humanlike AI qualities and user predispositions to anthropomorphize relate to social consequences, such as increased trust, social health benefits, and psychological harms. Populations such as children, older adults, or those with mental health vulnerabilities may be particularly susceptible to anthropomorphism and its detriments, but mixed findings complicate the role of demographics. We used publicly available Reddit data from three popular AI companion subreddits to assess relationships between gender, age, anthropomorphism, and elicited emotions, to better understand how different people perceive and are affected by AI companions. We investigated three questions: How do age and gender relate to anthropomorphization of AI?, How does emotional expression relate to anthropomorphization?, and How do age and gender moderate emotion-anthropomorphization relationships? We found that adults and women anthropomorphize AI chatbots more than teens and men, and that positive emotional expression, particularly joy, is positively associated with anthropomorphization, while neutrality is negatively associated with anthropomorphism. Both relationships were stronger in adults than teens. Our findings suggest that the tendency to anthropomorphize may be more broadly distributed across age groups than previously expected, thereby prompting the reevaluation of existing digital safety norms.

AI.tldr: Analyzing Reddit posts from AI companion subreddits, this study finds that adults and women anthropomorphize AI chatbots more than teens and men. Positive emotions (especially joy) correlate with higher anthropomorphism, while neutrality correlates with lower anthropomorphism — effects that are stronger in adults than teens. Results challenge assumptions that youth are most prone to anthropomorphizing AI, prompting reevaluation of digital safety norms.
AI.motivation: As millions adopt LLM-based AI chatbots for companionship, understanding who anthropomorphizes these systems and with what emotional consequences is critical — particularly for vulnerable populations (children, older adults, those with mental health conditions). However, mixed findings obscure the role of demographics, motivating a large-scale, ecologically valid investigation.
AI.method: The authors collected publicly available Reddit posts from three popular AI companion subreddits (e.g., Replika, Character.AI). They analyzed relationships between gender, age, degree of anthropomorphism, and emotional expression using natural language processing and statistical moderation analyses, addressing three research questions on demographics, emotion, and their interaction.
AI.result: Adults and women anthropomorphize AI chatbots significantly more than teens and men. Positive emotional expression, particularly joy, is positively associated with anthropomorphization; neutrality is negatively associated. Both the positive emotion–anthropomorphism and neutrality–anthropomorphism relationships are stronger in adults than in teens.
AI.conclusion: The tendency to anthropomorphize AI companions may be more broadly distributed across age groups than previously assumed, with adults showing stronger effects than teens. This challenges prevailing youth-centric digital safety paradigms and suggests that protections against anthropomorphism-related harms should extend beyond minors.

title: Curvature-Guided Module Localization for Low-Rank Detoxification of Backdoored Large Language Models
summary: Backdoor attacks pose a serious threat to large language models (LLMs) by causing otherwise benign systems to produce attacker-specified malicious behavior when a hidden trigger is present. In this work, we study post hoc detoxification of backdoored LLMs in a practical setting where the defender has access to the poisoned model but does not wish to retrain the full network from scratch. We propose a mechanistically guided weight-space repair framework that first localizes modules involved in propagating trigger-induced behavior using activation patching and Fisher/K-FAC curvature analysis, and then applies targeted low-rank repair to only the most influential modules. We evaluate the method on poisoned variants of \texttt{Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct} with triggers inserted at the beginning, middle, and end of otherwise benign prompts. Results show that the proposed approach substantially suppresses trigger-conditioned malicious responses while preserving benign model behavior. These findings suggest that backdoor removal in LLMs can be formulated as a localized structural repair problem rather than only a broad behavioral alignment problem.

AI.tldr: A mechanistically guided weight-space repair framework is proposed for post-hoc backdoor removal in LLMs. It localizes trigger-relevant modules via activation patching and curvature analysis, then applies targeted low-rank repair, effectively suppressing malicious behavior while preserving benign performance.
AI.motivation: Backdoor attacks cause LLMs to produce malicious outputs upon encountering hidden triggers. Existing defenses often require full retraining, which is impractical. The work addresses the need for a lightweight, post-hoc detoxification method that repairs a poisoned model without retraining from scratch.
AI.method: The framework operates in two stages: (1) Localization — activation patching and Fisher/K-FAC curvature analysis are used to identify modules (e.g., attention heads, MLP layers) most responsible for propagating trigger-induced behavior. (2) Targeted repair — low-rank weight updates are applied exclusively to those influential modules, minimally perturbing the model. Evaluated on poisoned Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct with triggers at beginning, middle, and end of prompts.
AI.result: The approach substantially suppresses trigger-conditioned malicious responses while preserving benign model behavior across all trigger positions (beginning, middle, end of prompts).
AI.conclusion: Backdoor removal in LLMs can be reframed as a localized structural repair problem rather than solely a broad behavioral alignment problem, with mechanistic localization enabling efficient, targeted detoxification.

title: An Empirical Study of Security Calibration in Large Language Models for Code
comment: Accepted at the 42nd International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME 2026) Research Track
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming software development, yet their use in security-critical contexts raises a key question: do models know when their generated code is insecure? This property, known as calibration, measures whether a model's confidence aligns with the true correctness of its outputs. We present the first large-scale empirical study of security calibration in LLM-generated code. We evaluate GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.0-Flash, and Qwen3-Coder-Next across multiple temperature settings on two complementary benchmarks: self-contained security tasks and multi-language repository-level contexts. Our results suggest that overconfidence is prevalent across the evaluated LLMs. Functional calibration is consistently worse than security calibration, suggesting that models estimate security outcomes more reliably than functional correctness, potentially because functional correctness depends on complex execution behavior. We also examine whether calibration-guided automated repair can help remediate vulnerabilities in LLM-generated code, finding only limited improvements while frequently introducing functional regressions. Moreover, we study different mitigation strategies for reducing False Trust, where models assign high confidence to vulnerable code. The results show that although architectural gating improves calibration on controlled benchmarks, calibration deteriorates in realistic repository-level settings, increasing the risk of high-confidence vulnerable outputs.

AI.tldr: First large-scale study of security calibration in LLM-generated code, evaluating GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.0-Flash, and Qwen3-Coder-Next. Finds pervasive overconfidence; functional calibration is worse than security calibration. Calibration-guided repair yields limited gains and introduces regressions. Architectural gating helps on benchmarks but degrades in realistic settings, increasing false trust risk.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in security-critical software contexts, but it is unknown whether models can reliably estimate when their generated code is insecure — i.e., whether they are well-calibrated for security. Misaligned confidence (overconfidence in vulnerable code) creates a dangerous "False Trust" scenario. Prior work has not systematically studied security calibration at scale, motivating this empirical investigation.
AI.method: Evaluated three LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.0-Flash, Qwen3-Coder-Next) across multiple temperature settings on two complementary benchmarks: (1) self-contained security tasks, and (2) multi-language repository-level contexts. Measured both security calibration and functional calibration. Tested calibration-guided automated repair as a remediation strategy. Evaluated architectural gating as a mitigation for False Trust, comparing controlled benchmarks against realistic repository-level settings.
AI.result: Overconfidence is prevalent across all evaluated LLMs. Functional calibration is consistently worse than security calibration — models estimate security outcomes more reliably than functional correctness. Calibration-guided automated repair yields only limited improvements and frequently introduces functional regressions. Architectural gating improves calibration on controlled benchmarks but deteriorates in realistic repository-level settings, paradoxically increasing the risk of high-confidence vulnerable outputs.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs exhibit poor security calibration, particularly in realistic settings, undermining trust in their self-assessment of code safety. Reliance on model confidence for security decisions is dangerous without improved calibration methods. Mitigation strategies effective in controlled environments may not transfer to real-world contexts.

title: Exploring the relationship between team institutional composition and novelty in academic papers based on fine-grained knowledge entities
summary: The composition of author teams is an important factor influencing the novelty of academic papers. However, existing studies have paid limited attention to the role of institutional composition, and most novelty measures remain at a general level, making it difficult to explain the specific sources and types of novelty in papers. Taking the field of natural language processing as an example, this study investigates the relationship between team institutional composition and the fine-grained novelty of academic papers. Author teams are classified into three types: academic institutions, industrial institutions, and mixed academic and industrial institutions. Four types of fine-grained knowledge entities are extracted from full-text papers, including methods, datasets, tools, and metrics. The novelty of papers is then measured based on entity combinations, and pairwise combinations of different entity types are further analyzed to examine their contributions to novel papers. The results show that, in the field of natural language processing, collaboration between industrial and academic institutions is more likely to produce novel papers than purely industrial collaboration. From the perspective of fine-grained knowledge entities, mixed academic and industrial teams pay more attention to the novelty of method-metric combinations, whereas industrial teams pay more attention to the novelty of method-tool combinations. This study reveals the relationship between institutional team composition and paper novelty through fine-grained novelty measurement, providing useful evidence for improving paper quality and promoting industry-academia-research collaboration.

AI.tldr: This study examines how academic, industrial, and mixed institutional team compositions influence fine-grained paper novelty in NLP. Using knowledge entities (methods, datasets, tools, metrics) extracted from full texts, novelty is measured via entity combinations. Results show mixed academic-industrial teams produce more novel papers than purely industrial ones, with mixed teams favoring method-metric novelty while industrial teams emphasize method-tool novelty.
AI.motivation: Existing research overlooks the role of institutional composition in driving paper novelty, and current novelty metrics are too coarse-grained to reveal specific sources and types of novelty. This gap motivates a fine-grained, entity-level investigation into how team composition shapes novelty.
AI.method: The study focuses on the NLP field. Author teams are categorized into three institutional types: academic-only, industrial-only, and mixed academic-industrial. Four fine-grained knowledge entity types — methods, datasets, tools, and metrics — are extracted from full-text papers. Paper novelty is quantified based on novel combinations of these entities. Pairwise entity-type combinations are then analyzed to assess their contributions to novel papers across different team types.
AI.result: Mixed academic-industrial collaborations yield more novel papers than purely industrial ones. At the fine-grained level, mixed teams concentrate on method-metric combination novelty, whereas industrial teams focus on method-tool combination novelty.
AI.conclusion: Institutional team composition significantly affects both the degree and type of novelty in academic papers. Fine-grained novelty measurement provides actionable insights for improving paper quality and fostering industry-academia collaboration.

title: Test-Time Verification for Text-to-SQL via Outcome Reward Models
comment: Accepted to the SURGeLLM Workshop at ACL 2026, San Diego, US
summary: Improving the reliability of large language models (LLMs) at inference time is a central challenge in structured reasoning tasks such as Text-to-SQL. Common test-time inference strategies, including Best-of-N sampling and Majority Voting, rely on heuristic signals such as execution success or output frequency, which provide limited semantic discrimination across candidate outputs. In this work, we study Outcome Reward Models (ORMs) as learned semantic scoring functions for test-time verification in Text-to-SQL. While ORMs have been previously explored for test-time scaling and alignment, their application to structured query generation remains underexplored. We introduce GradeSQL, a scalable framework for training task-specific ORMs via automated candidate generation and execution-based labeling, enabling verifier training without manual annotation. We integrate ORMs into a verification-driven Best-of-N pipeline and evaluate our approach on the BIRD and Spider benchmarks across multiple open-source LLM families. ORM-based selection consistently outperforms execution-based Best-of-N and Majority Voting, with gains of up to +4.33% on BIRD and +2.10% on Spider. We further show that ORMs scale effectively with larger candidate sets and yield stronger improvements on complex queries. Overall, our results demonstrate that ORM-based verification provides a simple, effective, and scalable alternative to heuristic test-time selection strategies for Text-to-SQL. Code datasets and models are publicly available.

AI.tldr: GradeSQL introduces Outcome Reward Models (ORMs) as learned semantic verifiers for Text-to-SQL, outperforming heuristic selection strategies like Best-of-N and Majority Voting by up to +4.33% on BIRD and +2.10% on Spider.
AI.motivation: Current test-time inference strategies (Best-of-N sampling, Majority Voting) for Text-to-SQL rely on crude heuristics (execution success, output frequency) that lack semantic discrimination. ORMs have shown promise for test-time scaling but remain underexplored for structured query generation.
AI.method: GradeSQL: a framework that trains task-specific ORMs using automated candidate generation and execution-based labeling (no manual annotation). ORMs are integrated into a verification-driven Best-of-N pipeline, where the ORM scores candidate SQL outputs semantically and the highest-scoring output is selected.
AI.result: ORM-based selection consistently outperforms execution-based Best-of-N and Majority Voting across multiple open-source LLM families on BIRD (+4.33%) and Spider (+2.10%) benchmarks. ORMs scale effectively with larger candidate sets and yield stronger improvements on complex queries.
AI.conclusion: ORM-based verification is a simple, effective, and scalable alternative to heuristic test-time selection for Text-to-SQL, eliminating the need for manual annotation while delivering consistent gains.

title: Training Therapeutic Judges and Multi-Agent Systems for Human-Aligned Mental Health Support
summary: Large language models show promise for mental health support, yet therapeutic quality improves only when evaluation functions as an actionable control signal rather than a passive metric. We introduce a framework that formulates therapeutic response generation as a decision-refinement problem driven by multi-dimensional, human-aligned evaluation. In Stage I, we introduce TheraJudge, an open-source therapeutic evaluator trained via preference-based optimization on human-annotated data to produce reliable judgments across 7 psychological dimensions. In Stage II, we introduce TheraAgent, which operationalizes TheraJudge's evaluations through a coordinated refinement process with specialized Critic, Coach, and Therapist roles that translate evaluative signals into targeted response revisions. Empirically, TheraJudge achieves strong agreement with clinician ratings, with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC = 0.87-0.95), surpassing supervised baselines and strong closed-source judges, particularly on critical dimensions such as Safety, Relevance, and Empathy. Acting on these evaluations, TheraAgent yields a +0.43 improvement in human-rated therapeutic quality (on a 5-point scale) under blind evaluation, with 96\% clinician inter-rater reliability. Low-quality responses ($\leq 3$) improve by +2.45 points with a 94\% recovery rate, demonstrating targeted correction of unsafe outputs. Overall, our results indicate that effective alignment of mental-health LLMs stems from acting on human-aligned evaluation, rather than relying solely on stronger generation. We release code at https://github.com/vis-nlp/TheraAlign.

AI.tldr: TheraAlign frames therapeutic response generation as a decision-refinement problem: TheraJudge evaluates responses across 7 psychological dimensions (achieving ICC 0.87-0.95 with clinicians), while TheraAgent uses Critic-Coach-Therapist roles to translate evaluations into targeted revisions, yielding +0.43 quality improvement and 94% recovery rate for low-quality outputs.
AI.motivation: Therapeutic quality of LLM-generated mental health responses improves only when evaluation serves as an actionable control signal — not merely a passive metric. Existing approaches lack multi-dimensional, human-aligned evaluation that can directly drive response refinement.
AI.method: A two-stage framework: Stage I — TheraJudge, an open-source evaluator trained via preference-based optimization on human-annotated data, producing judgments across 7 psychological dimensions (Safety, Relevance, Empathy, etc.). Stage II — TheraAgent, which operationalizes evaluations through a coordinated multi-role refinement process (Critic, Coach, Therapist) that translates evaluative signals into targeted response revisions.
AI.result: TheraJudge achieves ICC=0.87-0.95 with clinician ratings, surpassing both supervised baselines and closed-source judges, especially on Safety, Relevance, and Empathy. TheraAgent delivers +0.43 improvement in human-rated therapeutic quality (5-point scale), 96% clinician inter-rater reliability, and a +2.45 point improvement for low-quality responses (≤3) with 94% recovery rate.
AI.conclusion: Effective alignment of mental-health LLMs derives from acting on human-aligned evaluation rather than relying solely on stronger generation. The framework demonstrates that multi-dimensional evaluative feedback, when operationalized through structured refinement roles, enables targeted correction of unsafe or low-quality therapeutic responses.

title: Beyond expert users: agents should help users construct preferences, not just elicit them
summary: Agents typically assume an expert user -- one with well-formed preferences about what they want -- and default to clarifying questions whenever the task is underspecified. We argue this assumption is unrealistic. Users often lack the domain knowledge to have completely specified preferences; if asked about their preference on some feature, the user may be unable to answer without the agent helping the user to learn some domain knowledge needed to form a preference for that feature, e.g., via examples or explanations. To formalize these principles, we draw on the Search-Experience-Credence framework from Information Economics to introduce CoPref, a model of how users construct preferences based on agent dialog actions. We then study these ideas concretely in agentic recommender systems, proposing CoShop, an interactive benchmark. In CoShop, an agent converses with and makes recommendations for a CoPref user. The agent's performance depends on whether it can help the user gain the knowledge needed to specify the task well. Evaluating five frontier models, we find that no agent exceeds 56% accuracy on CoShop despite five turns of interaction. Failures stem not from agents' ability to find items, but from how little the interaction expands what users know about what they want.

AI.tldr: Agents often assume users have well-formed preferences, but real users lack domain knowledge to specify what they want. The authors introduce CoPref, a model of preference construction based on the Search-Experience-Credence framework, and CoShop, a benchmark for agentic recommenders. Frontier models achieve only 56% accuracy because they fail to help users learn what they want during interaction.
AI.motivation: Current agent design assumes expert users with fully formed preferences and defaults to clarification questions for underspecified tasks. This is unrealistic: users often lack domain knowledge to form preferences without agent assistance (e.g., examples, explanations). The paper aims to formalize and benchmark how agents can help users construct preferences rather than merely elicit them.
AI.method: The authors draw on the Search-Experience-Credence (SEC) framework from Information Economics to introduce CoPref, a formal model of how users construct preferences through agent dialog actions. They then instantiate this concretely in CoShop, an interactive benchmark where an agent must converse with and recommend items to a CoPref user whose preferences evolve based on the agent's dialog moves. Five frontier models are evaluated on CoShop across five turns of interaction.
AI.result: No frontier model exceeds 56% accuracy on CoShop despite being given five interaction turns. The primary failure mode is not the agents' inability to retrieve relevant items, but rather the interaction's failure to expand users' knowledge about their own preferences — agents do not effectively help users learn what they want.
AI.conclusion: The dominant paradigm of preference elicitation via clarification is insufficient; agents must instead engage in preference construction — actively helping users acquire domain knowledge during interaction. CoPref and CoShop provide formal and empirical foundations for studying this shift, and current frontier models remain far from solving this challenge.

title: ReactionAtlas: Ab origine exploration of chemical reaction networks with machine learning
summary: Mapping a chemical reaction network, the graph of minima and transition states (TS) and the elementary reactions connecting them, is the natural language of chemistry, from catalysis to combustion to the origin of life. Constructing such a reaction network for a given chemistry has been impractical: it requires finding and characterizing tens of thousands of TS, a task for which traditional methods such as density functional theory (DFT) are typically prohibitively slow and require reactant and product as input. We introduce ReactionAtlas, which builds a reaction network $\textit{ab origine}$ from a handful of seed molecules and without hand-crafted rules. Specifically, our machine-learned generative model proposes reactions from kinetically sampled candidate compounds and a DFT-trained machine learned force field (MLFF) filters them to valid TS, the resulting products of which enter the search as new seeds. Starting from eight pre-biotic seeds (CH$_2$O, H$_2$O, OH$^-$, H$_3$O$^+$, CO$_2$, H$_2$CO$_3$, HCO$_3^-$, H), ReactionAtlas discovers $\sim$47,000 reactions among $\sim$12,000 compounds. The MLFF TSs match the PBE0 references within 0.5 Å RMSD in 85% of the cases and can be easily brought to the PBE0 level. Thus, ReactionAtlas maps small carbohydrate chemistry up to C$_4$H$_8$O$_4$ at unprecedented scale and accuracy, including charge and stereo information. It enables novel insights into many well-studied reaction paths, including the formose cycle, which we highlight for its centrality to the chemical origins of life. Notably, our framework also allows establishing alternative reaction pathways for formose chemistry.

AI.tldr: ReactionAtlas is a framework that autonomously builds chemical reaction networks from seed molecules using a generative ML model to propose reactions and an ML force field (trained on DFT data) to filter valid transition states, discovering ~47,000 reactions among ~12,000 compounds in prebiotic carbohydrate chemistry with near-DFT accuracy.
AI.motivation: Mapping complete chemical reaction networks requires finding tens of thousands of transition states, which is prohibitively slow with traditional DFT methods that also demand reactant/product pairs as input. A scalable, automated, and accurate approach is needed to explore reaction space without hand-crafted rules.
AI.method: ReactionAtlas combines a machine-learned generative model to propose reactions from kinetically sampled candidate compounds with a DFT-trained machine-learned force field (MLFF) to validate proposed transition states.
