Products from validated reactions become new seeds, enabling iterative, breadth-first network expansion. Starting from eight prebiotic seed molecules, the framework grows the network autonomously, later refining MLFF TS geometries to the PBE0 DFT level.
AI.result: Starting from eight prebiotic seeds, ReactionAtlas discovered ~47,000 reactions among ~12,000 compounds, mapping small carbohydrate chemistry up to C₄H₈O₄ with charge and stereo resolution. MLFF transition states matched PBE0 references within 0.5 Å RMSD in 85% of cases. The framework revealed novel insights into well-studied pathways including the formose cycle and identified alternative reaction pathways for formose chemistry.
AI.conclusion: ReactionAtlas demonstrates that autonomous, large-scale reaction network construction is now feasible without hand-crafted rules, achieving DFT-level accuracy at a fraction of the cost. This enables systematic exploration of complex chemistries relevant to prebiotic chemistry, catalysis, and combustion, with the formose reaction network serving as a key case study for understanding the chemical origins of life.

title: Ethics and Social Responsibility in AI-Assisted Interviewing: An LLM-in-the-Loop Study of AI-Generated Follow-Up Questions
comment: This work has been accepted to CHIWORK '26
summary: Semi-structured interviews rely on timely, context-sensitive follow-up questions, yet interviewers' cognitive load and limited domain familiarity can constrain probing depth. We report findings from an LLM-in-the-loop Wizard-of-Oz (WoZ) study that simulates an AI follow-up assistant in live interviewing while preserving human oversight. In our setup, a co-interviewer selectively relayed and could edit AI-generated follow-up questions (AGQs) produced in real time by GPT-4o, enabling a realistic approximation of deployment without fully automating the interaction. Across 17 interviewers with varied qualitative-method expertise, participants raised five interlocking concerns: (1) harmful or discriminatory language and unpredictable interaction harms, (2) undermining interviewees' sense of respect through divided attention and missing nonverbal cues, (3) technology-based participation inequality, (4) unclear responsibility when harms occur, and (5) privacy, disclosure, and compliance risks when AI listens, records, or transcribes sensitive content. We translate these concerns into design and governance implications for safer, more respectful, and more accountable AI-assisted interviewing.

AI.tldr: A Wizard-of-Oz study with 17 interviewers tested GPT-4o as a real-time follow-up question generator in semi-structured interviews. Participants identified five concern clusters: harmful language, diminished respect from divided attention, participation inequality, unclear responsibility, and privacy risks. The paper translates these into design and governance recommendations for AI-assisted interviewing.
AI.motivation: Semi-structured interviews demand timely, context-sensitive follow-up questions, but interviewers face high cognitive load and often lack deep domain familiarity, which limits probing depth. The authors seek to explore whether an AI follow-up assistant can alleviate this burden while surfacing the risks and concerns that arise when such a system is introduced into live interviewing contexts.
AI.method: An LLM-in-the-loop Wizard-of-Oz (WoZ) study where a co-interviewer selectively relayed and could edit AI-generated follow-up questions (AGQs) produced in real time by GPT-4o. This preserved human oversight while realistically approximating a deployed AI assistant. Seventeen interviewers with varied qualitative-method expertise participated.
AI.result: Participants raised five interlocking concerns: (1) harmful/discriminatory language and unpredictable interaction harms; (2) undermining interviewees' sense of respect via divided attention and missed nonverbal cues; (3) technology-based participation inequality; (4) unclear responsibility when harms occur; and (5) privacy, disclosure, and compliance risks when AI listens to or records sensitive content.
AI.conclusion: The five concern clusters are translated into concrete design and governance implications aimed at making AI-assisted interviewing safer, more respectful, and more accountable, without advocating for full automation.

title: Certified Speculative Execution for Untrusted AI Agents
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures, 24 tables. Includes a technical appendix (full proofs and all supplementary tables)
summary: Hard-constrained sequential decision systems have no certified way to spend the test-time compute of modern AI: executing the multi-step drafts of a learned policy or a frozen LLM forfeits the feasibility guarantee a trusted solver provides, while invoking the solver at every step forfeits the speed the AI offers. Certificate-Gated Prefix Acceptance (CGPA) closes this gap with a certified speculative-execution contract for untrusted AI agents: a trusted verifier rejects constraint-violating transitions exactly, a conformally calibrated value boundary gates the longest low-cost prefix within a per-segment regret budget, and the rest defers to the solver, so safety, regret, and speed decouple by construction. The contract drives every untrusted proposal source - adversarial drafters and six heterogeneous frozen LLMs (including a 12B model that violates constraints in 98% of direct rollouts) - to zero applied violations; a certificate-aware learned boundary, conformally calibrated, drives mean regret three orders of magnitude below unguarded acceptance, to within sampling noise of the stepwise oracle (95% CI spanning zero), and under calendar shift a learned proposal source overtakes it on 15 of 18 held-out days. On a deployment-scale unit-commitment instance it turns a frozen 8B LLM into a 2.96x per-episode wall-clock speedup at 2.1% regret, outpacing the domain heuristic (1.79x) and a safe receding-horizon baseline (1.07x): the more capable the untrusted source, the faster the certified system, at guarantees that never change.

AI.tldr: Certificate-Gated Prefix Acceptance (CGPA) is a certified speculative-execution framework that decouples safety, regret, and speed in hard-constrained sequential decision systems by allowing untrusted AI agents (including constraint-violating LLMs) to propose multi-step action prefixes that are gated by a trusted verifier and a conformally calibrated value boundary, deferring to a trusted solver only when necessary — delivering zero constraint violations and near-oracle regret while achieving up to 2.96× wall-clock speedup over solver-only execution.
AI.motivation: Modern AI systems (learned policies, frozen LLMs) offer speed but lack feasibility guarantees in hard-constrained sequential decision problems, while trusted solvers guarantee feasibility but are slow when invoked at every step. No existing approach certifiably combines the speed of untrusted AI with the safety of a solver.
AI.method: CGPA formulates a certified speculative-execution contract with three components: (1) a trusted verifier that rejects constraint-violating transitions with certainty; (2) a conformally calibrated value boundary that accepts the longest low-cost prefix within a per-segment regret budget, using conformal prediction to provide statistical guarantees; and (3) a fallback to the trusted solver for any rejected portion. The framework applies to arbitrary untrusted proposal sources — adversarial drafters, learned policies, and frozen LLMs — with the contract decoupling safety, regret, and speed by construction.
AI.result: Across adversarial drafters and six heterogeneous frozen LLMs (including a 12B model with 98% direct-rollout constraint violation rate), CGPA achieves zero applied violations. A certificate-aware learned boundary with conformal calibration drives mean regret three orders of magnitude below unguarded acceptance, within sampling noise of the stepwise oracle (95% CI spanning zero). Under calendar shift, a learned proposal source overtakes the oracle on 15 of 18 held-out days. On a deployment-scale unit-commitment instance, an 8B frozen LLM achieves 2.96× per-episode wall-clock speedup at 2.1% regret, outperforming the domain heuristic (1.79×) and a safe receding-horizon baseline (1.07×).
AI.conclusion: CGPA demonstrates that certified speculative execution can harness the speed of untrusted AI agents (including highly capable but unreliable LLMs) for hard-constrained sequential decision problems without sacrificing safety or incurring meaningful regret. The core insight is that more capable untrusted sources yield faster certified systems, while guarantees remain invariant.

title: FeatX: Editing Software by Editing Features for Repository-Level Code Evolution
comment: 4 pages, Accepted to the Tools and Datasets Track of ASE 2026
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for software evolution, yet most interaction paradigms remain code-centric and require manual context management and prompt iteration. We present FeatX, a feature-oriented tool for editing software by editing features. Given an existing repository, FeatX extracts a hierarchical epic-feature structure with explicit feature-to-code mappings, then invokes a three-stage Evolution Agent to translate feature edits into code patches. The workflow is exposed through four coordinated panels. Across a controlled user study and replay experiments on 38 real-world feature-editing commits, FeatX significantly reduces cognitive load and improves usability compared with vanilla ChatGPT. It also achieves a 42.6\% relative improvement in function-level modification localization F1 over strong LLM baselines, at substantially lower cost (\$0.07 in total). The tool and collected dataset are available at https://github.com/a496263365/FeatX/tree/demo, with a demonstration video at https://youtu.be/OZqKZ4Ii-yM.

AI.tldr: FeatX is a feature-oriented software evolution tool that extracts hierarchical epic-feature structures with code mappings and uses a three-stage Evolution Agent to translate feature edits into code patches, reducing cognitive load and improving localization F1 by 42.6% over LLM baselines at very low cost.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based software evolution tools are code-centric, requiring developers to manually manage context and iteratively refine prompts. There is a need for a higher-level, feature-oriented interaction paradigm that reduces cognitive burden and better aligns with how developers reason about software changes.
AI.method: FeatX operates in two phases: (1) Feature Extraction — parsing a repository to produce a hierarchical epic-feature structure with explicit feature-to-code mappings; (2) Three-stage Evolution Agent — translating feature-level edits into code patches. The interface consists of four coordinated panels for structured interaction.
AI.result: In a controlled user study and replay experiments on 38 real-world feature-editing commits, FeatX significantly reduced cognitive load and improved usability over vanilla ChatGPT. It achieved a 42.6% relative improvement in function-level modification localization F1 over strong LLM baselines, with total costs as low as $0.07.
AI.conclusion: A feature-oriented interaction paradigm with structured feature-to-code mappings and agent-driven code generation can substantially outperform code-centric LLM workflows in both usability and accuracy for software evolution tasks, while remaining cost-effective.

title: Building a Multimodal Dataset of Academic Paper for Keyword Extraction
summary: Up to this point, keyword extraction task typically relies solely on textual data. Neglecting visual details and audio features from image and audio modalities leads to deficiencies in information richness and overlooks potential correlations, thereby constraining the model's ability to learn representations of the data and the accuracy of model predictions. Furthermore, the currently available multimodal datasets for keyword extraction task are particularly scarce, further hindering the progress of research on multimodal keyword extraction task. Therefore, this study constructs a multimodal dataset of academic paper consisting of 1000 samples, with each sample containing paper text, images, audios and keywords. Based on unsupervised and supervised methods of keyword extraction, experiments are conducted using textual data from papers, as well as text extracted from images and audio. The aim is to investigate the differences in performance in keyword extraction task with respect to different modal information and the fusion of multimodal information. The experimental results indicate that text from different modalities exhibits distinct characteristics in the model. The concatenation of paper text, image text and audio text can effectively enhance the keyword extraction performance of academic papers.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the limitation of text-only keyword extraction by introducing a multimodal dataset (1000 academic paper samples with text, images, audio, and keywords) and demonstrates that fusing textual information from all three modalities improves keyword extraction performance compared to using any single modality alone.
AI.motivation: Current keyword extraction relies solely on textual data, ignoring visual and audio modalities. This neglect leads to information poverty, missed cross-modal correlations, and constrained representation learning, ultimately limiting prediction accuracy. Additionally, the scarcity of multimodal datasets for keyword extraction further impedes research progress in this direction.
AI.method: The authors construct a multimodal academic paper dataset comprising 1000 samples, each containing paper text, images, audio, and ground-truth keywords. Text is extracted from images (via OCR or captioning) and audio (via automatic speech recognition). Experiments are conducted using both unsupervised and supervised keyword extraction methods. Performance is compared across individual modalities (text-only, image-derived text, audio-derived text) and their fusion (concatenation of all three).
AI.result: Text from different modalities exhibits distinct characteristics when processed by keyword extraction models. Concatenating paper text, image text, and audio text effectively enhances keyword extraction performance for academic papers compared to any single modality.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal information fusion — specifically combining textual content from paper body text, images, and audio — provides complementary signals that improve keyword extraction accuracy. The study highlights the value of constructing multimodal datasets and encourages further research into modality fusion for information extraction tasks.

title: Multilingual Polarization Detection Using Transformer-Based Models with Class Weighting and Threshold Tuning
summary: This paper describes our submission to SemEval-2026 Task 9 on detecting multilingual, multicultural, and multievent online polarization. We address all three subtasks: binary polarization detection, polarization type classification, and manifestation identification for English and Swahili. Our approach leverages transformer-based models (RoBERTa-base for English, AfroXLMR-base for Swahili) with class-weighted loss functions to address severe label imbalance and per-label threshold tuning to optimize multi-label classification. On the test set, we achieve F1 macro scores of 0.7901 (English) and 0.7910 (Swahili) for Subtask 1, 0.4615 (English) and 0.4808 (Swahili) for Subtask 2 and 0.4791 (English) and 0.5830 (Swahili) for Subtask 3, which give competitive performance on the leaderboard, demonstrating the effectiveness of our methods for handling imbalanced multi-label polarization detection. Our error analysis reveals that models struggle with dehumanization detection and lack of empathy.

AI.tldr: A SemEval-2026 submission using RoBERTa and AfroXLMR with class-weighted loss and per-label threshold tuning for multilingual polarization detection across three subtasks, achieving competitive F1 scores on English and Swahili.
AI.motivation: Address the challenge of detecting multilingual, multicultural, and multi-event online polarization with severe label imbalance across binary detection, type classification, and manifestation identification subtasks.
AI.method: Transformer-based models: RoBERTa-base for English and AfroXLMR-base for Swahili. Class-weighted loss functions handle label imbalance; per-label threshold tuning optimizes multi-label classification performance.
AI.result: Subtaks 1 F1 macro: 0.7901 (EN), 0.7910 (SW). Subtask 2: 0.4615 (EN), 0.4808 (SW). Subtask 3: 0.4791 (EN), 0.5830 (SW). Competitive leaderboard performance. Error analysis shows difficulty with dehumanization and lack-of-empathy detection.
AI.conclusion: Class-weighted loss and threshold tuning effectively mitigate label imbalance in multilingual polarization detection. Dehumanization and lack of empathy remain challenging for current models.

title: Why Solve It Twice? Hierarchical Accumulation of Skills for Transfer-Efficient ML Engineering
comment: 19 pages. Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Deep Learning for Code (DL4C)
summary: ML engineering agents waste compute rediscovering known techniques because every competition is a cold start. We present HASTE, a hierarchical multi-agent system that organizes cross-competition knowledge into three scope tiers (global, domain, and competition-specific), each coupled to a matching agent level. An orchestrator coordinates domain specialists and promotes learning between tiers via LLM-driven abstraction. A controlled ablation provides evidence for scoped loading: holding a 159-skill inventory constant across 8 competitions, tiered loading achieves a 100% medal rate while flat loading reaches only 62.5%, the same medal rate as loading no skills, and consumes 2x the output tokens. On the full MLE-Bench Lite benchmark (22 Kaggle competitions), HASTE reaches a medal rate of 77.3% using Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 12h per competition. In a cold-start run, the system begins with no accumulated skills. In warm-start runs, it reloads skills learned from earlier competitions, using only global and domain-level skills for transfer across competitions. Warm starts use 52% fewer refinement iterations, and the fraction of proposed changes kept by the agent rises from 42% at low inventory to 85% once 50+ skills are available. These results suggest that better knowledge organization can partly substitute for model strength and compute budget in ML-engineering agents.

AI.tldr: HASTE introduces a hierarchical multi-agent system with three-tiered knowledge scoping (global, domain, competition-specific) that reuses skills across ML competitions. Tiered loading achieves 100% medal rate vs 62.5% for flat loading, and warm-start runs use 52% fewer refinement iterations, demonstrating that knowledge organization can substitute for model strength and compute.
AI.motivation: ML engineering agents in competition settings waste compute by rediscovering known techniques from scratch each time ("cold start"). The authors aim to solve the knowledge transfer problem across competitions by organizing learned skills into reusable tiers.
AI.method: HASTE uses a hierarchical multi-agent architecture with three scope tiers (global, domain, competition-specific), each matched to an agent level. An orchestrator coordinates domain specialists and uses LLM-driven abstraction to promote learning between tiers. Skills are stored in a 159-skill inventory and selectively loaded based on scope relevance. The system is evaluated on MLE-Bench Lite (22 Kaggle competitions) using Claude Sonnet 4.6, with both cold-start (no prior skills) and warm-start (reloaded skills) configurations.
AI.result: Tiered loading achieves 100% medal rate vs 62.5% for both flat loading and no-skill baselines, with flat loading consuming 2x the output tokens. On the full benchmark, HASTE reaches 77.3% medal rate. Warm starts use 52% fewer refinement iterations, and the fraction of proposed changes kept rises from 42% (low inventory) to 85% (50+ skills available).
AI.conclusion: Better knowledge organization through hierarchical scoping can partially substitute for model strength and compute budget in ML engineering agents. The tiered architecture enables effective cross-competition transfer learning, reducing both iteration count and wasted computation.

title: Investigating Multi-Agent Deliberation in Law
comment: This manuscript has been accepted for presentation at the AIDA2J Workshop during the 21st International Conference of AI & Law in Singapore, June 8 2026
summary: Artificial Intelligence is increasingly applied to the field of law, and has the potential to increase access to justice. One particular movement that is gaining traction is that of agentic AI, wherein AI agents, based on Large Language Models (LLMs) can take autonomous actions. In particular, multi-agent approaches in the legal domain remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we investigate multi-agent deliberation methods for legal reasoning tasks using LLMs. We explore multi-agent deliberation (MAD) and introduce two novel multi-agent frameworks inspired by courtroom procedures and legal argumentation. Our experiments on both legal and non-legal benchmarks reveal that multi-agent frameworks achieve comparable overall performance to baseline large language models, but produce significantly distinct answers. Notably, these approaches can successfully solve cases that the baseline fails to address, and vice versa. We conduct a qualitative evaluation and highlight scenarios where multi-agent frameworks outperform monolithic approaches. For example, multi-agent approaches appear better suited for answering questions that require critical thinking from multiple perspectives. Our work positions multi-agent systems as a promising direction for AI in the legal domain, while demonstrating the potential of law-inspired multi-agent approaches for deliberation.

AI.tldr: This paper explores multi-agent deliberation (MAD) methods for legal reasoning using LLMs, introducing two novel frameworks inspired by courtroom procedures and legal argumentation. Experiments show multi-agent systems achieve comparable performance to monolithic LLMs but produce distinct, sometimes complementary results, excelling in tasks requiring multi-perspective critical thinking.
AI.motivation: AI, particularly agentic AI using LLMs, is increasingly applied to law with potential to improve access to justice. However, multi-agent approaches in the legal domain remain largely unexplored. The authors aim to investigate whether multi-agent deliberation frameworks, inspired by legal procedures, can enhance legal reasoning compared to monolithic LLM approaches.
AI.method: The authors introduce two novel multi-agent deliberation frameworks inspired by courtroom procedures and legal argumentation. They implement these frameworks using LLMs and conduct experiments on both legal and non-legal benchmarks, comparing multi-agent system performance against baseline monolithic LLMs. A qualitative evaluation is also performed to identify scenarios where multi-agent approaches outperform single-agent ones.
AI.result: Multi-agent frameworks achieve comparable overall performance to baseline LLMs but produce significantly distinct answers. Critically, multi-agent systems can successfully solve cases where baseline models fail, and vice versa. Multi-agent approaches particularly excel at questions requiring critical thinking from multiple perspectives.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent systems represent a promising direction for AI in the legal domain. Law-inspired multi-agent deliberation frameworks offer unique advantages over monolithic approaches, particularly for tasks demanding multi-perspective reasoning, positioning them as a valuable complement to existing LLM-based legal AI systems.

title: Revocable Learned State via Process Sidecars
summary: Language models are often adapted in stages: a public skill phase, a private memory phase, and a later safety phase that learns to refuse outputs tied to the remembered entities. Revoking the memory after the safety phase is not the same problem as subtracting the memory update: the later safety optimizer has transported the memory direction. We introduce process sidecars, a two-coefficient edit family $\hatθ(λ,γ)=θ_{\mathrm{AMS}}-λΔ_{\mathrm{M}}-γ\hat{R}_{\mathrm{S}\leftarrow\mathrm{M}}$, with $\hat{R}_{\mathrm{S}\leftarrow\mathrm{M}}=\hat{J}_{\mathrm{S},\varepsilon}(Δ_{\mathrm{M}})-Δ_{\mathrm{M}}$, where $\hat{J}_{\mathrm{S},\varepsilon}$ is a centered secant through the realized future AdamW safety-training process. The implementation uses $\varepsilon=1$ at the natural memory-edit scale; it reuses $θ_{\mathrm{AMS}}$ as the positive endpoint and computes one additional safety trace at $θ_{\mathrm{A}}-Δ_{\mathrm{M}}$. We prove two things. First, the exact sidecar, using the true transported direction $R_{\mathrm{S}\leftarrow\mathrm{M}}$ rather than the secant estimate, at $(λ,γ)=(1,1)$ recovers the counterfactual safety-only oracle $θ_{\mathrm{AS}}$ up to second order; the proof treats AdamW as an augmented-state map over parameters, first moments, and second moments. Second, this process information is necessary: whenever future safety training bends the memory direction, every scalar task-arithmetic edit leaves first-order counterfactual error, while the process-sidecar edit is second-order accurate. Across three models, the validation-selected 2D edit improves held-out refusal closure over naive task arithmetic in all trials, and over the $γ=λ$ process-JVP subfamily, the diagonal slice of the cached 2D grid, in all paired trials.

AI.tldr: Process sidecars are a two-coefficient model editing method that accounts for how safety fine-tuning transports memory update directions through the AdamW optimizer, achieving second-order accurate counterfactual edits compared to first-order error in standard task arithmetic.
AI.motivation: When language models undergo sequential adaptation (public skill → private memory → safety), simply subtracting the memory update after safety training fails because the safety optimizer has "transported" the memory direction. The authors aim to recover the counterfactual safety-only model without retaining the private memory.
AI.method: Introduce process sidecars: a two-parameter edit family $\hat{\theta}(\lambda,\gamma) = \theta_{\text{AMS}} - \lambda\Delta_M - \gamma\hat{R}_{S\leftarrow M}$, where $\hat{R}_{S\leftarrow M}$ estimates the transported memory direction using a centered secant approximation through the AdamW safety-training trajectory. Implementation uses $\varepsilon=1$, reuses $\theta_{\text{AMS}}$ as the positive endpoint, and computes one additional safety trace at $\theta_A - \Delta_M$. The method is theoretically analyzed treating AdamW as an augmented-state map over parameters, first moments, and second moments.
AI.result: The exact sidecar at $(\lambda,\gamma)=(1,1)$ recovers the counterfactual safety-only oracle $\theta_{\text{AS}}$ up to second order. Standard task-arithmetic edits leave first-order counterfactual error whenever safety training bends the memory direction. Across three models, the validation-selected 2D edit improves held-out refusal closure over naive task arithmetic in all trials, and over the $\gamma=\lambda$ process-JVP subfamily in all paired trials.
AI.conclusion: Process information from the safety training trajectory is necessary for accurate memory revocation; the proposed process-sidecar method provides a computationally efficient, second-order accurate solution using only one additional safety trace.

title: Evaluating Interactivity: Toward Automated Assessment of AI-Generated Explorable Explanations
summary: While large language models now enable rapid generation of interactive learning materials, evaluating the interaction quality of these explorable explanations remains an open challenge. Existing benchmarks largely focus on code executability or visual fidelity, providing limited insight into dynamic interaction behaviors such as learner-controlled state transitions and context-sensitive system responses, which are factors that critically shape learners' conceptual understanding. We present EE-Eval, an automated evaluation framework that formalizes interactivity as a finite space of learner-controllable states and transitions, represented as a Finite State Machine (FSM). By extracting FSMs from AI-generated explorable explanations, EE-Eval externalizes implicit interaction logic into an explicit, machine-interpretable graph. Evaluation is performed by comparing each generated FSM to an ideal FSM that encodes pedagogical intent, using a combination of graph-based metrics and embedding-based comparison of states, actions, and feedback to measure their structural and semantic similarity. Across thousands of generated explorable explanations spanning 127 concepts and produced by 6 AI models, EE-Eval consistently differentiates interaction quality beyond surface-level criteria such as functional correctness or visual quality, and exhibits substantially stronger alignment with human judgments of interactivity and pedagogical effectiveness than existing baselines. By framing interactivity as testable behavioral models rather than an emergent byproduct of LLM generation, EE-Eval transforms evaluation into a reflective diagnostic tool, enabling pedagogically grounded and actionable human-AI collaboration in creating interactive educational content.

AI.tldr: EE-Eval evaluates the interaction quality of AI-generated explorable explanations by extracting finite state machines and comparing them against ideal pedagogical FSMs using graph-based and embedding-based metrics.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for AI-generated interactive learning materials focus on surface-level criteria (code executability, visual fidelity) and fail to capture dynamic interaction behaviors like learner-controlled state transitions and context-sensitive responses that critically affect conceptual understanding.
AI.method: EE-Eval formalizes interactivity as a Finite State Machine (FSM) representing learner-controllable states and transitions. It extracts FSMs from AI-generated explorable explanations, then compares each generated FSM to an ideal, pedagogically-intended FSM using graph-based structural metrics and embedding-based semantic similarity of states, actions, and feedback.
AI.result: Evaluated across thousands of generated explorable explanations covering 127 concepts from 6 AI models, EE-Eval consistently differentiated interaction quality beyond surface-level criteria and showed substantially stronger alignment with human judgments of interactivity and pedagogical effectiveness than existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: By framing interactivity as testable behavioral models (FSMs) rather than an emergent byproduct of LLM generation, EE-Eval transforms evaluation into a reflective diagnostic tool that enables pedagogically grounded human-AI collaboration in creating interactive educational content.

title: Secure-CHG: A Comprehensive Framework for Robust and Fair Federated Learning via Hybrid Defense and Contribution-Aware Trust
summary: Federated Learning (FL) is highly susceptible to stealthy backdoor attacks, which aim to force a model into predicting an attacker-chosen target class for inputs containing a specific trigger. However, existing statistical defenses primarily focus on the early stages of model convergence. In this paper, we identify a fundamental vulnerability termed ``Late-stage Failure.'' We demonstrate that as the global model converges, decaying gradient norms render malicious and benign updates morphologically indistinguishable. This vanishing statistical variance effectively blinds traditional defenses, enabling adaptive adversaries to remain dormant and subsequently hijack the training process. To overcome these constraints, we propose Secure-CHG, a hybrid framework that pivots the defense paradigm from superficial morphological detection toward intrinsic semantic contribution verification. Secure-CHG employs an adaptive defense pipeline: a cascaded statistical filter stabilizes optimization during the early oscillatory phase, while a novel CHG-Shapley mechanism takes over during late-stage convergence. By leveraging sample hardness (i.e., local training loss) to project updates into a composite Hardness-Gradient space, it effectively amplifies adversarial semantic traces, enabling the isolation of stealthy attackers even as gradient norms vanish. Furthermore, we derive a closed-form solution for CHG-Shapley, facilitating low-complexity, retraining-free node valuation and trust-modulated aggregation. Extensive evaluations on CIFAR-10, MedMNIST, and NEU-SDDB demonstrate that Secure-CHG effectively mitigates Late-stage Failure. Specifically, it significantly suppresses advanced backdoor attacks, reducing their attack success rate by 2.3$\times$ and 2.0$\times$ relative to the mainstream Krum and Trimmed Mean baselines, respectively.

AI.tldr: Federated learning suffers from "Late-stage Failure," where converging gradient norms make malicious and benign updates indistinguishable to statistical defenses. The proposed Secure-CHG framework switches from morphological detection to semantic contribution verification using a cascaded statistical filter for early stages and a CHG-Shapley mechanism for late-stage convergence, suppressing backdoor attacks by 2.0-2.3× over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing statistical defenses against backdoor attacks in federated learning focus on early-stage convergence, where gradient norms are large enough to distinguish malicious from benign updates. However, as the global model converges, decaying gradient norms cause malicious and benign updates to become morphologically indistinguishable — a vulnerability the authors term "Late-stage Failure." This blinds traditional defenses and allows adaptive adversaries to remain dormant before hijacking training.
AI.method: Secure-CHG is a hybrid defense framework with two phases: (1) a cascaded statistical filter that stabilizes optimization during the early oscillatory phase, and (2) a novel CHG-Shapley mechanism activated during late-stage convergence. The CHG-Shapley mechanism projects updates into a composite Hardness-Gradient space using sample hardness (local training loss), amplifying adversarial semantic traces. A closed-form solution enables low-complexity, retraining-free node valuation and trust-modulated aggregation.
AI.result: Evaluations on CIFAR-10, MedMNIST, and NEU-SDDB show Secure-CHG effectively mitigates Late-stage Failure. It reduces the attack success rate of advanced backdoor attacks by 2.3× compared to Krum and 2.0× compared to Trimmed Mean baselines.
AI.conclusion: The Late-stage Failure vulnerability fundamentally undermines statistical defenses in FL. Shifting from morphological detection to semantic contribution verification via CHG-Shapley provides robust protection against stealthy backdoor attacks throughout the entire training lifecycle.

title: A Multi-Dimensional, Per-Pass Empirical Study of the LLVM Optimization Pipeline
summary: Quantifying the marginal impact of individual optimization passes underpins phase ordering, pass selection, optimization design, and analysis of pass/hardware interactions. In LLVM -- the standard backend for C/C++, Rust, and ML stacks via MLIR -- interactions among optimization passes, measurement noise, and pipeline scale make this difficult. We present a systematic, empirical study of the LLVM -O3 optimization pipeline. We decompose the pipeline into cumulative per-pass prefixes. We then measure execution time, compile time, binary size, hardware counters, and RAPL energy across 84,750 measurements covering 113 cumulative prefixes of the -O3 pipeline evaluated on 30 PolyBench/C kernels under rigorous noise mitigation. On these compute-bound affine kernels, the pipeline is non-monotone (6.6-9.7% of transitions regress) and strongly back-loaded (the median non-regressing kernel needs 84.8% of the pipeline for 80% of its speedup). Most gains are driven by a small Pareto-dominant core of passes, while the final -O3 configuration is Pareto-dominated on (size, speedup) for 29 of 30 kernels. We further show that IR instruction count is an unreliable predictor of runtime, that runtime-targeted passes are de facto energy-targeted (30-60% savings), and that the search-free idealized-additive upper bound on losses due to phase interference is 46.35%. These findings enable more informed pass pruning, cost-model calibration, and autotuning.

AI.tldr: A systematic empirical study of the LLVM -O3 optimization pipeline reveals it is non-monotone, strongly back-loaded, and driven by a small core of Pareto-dominant passes. IR instruction count poorly predicts runtime, runtime-oriented passes also save energy, and phase-interference losses could reach 46.35%.
AI.motivation: Quantifying the marginal impact of individual optimization passes is essential for phase ordering, pass selection, optimization design, and understanding pass/hardware interactions. However, LLVM's complexity, interacting passes, measurement noise, and pipeline scale make such quantification difficult.
AI.method: The authors decompose the LLVM -O3 pipeline into 113 cumulative per-pass prefixes and conduct 84,750 measurements across 30 PolyBench/C kernels. They measure execution time, compile time, binary size, hardware counters, and RAPL energy under rigorous noise mitigation, analyzing monotonicity, back-loading, Pareto dominance, IR instruction count predictiveness, energy effects, and idealized phase-interference bounds.
AI.result: The pipeline is non-monotone (6.6–9.7% of transitions regress) and strongly back-loaded (median non-regressing kernel needs 84.8% of the pipeline for 80% of speedup). A small Pareto-dominant pass core drives most gains; the final -O3 configuration is Pareto-dominated on (size, speedup) for 29/30 kernels. IR instruction count unreliably predicts runtime. Runtime-targeted passes yield 30–60% energy savings. The idealized-additive upper bound on phase-interference losses is 46.35%.
AI.conclusion: These findings enable more informed pass pruning, cost-model calibration, and autotuning by exposing the non-monotonic, back-loaded nature of -O3, the limited predictive value of IR instruction counts, and the significant energy co-benefits of runtime-oriented passes.

title: RoPoLL: Robust Panel of LLM Judges
summary:
The LLM Jury, a Panel of LLM Evaluators (PoLL) reporting consensus scores, has become a practical alternative to single-judge LLM evaluation, yet its statistical behavior remains poorly understood. We formalize the LLM Jury under the Huber contamination model and show that PoLL incurs unbounded bias
  under any positive contamination, regardless of jury size, whenever a single judge fails in a biased, LLM-typical way (mode collapse, sycophancy, safety refusal). Framing jury consensus as classical robust mean estimation, we propose RoPoLL (Robust Panel of LLM-as-Judge), which preserves the PoLL
  panel but replaces the aggregation function with a robust mean estimator, instantiated with the geometric median (GM): tuning-free, with the optimal finite-sample breakdown point 1/2. A finite-sample error bound and a matching information-theoretic minimax lower bound agree on the parametric rate
  sigma*sqrt(d/N) and differ on the breakdown floor by a factor of sqrt(d), a statistical-computational gap that polynomial-time RoPoLL pays relative to the intractable Tukey halfspace median. Across 13 open-weight judges (4B-675B), three reward-model benchmarks, and four corruption regimes at rates up
  to 50%, RoPoLL dominates PoLL on every biased corruption type: by about 19% on cross-dimensional attacks at matched compute, and by orders of magnitude on heavy-tailed Byzantine adversaries. A 3-judge RoPoLL committee at 38B beats Mistral-Large-3 (675B) by 1.31x on HelpSteer-2 under 30% bimodal-random
  corruption, an 18x parameter advantage at better accuracy; a Noisy-GT control confirms the premium is paid against biased contamination, not benign imprecision.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes LLM jury evaluation under the Huber contamination model, showing that standard consensus aggregation (PoLL) suffers unbounded bias under any positive contamination. The authors propose RoPoLL, which replaces the aggregation function with a robust mean estimator (geometric median), achieving optimal breakdown point and dominating PoLL across diverse corruption regimes.
AI.motivation: LLM-as-Judge evaluation increasingly uses panels (PoLL) for consensus scoring, but the statistical robustness of such juries against biased or corrupted judges — e.g., mode collapse, sycophancy, safety refusal — is poorly understood. There is a need to characterize failure modes and design provably robust alternatives.
AI.method: The authors (1) formalize the LLM Jury under the Huber contamination model, proving PoLL incurs unbounded bias under any positive contamination when a single judge fails; (2) reframe jury consensus as robust mean estimation; (3) propose RoPoLL using the geometric median (GM) as a tuning-free aggregation function with optimal finite-sample breakdown point of 1/2; and (4) derive finite-sample error bounds and information-theoretic minimax lower bounds, identifying a sqrt(d) statistical-computational gap relative to the Tukey halfspace median.
AI.result: RoPoLL dominates PoLL on every biased corruption type across 13 open-weight judges (4B–675B), three reward-model benchmarks, and four corruption regimes up to 50%. It improves ~19% on cross-dimensional attacks at matched compute and by orders of magnitude on heavy-tailed Byzantine adversaries. A 3-judge RoPoLL at 38B beats Mistral-Large-3 (675B) by 1.31× on HelpSteer-2 under 30% bimodal corruption, representing an 18× parameter advantage at better accuracy. A Noisy-GT control confirms gains are specifically against biased contamination, not benign imprecision.
AI.conclusion: RoPoLL provides a principled, tuning-free robust aggregation framework for LLM juries, establishing that geometric median-based consensus yields strong theoretical guarantees and empirical dominance over standard PoLL under realistic LLM-specific corruption regimes, with practical efficiency using small committees.

title: Predictable GRPO: A Closed-Form Model of Training Dynamics
summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has become a standard tool for improving the reasoning ability of large language models, yet its training dynamics are still described empirically: reward trajectories are fit with low-parameter functional forms whose constants carry no mechanistic meaning, and hyperparameter choices remain a matter of trial and error.  We develop a first-principles reduced-order model of these dynamics. The reduction has three consequences. First, it subsumes the empirical single-exponential saturation law as its overdamped limit, recasting the fitted plateau, timescale, and size exponent as the fixed point, inverse stiffness, and curvature-scaling exponent of the underlying potential, and adding, through the retained inertial term, the slow-start phase the single exponential cannot represent. Second, it yields predictions tied to independently measurable quantities rather than fitted ones: group-size invariance of the deterministic trajectory with a $1/G$ stationary fluctuation, a sharp stability threshold in the refresh interval, and an overdamped-to-oscillatory transition. Third, it furnishes diagnostics that separate failure modes a reward curve alone conflates -- reward hacking, advantage degeneracy, policy concentration, and dynamical instability. Across three models and two group sizes, the closed-form trajectory fits training reward to $R^2 \geq 0.91$ and the predicted group-size invariance holds on both the reward curve and out-of-distribution transfer to eight math benchmarks. The stability and oscillatory predictions are exercised in a controlled exact-reduction setting where the mean-field assumption holds exactly: a softmax-bandit reduction reproduces the predicted overdamped-to-oscillatory transition and locates the refresh-interval stability threshold at the independently measured stiffness, with a deep-network demonstration left to future work.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a first-principles reduced-order model of GRPO training dynamics, replacing empirical curve-fitting with a mechanistic potential-based description that predicts group-size invariance, stability thresholds, and overdamped-to-oscillatory transitions, validated with R² ≥ 0.91 on real models and exact reproduction in a softmax-bandit setting.
AI.motivation: Existing understanding of GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) training dynamics is purely empirical — reward trajectories are fit with low-parameter functional forms whose constants carry no mechanistic meaning, and hyperparameter selection remains trial-and-error. A principled, predictive theory is lacking.
AI.method: The authors derive a reduced-order mean-field model of GRPO dynamics from first principles. The reduction yields a second-order dynamical system that recovers the empirical single-exponential saturation law as its overdamped limit, while also capturing inertial slow-start effects. From this model they analytically derive three predictions: (1) deterministic trajectory invariance under group size G, with 1/G stationary fluctuations; (2) a sharp refresh-interval stability threshold; and (3) an overdamped-to-oscillatory transition. Validation spans three models, two group sizes, and out-of-distribution transfer to eight math benchmarks, plus a controlled softmax-bandit exact-reduction experiment.
AI.result: The closed-form trajectory fits training reward with R² ≥ 0.91. Group-size invariance holds on both the reward curve and out-of-distribution transfer across eight math benchmarks. In the softmax-bandit reduction, the predicted overdamped-to-oscillatory transition is reproduced and the refresh-interval stability threshold is located at the independently measured stiffness.
AI.conclusion: The reduced-order model provides a mechanistic, predictive framework for GRPO dynamics, replacing trial-and-error hyperparameter tuning with diagnostics that separate distinct failure modes (reward hacking, advantage degeneracy, policy concentration, dynamical instability). The deep-network demonstration of the stability/oscillatory predictions is left to future work.

title: From Idea to Prototype in an Afternoon: Scaffolded, AI-Assisted Rapid VA Prototyping
summary: Testing a new visual-analytics idea usually takes months: one needs to find a realistic data set, clean it, and implement an interactive prototype. We describe a case where a workflow language and an AI assistant reduced this effort to one afternoon. The idea under test: relax the Pareto frontier with a tolerance and group the surviving options into recurring types -- ``constellations'' on a ``soft sky''. Using the Artifact--Transform Workflow Language (ATWL) as a scaffold, we obtained a consistent workflow in minutes and a running prototype in a few hours. We derive three lessons. The scaffold matters: without ATWL the assistant produced a naive workflow. The scaffold alone is not enough: the first implementation was only average, and expert knowledge injection was needed to reach state-of-the-art quality. Finally, the way the scaffold is used matters: controlled experiments show that a language definition and a library of examples support different aspects of the task, that providing both at once reduces quality because template following displaces creative content, and that scaffolds work best when introduced after an initial unconstrained design pass. We argue that the field needs a typology of human knowledge injection, in a form that is both human-editable and machine-accessible.

AI.tldr: A workflow language (ATWL) combined with an AI assistant reduced the time to test a new visual-analytics idea from months to an afternoon. The idea involves relaxing the Pareto frontier with a tolerance and grouping surviving options into recurring "constellations." The study finds that scaffolds (language + examples) matter, but expert knowledge injection is critical; providing both language and examples simultaneously reduces quality due to template-following displacing creativity. Scaffolds work best when introduced after an initial unconstrained design pass.
AI.motivation: Testing visual-analytics ideas is prohibitively time-consuming, requiring months for data set acquisition, cleaning, and prototype implementation. The authors seek to demonstrate that a structured workflow language combined with AI assistance can dramatically accelerate this pipeline, and to derive design lessons about how scaffolds should be used in human-AI collaboration.
AI.method: The authors use the Artifact–Transform Workflow Language (ATWL) as a scaffold alongside an AI assistant to implement a visual-analytics concept (soft Pareto frontier with constellation grouping). They conduct controlled experiments varying the presence of a language definition, a library of examples, both, or neither, and compare the effect of introducing scaffolds before versus after an initial unconstrained design pass.
AI.result: Without ATWL, the AI produced a naive workflow. With ATWL alone, the implementation was only average. Expert knowledge injection was needed for state-of-the-art quality. Providing both a language definition and example library simultaneously reduced quality because template-following displaced creative content. Scaffolds were most effective when introduced after an initial unconstrained design pass.
AI.conclusion: The field needs a typology of human knowledge injection that is both human-editable and machine-accessible. Scaffolds (language definitions, example libraries) are valuable but their timing and combination matter critically; they should be introduced after unconstrained exploration to avoid stifling creativity.

title: Probe Choice Changes Canary-Memorization Verdicts: Three Post-Hoc Disagreement Case Studies in a Text-Dominant LoRA-Tuned Autoregressive Testbed
comment: ICML 2026 FoGen Workshop camera-ready. 17 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables
summary: We audit a fixed prefix-window mean-NLL memorization probe (K=20) on a Qwen2.5-VL-7B canary testbed and report three post-hoc cases where it disagrees with full-span secret NLL or greedy exact-recall. C3 (false negative, window truncation): damage lands on hex tokens outside K=20; the probe stays flat while hit@1 drops. C4 (false positive, non-secret drift): the probe moves, but approximately 99% sits on non-secret preamble; the secret span and hit@1 are unchanged. C5 (ambiguous in-window drop): the probe falls on an undertrained baseline while full-span hex is positive and hit@1=0. Recommendation: report (i) full-span secret NLL, (ii) a span-localised decomposition, (iii) behavioural exact-recall at k>=4, and (iv) decoy probes before asserting secret-specificity. Evidence is on controlled canaries in one backbone; magnitudes are testbed-specific.

AI.tldr: Auditing a prefix-window memorization probe on Qwen2.5-VL-7B reveals three failure modes (false negatives, false positives, ambiguous drops) compared to full-span secret NLL and exact-recall, prompting recommendations for more rigorous memorization auditing.
AI.motivation: To assess the reliability of fixed prefix-window mean-NLL probes for detecting memorization in vision-language models, and to identify conditions under which such probes produce misleading signals relative to ground-truth metrics like full-span secret NLL and greedy exact-recall.
AI.method: A controlled canary testbed is constructed on Qwen2.5-VL-7B using a fixed prefix-window mean-NLL memorization probe with K=20. Post-hoc case analysis is performed on three disagreement scenarios (C3, C4, C5) comparing the probe's output against full-span secret NLL and hit@1 exact-recall metrics.
AI.result: Three failure cases identified: C3 (false negative) — damage tokens fall outside the K=20 window, probe stays flat while hit@1 drops; C4 (false positive) — probe movement largely driven by non-secret preamble (~99%), secret span and hit@1 unchanged; C5 (ambiguous in-window drop) — probe falls on an undertrained baseline while full-span hex NLL is positive and hit@1=0.
AI.conclusion: The authors recommend reporting (i) full-span secret NLL, (ii) span-localised decomposition, (iii) behavioural exact-recall at k≥4, and (iv) decoy probes before asserting secret-specificity. Findings are limited to controlled canaries on a single backbone.

title: Mutating the "Immutable": A Large-Scale Study of Git Tag Alterations
summary: Git tags are commonly viewed as immutable references in software development, marking releases and specific repository states that underpin build reproducibility and software supply-chain integrity. Despite their intended immutability, Git allows tags to be altered through deletion or modification via force-pushed updates. The prevalence of such alterations threatens reproducible builds and dependency integrity. We conduct the first large-scale empirical study of tag alterations in public code repositories, analyzing 328.4 M software repositories from Software Heritage and identifying 10.2 M tag alterations affecting 189 k unique repositories. A cross-analysis with Nixpkgs reveals that 32 packages reference tags altered in our dataset, with 7 exhibiting confirmed build errors, providing concrete evidence that tag alterations break reproducible package builds. Our findings challenge the widespread assumption that tags are immutable anchors for released software. We therefore recommend that build systems and package managers pin dependencies to cryptographic commit hashes, that development forges expose tagmutation audit logs, and that the community adopt systematic monitoring of tag alterations as a standard supply-chain security practice.

AI.tldr: First large-scale empirical study of Git tag alterations across 328.4M repositories, finding 10.2M alterations in 189k repos. Cross-analysis with Nixpkgs shows tag mutations directly cause reproducible build failures, challenging the assumption of tag immutability and recommending commit-hash pinning and audit logging.
AI.motivation: Git tags are widely assumed to be immutable references that anchor reproducible builds and supply-chain integrity. However, Git permits tag deletion and force-pushed modification. No prior large-scale empirical study has quantified the prevalence or downstream consequences of tag alterations, leaving a critical blind spot in software supply-chain security.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 328.4 million public software repositories from the Software Heritage archive to detect tag alterations (deletions and force-pushed modifications). They cross-referenced the identified altered tags against Nixpkgs, a reproducible build package ecosystem, to empirically assess whether altered tags cause concrete build failures.
AI.result: They identified 10.2 million tag alterations across 189,000 unique repositories. The Nixpkgs cross-analysis revealed 32 packages referencing altered tags, of which 7 exhibited confirmed build errors, providing direct evidence that tag mutations break reproducible builds.
AI.conclusion: Tag immutability is an unreliable assumption. The authors recommend that build systems and package managers pin dependencies to cryptographic commit hashes, that code forges expose tag-mutation audit logs, and that systematic monitoring of tag alterations be adopted as a standard supply-chain security practice.

title: Beyond Clean Text: Evaluating Encoder and Decoder Robustness for Bangla Event Detection in Noisy Text
summary: Event detection (ED) systems are typically evaluated on clean, curated text, leaving their robustness to real-world noise largely unexplored, particularly for low-resource languages such as Bangla. We introduce a generalized Bangla news event ontology and a benchmark comprising 9,979 annotated sentences across 40 event subtypes, spanning clean news text, real-world Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) transcripts, and orthographically corrupted text. We systematically evaluate fine-tuned encoder-only models (BanglaBERT and XLM-R) alongside instruction-tuned decoder-only large language models (Llama 3 and Gemma 3). Our results reveal a clear architectural trade-off: encoder models achieve higher performance on clean text but degrade substantially under noise, whereas decoder-only LLMs are markedly more robust, particularly when event triggers are corrupted. We further show that embedding annotation guidelines during instruction tuning establishes a higher performance baseline on noisy text but yields inconsistent reductions in performance degradation across noisy conditions. Finally, model scaling consistently improves the robustness of decoder-only LLMs, while combined training on clean and noisy data serves as an effective regularization strategy that disproportionately benefits encoder architectures, significantly narrowing the robustness gap.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Bangla news event ontology and noisy-text benchmark, showing encoder-only models excel on clean text but degrade under noise, while decoder-only LLMs are more robust—especially with instruction tuning, model scaling, and mixed-domain training.
AI.motivation: Event detection systems are predominantly evaluated on clean, curated text, with little understanding of their robustness under real-world noise conditions (e.g., ASR errors, orthographic corruption). This gap is especially acute for low-resource languages like Bangla, where no annotated noisy-text benchmark exists.
AI.method: The authors construct a generalized Bangla news event ontology with 40 event subtypes and a benchmark of 9,979 annotated sentences spanning three conditions: clean news text, ASR transcripts, and orthographically corrupted text. They systematically compare fine-tuned encoder-only models (BanglaBERT, XLM-R) against instruction-tuned decoder-only LLMs (Llama 3, Gemma 3), and evaluate the effects of embedding annotation guidelines during instruction tuning, model scaling, and combined clean+noisy training.
AI.result: Encoder-only models achieve higher absolute performance on clean text but suffer substantial degradation under noise. Decoder-only LLMs exhibit significantly greater robustness, particularly when event triggers are corrupted. Instruction tuning with annotation guidelines raises the baseline on noisy text but does not consistently reduce performance degradation across noise conditions. Model scaling consistently improves decoder-only LLM robustness, and combined clean+noisy training serves as an effective regularizer that disproportionately benefits encoder architectures, narrowing the robustness gap.
AI.conclusion: Architectural choice fundamentally determines noise robustness in Bangla event detection: decoder-only LLMs offer superior resilience to real-world corruption. Instruction tuning with task guidelines and mixed-domain training are practical strategies for improving robustness, with the latter being especially beneficial for encoder models. The benchmark and ontology provide a foundation for future work on low-resource, noise-robust event detection.

title: HyPOLE: Hyperproperty-Guided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning under Partial Observation
summary: Formal specification is a powerful tool to guide the learning process and provides significant advantages over reward shaping: (1) mathematical rigor; (2) expressiveness to specify objectives and constraints, and (3) the ability to define tactics to achieve objectives. However, these benefits remain largely unexplored in the context of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL). This paper introduces HyPOLE, a novel framework for MARL under partial observability, where learning is guided by the expressive power of the so-called hyperproperties and, in particular, the temporal logic HyperLTL. We integrate Centralized Training for Decentralized Execution (CTDE) techniques with HyPOLE to synthesize decentralized policies, and our evaluation on SMAC, MessySMAC, and WildFire benchmark demonstrates clear advantages over baselines.

AI.tldr: HyPOLE is a MARL framework that uses HyperLTL temporal logic specifications (hyperproperties) to guide learning under partial observability, integrated with CTDE for decentralized policy synthesis, showing superior performance on SMAC, MessySMAC, and WildFire benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Formal specification offers mathematical rigor, expressiveness for objectives/constraints, and tactic definitions — advantages over reward shaping — yet these benefits remain unexplored in MARL. The authors aim to bridge this gap, particularly for partially observable multi-agent settings.
AI.method: HyPOLE framework combines hyperproperty specifications (HyperLTL temporal logic) with Centralized Training for Decentralized Execution (CTDE) to synthesize decentralized policies. HyperLTL enables expressing relational properties across multiple execution traces, guiding the MARL training process under partial observability.
AI.result: Evaluation on SMAC, MessySMAC, and WildFire benchmarks demonstrates clear advantages over baseline methods, validating the effectiveness of HyperLTL-guided learning in multi-agent partially observable environments.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging hyperproperties and HyperLTL within MARL is a promising direction, offering rigorous specification-driven learning that outperforms existing reward-shaping approaches in decentralized multi-agent settings.

title: Gradient Smoothing: Coupling Layer-wise Updates for Improved Optimization
comment: Published in the Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: Deep neural networks with repeated architectural blocks, such as transformers, often exhibit structured relationships across layers that emerge during training. Motivated by this observation, we introduce \emph{Depth-wise Gradient Augmentation}, a general optimization paradigm in which the update applied to each layer is obtained by transforming the collection of block-wise optimizer updates along the depth dimension. Within this framework, we study \emph{Gradient Smoothing}, a family of depth-wise smoothing methods, and instantiate it with a simple local \emph{Window Smoothing} operator. The resulting method operates directly on block-wise updates produced by arbitrary base optimizers (e.g., SGD, Adam, Muon), incurs minimal computational overhead, and is compatible with existing optimization pipelines. We evaluate Gradient Smoothing across a diverse set of architectures and training regimes, including language model pretraining, RL post-training of LLMs for reasoning, diffusion modeling, and image classification with Vision Transformers. Across these settings, Gradient Smoothing consistently improves optimization and generalization performance without modifying model architectures or training objectives. We further show that it promotes more structured representation evolution across depth, consistent with its interpretation as a structured depth-wise preconditioning method. Together, these results establish Depth-wise Gradient Augmentation as a promising framework for exploiting cross-depth structure in optimization and demonstrate Gradient Smoothing as a simple and broadly applicable instantiation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Depth-wise Gradient Augmentation, a framework that transforms optimizer updates across layers using depth-wise operations. Its practical instantiation, Gradient Smoothing via Window Smoothing, applies a local smoothing operator to block-wise gradients. This lightweight, optimizer-agnostic method consistently improves performance across diverse tasks—language model pretraining, LLM RL post-training, diffusion models, and ViT classification—by promoting structured representation evolution across depth.
AI.motivation: Deep networks with repeated blocks (e.g., Transformers) exhibit structured cross-layer relationships that emerge during training, yet standard optimizers treat each layer independently. The authors aim to exploit this latent depth-wise structure to improve optimization without altering architectures or objectives.
AI.method: The authors propose Depth-wise Gradient Augmentation, where per-layer updates are transformed along the depth dimension. They instantiate this with Gradient Smoothing using a local Window Smoothing operator that smooths block-wise optimizer updates (from SGD, Adam, Muon, etc.) across neighboring layers. The method is compatible with existing pipelines and adds minimal overhead.
AI.result: Gradient Smoothing consistently improves optimization and generalization across language model pretraining, RL-based LLM post-training for reasoning, diffusion modeling, and ViT image classification, without modifying architectures or training objectives.
AI.conclusion: Depth-wise Gradient Augmentation is a promising framework for exploiting cross-depth structure in optimization. Gradient Smoothing serves as a simple, broadly applicable instantiation that promotes structured representation evolution and effectively serves as a depth-wise preconditioner.

title: Investigating LLM-Powered Dissenting Minority Support in Power-Imbalanced Group Decision-Making: Counterargument and Mediation as Intervention Strategies
summary: Minority viewpoints are often suppressed in power-imbalanced group decision-making due to social pressure to comply with the majority. To address this problem, we developed an LLM-powered dissenting minority support system that aimed to foster attention to minority views through either AI-generated counterarguments or AI-mediated messages. We conducted a mixed-method experiment with 96 participants in 24 groups, comparing minority members' experiences across baseline, AI-counterargument, and AI-mediated message conditions. Our findings revealed a nuanced trade-off: AI-generated counterarguments fostered a more flexible atmosphere and enhanced satisfaction, while AI-mediated messaging increased minority participation but unexpectedly reduced their psychological safety. This research contributes empirical evidence on how different AI implementations affect group dynamics, identifies a critical support paradox between participation and psychological safety, provides design implications for future systems, and highlights ethical challenges in implementing AI-mediated communication in hierarchical settings. These insights advance understanding of designing more equitable AI support for power-imbalanced group decision-making.

AI.tldr: An LLM-powered system was developed to support minority viewpoints in group decisions, tested across 96 participants. AI-generated counterarguments improved atmosphere and satisfaction, while AI-mediated messages boosted participation but reduced psychological safety—revealing a "support paradox" with key design and ethical implications.
AI.motivation: In power-imbalanced group decision-making, minority viewpoints are frequently suppressed due to conformity pressure toward majority opinions. Existing approaches lack empirical understanding of how AI-based interventions could mitigate this suppression, motivating the need to design and evaluate systems that foster equitable attention to dissenting views.
AI.method: A mixed-method experiment was conducted with 96 participants organized into 24 groups across three conditions: (1) a baseline with no AI support, (2) an AI-counterargument condition where the LLM generated dissenting arguments, and (3) an AI-mediated message condition where the LLM rephrased or channeled minority contributions. Both quantitative and qualitative measures captured minority members' experiences, group dynamics, participation, satisfaction, and psychological safety.
AI.result: A nuanced trade-off emerged: AI-generated counterarguments fostered a more flexible group atmosphere and enhanced overall satisfaction, whereas AI-mediated messaging increased minority participation but paradoxically decreased their sense of psychological safety. These divergent outcomes constitute a "support paradox" between encouraging participation and preserving psychological safety.
AI.conclusion: The study contributes empirical evidence on how distinct AI implementation strategies differentially shape group dynamics in hierarchical settings. It surfaces a critical design tension—the support paradox—between participation and psychological safety, offers design implications for future systems, and highlights ethical challenges in AI-mediated communication within power-imbalanced contexts, advancing the goal of more equitable AI-assisted group decision-making.

title: Securing the AI Agent: A Unified Framework for Multi-Layer Agent Red Teaming
summary: The fast growth of open-source AI infrastructure, from model serving engines and agent platforms to the Model Context Protocol (MCP) ecosystem and the language models themselves, has outpaced the security tooling available to defend it. We present AI-Infra-Guard, an open-source framework that organizes AI red teaming around a single observation: the attack surface of an AI agent is stratified across layers (infrastructure, protocol/tool, agent behavior, and model), and no single detection paradigm fits all of them. The framework therefore matches a paradigm to each layer, from deterministic rule matching over 75+ AI components and 1{,}400+ vulnerability rules, through LLM-driven agentic auditing of MCP servers and agent-skill packages and multi-turn black-box agent red teaming, to a jailbreak harness with 26+ attack operators over sixteen datasets. To our knowledge it is the only open-source framework to span all of these, including supply-chain auditing of the agent skills that increasingly extend AI agents. We release AI-Infra-Guard as open source so that \emph{layer-paradigm matching} can serve as a practical foundation for agent security and a shared base for the community to build on.

AI.tldr: AI-Infra-Guard is an open-source AI red-teaming framework that matches distinct detection paradigms to each layer of the AI agent attack surface (infrastructure, protocol/tool, agent behavior, model), spanning deterministic rules, LLM-driven auditing, multi-turn red teaming, and jailbreak testing.
AI.motivation: The rapid growth of open-source AI infrastructure — including serving engines, agent platforms, the MCP ecosystem, and language models — has outstripped available security tooling. No single detection paradigm adequately covers all layers of the AI agent attack surface.
AI.method: Layer-paradigm matching: (1) deterministic rule matching across 75+ AI components and 1,400+ vulnerability rules for the infrastructure layer; (2) LLM-driven agentic auditing for MCP servers and agent-skill packages; (3) multi-turn black-box agent red teaming; (4) a jailbreak harness with 26+ attack operators evaluated over sixteen datasets. Includes supply-chain auditing of agent skills.
AI.result: AI-Infra-Guard is, to the authors' knowledge, the only open-source framework spanning all layers of the AI agent attack surface, including supply-chain auditing of agent-skill packages.
AI.conclusion: Layer-paradigm matching provides a practical foundation for agent security. The framework is released open-source to serve as a shared community base for AI security research and defense.

title: A Self-Negotiation Framework for Ethical Decision-Making during Task Interruptions in Service Robots
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
summary: Service robots operating in public environments frequently encounter interruptions when multiple users request service simultaneously. Resolving such conflicts requires ethical decision-making, as prioritizing one user request can disadvantage another. Current approaches rely on static rules or centralized arbitration and do not support autonomous, ethics-based conflict resolution. This paper addresses the question of how a single robot can arbitrate between multiple users during task interruptions and make ethically aligned decisions without relying on external coordination. We introduce a self-negotiation framework that represents each user by an ethical profile that captures their contextual ethical preferences and conditions, and resolves conflicts through an internal negotiation process. The framework is implemented in a modular ROS-based implementation and evaluated in simulation with a realistic interruption scenario. The results show that the system consistently produces user ethical preference-aligned outcomes, supports multilateral negotiation among users, and responds within 1.5 seconds, with near-linear runtime growth under increasing user input.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a self-negotiation framework enabling a single service robot to autonomously resolve multi-user interruptions through ethical preference-aligned decision-making, using internal negotiation among user ethical profiles, with sub-1.5s response times demonstrated in simulation.
AI.motivation: Service robots in public environments face interruptions from multiple simultaneous user requests and must make ethically sound arbitration decisions, yet existing solutions rely on static rules or centralized coordination and lack autonomous, ethics-based conflict resolution capabilities.
AI.method: The authors propose a self-negotiation framework where each user is represented by an ethical profile encoding their contextual preferences and conditions. Conflict resolution occurs through an internal multilateral negotiation process within the robot. The system is implemented as a modular ROS-based architecture and evaluated in simulation using a realistic interruption scenario.
AI.result: The framework consistently produces outcomes aligned with user ethical preferences, supports multilateral negotiation among multiple users, and responds within 1.5 seconds. Runtime growth scales near-linearly with increasing user input.
AI.conclusion: Self-negotiation based on individual ethical profiles is a viable approach for autonomous, ethics-aligned conflict resolution in service robots, offering scalable performance without external arbitration infrastructure.

title: Bridging Scientific Heritage: An Arabic--Russian Parallel Corpus and LLM Benchmark for Sustainable Knowledge Transfer
summary: Russian and Arabic are among the major languages of scientific communication. Language barriers impede the exchange of research results between these communities, which affects international collaboration and the progress of sustainability-related research. We present a benchmark for Arabic--Russian scientific translation. The benchmark includes a hybrid parallel corpus of about 27,000 sentence pairs, compiled from scientific abstracts and general-domain texts (religion, news, conversations). We fine-tune three multilingual language models -- mT5-base (580M parameters), NLLB-200-distilled-1.3B (1.3B), and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (7B) -- using LoRA with ranks 8, 16, 32, and 64. The Qwen2.5-7B model with QLoRA (rank 8) yields BLEU 23.15, chrF 43.89, BERTScore 0.906, and COMET 0.758. These are +4.36 BLEU and +0.051 COMET above the zero-shot baseline. Few-shot prompting with three examples does not improve performance, indicating that domain-specific fine-tuning is required. We release the models, the corpus, and the evaluation code. By lowering the language barrier for scientific texts, the work enables knowledge exchange between Arabic-speaking and Russian-speaking researchers. It contributes to sustainable partnerships (UN SDG 17) and innovation infrastructure (SDG 9), aligning with the conference's focus on technology-driven sustainable development.

AI.tldr: A benchmark and fine-tuned models for Arabic--Russian scientific translation are presented, with the best model (Qwen2.5-7B with QLoRA rank 8) achieving BLEU 23.15, outperforming zero-shot baselines by +4.36 BLEU. Few-shot prompting proved ineffective, confirming the necessity of domain-specific fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Russian and Arabic are major scientific languages, but language barriers hinder research exchange and international collaboration, particularly in sustainability-related fields. No dedicated Arabic--Russian scientific translation benchmark or models previously existed.
AI.method: A hybrid parallel corpus of ~27,000 sentence pairs was compiled from scientific abstracts and general-domain texts. Three multilingual models (mT5-base, NLLB-200-distilled-1.3B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) were fine-tuned using LoRA with ranks 8, 16, 32, and 64. Evaluation used BLEU, chrF, BERTScore, and COMET metrics, with zero-shot and few-shot baselines for comparison.
AI.result: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with QLoRA (rank 8) achieved the best results: BLEU 23.15, chrF 43.89, BERTScore 0.906, COMET 0.758 — gains of +4.36 BLEU and +0.051 COMET over zero-shot. Few-shot prompting with three examples yielded no improvement, underscoring the need for domain-specific fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific fine-tuning is essential for low-resource scientific translation pairs like Arabic--Russian. The released models, corpus, and code lower language barriers and support UN SDGs 9 and 17 by fostering sustainable international research partnerships.

title: MultiUAV-Plat: An LLM-Oriented Platform, Benchmark and Framework for Multi-UAV Collaborative Task Planning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) provide a promising interface for high-level robotic task planning, but their use in multi-UAV collaboration remains difficult to evaluate systematically. Existing UAV simulators mainly emphasize dynamics, perception, or low-level control, while existing LLM-agent benchmarks rarely capture aerial-robotics constraints such as partial observability, spatial coverage, UAV assignment, and multi-vehicle coordination. To bridge this gap, we present MultiUAV-Plat, a lightweight, easy-to-use, LLM-agent-oriented simulation platform for multi-UAV collaborative task planning. The platform exposes concise RESTful APIs, agent-facing observations, role-based information access, hidden validation logic, and optional 2D/3D visualization, allowing agents to solve missions through realistic tool interaction rather than privileged simulator access. Built on this platform, the MultiUAV-Plat Benchmark contains 75 mission sessions, 1500 natural-language tasks, and 9396 validation checks across target assignment, area search, and area assignment and patrol scenarios. We further propose Agent4Drone, a task-specific LLM agent framework that structures multi-UAV behavior into memory, observation, task understanding, planning, execution, and verification. In a full paired benchmark comparison, Agent4Drone achieves a 57.9% task pass rate, a 74.6% average task check pass rate, and a 72.0% global check pass rate, substantially outperforming a ReAct baseline at 30.6%, 47.9%, and 43.1%, respectively. Agent4Drone also reduces the total failed task rate from 32.4% to 12.9%. These results demonstrate that MultiUAV-Plat and MultiUAV-Plat Benchmark provide a reproducible foundation for studying LLM-driven multi-UAV autonomy under realistic information and execution constraints.
