AI.tldr: MultiUAV-Plat is a lightweight simulation platform and benchmark for evaluating LLM-based agents in multi-UAV collaborative task planning. It features realistic constraints like partial observability and role-based access. Agent4Drone, a structured LLM agent framework, significantly outperforms the ReAct baseline, achieving 57.9% task pass rate vs. 30.6%.
AI.motivation: Current UAV simulators focus on low-level control/dynamics, while LLM-agent benchmarks ignore aerial-robotics constraints (partial observability, spatial coverage, multi-vehicle coordination). There is no systematic way to evaluate LLMs for multi-UAV collaborative task planning, creating a critical evaluation gap.
AI.method: The authors built MultiUAV-Plat, a lightweight simulation platform exposing RESTful APIs with agent-facing observations, role-based information access, hidden validation logic, and optional 2D/3D visualization. On this platform, they created the MultiUAV-Plat Benchmark (75 sessions, 1500 tasks, 9396 checks) across target assignment, area search, and area assignment/patrol scenarios. They also proposed Agent4Drone, an LLM agent framework with six structured modules: memory, observation, task understanding, planning, execution, and verification.
AI.result: Agent4Drone achieved a 57.9% task pass rate, 74.6% average task check pass rate, and 72.0% global check pass rate, substantially outperforming the ReAct baseline (30.6%, 47.9%, 43.1%). The total failed task rate dropped from 32.4% (ReAct) to 12.9% (Agent4Drone).
AI.conclusion: MultiUAV-Plat and its benchmark provide a reproducible, standardized foundation for studying LLM-driven multi-UAV autonomy under realistic information and execution constraints. Agent4Drone's structured decomposition of multi-UAV behavior proves effective over simpler LLM-agent paradigms like ReAct.

title: AgRefactor: Self-Evolving Agentic Workflow for HLS Compatibility and Performance
summary: High-Level Synthesis (HLS) provides a fast path from concepts to silicon, but converting real-world software into synthesizable HLS code remains challenging due to restrictive language support and the gap between software and hardware programming practices. Existing automated and LLM-based refactoring approaches partially address this problem, yet they often lack flexibility, struggle to scale, and incur high computational costs. We introduce AgRefactor, an LLM-based multi-agent workflow for refactoring software into HLS-compatible programs. AgRefactor incorporates a self-evolving memory system that accumulates and retrieves factual and strategic knowledge across tasks, improving robustness and efficiency on unseen programs. To reduce cost and enhance scalability, it integrates automated refactoring tools, enabling agents to balance LLM-driven rewrites with efficient tool-based transformations. On 9 out of 11 challenging real-world benchmarks, which are 5-10x longer than the most complex cases studied in prior work, AgRefactor outperforms or matches the state-of-the-art automated refactoring tool and a strong LLM-based baseline built on the same framework backbone. Further agentic performance optimization yields a 6.51x geometric mean speedup over the SoTA pragma tuning tool and a 1.20x speedup over optimized open-source designs with less than 20% extra resources. AgRefactor is fully-automated and open-sourced.

AI.tldr: AgRefactor is an LLM-based multi-agent system with a self-evolving memory that refactors real-world software into HLS-compatible code, outperforming prior automated and LLM-based methods on 9/11 challenging benchmarks while achieving significant performance speedups with modest resource overhead.
AI.motivation: Converting real-world software into synthesizable HLS code is difficult due to restrictive language support and the gap between software and hardware programming practices. Existing automated and LLM-based refactoring approaches lack flexibility, struggle to scale, and incur high computational costs.
AI.method: AgRefactor uses an LLM-based multi-agent workflow with a self-evolving memory system that accumulates factual and strategic knowledge across tasks. It integrates automated refactoring tools alongside LLM-driven rewrites, enabling agents to balance flexible reasoning with efficient tool-based transformations for cost reduction and scalability.
AI.result: On 9 of 11 challenging real-world benchmarks (5-10x longer than prior work's most complex cases), AgRefactor outperforms or matches the SoTA automated refactoring tool and a strong LLM baseline. Agentic performance optimization yields a 6.51x geometric mean speedup over the SoTA pragma tuning tool and 1.20x speedup over optimized open-source designs with under 20% extra resource overhead.
AI.conclusion: AgRefactor demonstrates that a multi-agent LLM architecture augmented with persistent memory and integrated tool use can effectively automate complex software-to-HLS refactoring at scale, achieving superior performance with manageable resource costs. The system is fully automated and open-sourced.

title: Mind the Residual Gap: Probabilistic Downscaling under Real-World Bias
summary: Probabilistic downscaling is the task of modeling the conditional distribution of high-resolution fields given coarse inputs, and is a central challenge to atmospheric science, climate modeling, and other multiscale physical systems. A widely used paradigm decomposes the problem into a deterministic mean predictor followed by a stochastic residual generator. While effective in idealized settings, this mean--residual approach frequently produces biased and under-dispersive ensembles in real-world applications. Is this merely generic predictive uncertainty miscalibration? We show that the root cause is more fundamental: residual target misspecification, the residual distribution induced during training differs systematically from the one required at test time due to downscaling bias. To close this gap, we introduce ReMatch (Residual Distribution Matching). ReMatch aligns the training residual distribution toward the test-time regime via optimal transport in a low-dimensional PCA space. This preserves the statistical benefits of the mean--residual framework while reducing the train--test mismatch in the residual targets seen by the stochastic generator. On a controlled synthetic benchmark with varying bias levels and a real-world HRRR--ERA5 wind field downscaling task, ReMatch substantially reduces under-dispersion, improves calibration (SSR and CRPS), and outperforms strong baselines, including the standard mean--residual model and its variants, as well as state-of-the-art super-resolution models. Our code is available at https://github.com/sdean-group/ReMatch.git.

AI.tldr: ReMatch addresses the fundamental problem of residual target misspecification in probabilistic downscaling by aligning training residual distributions with test-time regimes via optimal transport in PCA space, reducing under-dispersion and improving calibration.
AI.motivation: The standard mean--residual paradigm for probabilistic downscaling suffers from biased, under-dispersive ensembles. The authors identify that this is not merely generic calibration error but a deeper issue: residual target misspecification — the residual distribution during training systematically differs from that needed at test time due to downscaling bias in the deterministic mean predictor.
AI.method: ReMatch (Residual Distribution Matching) aligns the training residual distribution toward the test-time regime using optimal transport in a low-dimensional PCA space. This corrects the train--test mismatch in residual targets while preserving the statistical advantages of the mean--residual decomposition framework.
AI.result: On a controlled synthetic benchmark with varying bias levels and a real-world HRRR--ERA5 wind field downscaling task, ReMatch substantially reduces under-dispersion, improves calibration metrics (SSR and CRPS), and outperforms strong baselines including standard mean--residual models and state-of-the-art super-resolution approaches.
AI.conclusion: Residual target misspecification is a fundamental flaw in the mean--residual downscaling paradigm, and ReMatch provides an effective, principled correction via optimal transport, yielding better-calibrated probabilistic forecasts in both synthetic and real-world atmospheric science settings.

title: The Decomposition Is the Fingerprint: Per-Component Identity for Agent Skills
summary: AI agents increasingly acquire and execute skills at runtime: bundles of prompt instructions, executable code, and tool declarations fetched from marketplaces and other agents. Governing them needs a stable notion of skill identity, yet cryptographic hashing is engineered to destroy the very similarity we need, as a one-character edit scrambles the digest. We present a compact, locality-sensitive fingerprint that embeds each component of a skill and projects it to bits with a multi-bank SimHash, giving a fixed 120-byte signature compared in constant time by Hamming distance. Our central claim is that keeping the fingerprint as a per-component triple (prompt, code, tools), rather than a single score, is what makes it useful: the triple recovers skill-family identity through paraphrase, renaming, refactoring, and controlled code translation when another component remains shared, while independent multilingual reimplementation is not recovered; it also localizes which component carries the reuse. We claim lineage, not behavioral equivalence: identity supplies the structural axis of a registry and leaves safety to behavioral verification. The fingerprint reaches an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.974 (95% CI [0.956, 0.994]) over 4,950 pairwise comparisons while using 77x fewer bits than the embedding it approximates, with ranking preserved in expectation and finite-bit concentration; the per-component split turns one number into relationship classification, families, novelty, and a portable "SkillBOM" for a skill registry. On a 906-skill injection benchmark the fingerprint recognizes injected skills as tampered copies of a known base and localizes the change, but recognition is not trust: it remains, by design, an identity signal complementary to behavioral verification rather than a safety verdict.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a locality-sensitive fingerprint for AI skills that uses per-component SimHash to create compact 120-byte signatures. Unlike cryptographic hashes, these fingerprints survive paraphrase, refactoring, and controlled translation, enabling skill identity tracking across marketplaces. Achieves AUC 0.974 while using 77× fewer bits than the embedding it approximates. The per-component triple structure localizes which part carries reuse and distinguishes genuine skill-family variants from independent reimplementations.
AI.motivation: AI skills (prompt instructions, code, tool declarations) are increasingly traded and reused at runtime across agents and marketplaces. Governing this ecosystem requires stable skill identity. However, cryptographic hashing is deliberately brittle: a single-character change produces an entirely different digest, making it useless for detecting near-duplicate or derived skills. A fingerprint that tolerates benign variation while still discriminating independent implementation is needed for registries, provenance tracking, and tamper detection.
AI.method: The method embeds each of three skill components (prompt, code, tools) separately using a multi-bank SimHash, projecting high-dimensional embeddings to fixed bit vectors. The three per-component fingerprints concatenate into a 120-byte signature. Similarity is measured by Hamming distance in constant time. The per-component triple (rather than a single fused score) enables: (1) recovery of skill-family identity through paraphrase, renaming, refactoring, and controlled code translation when another component is shared; (2) non-recovery of independent multilingual reimplementations; and (3) localization of which component carries the reuse. A SkillBOM (Skill Bill of Materials) format is proposed for registries.
AI.result: The fingerprint achieves AUC 0.974 (95% CI [0.956, 0.994]) over 4,950 pairwise comparisons, using 77× fewer bits than the embedding it approximates. Ranking is preserved in expectation with finite-bit concentration guarantees. On a 906-skill injection benchmark, the fingerprint correctly recognizes injected skills as tampered copies of a known base and localizes the changed component. The per-component split enables relationship classification, family grouping, and novelty detection.
AI.conclusion: The fingerprint provides a structural identity signal for AI skill registries, not a behavioral safety verdict. It is explicitly designed as complementary to behavioral verification: identity (lineage/provenance) supplies the organizational axis of a registry, while safety judgments remain the domain of behavioral testing. Recognition of tampered copies is not trust; the fingerprint signals "this is derived from X" but deliberately defers the trust decision to downstream verification.

title: MOA: A Profiling-Guided LLM Framework for Memory-Optimization Automation at Codebase Scale
summary: Modern large-scale software systems often suffer from pervasive memory inefficiencies (e.g., bloat, churn), leading to excessive resource costs and performance degradation. Existing optimization workflows lack end-to-end automation, forcing developers to manually synthesize complex tool outputs into actionable and semantics-preserving fixes, precluding scalability in large codebases. To address this, this paper presents MOA, an LLM-driven framework that automatically detects and repairs recurring memory inefficiencies across production-scale codebases. Specifically, MOA operates through three agents: an Analyzer that mines anti-patterns from profiling data, a Checker Generator that synthesizes static analyzers through template-guided refinement, and a Patcher that generates optimization patches via state-machine-driven workflows. Our evaluation on OpenHarmony, an open-source operating system with over 100 million lines of C/C++ code, shows that MOA identifies 13 anti-patterns (9 previously unknown) from 3 profiled services, detects over 10,000 inefficiencies across a broader set of 7 services, and generates 769 patches with 92.5% expert acceptance rate, achieving 42.2% heap reduction and 10.6% binary size reduction on average. We envision MOA as a valuable tool for performance engineering at production scale.

AI.tldr: MOA is an LLM-driven framework with three agents (Analyzer, Checker Generator, Patcher) that automatically detects and repairs memory inefficiencies in large-scale codebases, achieving 42.2% heap reduction and 92.5% expert acceptance rate on OpenHarmony's 100M+ LOC C/C++ codebase.
AI.motivation: Modern large-scale software systems suffer from pervasive memory inefficiencies (bloat, churn), but existing optimization workflows lack end-to-end automation, forcing developers to manually synthesize complex tool outputs into actionable, semantics-preserving fixes — a process that does not scale to large codebases.
AI.method: MOA employs a three-agent architecture: (1) an Analyzer agent that mines anti-patterns from profiling data, (2) a Checker Generator that synthesizes static analyzers via template-guided refinement, and (3) a Patcher that generates optimization patches using state-machine-driven workflows.
AI.result: Evaluated on OpenHarmony (100M+ lines of C/C++), MOA identified 13 anti-patterns (9 previously unknown) from 3 profiled services, detected over 10,000 inefficiencies across 7 services, and generated 769 patches with a 92.5% expert acceptance rate, yielding 42.2% heap reduction and 10.6% binary size reduction on average.
AI.conclusion: MOA demonstrates that LLM-driven, multi-agent automation is a viable and effective approach for performance engineering at production scale, enabling semantics-preserving detection and repair of memory inefficiencies across massive codebases.

title: Linguistic Distancing on Social Media: Indicators of Emotion Regulation Across Age Groups
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, Computational Affective Science Workshop
summary: Managing our emotional responses to events is key to emotional well-being, a process referred to as emotion regulation in psychology. Previous work has established that the degree to which we distance events is a type of emotion regulation. When we psychologically distance from events there can be markers in our language. These markers have been referred to as linguistic distancing. We build upon a previous metric to operationalize linguistic distancing, and explore how it changes across the lifespan. We explore this systematically by analyzing large amounts of social media text, a venue where people express their emotions. By investigating how distancing varies across age groups we can better understand how emotion regulation varies with age and provide initial benchmarks on social media data. We provide additional evidence further strengthening the hypothesis that linguistic distancing occurs in proportionally more instances with age. These findings align with past work in psychology which indicate improved well-being with older age. Better understanding how linguistic distancing changes with age is important because it functions as a marker of well-being and can inform effective health interventions. We provide a foundation for further exploring emotion regulation through linguistic distancing in text data.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how linguistic distancing—a language-based marker of emotion regulation—changes across the lifespan by analyzing large-scale social media text, finding that distancing increases proportionally with age, consistent with established psychological findings of improved emotional well-being in older adults.
AI.motivation: To systematically understand how emotion regulation, operationalized through linguistic distancing, varies across age groups using social media data, and to provide benchmarks that can inform health interventions.
AI.method: The authors build upon a previous metric for operationalizing linguistic distancing and apply it to large-scale social media text data, systematically analyzing how distancing markers vary across different age groups.
AI.result: Linguistic distancing occurs in proportionally more instances with increasing age, providing additional evidence that strengthens the hypothesis of age-related increases in this form of emotion regulation.
AI.conclusion: The findings align with prior psychological research indicating improved well-being with older age. Linguistic distancing serves as a well-being marker with potential to inform effective health interventions, and the work lays a foundation for further exploration of emotion regulation through text data.

title: TreeAgent: A Generalizable Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Bias Labeling in Forestry via Compiled Expert Rules and Vision-Language Models
summary: Human-labeled data are widely used as reference annotations in ML, despite known variability across annotators in many expert-driven domains. In addition, expert annotation is slow, inconsistent, and remains a major bottleneck for scaling tasks like tree height bias classification in forestry remote sensing. We propose a multi-agent system (MAS) that orchestrates expert decision trees with Vision-Language Models (VLMs), treating the decision tree as a structural prior while VLMs perform localized semantic perception at individual nodes, with multi-agent voting to mitigate VLM stochasticity. We formalize a Decoupled Declarative Decision (D3) Framework that enables zero-modification generalization across diverse expert-defined decision structures. On a tree bias classification testbed, our framework outperforms supervised ML baselines and reduces the amount of expert labeling effort required. These results suggest that agentic orchestration of VLMs with expert priors can reproduce expert-defined labeling procedures at substantially lower annotation cost while maintaining interpretability.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent system combining expert decision trees with Vision-Language Models (VLMs) is proposed to automate expert-level annotation. The Decoupled Declarative Decision (D3) Framework enables VLMs to perform localized semantic perception at decision tree nodes with multi-agent voting to reduce stochasticity, outperforming supervised baselines on tree height bias classification while drastically reducing expert labeling effort.
AI.motivation: Expert human annotation is slow, inconsistent, and a major bottleneck for scaling tasks in remote sensing (e.g., tree height bias classification). Variability across annotators and high labeling costs motivate automation that retains expert knowledge structure without requiring large volumes of labeled data.
AI.method: The authors propose a multi-agent system (MAS) that uses expert-defined decision trees as structural priors. VLMs are deployed at individual decision tree nodes to perform localized semantic perception, with multi-agent voting mitigating VLM stochasticity. They formalize this as the Decoupled Declarative Decision (D3) Framework, which supports zero-modification generalization across different expert-defined decision structures.
AI.result: On a tree bias classification testbed, the D3 framework outperforms supervised ML baselines and significantly reduces the amount of expert labeling effort required, while maintaining interpretability.
AI.conclusion: Agentic orchestration of VLMs with expert priors can reproduce expert-defined labeling procedures at substantially lower annotation cost while preserving interpretability, offering a scalable alternative to traditional expert annotation pipelines.

title: Neuro-Bayesian-Symbolic Residual Attention Shallow Network: Explainable Deep Learning for Cybersecurity Risk Assessment
comment: 19 pages, Submitted to IJCCC (Online ISSN 1841-9844, ISSN-L 1841-9836), June 25, 2026
summary: We introduce the Neuro-Bayesian-Symbolic Residual Attention Shallow Network (NBS-RASN), a hybrid neural architecture for explainable cybersecurity risk assessment in open-source ecosystems. Unlike deep models that trade interpretability for accuracy, our shallow network encodes domain knowledge, causal reasoning, and expert judgment as differentiable components. It uses 80 interpretable neurons across 12 layers, including a gatekeeper that enforces five epistemological axioms - precision, causality, falsifiability, transparency, and completeness - as hard constraints before propagation. Despite limited depth, the network exhibits deep-learning traits via residual attention and feedback loops, learning complex risk patterns without becoming a black box. It produces fully decomposable scores: a deterministic weighted component plus an expert adjustment, with each adjustment traceable to named amplifiers (blast radius, propagation speed, structural nature, default exposure, exploitation pattern, institutional criticality). We validate on 20 open-source projects covering all OWASP Top 10:2025 categories and language risk classes, achieving confidence scores of 0.79-0.97, and show that explainability is guaranteed by design, not by a training algorithm. This challenges the assumption that deep learning requires deep networks, proving that shallow networks with deep reasoning can outperform opaque models in high-stakes cybersecurity, where interpretability is essential.

AI.tldr: The NBS-RASN is a shallow hybrid neural architecture (80 neurons, 12 layers) that enforces five epistemological axioms as hard constraints via a gatekeeper mechanism, producing fully traceable cybersecurity risk scores with confidence of 0.79–0.97 across 20 open-source projects, demonstrating that shallow networks with deep reasoning can match or exceed deep models while maintaining guaranteed explainability.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning models for cybersecurity risk assessment trade interpretability for accuracy, producing opaque black-box decisions that are unacceptable in high-stakes security contexts where every risk score must be explainable, auditable, and traceable to specific causal factors.
AI.method: The authors propose NBS-RASN, a shallow network with 80 interpretable neurons across 12 layers, integrating three paradigms: (1) Neuro — differentiable neural components; (2) Bayesian — probabilistic reasoning; and (3) Symbolic — explicit domain knowledge encoding. A gatekeeper enforces five epistemological axioms (precision, causality, falsifiability, transparency, completeness) as hard constraints before propagation. Residual attention and feedback loops enable deep-learning-like pattern learning. The output is a decomposable score: a deterministic weighted component plus an expert adjustment traceable to six named amplifiers (blast radius, propagation speed, structural nature, default exposure, exploitation pattern, institutional criticality). Validation covers 20 open-source projects across all OWASP Top 10:2025 categories.
AI.result: The model achieves confidence scores ranging from 0.79 to 0.97 across the 20-project validation set spanning all OWASP Top 10:2025 categories. Explainability is guaranteed architecturally rather than post-hoc, with every risk score decomposable into its constituent amplifiers.
AI.conclusion: The work challenges the prevailing assumption that deep networks are necessary for deep reasoning, demonstrating that shallow architectures augmented with symbolic constraints, Bayesian reasoning, and residual attention can outperform opaque deep models in high-stakes domains where interpretability is non-negotiable.

title: Partition-Guided Distance Saliency: Bridging Decision and Objective Spaces in Many-Objective Optimization
comment: The 4th World Conference on eXplainable Artificial Intelligence 01-03 July, 2026 Fortaleza, Brazil Building transparent AI
summary: Explainability in Many-Objective Optimization (MaO) is currently hindered by the escalating complexity of the Pareto front, which renders the relationship between high-dimensional decision variables and objective outcomes increasingly opaque. As the number of objectives exceeds the limits of traditional visualization, decision-makers encounter a ``cognitive drought'' in identifying relevant trade-offs or specifying target regions without a priori knowledge. To bridge this interpretability gap, we introduce the {Partition-Guided Distance Saliency (PGDS)} framework, a novel XAI approach designed for continuous optimization landscapes. Our framework automates the explanation process through a three-stage pipeline that prioritizes geometric intuition over abstract rules. First, we employ a surrogate model that learns how geometric distances in the decision space map to proximity in the objective space. Second, to address the difficulty of manual target selection in high dimensions, the framework automatically partitions the objective landscape into distinct regions and identifies local ``Dominating Points'' to serve as automated targets for improvement. Third, we quantify how sensitive a solution's position is to each decision variable by measuring the distance shifts induced by perturbations to each variable. This allows PGDS to categorize features as either ``Drivers'' which facilitate convergence toward preferred regions, or ``Blockers'' which represent geometric constraints hindering further progress. Validation on 10-objective benchmarks and a physics-informed engineering problem (Welded Beam) demonstrates that PGDS provides differentiated, actionable insights that traditional visualization and rule-based XAI methods fail to provide.

AI.tldr: PGDS is an XAI framework for Many-Objective Optimization that automates explanation by learning distance mappings, partitioning the objective landscape into regions with Dominating Points, and classifying decision variables as Drivers or Blockers based on perturbation-induced distance shifts.
AI.motivation: In Many-Objective Optimization (MaO), the high-dimensional Pareto front creates a "cognitive drought" where decision-makers cannot interpret relationships between decision variables and objectives, nor specify meaningful target regions without prior knowledge. Traditional visualization fails beyond 2-3 objectives.
AI.method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) A surrogate model learns the mapping from geometric distances in decision space to proximity in objective space. (2) The objective landscape is automatically partitioned into distinct regions, each with a local "Dominating Point" serving as an automated improvement target. (3) Variable-wise perturbation analysis quantifies how distance shifts, categorizing each variable as a "Driver" (facilitates convergence toward preferred regions) or a "Blocker" (geometric constraint hindering progress).
AI.result: Validation on 10-objective benchmark problems and a Welded Beam physics-informed engineering problem showed that PGDS provides differentiated, actionable insights beyond what traditional visualization and rule-based XAI methods can offer.
AI.conclusion: PGDS successfully bridges the interpretability gap in MaO by replacing opaque high-dimensional trade-off analysis with a geometrically intuitive, automated explanation framework that yields actionable feature-level guidance for decision-makers.

title: What Counts as an Error? Dual-Reference Benchmarking for Atypical ASR
summary: ASR systems have been often reported to underperform on atypical speech. An often conflated compounding factor is the existence of two valid transcription references: verbatim (actual produced speech, including repetitions/prolongations) and intended (the canonical form of the text with disfluencies removed) in atypical speech recognition depending on context and use-case. Most ASR evaluations conflate this duality into a single ground truth and reward systems that delete disfluencies, ignoring verbatim faithfulness. We benchmark 11 ASR models from encoder-decoder, CTC and transducer families using both verbatim and intended references on atypical stuttered speech as a case study. Our quantitative assessment underlines the disparity in model performance and rankings using the two transcript styles. Through this analysis, we highlight the importance of selecting a suitable transcription reference for valid model selection depending on the use-case, particularly for atypical ASR.

AI.tldr: ASR systems are typically evaluated on atypical speech using a single ground truth that conflates verbatim and intended transcriptions, unfairly penalizing models that preserve disfluencies. The authors benchmark 11 ASR models on stuttered speech using both reference types, revealing significant performance disparities and ranking changes, underscoring the need to align transcription reference choice with the specific use-case.
AI.motivation: Atypical speech (e.g., stuttered speech) presents a dual-transcription problem: verbatim captures actual produced speech including disfluencies, while intended captures the canonical, cleaned form. Most ASR evaluations collapse these into a single ground truth, typically the intended form, thereby rewarding models that delete disfluencies and ignoring verbatim faithfulness. This conflation leads to misleading performance assessments and suboptimal model selection for use-cases requiring verbatim output.
AI.method: The authors benchmark 11 ASR models spanning encoder-decoder, CTC, and transducer architectures on atypical stuttered speech. They evaluate each model separately against both verbatim and intended transcription references, then quantitatively compare the resulting performance metrics (e.g., WER) and model rankings across the two reference styles.
AI.result: The evaluation reveals substantial disparities in both absolute performance scores and relative model rankings when using verbatim versus intended transcription references. Models that preserve disfluencies perform better under verbatim evaluation but are penalized under intended references, and vice versa.
AI.conclusion: Selecting the appropriate transcription reference is critical for valid ASR model evaluation and selection, particularly for atypical speech. The choice must align with the downstream use-case (e.g., verbatim for clinical documentation vs. intended for readability-focused applications). Conflating the two leads to misleading conclusions about model quality.

title: CSO-LLM: Class Subspace Orthogonalization for Post-Training Backdoor Detection and Trigger Inversion in LLMs
summary: While post-training backdoor detection and trigger inversion schemes have been developed for AIs used e.g. for images, there is a paucity of such methods for LLMs. First, the LLM input space is discrete, with up to 150,000^k k-tuples to consider with k the token-length of a putative trigger. Second, one must blacklist tokens typical of the putative target response (class) of an attack, as such tokens may give false detection signals. However, a comprehensive blacklist is not available, in general, for a given domain. We develop a highly effective detection and inversion framework for LLMs treated as classifiers. Central to our approach is class subspace orthogonalization (CSO), a novel plug-and-play paradigm for backdoor detection that serves two fundamental roles when applied to LLMs: i) it enhances both sensitivity and specificity of a baseline detector; ii) it provides a form of implicit blacklisting, as it penalizes against inclusion, in a candidate trigger, of tokens that induce signal perturbations "in the direction of" the putative target class of an attack. One version of our detector performs continuous optimization in token embedding space, while a companion trigger-inversion and detection method performs greedy accretion in discrete token space. Our methods give both strong detection performance and accurate inversion of ground-truth triggers on several LLM classification domains, and for several different LLM architectures.

AI.tldr: A novel backdoor detection and trigger inversion framework for LLMs as classifiers, using Class Subspace Orthogonalization (CSO) to enhance detection sensitivity/specificity and provide implicit blacklisting, with both continuous optimization and discrete greedy accretion methods.
AI.motivation: Existing backdoor detection/trigger inversion methods are well-studied for image models but scarce for LLMs due to two challenges: (1) the discrete and combinatorially vast input space (up to 150,000^k token sequences), and (2) the lack of comprehensive blacklists to exclude tokens that resemble target-class responses, which would otherwise produce false detection signals.
AI.method: The authors propose Class Subspace Orthogonalization (CSO), a plug-and-play paradigm that (i) improves baseline detector sensitivity and specificity, and (ii) implicitly blacklists tokens that induce perturbations aligned with the target class direction. Two algorithm variants are developed: one performing continuous optimization in token embedding space for detection, and another using greedy accretion in discrete token space for joint trigger inversion and detection.
AI.result: The methods achieve strong backdoor detection performance and accurate ground-truth trigger inversion across multiple LLM classification domains and several different LLM architectures.
AI.conclusion: CSO-based methods effectively address the unique challenges of LLM backdoor detection, offering both reliable detection and precise trigger recovery without requiring explicit blacklists, and generalize well across diverse LLM architectures and classification tasks.

title: Failure-Based Testing for Deep Reinforcement Learning Agents
summary:
Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) agents have been widely adopted across diverse domains to address challenging decision-making problems, such as autonomous driving and robotic control. Given that many of these applications are safety- and security-critical, rigorous testing of DRL agents is indispensable. Existing testing methods are typically guided by reward signals to detect failures. However, for well-trained agents, whose performance approaches optimal levels in standard operating conditions, reward signals remain generally high, making current methods ineffective at uncovering critical failures.
  To address these challenges, we propose a novel failure-based method that leverages task-induced failure insights to enhance failure detection capability while reducing the number of tests required. Since DRL agents are inherently designed with human-defined tasks, they provide valuable cues about task difficulty. Intuitively, a DRL agent is more likely to fail when confronted with a more difficult task; therefore, PRT prioritizes these tasks. Building on this foundation, we propose Prior Random Testing, a black-box failure-based testing method that enables targeted prioritization while preserving the diversity of generated test cases. Guided by task-induced failure insights, PRT prioritizes failure-prone regions of the input domain, thereby facilitating efficient failure detection.
  PRT is evaluated on four widely used benchmarks and compared with different state-of-the-art methods including fuzzing, search-based and generative-based methods. PRT ranks among the top performers in terms of both the cost of finding the first failure and the diversity of test cases. Notably, compared to random testing, PRT achieves better diversity and reduces the testing cost by over 50%.

AI.tldr: PRT (Prior Random Testing) is a black-box failure-based testing method for Deep Reinforcement Learning agents that prioritizes failure-prone input regions using task-induced difficulty cues, achieving over 50% reduction in testing cost compared to random testing while maintaining test case diversity.
AI.motivation: Existing DRL testing methods rely on reward signals to detect failures, but well-trained agents operating near-optimal levels produce consistently high rewards, rendering reward-guided methods ineffective at uncovering critical failures in safety- and security-critical applications like autonomous driving and robotic control.
AI.method: PRT leverages task-induced failure insights — the intuition that harder tasks lead to higher failure probability — to prioritize testing in failure-prone input regions. It is a black-box method that combines targeted prioritization with diversity preservation, using the agent's human-defined task structure as a cue for difficulty estimation without requiring access to internal model parameters.
AI.result: Evaluated on four benchmarks against fuzzing, search-based, and generative-based methods, PRT ranks among top performers in both cost of finding the first failure and test case diversity. It reduces testing cost by over 50% compared to random testing while achieving superior diversity.
AI.conclusion: Task-induced failure insights provide an effective, lightweight signal for prioritizing DRL testing efforts. PRT demonstrates that exploiting inherent task difficulty cues can substantially improve failure detection efficiency without sacrificing test diversity, offering a practical solution for testing well-trained DRL agents.

title: From Propositional to Perceptual Asymmetry: Extending Frictive Policy Optimization to Asymmetric Partial Information Dialogue
comment: 11 pages. To appear in Proceedings of SIGDIAL 2026
summary: Frictive Policy Optimization (FPO; Pustejovsky et al., 2025) treats friction in collaborative dialogue -- misalignment, misunderstanding, repair -- as an epistemic signal essential to common-ground construction, rather than noise to be minimized. However, FPO and its implementations assume shared perceptual contexts, where friction arises from differently interpreted propositions over the same scene, which we define as propositional asymmetry. We extend FPO to perceptual asymmetry, where participants hold asymmetric partial information and the same referring expression yields different denotations depending on whose information state grounds the reference. We evaluate this through cross-corpora analysis and LLM probing on referentially asymmetric dialogue tasks, primarily the HCRC MapTask (Anderson et al., 1991). We find that FPO's friction functional is empirically valid only when evaluated from within each participant's information horizon: different landmark configurations produce qualitatively distinct grounding failure modes, with a small class of ambiguous configurations driving a disproportionate share of misunderstandings through trajectories that appear successful but silently diverge. The LLM probe confirms that having the "right perspective" matters more than having all perspectives: the informed single viewpoint outperforms omniscient access to both participants' contexts. We propose two annotation refinements: subtype decomposition of pending grounding states and accommodation-aware alignment classification.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Frictive Policy Optimization (FPO) from propositional asymmetry to perceptual asymmetry, where interlocutors hold different partial information states. Through cross-corpora analysis of referentially asymmetric dialogue tasks (primarily HCRC MapTask) and LLM probing, the authors find that FPO's friction functional is only valid within each participant's information horizon. Key findings include: ambiguous landmark configurations disproportionately drive misunderstandings via silently divergent trajectories, and the informed single viewpoint outperforms omniscient access. They propose two annotation refinements: subtype decomposition of pending grounding states and accommodation-aware alignment classification.
AI.motivation: Existing FPO frameworks assume shared perceptual contexts where friction arises from propositional asymmetry (differently interpreted propositions over the same scene). Real-world collaborative dialogue, however, frequently involves perceptual asymmetry — participants hold asymmetric partial information, causing identical referring expressions to yield different denotations. The paper aims to test whether FPO's friction functional generalizes to these more ecologically valid settings.
AI.method: The authors conduct cross-corpora analysis on referentially asymmetric dialogue tasks (primarily the HCRC MapTask corpus) and employ LLM probing to evaluate FPO's friction functional under perceptual asymmetry. They analyze grounding failure modes across different landmark configurations and compare the "informed single viewpoint" condition against "omniscient access" to both participants' contexts.
AI.result: (1) FPO's friction functional is empirically valid only when evaluated from within each participant's information horizon. (2) Different landmark configurations produce qualitatively distinct grounding failure modes. (3) A small class of ambiguous configurations drives a disproportionate share of misunderstandings through trajectories that appear successful but silently diverge. (4) The LLM probe shows the informed single viewpoint outperforms omniscient access to both participants' contexts, demonstrating that having the "right perspective" matters more than having all perspectives.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that perceptual asymmetry poses a significant challenge to FPO and grounding theory more broadly. Two annotation refinements are proposed to improve modeling: subtype decomposition of pending grounding states and accommodation-aware alignment classification, which together better capture the nuanced failure modes arising from asymmetric information states in collaborative dialogue.

title: A Stationary-Distribution Theory for Triplet-Based Plateau Search in Random Forest Ensemble-Size Selection
summary:
The number of trees is a central computational parameter in Random Forests: increasing it reduces finite-ensemble variability but increases training and prediction cost. Plateau-based tuning adapts this parameter through local comparisons of out-of-bag scores at a geometric triplet of tree counts. After the remaining hyperparameters have stabilized, however, the central triplet point need not converge to a deterministic value; instead, it fluctuates around a stationary regime.
  This paper develops a stationary-distribution theory for this process. The central ensemble size $B_t$ is modeled as a birth-death Markov chain on a geometric grid, and its stationary distribution is derived through local balance. Under a leading centered folded-normal approximation, equilibrium equations are obtained for the original update rule and a symmetric modified variant, implying that the stationary center $B_*=O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$.
  The stationary spread is also characterized. A local Gaussian approximation and a Fokker-Planck interpretation give grid-level variance constants. After conversion to the ensemble-size scale, $σ_{B,*}=O(\varepsilon^{-2})$, while the variance is $O(\varepsilon^{-4})$. The leading relative spread is independent of $\varepsilon$ and controlled by the scale factor and update rule. These results interpret plateau-based Random Forest tuning as a stochastic process rather than a deterministic stopping rule.

AI.tldr: Plateau-based tuning of the number of trees in Random Forests is modeled as a birth-death Markov chain on a geometric grid. The stationary distribution is derived analytically, showing the central ensemble size and its variance both scale as O(ε⁻²) and O(ε⁻⁴) respectively, with the relative spread independent of the tolerance ε.
AI.motivation: The number of trees in Random Forests is a critical hyperparameter trading off ensemble variance against computational cost. Existing plateau-based tuning methods adaptively select this number, but after other hyperparameters stabilize, the tree count fluctuates rather than converging deterministically. Understanding this stationary behavior theoretically is essential for interpreting the tuning procedure as a stochastic process rather than a deterministic stopping rule.
AI.method: The authors model the central ensemble size B_t as a birth-death Markov chain on a geometric grid. Local balance conditions are used to derive the stationary distribution. A leading centered folded-normal approximation yields equilibrium equations for both the original update rule and a symmetrically modified variant. A local Gaussian approximation combined with a Fokker-Planck interpretation provides grid-level variance constants, which are then converted to the ensemble-size scale.
AI.result: Under the folded-normal approximation, the stationary center satisfies B_* = O(ε⁻²) as ε → 0. The stationary spread σ_{B,*} = O(ε⁻²) and the variance is O(ε⁻⁴). The leading relative spread is independent of ε and governed solely by the scale factor and update rule.
AI.conclusion: Plateau-based Random Forest tuning should be interpreted as a stochastic process whose ensemble size converges to a stationary distribution rather than a fixed deterministic value. The asymptotic scalings provide theoretical guarantees on the variability of the tuned tree count and offer guidance for practitioners on what to expect from the tuning procedure.

title: Automated High-Precision Extraction and Forensic Verification of Data-Bearing Vector Figures
summary: The quantitative record of science and engineering is increasingly carried by figures rather than text or tables, and a reader who needs the underlying numbers must usually re-digitize them by hand: slowly, imprecisely, and with no way to prove the result is faithful. Yet when a figure is stored as vector graphics, its data are not approximated by the picture but encoded in it: the renderer writes each marker and vertex at a printed precision that, for the dominant scientific toolchain, exceeds the data's own. We turn this into three contributions, one per shortcoming of hand digitization. First, a precision theory bounding how accurately data can be recovered for a given renderer and export format: bit-exact float32 for matplotlib markers, and a calibration-limited three to four significant figures end to end. Second, an automatic extractor that decodes a figure in one pass with no human in the loop, in place of the slow point-by-point tracing a digitizer demands. Third, a verification theory: recovery is injective except on a characterized, vanishingly small interval near zero; accidental agreement between unrelated data is astronomically unlikely; and a re-rendering certificate binds the recovered values to the markers, lines, and ticks the figure draws, not its text, making a result non-repudiable. With no ground truth used during recovery, decoded figures match external archives (Planck 2018 to 10^-9; the Keeling CO2 record to 5*10^-4, and one decoded figure independently reproduces a correction to the Chinchilla scaling-law confidence interval. We map the achievable precision across common renderers and their PDF, SVG, and EPS formats. What we deliver is certified data; the scientific significance of any particular dataset lies outside this paper's scope, and recovered values are candidates for human review, never accusations.

AI.tldr: A method to automatically extract precise, verifiable numerical data from vector-graphic scientific figures, with theoretical guarantees on precision, uniqueness, and non-repudiability.
AI.motivation: Scientific data is increasingly locked in figures rather than tables, forcing manual digitization that is slow, imprecise, and provides no fidelity proof. Vector graphics contain encoded data at high precision, but no existing method exploits this rigorously.
AI.method: Three theoretical-practical contributions: (1) a precision theory bounding recovery accuracy for matplotlib/renderer/format combinations; (2) a one-pass automatic extractor requiring no human intervention; (3) an injectivity verification theory with re-rendering certificates ensuring non-repudiability and near-zero chance of spurious agreement.
AI.result: Decoded figures match external archives with extreme fidelity: Planck 2018 to 10^-9 relative error, Keeling CO2 record to 5×10^-4. One decoded figure independently reproduced a published correction to the Chinchilla scaling-law confidence interval. Precision mapped across PDF, SVG, and EPS formats.
AI.conclusion: The system delivers certified, non-repudiable numerical data extracted automatically from vector figures. Scientific interpretation remains a human responsibility; recovered values are candidates for review, not accusations.

title: Maximizing Parallel Execution of Series-Parallel Task Graphs for Safety-Critical Embedded Control
summary: Safety-critical embedded control programs must complete each control cycle within a bounded period. Sequential execution on conventional processors can become a bottleneck when the dependency structure of the program contains subtasks that could be executed concurrently. This paper studies the Maximum Parallel Execution (MPE) problem for series-parallel task graphs under a staged batching model: compatible tasks inside one batch execute in parallel, while the selected batches are launched sequentially in a topological order that preserves precedence. We formulate MPE as a weighted clique-partitioning problem that minimizes the sum of batch execution times, with each batch cost determined by its slowest task. To solve this problem efficiently, we propose a Lagrangian-based Iterative Heuristic (LIH). LIH constructs a pricing-filtered restricted pool of feasible candidate batches from singleton columns and random greedy clique generation. It then applies Lagrangian pricing to guide column selection and uses a repair procedure to recover a legal clique partition. Experiments against a weighted mixed-graph-coloring branch-and-bound baseline and a randomized greedy baseline show that LIH matches the exact optimum in 91.25% of comparable instances, with an average gap of 0.073% and an average runtime of 18.19 ms. In the largest exact-reference node setting, the exact baseline requires hundreds of seconds on average, whereas LIH remains below 50 ms. We further present an end-to-end PLC ladder-logic case study in which PLCOpen-style programs are converted to MPE graphs, optimized by LIH, translated into FPGA-oriented HDL, and simulated against the original PLC scan execution.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the Maximum Parallel Execution (MPE) problem for embedded control programs with series-parallel task dependencies. It models MPE as a weighted clique-partitioning problem under a staged batching model and proposes a Lagrangian-based Iterative Heuristic (LIH) that achieves near-optimal solutions (91.25% exact match, 0.073% avg gap) in milliseconds, vastly outperforming exact branch-and-bound methods that require hundreds of seconds.
AI.motivation: Safety-critical embedded control systems (e.g., PLCs) must complete control cycles within strict deadlines. Sequential execution on conventional processors becomes a bottleneck when programs contain inherent concurrency. The authors aim to exploit this parallelism by transforming control programs into series-parallel task graphs and maximizing parallel execution under precedence constraints, thereby reducing cycle time and enabling deployment on faster hardware like FPGAs.
AI.method: The authors formulate MPE as a weighted clique-partitioning problem on a comparability graph derived from a series-parallel task DAG. Tasks are grouped into batches; batches execute sequentially in topological order, but tasks within a batch run in parallel (batch cost = max task time). They propose LIH: a heuristic that (1) builds a restricted pool of candidate cliques via singleton columns and random greedy generation, (2) applies Lagrangian pricing to guide clique selection, and (3) uses a repair procedure to produce a legal clique partition. They benchmark against an exact weighted mixed-graph-coloring branch-and-bound and a randomized greedy baseline. An end-to-end case study converts PLCOpen ladder-logic programs to MPE graphs, optimizes via LIH, and synthesizes FPGA HDL for simulation.
AI.result: LIH matches the exact optimum in 91.25% of comparable instances, with an average optimality gap of 0.073% and average runtime of 18.19 ms. In the largest exact-reference setting, the branch-and-bound baseline requires hundreds of seconds on average, while LIH stays under 50 ms. The FPGA-based case study demonstrates that LIH-optimized schedules significantly outperform traditional PLC scan execution.
AI.conclusion: The Lagrangian-based Iterative Heuristic (LIH) provides a highly effective and scalable solution to the MPE problem for series-parallel task graphs, combining near-optimal partitioning quality with millisecond-level runtime. It enables practical, automated transformation of PLC programs into parallel FPGA implementations, overcoming the sequential bottleneck of conventional embedded controllers.

title: Measuring Judgment Quality in Natural-Language Explanations: Evidence from Forecasting Tournaments
summary: Decision-makers routinely rely on expert judgments accompanied by written explanations, yet explanation quality is difficult to measure at scale. Forecasting tournaments offer a natural testing ground: probabilistic judgments are paired with natural-language rationales and scored against realized outcomes. We introduce Explanation Quality Markers (EQMs), a set of sixty theory-guided reasoning patterns scored by large language models (LLMs). In a pre-registered analysis of over 55,000 forecast-rationale pairs from a multiyear forecasting tournament, EQMs predict accuracy at both the forecast and forecaster levels, consistently outperforming pre-LLM text-analysis methods. More than 90% of statistically significant pattern-level EQM-accuracy correlations match our directional hypotheses. The signal is asymmetric: EQMs identify likely underperformers more reliably than they distinguish the very best forecasters. Benchmarked against traditional indicators of forecasting skill, EQMs are the strongest predictor at the forecast level and competitive at the forecaster level, though weaker than prior accuracy. Human ratings of rationale quality are less consistently correlated with accuracy and place disproportionate weight on rationale length. Results transfer to an independent forecasting study. EQMs provide a scalable, interpretable method for extracting judgment-relevant information from written explanations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Explanation Quality Markers (EQMs), a set of 60 theory-guided reasoning patterns scored by LLMs to evaluate written explanations accompanying probabilistic forecasts. Analyzing 55,000+ forecast-rationale pairs, EQMs consistently predict forecast accuracy, outperforming traditional text-analysis methods, and provide a scalable, interpretable tool for extracting judgment quality signals from explanations.
AI.motivation: Decision-makers frequently rely on expert judgments with written explanations, but measuring explanation quality at scale is notoriously difficult. Forecasting tournaments offer an ideal setting to study this, as probabilistic forecasts, natural-language rationales, and ground-truth outcomes are all available. The authors aim to develop and validate a scalable method for assessing whether explanations contain signals of judgment quality.
AI.method: The authors developed 60 Explanation Quality Markers (EQMs) — theory-guided reasoning patterns spanning dimensions like coherence, calibration, metacognition, and evidential reasoning. LLMs were used to score these markers on over 55,000 forecast-rationale pairs from a multiyear forecasting tournament. EQMs were then tested as predictors of forecast-level and forecaster-level accuracy, compared against pre-LLM text-analysis methods (e.g., LIWC) and human ratings, and validated on an independent forecasting study.
AI.result: EQMs significantly predicted forecast accuracy at both forecast and forecaster levels, consistently outperforming pre-LLM methods. Over 90% of significant EQM-accuracy correlations aligned with directional hypotheses. The signal was asymmetric: EQMs more reliably identified likely underperformers than top forecasters. Compared to traditional skill indicators, EQMs were the strongest predictor at the forecast level and competitive at the forecaster level (though weaker than past accuracy). Human ratings of rationale quality correlated less consistently with accuracy and over-weighted rationale length.
AI.conclusion: EQMs provide a scalable, interpretable method for extracting judgment-relevant information from written explanations. They offer practical value for decision-makers seeking to evaluate the quality of expert reasoning without relying solely on track records, and highlight the potential of LLMs to operationalize theory-driven text analysis at scale.

title: AgentBound: Verifiable Behavioral Governance for Autonomous AI Agents
summary:
Autonomous AI agents increasingly perform consequential actions on behalf of human principals, including financial transactions, external communications, and enterprise workflows. Existing agent infrastructure relies on identity federation and delegated authorization to authenticate workloads and control resource access, but it cannot determine whether an authorized action should be executed under the current behavioral and operational context.
  We present AgentBound, a runtime governance framework that provides verifiable behavioral oversight for autonomous AI agents. AgentBound evaluates each proposed action using three independent authorities: delegated authorization, owner-signed behavioral constitutions, and site action contracts. Their judgments are conservatively composed through a formal decision model to determine whether an action should be permitted, reviewed, or denied before execution.
  To provide accountability, AgentBound generates cryptographically verifiable governance receipts that bind every action to the exact delegation, policy, and semantic artifacts governing the decision, enabling independent replay verification and policy provenance. The framework also introduces standing delegation for long-running agents, allowing periodic workloads to operate under continuously refreshed governance policies while preserving revocability and bounded authority.
  We present the formal foundation, system architecture, governance receipt protocol, and AgentBound-Bench, a benchmark framework for evaluating governance correctness, authority composition, and accountability. Rather than replacing model alignment, AgentBound complements it by providing a deterministic governance layer between authorization and execution, transforming governance from a process that must be trusted into one that can be independently verified.

AI.tldr: AgentBound is a runtime governance framework for autonomous AI agents that evaluates each proposed action using three independent authorities (delegated authorization, behavioral constitutions, and site action contracts), composed through a formal decision model. It produces cryptographically verifiable governance receipts for accountability and introduces standing delegation for long-running agents. The framework complements model alignment by providing a deterministic, independently verifiable governance layer between authorization and execution.
AI.motivation: Existing agent infrastructure relies on identity federation and delegated authorization for access control but lacks the ability to determine whether an authorized action is contextually appropriate at runtime. As autonomous AI agents perform increasingly consequential actions (financial transactions, enterprise workflows), there is a need for verifiable behavioral oversight that goes beyond simple authorization checks.
AI.method: AgentBound employs a three-authority governance model: (1) delegated authorization for traditional access control, (2) owner-signed behavioral constitutions defining permissible agent conduct, and (3) site action contracts specifying action-level constraints. These judgments are conservatively composed via a formal decision model outputting permit/review/deny decisions. The framework generates cryptographically verifiable governance receipts binding each action to its governing artifacts, enabling replay verification. It also introduces standing delegation for periodically refreshed governance in long-running agents.
AI.result: The paper presents the formal foundation, system architecture, governance receipt protocol, and AgentBound-Bench — a benchmark framework for evaluating governance correctness, authority composition, and accountability.
AI.conclusion: AgentBound transforms governance from a trust-based process into one that can be independently verified, providing a deterministic governance layer between authorization and execution that complements rather than replaces model alignment.

title: A Transferable Learned Temporal Prior for Transmission Reconstruction and Decision-Relevant Uncertainty in Real Outbreak Labels
summary: Outbreak transmission reconstruction treats epidemiological timing and transmission labels as deterministic ground truth; neither has been systematically evaluated. We trained a logistic regression temporal prior on eleven disease families, locked all parameters before accessing any target outbreak data, and applied it without refitting to a strict Andes virus (ANDV) parent-ranking benchmark of 29 tasks. The locked prior achieved mean reciprocal rank (MRR) 0.571 versus 0.274 and Top-1 accuracy 37.9% versus 13.8% against the best source-trained parametric baseline (permutation p <= 0.0002; 7-8 reversals to lose MRR significance). A phylogenetic concordance audit of 75 NYC mpox inter-host pairs - independent label-reliability evidence rather than a prior validation - found that 54.67% (exact 95% CI: 42.75-66.21%) were genomically unresolved or unsupported. Retaining uncertain edges in ANDV and Guangdong Delta graphs shifted top-5 source-priority sets (Jaccard 0.429-0.667). Transmission-label uncertainty was measurable in the outbreak evidence modules examined, and retaining uncertain links changed which source cases were prioritized for intervention.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the common assumption that transmission labels in outbreak reconstruction are deterministic ground truth. Using a locked logistic regression temporal prior across 11 disease families, it significantly outperforms parametric baselines on an Andes virus benchmark. A phylogenetic audit of mpox data reveals over half of inter-host pairs are genomically unresolved. Retaining uncertain edges meaningfully changes source-priority sets, demonstrating that transmission-label uncertainty is measurable and consequential for intervention targeting.
AI.motivation: Outbreak transmission reconstruction typically treats epidemiological timing and transmission labels as deterministic ground truth, but this assumption has never been systematically evaluated. The authors aim to quantify transmission-label uncertainty and assess how it affects outbreak inference and intervention prioritization.
AI.method: A logistic regression temporal prior was trained on eleven disease families with all parameters locked before accessing any target outbreak data. This locked prior was applied without refitting to a strict Andes virus (ANDV) parent-ranking benchmark of 29 tasks. Mean reciprocal rank (MRR) and Top-1 accuracy were compared against the best source-trained parametric baseline, with permutation tests for significance. A phylogenetic concordance audit of 75 NYC mpox inter-host pairs provided independent label-reliability evidence. Uncertain edges were retained in ANDV and Guangdong Delta graphs to measure shifts in top-5 source-priority sets via Jaccard index.
AI.result: The locked prior achieved MRR 0.571 vs. 0.274 and Top-1 accuracy 37.9% vs. 13.8% against the best parametric baseline (permutation p ≤ 0.0002; 7–8 reversals needed to lose MRR significance). The mpox audit found 54.67% (95% CI: 42.75–66.21%) of inter-host pairs were genomically unresolved or unsupported. Retaining uncertain edges in ANDV and Guangdong Delta graphs shifted top-5 source-priority sets with Jaccard indices of 0.429–0.667.
AI.conclusion: Transmission-label uncertainty is measurable in outbreak evidence modules, and retaining uncertain links substantively changes which source cases are prioritized for intervention. This calls for systematic incorporation of uncertainty rather than treating transmission labels as ground truth in outbreak reconstruction.

title: Witness Complexity of Short Descriptions: A Cryptographic Perspective
summary: In cryptographic practice, where protocols impose strict time bounds, implementations demand predictable resource usage, and real-world systems require immediate verification for security and usability, a short key or certificate is useful only if it can be expanded or verified within a bounded time; otherwise a compact representation that requires superpolynomial work to expand offers no operational guarantee within a bounded-time protocol. This paper formalises that gap by introducing \emph{witness complexity} \(\gam(x)\), the minimum running time over near-shortest descriptions of a string on a universal Turing machine. \(\gam\) differs from Shannon entropy and Kolmogorov complexity \(\KC\): low \(\KC\) can coexist with high \(\gam\). We prove invariance up to polynomial factors; a conditional separation (assuming \(\PneqNP\)). An unconditional lower bound from incomputability of \(\KC\); a biconditional characterisation of \(\PeqNP\) via the class-relative variant \(\gP\); and polynomial-time tractability for structured \(\classNP\) families. Part II develops companion measures and shows an unconditional gap between grammar size and derivation cost, positioning \(\gam\) as a metric for the usability of keys and certificates.

AI.tldr: Introduces witness complexity (γ), a time-bounded analogue of Kolmogorov complexity measuring the minimum runtime on a universal Turing machine over near-shortest descriptions. Proves invariance, conditional separations from K, connections to P vs NP, and applies the concept to cryptographic key/certificate usability.
AI.motivation: In cryptographic practice, a short key or certificate is only useful if it can be expanded/verified within bounded time. Standard notions like Shannon entropy and Kolmogorov complexity fail to capture this operational requirement, motivating a complexity measure that jointly accounts for description length and expansion time.
AI.method: Formally defines witness complexity γ(x) as the minimum running time over near-shortest descriptions on a universal Turing machine. Proves polynomial-factor invariance. Establishes conditional separation from Kolmogorov complexity assuming P≠NP, an unconditional lower bound via K-incomputability, a biconditional characterization of P=NP via class-relative variant γ^P, and polynomial-time tractability for structured NP families. Part II develops companion measures and demonstrates an unconditional grammar-size vs. derivation-cost gap.
AI.result: Key results: (1) γ is invariant up to polynomial factors; (2) conditional separation: low K does not imply low γ unless P=NP; (3) unconditional lower bound from the incomputability of K; (4) P=NP is equivalent to γ^P being polynomial; (5) structured NP families admit polynomial-time γ computation; (6) unconditional gap between grammar size and derivation cost.
AI.conclusion: Witness complexity γ provides a principled metric for the usability of compact cryptographic objects (keys, certificates) in bounded-time protocols, capturing the gap between having a short description and being able to efficiently use it. The measure bridges Kolmogorov complexity, computational complexity, and practical cryptographic engineering.

title: Digital Innovation through Knowledge Processes
summary: The artefact at the intersection of knowledge and process management is the process, which describes how enterprises are generating value. In knowledge management literature the relation of knowledge and processes is discussed, often leading to the definition of knowledge intensive processes, which entail a high level of human involvement. The process management community on the other hand focuses on the formalization of processes as models that can be executed, monitored, and improved. In this paper we explore the relationship of process resources such as data, objects, artefacts and humans, in order to come to more universal definition of knowledge intensive processes. For this purpose, we analyze different patterns that frequently occur in knowledge management processes, how they are represented in process models, and which types of knowledge are represented by them. The results comprise a categorization of process models into 6 categories that allow to easily see the knowledge intensity as well as a collection of common knowledge process patterns. The patterns were derived from a real-world knowledge gathering process, which includes a wide array of patterns and concepts detailed in this paper. We think that a holistic view on knowledge intensive processes, how to model, execute, monitor, and asses their impact, will speed up and improve the quality of digital transformation projects.

AI.tldr: This paper explores the intersection of knowledge management and process management by analyzing how process resources (data, objects, artifacts, humans) relate to knowledge intensity. It derives 6 categories for classifying process models by knowledge intensity and identifies common knowledge process patterns from a real-world case, aiming to improve digital transformation projects.
AI.motivation: Existing literature treats knowledge-intensive processes from separate disciplinary perspectives: knowledge management emphasizes human involvement, while process management focuses on formal executable models. The authors seek a unified, holistic definition of knowledge-intensive processes that bridges both views and supports modeling, execution, monitoring, and impact assessment.
AI.method: The authors analyze the relationship among process resources (data, objects, artifacts, humans), examine recurring patterns in knowledge management processes and their representation in process models, and identify which knowledge types they embody. Patterns were derived from a real-world knowledge gathering process.
AI.result: A categorization of process models into 6 categories reflecting knowledge intensity, plus a collection of common knowledge process patterns derived from real-world data.
AI.conclusion: A holistic view on knowledge-intensive processes — covering modeling, execution, monitoring, and impact assessment — can accelerate and improve the quality of digital transformation projects.

title: Wait, am I Being Fair? Characterizing Deductive Stereotyping and Mitigating It with Fair-GCG
summary: Warning: This paper contains several toxic and offensive statements. While reasoning generally improves fairness in recent large language models (LLMs), failures persist. In this work, we identify a failure mode, deductive stereotyping, in which models apply population-level statistical regularities to individual cases, producing logically coherent yet socially biased inferences. We provide a statistical interpretation of this phenomenon. To steer models toward fairness-aware reasoning, we propose a reasoning-time injection framework. We further introduce Fair-GCG to systematically discover effective injection phrases. Injection phrases discovered by Fair-GCG improve performance across multiple fairness benchmarks, generalize from smaller to larger LLMs, improves reasoning-level fairness, reduces bias in open-ended generation, and transfer to real-world fairness-sensitive tasks.

AI.tldr: LLMs exhibit "deductive stereotyping" — logically coherent reasoning that applies population-level statistical regularities to individuals, producing socially biased inferences. The authors propose a reasoning-time injection framework and Fair-GCG, a method to discover effective fairness injection phrases, which improve fairness across benchmarks, generalize across model sizes, and transfer to real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: While reasoning generally improves LLM fairness, failures persist. The authors identify a specific failure mode — deductive stereotyping — where models make statistically grounded but socially biased inferences about individuals. Addressing this requires a method that steers reasoning toward fairness awareness without retraining or fine-tuning.
AI.method: The authors (1) formally characterize "deductive stereotyping" with a statistical interpretation; (2) propose a reasoning-time injection framework that inserts fairness-aware phrases into the model's reasoning process at inference time; and (3) introduce Fair-GCG, a systematic search method (building on Greedy Coordinate Gradient) to automatically discover effective injection phrases rather than relying on manual prompt engineering.
AI.result: Fair-GCG-discovered injection phrases improve performance across multiple fairness benchmarks, generalize from smaller to larger LLMs, enhance reasoning-level fairness, reduce bias in open-ended generation, and successfully transfer to real-world fairness-sensitive tasks.
AI.conclusion: Deductive stereotyping is a consequential failure mode in LLM reasoning that can be mitigated through inference-time interventions. The Fair-GCG framework provides an effective, generalizable, and transferable approach to steering models toward fairness-aware reasoning without modifying model weights.

title: When Regulation Has Memory: Hysteresis and Control Burden in Artificial Agency
summary:
Adaptive agents are usually judged by what they do, but an agent can appear stable while the internal effort required to keep it stable is increasing. This hidden regulatory burden matters for artificial agents operating under noise, delay, or changing demands: two systems may reach similar internal states while one requires much more corrective control to get there.
  Here, we study whether that burden depends on history. Using a computational model of adaptive uncertainty regulation, we drive an artificial agent through a continuous change in its uncertainty target and then reverse the change without resetting the agent. This creates a simple test for carryover: does the controller respond only to the current target, or does the path by which the agent reached that target still matter?
  The simulations show a clear history-dependent effect. The adaptive gain required to regulate the agent forms a reproducible hysteresis loop, meaning that the same target can require different levels of control depending on whether the agent is moving toward or returning from a more demanding regime. The timing of regulation also matters. When stabilization is available before disturbance exposure, the agent generally requires less adaptive gain than when it can only recover after disturbance has already acted.
  The state-level coherence measure also shows path dependence, but the timing effect is much clearer in regulatory gain. The main difference is therefore not that anticipatory regulation produces a completely different state. Rather, it reaches comparable regulated behavior with lower modeled control demand. These results suggest that adaptive agents should be evaluated not only by whether they remain organized, but by how much regulation they must recruit to do so.

AI.tldr: Adaptive agents exhibit history-dependent regulatory burden: the same target state can require different amounts of control depending on the path taken to reach it. Simulations reveal hysteresis in adaptive gain and show that anticipatory stabilization reduces control demand compared to post-disturbance recovery.
AI.motivation: Agents are typically judged by observable behavior/stability, but this neglects the hidden regulatory effort (control demand) required to maintain that stability. The authors investigate whether this regulatory burden depends on the agent's history — i.e., does the path matter, not just the current state?
AI.method: A computational model of adaptive uncertainty regulation is used. An artificial agent is driven through a continuous change in its uncertainty target, then the change is reversed without resetting the agent. This creates a test for carryover/hysteresis effects in the controller's adaptive gain, comparing anticipatory stabilization versus post-disturbance recovery conditions.
AI.result: A clear history-dependent effect emerges: adaptive gain forms a reproducible hysteresis loop — the same uncertainty target demands different levels of control depending on whether the agent is moving toward or returning from a demanding regime. Anticipatory stabilization (before disturbance) requires less adaptive gain than post-disturbance recovery. The state-level coherence measure also shows path dependence, but the timing effect is much clearer in regulatory gain.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive agents should be evaluated not only by whether they remain organized, but by how much regulation they must recruit to do so. The path to a state matters as much as the state itself when assessing control efficiency.

title: Behavior Cloning is Not All You Need: The Optimality of On-Policy Distillation for Noisy Expert Feedback
