summary: Imitation Learning is a natural framework for learning in sequential decision-making systems and has emerged as the dominant paradigm through which we understand language model training. A central puzzle is that, while in theory offline IL can be horizon-free and optimal, in practice online methods such as on-policy distillation often outperform offline methods such as supervised fine-tuning. We propose a noisy expert model to explain this gap, in which the learner only has access to a noisy version of the expert's policy, but wishes to compete against the reward achieved by a clean expert, motivated by the fact that in many applications, e.g. training language models to perform long chains of thought, the expert is often imperfect. In this setting, we show a sharp separation between offline and online IL. Offline learning from noisy trajectories is fundamentally hard: to compete with the clean expert, the sample complexity must grow exponentially, in contradistinction to the clean expert setting where no explicit horizon dependence exists. In contrast, we prove that online interaction with the noisy expert via a novel variant of OPD enables polynomial dependence on the horizon in general. We further show that, under a natural condition on the expert noise distribution, which we show to be necessary for any horizon-free sample complexity, one can obtain such a guarantee, although our proposed algorithm sacrifices statistical efficiency in its dependence on the size of the policy class. Our analysis leads to an alternative loss function that is commonly considered empirically for LM training. We further provide algorithms and lower bounds, and extend our results to the more realistic setting of unknown corruption when the clean expert is deterministic, thereby providing a theoretical foundation for why OPD can outperform SFT when training language models from imperfect teachers.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a theoretical gap between offline and online imitation learning when learning from noisy/imperfect experts, proving that offline IL requires exponential sample complexity while a novel online method (OPD variant) achieves polynomial horizon dependence, providing a theoretical foundation for why on-policy distillation outperforms supervised fine-tuning in language model training.
AI.motivation: In theory, offline imitation learning can be horizon-free and optimal, yet in practice, online methods like on-policy distillation (OPD) consistently outperform offline methods like supervised fine-tuning (SFT), especially when training language models on long chains of thought with imperfect teachers. The paper aims to explain this gap by modeling the expert as noisy/imperfect.
AI.method: The authors propose a noisy expert model where the learner only observes a noisy version of the expert's policy but must compete with the clean expert's reward. They analyze sample complexity lower bounds for offline IL (showing exponential horizon dependence) and propose a novel online OPD variant achieving polynomial dependence. They further extend results to unknown corruption with deterministic clean experts, and derive an alternative loss function aligned with empirical LM training practices.
AI.result: A sharp separation is established: offline IL from noisy trajectories requires sample complexity exponential in the horizon to compete with the clean expert, while online interaction via the novel OPD variant achieves polynomial dependence. Under a natural noise condition (shown necessary for any horizon-free guarantee), a horizon-free result is obtained, though with suboptimal dependence on policy class size. These results extend to unknown corruption settings.
AI.conclusion: The noisy expert model provides a rigorous theoretical justification for why online methods (OPD) empirically outperform offline methods (SFT) when learning from imperfect teachers, particularly relevant for training language models on complex reasoning tasks involving long chains of thought.

title: EnclaveX: End-to-End Confidential AI with CPU/GPU TEEs
summary:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly proliferated, driving widespread adoption of AI applications. Most deployments rely on centralized infrastructures such as Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, or AWS, requiring users to share sensitive data and training or fine-tuning code. This dependence raises significant security and privacy concerns, as cloud providers must be trusted to ensure confidentiality and integrity.
  Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) e.g., Intel SGX/TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, and ARM CCA have been introduced to mitigate these risks. More recently, NVIDIA has developed GPU TEEs (e.g., H100/H200), yet comprehensive evaluations of end-to-end workflows that integrate CPU and GPU TEEs remain limited. Critical aspects, including performance overhead, remote attestation, and security guarantees for AI/LLM applications, have not been sufficiently studied.
  This paper addresses this gap by presenting an end-to-end workflow that combines CPU and GPU TEEs. We propose mechanisms to ensure confidentiality and integrity at both the VM level (via Intel TDX and AMD SEV-SNP) and the application level, highlighting vulnerabilities such as Kubernetes administrators' ability to access confidential VM contents. Finally, we evaluate the performance overhead of our system using industry benchmarks, focusing on configurations that integrate Intel TDX with NVIDIA H200 GPUs.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an end-to-end workflow combining CPU and GPU TEEs (Intel TDX/AMD SEV-SNP with NVIDIA H200 GPUs) for LLM deployments, addressing confidentiality and integrity at both VM and application levels while identifying vulnerabilities like Kubernetes admin access to confidential VMs, and evaluating performance overhead.
AI.motivation: The widespread deployment of LLMs on centralized cloud infrastructures forces users to share sensitive data and code with cloud providers, creating significant security and privacy risks. While TEEs exist for both CPUs and GPUs, comprehensive evaluations of integrated CPU-GPU TEE workflows—covering performance overhead, remote attestation, and security guarantees for AI/LLM applications—are lacking.
AI.method: The authors design and implement an end-to-end system architecture that integrates CPU TEEs (Intel TDX and AMD SEV-SNP) with GPU TEEs (NVIDIA H100/H200). They propose mechanisms for confidentiality and integrity at both the VM level and application level, analyze attack surfaces including Kubernetes administrator access to confidential VMs, and benchmark performance overhead using industry-standard metrics.
AI.result: The paper identifies vulnerabilities where Kubernetes administrators can access confidential VM contents. Performance overhead is evaluated using industry benchmarks on configurations pairing Intel TDX with NVIDIA H200 GPUs, though specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The study fills a critical gap in understanding integrated CPU-GPU TEE deployments for LLM workloads, demonstrating that while such architectures can mitigate cloud-trust risks, practical vulnerabilities (e.g., orchestration-layer attacks) and performance trade-offs must be carefully managed.

title: Falsification, Not Exposure: An Internally Preregistered Placebo-Controlled Decomposition of Self-Repair Feedback in Frozen Small Code Models
summary: In deployment settings where retraining is infeasible, small frozen code models are routinely asked to repair a failed program after seeing their own failing output, usually treated as a retry mechanism. From a Popperian view, a generated program is a conjecture and a test-execution violation is an oracle-relative, executable counterexample, so feedback's value should be attributed not to re-exposure to failing code but to whether the conjecture is opened to external, executable criticism. As the third stage of a falsification-centered measurement program, this study builds a placebo-controlled instrument that decomposes the feedback packet against a blind-resampling baseline at matched output-generation budget and against content-free, shape-matched placebos. The contribution is not a new repair algorithm but a reflexive methodology (packet decomposition, placebo mirroring, matched-budget discordant-pair tests, fresh-generation confirmation, executable audits) that makes both the model's program conjecture and the researcher's "feedback content works" claim falsifiable. Across six HumanEval+/MBPP+ cells with three 0.5B-1.5B frozen models, 290 dead task-cell units (no best-of-8 candidate passing the public tier) were evaluated; the main run produced 7,000 fresh generations and a preregistered follow-up 1,400 more. Blind resampling exceeded bare-code retry by +18 net unlocks (25/7, Holm p=0.0021). Code-plus-facts recovered +18 over bare code (21/3, p=0.00042) and +15 over a generic-bullet placebo (p=0.0041). An instruction-only effect was not distinguishable (+3, p=0.36). Code-plus-facts and blind resampling tied at 26 unlocks each (not equivalence). Six external-controller follow-ups tied a content-free shape placebo. In this regime, falsification helped not as vocabulary or self-critique, but as comparison with external, executable counterexamples.

AI.tldr: This study introduces a falsification-centered methodology to evaluate whether feedback content genuinely helps frozen code models repair failing programs. Using placebo-controlled, matched-budget experiments across six benchmarks with small models, the authors find that blind resampling and code-plus-facts feedback both outperform bare-code retry, while instruction-only feedback does not. The core finding: the value of feedback lies in exposing the model to external, executable counterexamples rather than re-exposure to its own failing output.
AI.motivation: Current practice treats code model repair as a simple retry mechanism where models see their own failing output. From a Popperian (falsificationist) perspective, this conflates mere re-exposure with genuine learning from executable counterexamples. The authors aim to build a rigorous, placebo-controlled measurement framework that makes both the model's program conjectures and the researcher's "feedback works" claim falsifiable.
AI.method: A placebo-controlled instrument with several key components: (1) packet decomposition separating code, facts, instructions, and shape; (2) placebo mirroring creating content-free, shape-matched placebos; (3) matched-budget discordant-pair tests controlling generation budget; (4) fresh-generation confirmation; (5) executable audits. Experiments span six HumanEval+/MBPP+ cells with three frozen models (0.5B–1.5B), evaluating 290 dead task-cell units (no best-of-8 candidate passing public tests). Main run: 7,000 fresh generations; preregistered follow-up: 1,400 more.
AI.result: Blind resampling exceeded bare-code retry by +18 net unlocks (25/7, Holm-corrected p=0.0021). Code-plus-facts outperformed bare code by +18 (21/3, p=0.00042) and a generic-bullet placebo by +15 (p=0.0041). Instruction-only effect was not distinguishable from zero (+3, p=0.36). Code-plus-facts and blind resampling tied at 26 unlocks each (not statistically equivalent). Six follow-up external-controller conditions tied the content-free shape placebo.
AI.conclusion: In this frozen-model regime, falsification helps not through vocabulary exposure or self-critique, but through comparison with external, executable counterexamples. The contribution is a reflexive methodology for making feedback-content claims rigorously testable, rather than a new repair algorithm.

title: CORTEX: Token-Level Hallucination Detection in RAG via Comparative Internal Representations
summary: In this paper, we propose CORTEX, a token-level hallucination detection method for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). In long-form RAG outputs, hallucinations often arise in localized spans rather than throughout an entire response. CORTEX therefore identifies ungrounded content at the token level, enabling fine-grained localization of hallucinations. The key intuition behind CORTEX is that tokens grounded in retrieved documents should be more strongly influenced by those documents than hallucinated tokens. To capture this document-induced effect, CORTEX compares internal representations of a large language model (LLM) under two conditions: with and without the retrieved documents. Instead of relying solely on each token's immediate sensitivity to the retrieved documents, CORTEX also leverages the propagation of document-grounded information through preceding tokens, reducing false positives for tokens whose evidence has already been absorbed into the context. Finally, CORTEX applies post-processing smoothing step that models the tendency of hallucination labels to persist over contiguous spans, reducing local noise and encouraging span-consistent predictions. Experiments on two RAG benchmarks and three LLMs show that CORTEX substantially improves token-level hallucination detection, with each component consistently contributing to performance gains.

AI.tldr: CORTEX is a token-level hallucination detection method for RAG that identifies ungrounded spans by comparing LLM representations with and without retrieved documents, incorporating contextual propagation and span-smoothing to improve localization accuracy.
AI.motivation: Hallucinations in long-form RAG outputs typically occur in localized spans rather than uniformly across the entire response. Existing detection methods lack the granularity to pinpoint these specific ungrounded tokens, motivating a fine-grained, token-level detection approach.
AI.method: CORTEX operates in three stages: (1) It compares the internal LLM representations of each token under two conditions—with and without retrieved documents—to measure document-induced influence. (2) It leverages propagation of grounded information through preceding tokens to reduce false positives, recognizing that a token's evidence may already be absorbed into prior context. (3) A post-processing smoothing step models the tendency of hallucination labels to persist over contiguous spans, reducing local noise and enforcing span-consistent predictions.
AI.result: Experiments on two RAG benchmarks and three LLMs demonstrate that CORTEX substantially improves token-level hallucination detection, with ablation results confirming that each component (document influence comparison, propagation through preceding tokens, and span smoothing) consistently contributes to performance gains.
AI.conclusion: CORTEX provides an effective fine-grained hallucination detection method for RAG systems by exploiting differences in LLM representations induced by retrieved documents, and the multi-component design proves both individually and collectively beneficial for accurate token-level detection.

title: A Three-Phase Foundation Model for Tax-Aware Personalized Portfolio Management
summary: We present a three-phase deep reinforcement learning system for personalized portfolio management that addresses three limitations shared by all prior financial RL work: 1) ticker lock-in, 2) monolithic objectives , and 3) static user models. Phase 1 pretrains a ticker-identity-free cross asset encoder via self-supervised learning on a multi-asset corpus, augmented by a frozen parallel branch using Chronos, a T5-based time series foundation model, fused via a learned gating mechanism. To our knowledge, this is the first application of a time series foundation model to portfolio management RL. The encoder generalizes to any publicly traded asset via a 50-dimensional observable metadata vector that requires no retraining for new tickers. Phase 2 fine-tunes a MoE (Mixture of Experts) portfolio actor critic with PPO under an objective-conditioned reward that simultaneously serves six distinct investment goals sampled per episode: short-term alpha, short-term gain, long-term gain, capital preservation, tax-loss harvesting, and long-term-gains-only. A MoE architecture assigns each objective to a specialized expert head (momentum, growth, defensive, tax-aware), and a learned intent router blends experts based on the active objective and current market regime, which eliminates cross-objective gradient conflict. Phase 3 adds a lightweight personalization layer further adapted at inference time to each individual via a 76-parameter LoRA module fine-tuned on real brokerage transaction history, inferring investment objectives from revealed trading behavior rather than questionnaires. A natural language intent parser converts free-form goals directly into structured investment objective parameters.

AI.tldr: A three-phase deep RL system for personalized portfolio management that overcomes ticker lock-in, monolithic objectives, and static user models by combining a ticker-agnostic encoder (augmented with a Chronos time-series foundation model), a Mixture-of-Experts PPO architecture supporting six distinct investment goals, and a LoRA-based personalization layer inferred from real trading behavior.
AI.motivation: Existing financial RL systems suffer from three core limitations: (1) ticker lock-in — models are tied to specific assets and cannot generalize to new tickers without retraining; (2) monolithic objectives — a single reward function cannot simultaneously serve diverse investment goals; and (3) static user models — user preferences are typically captured through questionnaires rather than adapting to actual behavior. This paper aims to address all three simultaneously.
AI.method: A three-phase architecture: Phase 1 pretrains a ticker-identity-free cross-asset encoder via self-supervised learning on multi-asset data, augmented by a frozen Chronos (T5-based time-series foundation model) branch fused through a learned gating mechanism; assets are represented by a 50-dimensional metadata vector enabling zero-shot generalization. Phase 2 fine-tunes a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) actor-critic with PPO under an objective-conditioned reward supporting six goals (short-term alpha, short-term gain, long-term gain, capital preservation, tax-loss harvesting, long-term-gains-only), with specialized expert heads (momentum, growth, defensive, tax-aware) routed by a learned intent router based on active objective and market regime. Phase 3 adds a 76-parameter LoRA module fine-tuned on brokerage transaction history for personalized adaptation, plus a natural language intent parser that maps free-form goals to structured investment parameters.
AI.result: The paper claims this is the first application of a time-series foundation model (Chronos) to portfolio management RL. The ticker-agnostic encoder generalizes to any publicly traded asset without retraining. The MoE architecture eliminates cross-objective gradient conflict by isolating objectives to specialized expert heads.
AI.conclusion: The proposed three-phase system successfully addresses ticker lock-in, monolithic objectives, and static user models through a modular design combining foundation models, mixture-of-experts, and lightweight LoRA personalization, enabling a generalizable, multi-objective, and adaptive portfolio management agent.

title: Personalizing Marketplace Policies with Competing Objectives and Constrained Experiments: Evidence from a Job Marketplace
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at ACM SIGKDD 2026 (Applied Data Science Track)
summary:
Two-sided marketplaces connect distinct user groups whose interests often conflict -- improving outcomes on one side could degrade the other side's experience. To address this challenge, we deploy an integrated framework for personalizing free-value thresholds -- a policy governing the scope of complimentary services for job listings -- across a two-sided job marketplace connecting millions of employers and job seekers. Our personalized policy delivers statistically significant and economically sizable lift in the target metric while respecting engagement guardrail constraints.
  Direct application of standard uplift methods proves insufficient here for two reasons. First, cross-side externalities demand multi-objective optimization: maximizing employer-side metrics risks harming job seeker engagement, with effects varying substantially across job segments. Second, marketplace interference necessitates cluster-level randomization, limiting us to few discrete treatment levels -- effectively a form of positivity violation that rules out methods designed for continuous treatments.
  We contribute an integrated framework with three components. Our ensemble-based hybrid ranking models target and guardrail metrics separately, cutting guardrail risk by over 10% for equivalent target gains compared to single-objective approaches. A treatment effect extrapolation method extends our estimates from limited experimental variation to untested policy levels, relying on monotonicity assumptions that we validate empirically. Finally, we present production deployment, where post-launch data confirms both extrapolation accuracy and guardrail compliance.
  Our deployed system demonstrates that principled methodology can enable meaningful personalization even when experiments are severely constrained and different objectives compete -- common conditions that characterize many real-world marketplaces.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an integrated framework for personalizing free-value thresholds in a two-sided job marketplace, addressing challenges of cross-side externalities and experimental constraints. The approach combines ensemble hybrid ranking models, treatment effect extrapolation with monotonicity assumptions, and production validation, achieving significant metric lifts while respecting guardrails.
AI.motivation: Two-sided marketplaces face inherent tension: optimizing for one user group (e.g., employers) can harm another (e.g., job seekers). Standard uplift methods fail due to (1) cross-side externalities requiring multi-objective optimization, and (2) marketplace interference necessitating cluster-level randomization, which creates a positivity violation that rules out continuous-treatment methods.
AI.method: The framework has three components: (1) ensemble-based hybrid ranking models that separately target primary and guardrail metrics, reducing guardrail risk by over 10% for equivalent target gains versus single-objective approaches; (2) a treatment effect extrapolation method that extends estimates from limited discrete experimental levels to untested policy levels, using empirically validated monotonicity assumptions; (3) production deployment with post-launch validation confirming extrapolation accuracy and guardrail compliance.
AI.result: The personalized policy delivered statistically significant and economically sizable lift in the target employer-side metric while respecting job seeker engagement guardrails. Post-launch data confirmed both the accuracy of the treatment effect extrapolation and compliance with guardrail constraints.
AI.conclusion: Principled methodology can enable meaningful personalization even under severely constrained experiments and competing objectives — conditions common in real-world marketplaces. The deployed system demonstrates practical viability of the integrated approach.

title: A forgery attack on the Block.co blockchain-based digital credential certification system
comment: 8 pages, 9 figures, accepted for presentation at the 2nd IEEE International Workshop on Blockchain and Distributed Ledger Technologies (BlockDLT 2026)
summary: Certification of digital documents, such as academic credentials, seems a particularly suitable application for the use of blockchain and distributed ledger technologies. Indeed, these technologies enable decentralized certification systems that rely on the immutability and persistence of their distributed ledgers. However, in the absence of a central trusted authority, it is not easy to guarantee the authenticity of the connection between the real identity of an academic institution and the digital identity of the certificate issuer. In this paper, we demonstrate that one of such systems, known as Block.co, has a vulnerability that allows the production of forged certificates that are recognized as valid by the system. Since this is an inherent limitation of the approach used for blockchain-based certification, our attack is likely to be extendable to other systems adopting the same approach.

AI.tldr: The paper exposes a vulnerability in the Block.co blockchain-based academic certification system that allows forged certificates to be recognized as valid, due to an inherent limitation in linking real-world institutional identity to on-chain digital identity without a central trusted authority.
AI.motivation: Blockchain-based digital document certification systems promise decentralized, immutable verification. However, without a central trusted authority, reliably binding a real-world academic institution's identity to its on-chain issuer identity is challenging. The authors aim to investigate whether existing systems like Block.co successfully address this identity-authenticity gap.
AI.method: The authors conduct a security analysis of the Block.co certification system, identifying and demonstrating a practical attack that exploits the disconnect between an institution's real-world identity and its blockchain-based digital identity, enabling the production of forged yet system-valid certificates.
AI.result: A concrete vulnerability was found in Block.co that allows forged certificates to pass as valid within the system. The root cause is identified as an inherent limitation of the underlying approach — not merely an implementation flaw — suggesting the attack is generalizable to other blockchain-based certification systems using the same design paradigm.
AI.conclusion: Blockchain-based certification systems lacking a robust mechanism to cryptographically bind real-world institutional identity to on-chain identity are fundamentally vulnerable to forgery attacks. The Block.co case illustrates a systemic weakness likely present in similar systems.

title: FormIDEAble: Safe and Socially-aware Autonomous Systems
summary: Autonomous agents operating in socio-critical settings must coordinate with humans under uncertainty while respecting explicit safety constraints. Existing approaches either account for social dynamics without formal guarantees or provide formal assurance while abstracting away human behaviour. We introduce FormIDEAble, a formally grounded approach for synthesising socially-aware cooperation strategies with safety guarantees. The cooperation between humans and the autonomous agent is modelled as a Priced Timed Markov Decision Process, and decision-making is formulated as a cost-bounded reachability problem. We illustrate the approach using an emergency evacuation scenario. Initial experimental evidence demonstrates the effectiveness of the approach and highlights the trade-offs between optimisation and safety guarantees. FormIDEAble provides a principled foundation for formally assured, socially-aware decision-making in socio-critical systems.

AI.tldr: FormIDEAble is a formal framework for synthesising socially-aware autonomous agent strategies with safety guarantees, modelling human-agent cooperation as a Priced Timed Markov Decision Process and solving it as a cost-bounded reachability problem.
AI.motivation: Current methods either handle social dynamics without formal safety guarantees, or provide formal assurance while ignoring human behaviour. There is a gap in unifying socially-aware coordination with verifiable safety in socio-critical settings.
AI.method: Models human-agent cooperation as a Priced Timed Markov Decision Process (PTMDP). Decision-making is cast as a cost-bounded reachability problem, enabling synthesis of strategies that respect explicit safety constraints while accounting for social interaction under uncertainty.
AI.result: Illustrated via an emergency evacuation scenario. Initial experiments show the approach is effective and reveal trade-offs between optimisation objectives and safety guarantees.
AI.conclusion: FormIDEAble provides a principled, formally assured foundation for socially-aware decision-making in socio-critical autonomous systems.

title: Truth or Sophistry? LoFa: A Benchmark for LLM Robustness Against Logical Fallacies
comment: Accepted to ACL 2026 Main. 33 pages (9 pages main text)
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong semantic capabilities, yet their resilience to manipulative linguistic patterns such as logical fallacies remains underexplored. Prior work has primarily examined whether LLMs can identify or classify fallacies, leaving their robustness against fallacious persuasion insufficiently studied. To address this gap, we introduce LoFa (Logical Fallacy), a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLM robustness against fallacies. LoFa is constructed through a multi-agent pipeline that pairs factual questions with fallacious arguments, and is accompanied by a multi-round debate framework for assessing model resilience under sustained adversarial persuasion. To disentangle fallacy robustness from a model's inherent knowledge limitations, we further propose Logical Fallacy Resistance at k (LFR@k), a metric that quantifies resistance to fallacious attacks. Experiments show that LLMs exhibit varying levels of robustness across different fallacy types, revealing distinct vulnerability profiles among models.

AI.tldr: LoFa is a benchmark and LFR@k is a metric for evaluating how robust LLMs are against logical fallacies in adversarial persuasion settings, revealing that models have distinct vulnerability profiles across different fallacy types.
AI.motivation: Prior work on LLMs and logical fallacies focuses narrowly on fallacy identification/classification, neglecting the more critical question of whether LLMs can resist being persuaded by fallacious arguments. This gap motivates a systematic evaluation of LLM robustness against manipulative reasoning.
AI.method: (1) LoFa benchmark: constructed via a multi-agent pipeline that pairs factual questions with fallacious arguments. (2) A multi-round debate framework simulates sustained adversarial persuasion. (3) LFR@k metric: quantifies fallacy resistance while disentangling it from inherent knowledge limitations, measuring how many rounds (k) a model withstands before being swayed.
AI.result: LLMs exhibit varying robustness levels across different fallacy types, with each model showing distinct vulnerability profiles — some fallacies are more effective at persuading certain models than others.
AI.conclusion: LLM robustness against logical fallacies is non-uniform and model-specific. Evaluating and understanding these vulnerability profiles is essential for developing more resilient language models, and LoFa plus LFR@k provide the necessary tools for this assessment.

title: Beyond Compilation: Evaluating Faithful Natural-Language-to-Lean Statement Formalization
summary: Theorem-proving benchmarks evaluate proof search against fixed formal statements, but natural-language-to-Lean formalization must generate the formal statement itself. In this setting, compilation is only a validity check: a Lean declaration may type-check while omitting hypotheses, changing domains, or expressing a vacuous claim. We study faithful statement formalization as both an evaluation problem and a bottleneck-attribution problem. On a 400-entry graduate-level benchmark spanning real analysis, complex analysis, topology, and algebra, our protocol combines Lean compilation, cross-model semantic judging, and human expert calibration. The resulting picture is different from compile-rate evaluation: a full tool-augmented agent reaches 89.5% compilation but only 60.5% consensus faithfulness, exposing a 29.0-point compile-pass but consensus-unfaithful gap. Targeted human audits support the metric as a conservative decision boundary: across available case-level audits, 96.0% of consensus-positive outputs are human-confirmed faithful, while 82.4% of compile-pass consensus-negative outputs are human-confirmed semantic failures. Under this metric, existing one-shot formalizer models and prover-oriented Lean models remain low, suggesting that formal validity, proof-oriented Lean competence, and faithful statement generation should be reported separately. We then use a full $2^3$ factorial design to decompose three recurring interventions in formalization pipelines: parametric expert drafting, Mathlib/context search, and Lean elaboration feedback. Elaboration feedback is the largest validity intervention, but it also exposes a larger compile-pass semantic-failure bucket; search mainly improves grounding and selectivity; and fine-tuned drafting is largely substitutable in this tool stack once feedback and grounding are available.

AI.tldr: The paper examines "faithful statement formalization" — translating natural language math into Lean — going beyond mere compilation checks. Using a 400-entry graduate-level benchmark and a protocol combining compilation, cross-model semantic judging, and human calibration, it reveals a 29-point gap between compilation success (89.5%) and consensus faithfulness (60.5%). A factorial experiment decomposes three interventions (expert drafting, Mathlib search, elaboration feedback), finding elaboration feedback most improves validity but also expands the compile-pass/unfaithful gap.
AI.motivation: Existing theorem-proving benchmarks evaluate proof search against fixed formal statements, but NL-to-Lean formalization requires generating the formal statement itself. Compilation is insufficient as a validity check because a declaration can type-check while being semantically vacuous (missing hypotheses, wrong domains, trivial claims). The authors aim to study faithful statement formalization as both an evaluation problem and a bottleneck-attribution problem, arguing that formal validity, proof competence, and faithful generation should be reported separately.
AI.method: The authors construct a 400-entry graduate-level benchmark across real analysis, complex analysis, topology, and algebra. Their evaluation protocol combines three components: (1) Lean compilation as a basic validity filter, (2) cross-model semantic judging using multiple models to assess faithfulness, and (3) human expert calibration to validate the metric. For bottleneck analysis, they employ a full 2³ factorial design decomposing three interventions: parametric expert drafting (fine-tuned vs. general-purpose), Mathlib/context search (enabled vs. disabled), and Lean elaboration feedback (enabled vs. disabled).
AI.result: A full tool-augmented agent reaches 89.5% compilation but only 60.5% consensus faithfulness, a 29.0-point gap. Human audits confirm the metric's reliability: 96.0% of consensus-positive outputs are human-confirmed faithful, and 82.4% of compile-pass/consensus-negative outputs are human-confirmed semantic failures. Existing one-shot formalizers and prover-oriented Lean models perform poorly under this metric. The factorial experiment reveals elaboration feedback is the largest validity intervention but also widens the compile-pass semantic-failure bucket; search mainly improves grounding and selectivity; fine-tuned drafting is largely substitutable when feedback and grounding are available.
AI.conclusion: Faithful statement formalization is a distinct problem from proof search, and compilation-based evaluation alone is misleading. The authors recommend reporting formal validity, proof-oriented Lean competence, and faithful statement generation separately. Their faithfulness metric, validated by human calibration, provides a conservative decision boundary. The factorial analysis suggests that elaboration feedback is the most impactful single intervention but must be paired with semantic checking, while fine-tuned drafting becomes less critical in a well-grounded tool stack.

title: Quality-Aware Modulation for Diffusion Transformers
summary: Modern text-to-image diffusion models, such as diffusion transformers (DiT), rely on timestep or prompt embeddings to modulate the strength of the denoising process in each timestep. While this modulation communicates the current noise level, it does not provide any quality-aware information, which can lead to generated images that are unaligned, visually inconsistent, and lacking in fidelity. In this paper, we propose the Quality Representation Module (QRM), a lightweight transformer module that learns a quality-aware representation based on existing model inputs, and produces a set of vectors $M_{qrm}$. These vectors adjust the adaptive LayerNorm modulation within the DiT transformer blocks, thereby injecting a quality-sensitive signal into the denoising parameters. The QRM introduces no significant changes to the sampling schedule or diffusion backbone. Experiments include ablations on QRM training losses and architectures, as well as empirical results demonstrating consistent image quality improvements over baseline DiT-based models.

AI.tldr: QRM learns a quality-aware representation from existing model inputs to modulate DiT LayerNorm parameters, injecting quality-sensitive signals into the denoising process without altering the sampling schedule or backbone, yielding consistent image quality improvements.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion transformers (DiT) use timestep/prompt embeddings that carry noise-level and semantic information but lack explicit quality-aware signals, resulting in images that can be misaligned, visually inconsistent, or low-fidelity.
AI.method: Propose the Quality Representation Module (QRM), a lightweight transformer module that takes existing model inputs, learns a quality-aware representation, and outputs vectors M_qrm. These vectors adjust the adaptive LayerNorm modulation within DiT blocks, injecting quality-sensitive signals directly into denoising parameters without modifying the sampling schedule or backbone architecture.
AI.result: Experiments include ablation studies on QRM training losses and architectures, plus empirical results showing consistent image quality improvements over baseline DiT-based models.
AI.conclusion: QRM effectively supplements DiT models with quality-aware modulation, improving output fidelity and consistency with minimal architectural overhead and no changes to the diffusion sampling pipeline.

title: CVE-TTP KG: Knowledge Graph Linking Software Vulnerabilities to Attack Behaviors
summary: In the evolving threat landscape, adversaries exploit software vulnerabilities to launch sophisticated attacks, challenging traditional defenses. Although databases like CVE and NVD provide detailed technical information, they often lack links to attacker behaviors such as tactics and techniques, limiting effective threat interpretation and response. This work bridges this gap by connecting vulnerabilities with behavioral patterns from the MITRE ATT&CK framework. We construct a CVE-TTP Knowledge Graph that links CVEs to tactics and techniques using classification and relation extraction. Transformer-based models are developed for behavior identification, with CySecBERT achieving macro F1-scores of 87.71% (techniques) and 96.16% (tactics). Also, we created an annotated dataset with 24,820 entities and 43,608 relations for entity and relation extraction. The pipeline-based approach achieves macro F1-scores of 0.86 (entity extraction) and 0.99 (relation extraction), while a span-based joint model achieves 0.78. These outputs are integrated into a Neo4j-based Cyber Threat Knowledge Graph, enabling structured visualization of vulnerabilities.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs a CVE-TTP Knowledge Graph linking software vulnerabilities (CVEs) to MITRE ATT&CK tactics and techniques using Transformer-based classification and relation extraction, enabling structured threat intelligence visualization.
AI.motivation: Existing vulnerability databases (CVE, NVD) provide rich technical details but lack explicit connections to attacker behavioral patterns (tactics, techniques), hindering effective threat interpretation and response. Bridging CVEs with MITRE ATT&CK fills this gap.
AI.method: The authors develop a pipeline: (1) Transformer-based models (CySecBERT) for classifying CVEs into ATT&CK tactics (macro F1: 96.16%) and techniques (macro F1: 87.71%); (2) an annotated dataset of 24,820 entities and 43,608 relations for entity/relation extraction; (3) both a pipeline-based approach (macro F1: 0.86 entity, 0.99 relation) and a span-based joint model (macro F1: 0.78) for extraction; (4) integration into a Neo4j-based Cyber Threat Knowledge Graph.
AI.result: CySecBERT achieved macro F1-scores of 87.71% for technique classification and 96.16% for tactic classification. For entity and relation extraction, the pipeline approach reached 0.86 and 0.99 macro F1 respectively, while the joint model scored 0.78. The resulting knowledge graph enables structured vulnerability visualization.
AI.conclusion: The CVE-TTP Knowledge Graph successfully bridges CVE data with ATT&CK behavioral patterns, providing a structured, queryable resource that enhances threat intelligence analysis and cyber defense decision-making.

title: From Failure to Alignment: A Requirements Engineering Framework for Machine Learning Systems
summary:
Organisations designing, developing, and deploying machine learning systems (MLS) need to be able to check that these systems are trustworthy, and communicate this clearly to their stakeholders, be they different categories of users, engineers, or wider society. By focusing on stakeholders, Requirements Engineering is well positioned to drive the design and engineering of MLS that align with the needs of their stakeholders. Yet, we still need a systematic process for modelling and reasoning about requirements for MLS that is driven both by stakeholders' needs and constraints for MLS development.
  This paper proposes a framework entitled REAL (Requirements Engineering for mAchines that Learn - and Fail) to help develop MLS that align with stakeholders' needs by adopting a requirements engineering approach. This model-based framework is based on three principles. First, weaving together requirements for data, models, and the system as a whole. Second, using failure to drive the exploration of alternative requirements. Third, iterative and traceable refinement of MLS requirements.
  We demonstrate the proposed framework using an example from autonomous driving and show that REAL supports the development of MLS that better align with stakeholders' requirements. A replication package is available online.

AI.tldr: REAL is a model-based requirements engineering framework for machine learning systems that weaves together data, model, and system requirements, uses failure analysis to explore alternatives, and supports iterative, traceable refinement—demonstrated via an autonomous driving case study.
AI.motivation: Organisations developing ML systems lack a systematic, stakeholder-driven process for modelling and reasoning about ML requirements. Existing RE approaches do not adequately address the interplay between data, model, and system-level requirements, nor do they leverage failure analysis to iteratively refine requirements for trustworthy MLS.
AI.method: The REAL framework operates on three principles: (1) weaving together requirements for data, models, and the overall system; (2) using failure-driven exploration to identify alternative requirements; and (3) enabling iterative and traceable refinement of MLS requirements. It is model-based and demonstrated through an autonomous driving example, with a replication package provided.
AI.result: The REAL framework supports development of MLS that better align with stakeholder requirements by providing structured, traceable refinement driven by failure analysis. The autonomous driving case study illustrates how REAL captures the interdependencies among data, model, and system requirements.
AI.conclusion: REAL offers a systematic RE approach tailored to MLS, addressing gaps in current practice by integrating stakeholder needs, failure-driven iteration, and cross-layer traceability. It positions Requirements Engineering as a key driver for building trustworthy ML systems.

title: A Semantic-Layer-Mediated Agent for Natural Language to SQL over Heterogeneous Enterprise Databases
comment: Submitted to FITAT 2026 for peer review
summary: Natural language-to-SQL (NL2SQL) over real-world enterprise databases remains significantly more challenging than on academic benchmarks. Enterprise schemas often contain hundreds of physical tables with cryptic column names, heterogeneous SQL dialects, and complex analytical workloads requiring nested aggregations, temporal reasoning, and multi-table joins. We present a semantic-layer-mediated NL2SQL agent that decouples semantic intent from physical SQL execution. Rather than generating SQL directly over raw schemas, the agent reasons over a curated semantic layer through a compact intermediate representation called the Semantic Model Query (SMQ). A deterministic compiler translates each SMQ into dialect-specific SQL, providing verified building blocks that the agent composes into the final query. The system employs a constrained think-act loop, supports SQLite, BigQuery, and Snowflake backends, and is integrated into an end-to-end evaluation framework. Using Gemini 3 Pro, the system achieves 94.15% execution accuracy on the 547-task Spider2-snow benchmark, ranking third on the official leaderboard and substantially outperforming schema-only approaches. We describe the system architecture, SMQ representation, agent workflow, evaluation results, and discuss semantic-layer quality and the trade-off between improved grounding and overfitting.

AI.tldr: A semantic-layer-mediated NL2SQL agent using a Semantic Model Query (SMQ) intermediate representation achieves 94.15% execution accuracy on Spider2-snow, outperforming schema-only methods by reasoning over curated semantic models rather than raw enterprise schemas.
AI.motivation: Enterprise NL2SQL is far harder than academic benchmarks due to hundreds of physical tables, cryptic column names, heterogeneous SQL dialects, and complex analytical queries. Directly generating SQL over raw schemas fails to handle these challenges, motivating a decoupled approach that separates semantic intent from physical execution.
AI.method: A semantic-layer-mediated agent architecture that reasons over a curated semantic layer using a compact intermediate representation called Semantic Model Query (SMQ). The agent operates in a constrained think-act loop, composing queries from verified building blocks. A deterministic compiler translates SMQ into dialect-specific SQL for SQLite, BigQuery, and Snowflake. The system is integrated with an end-to-end evaluation framework and uses Gemini 3 Pro as the underlying model.
AI.result: The system achieves 94.15% execution accuracy on the 547-task Spider2-snow benchmark, ranking third on the official leaderboard and substantially outperforming schema-only approaches.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling semantic intent from physical SQL execution via a semantic layer and SMQ intermediate representation significantly improves NL2SQL performance on enterprise databases. The authors highlight the trade-off between improved grounding through curated semantics and the risk of overfitting to specific semantic models.

title: LabGuard: Grounding Natural-Language Laboratory Rules into Runtime Guards for Embodied Laboratory Agents
summary: Scientific embodied agents are increasingly capable of carrying out laboratory procedures, but executing these procedures safely in dynamic laboratory environments remains challenging. Current safety approaches often overlook the intermediate step of transforming laboratory natural language, including safety rules, manuals, protocols, and standard operating procedures, into machine-checkable runtime constraints. We introduce LabGuard (Laboratory Guard), a language-to-execution safety suite that grounds natural-language laboratory rules into executable specifications and deploys them as runtime guards. LabGuard includes three core components: LabGuard-IR, which defines a typed executable representation; LabGuard-Bench, which provides 812 supervised annotations expanded from 203 seed laboratory rules; and LabGuard-Grounder, which maps natural-language laboratory rules into LabGuard-IR. The resulting IR instances are handled by the LabGuard Pipeline, which compiles them into runtime monitors and applies them at the controller boundary. Experiments show that LabGuard generalizes to unseen laboratory-rule sources, achieves 79.4 task-scope F1, and reduces unsafe events from 39.5% to 23.8% after monitor compilation. In LabUtopia, its runtime monitors integrate with ACT, keeping interventions below 0.5% while preserving task success.

AI.tldr: LabGuard is a safety suite that translates natural-language laboratory rules into executable runtime monitors, reducing unsafe events from 39.5% to 23.8% in scientific embodied agents while preserving task success with minimal intervention.
AI.motivation: Scientific embodied agents operating in dynamic labs face safety challenges. Existing safety methods fail to bridge the gap between natural-language safety rules (protocols, SOPs, manuals) and machine-checkable runtime constraints, leaving a critical intermediate step unaddressed.
AI.method: LabGuard consists of three components: (1) LabGuard-IR, a typed intermediate representation for executable safety specifications; (2) LabGuard-Bench, a benchmark with 812 supervised annotations from 203 seed laboratory rules; and (3) LabGuard-Grounder, which maps natural-language rules into LabGuard-IR. The resulting IR instances are compiled by the LabGuard Pipeline into runtime monitors deployed at the controller boundary.
AI.result: LabGuard generalizes to unseen rule sources, achieves 79.4 task-scope F1, and reduces unsafe events from 39.5% to 23.8% after monitor compilation. In the LabUtopia environment, runtime monitors integrated with ACT keep interventions below 0.5% without compromising task success.
AI.conclusion: Grounding natural-language lab safety rules into executable runtime monitors is an effective approach for improving safety in embodied laboratory agents, enabling significant reduction of unsafe events with negligible impact on task performance.

title: Physics-informed Conditional Normalizing Flows for Angles-only Cislunar Orbit Determination
summary: Generative Astrodynamics is advanced in this work by extending generative modelling to an orbit determination problem in the cislunar environment. The task is formulated as conditional density estimation, aiming to infer the probability distribution of the initial state from angles-only measurements over short observation arcs. A normalising flow is trained on perturbed topocentric observations from Near Rectilinear Halo Orbits, enabling a flexible and potentially multimodal posterior representation. Given new measurements, the learned density is sampled to generate statistically consistent and physics-informed state hypotheses. These estimates are refined via nonlinear least-squares minimisation, providing a competitive warm start for classical algorithms.

AI.tldr: This work extends generative modelling to cislunar orbit determination by using normalising flows for conditional density estimation of initial states from short-arc angles-only observations, with posterior sampling refined via nonlinear least-squares to provide warm starts for classical algorithms.
AI.motivation: Orbit determination in the cislunar environment from short arcs of angles-only measurements is challenging due to weak observability and potentially multimodal posteriors. Classical iterative methods (e.g., least-squares) require good initial guesses and may converge poorly. The authors seek a data-driven approach that learns the underlying distribution over states conditioned on observations to generate statistically consistent, physics-informed initial guesses.
AI.method: The problem is framed as conditional density estimation. A normalising flow is trained on perturbed topocentric observations from Near Rectilinear Halo Orbits (NRHOs) to model the posterior distribution of the initial state given measurements. At inference, new measurements condition the learned density, from which state hypotheses are sampled. These samples are then refined via nonlinear least-squares minimisation, serving as warm starts for classical orbit determination algorithms.
AI.result: The normalising flow yields a flexible, potentially multimodal posterior representation over initial states. Sampling from this learned density produces statistically consistent state hypotheses that, after least-squares refinement, provide competitive warm starts for classical orbit determination algorithms in the cislunar regime.
AI.conclusion: Generative modelling, specifically normalising flows, can effectively capture complex posterior distributions for orbit determination under weak observability. The approach bridges data-driven generative methods and classical physics-based estimation, offering robust initialisation that mitigates convergence issues in traditional algorithms.

title: Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning based Intrusion Detection in Realistic IoT Networks
summary: The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly growing and expanding into various sectors, such as healthcare, transportation, smart homes, and more. Despite the benefits of using IoT devices, they present several challenges. Given the significant role these devices play in our lives, it is crucial to address issues related to their security and privacy. These devices are limited in resources, which complicates their security and the protection of the data that they manage. The paper aims to examine intrusion detection systems using the Gotham2025 dataset, generated through the Gotham testbed, which consists of 78 emulated IoT devices utilising various protocols, including MQTT, CoAP, and RTSP, to assist in safeguarding IoT networks from attacks. We conduct a comparative analysis between five machine learning algorithms, including Random Forest, XGBoost, Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, and Deep Neural Network. We demonstrate that the Random Forest Classifier was the top-performing model, achieving an F1-score of 0.99 in classifying attacks.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates five ML algorithms for IoT intrusion detection using the Gotham2025 dataset (78 emulated IoT devices, MQTT/CoAP/RTSP protocols), finding Random Forest achieves the best performance with an F1-score of 0.99.
AI.motivation: IoT devices are increasingly deployed across critical sectors but suffer from severe resource constraints that complicate security and data protection. There is a pressing need for effective intrusion detection systems tailored to the heterogeneous, resource-limited nature of IoT networks.
AI.method: The authors use the Gotham2025 dataset, generated from a testbed of 78 emulated IoT devices communicating via MQTT, CoAP, and RTSP protocols. They conduct a comparative analysis of five machine learning algorithms — Random Forest, XGBoost, Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, and Deep Neural Network — for classifying network attacks.
AI.result: Random Forest Classifier emerged as the top-performing model, attaining an F1-score of 0.99 for attack classification, outperforming XGBoost, Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, and Deep Neural Network.
AI.conclusion: ML-based intrusion detection, particularly using ensemble methods like Random Forest, can effectively safeguard resource-constrained IoT networks. The Gotham2025 dataset proves to be a valuable benchmark for evaluating IDS in multi-protocol IoT environments.

title: Digital Sovereignty as a Quality Attribute for Software Architectures
summary: Digital sovereignty (DS) is an increasingly important concept and political agenda throughout the world, including in the European Union (EU). However, the concept is also regrettably vague. With this critical point in mind, the paper presents an analysis of digital sovereignty as a quality attribute for software architectures in the context of cloud computing and the EU's policy frameworks for it. The analysis reveals that DS can be sharpened analytically by conceptualizing it as a quality attribute. The analysis further demonstrates how DS satisfies many of the classical properties of quality attributes for software architectures, including their measurability and validation, the trade-offs they involve, and the scenario-based methodology commonly used for analyzing them.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes digital sovereignty (DS) as a quality attribute for software architectures in cloud computing, contextualized within EU policy frameworks, demonstrating that DS satisfies classical quality attribute properties such as measurability, trade-offs, and scenario-based analysis.
AI.motivation: Digital sovereignty is an increasingly important yet regrettably vague concept in political agendas, particularly in the EU. The paper is motivated by the need to sharpen this concept analytically and make it operational for software architecture design in cloud computing contexts.
AI.method: The paper conducts a conceptual analysis by mapping digital sovereignty onto the established framework of software architecture quality attributes. It examines how DS aligns with classical quality attribute properties — including measurability, validation, trade-off analysis, and scenario-based methodology — within the specific context of EU cloud computing policy frameworks.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that DS can be sharpened analytically by conceptualizing it as a quality attribute. It further demonstrates that DS satisfies many classical properties of quality attributes, including measurability and validation, inherent trade-offs, and compatibility with scenario-based architectural analysis methods.
AI.conclusion: Conceptualizing digital sovereignty as a software architecture quality attribute offers a rigorous, operational pathway to reduce the concept's vagueness and integrate it systematically into cloud system design, particularly aligned with EU policy objectives.

title: Reference-Based Prosody and Rhythm Evaluation for Spoken Dialogue Systems
summary: Speech-to-speech (S2S) AI agents are advancing rapidly, yet evaluation lacks interpretable speech-native measures for conversational prosody and rhythm. Because $F_0$, speaking rate, articulation rate, and pausing shift with model-predicted speaker traits and interaction state, pooled human statistics can be poorly calibrated for evaluating a particular output. Using 4000+ hours of dyadic English conversation from the Seamless Interaction dataset, we construct matched reference regimes for $F_0$ mean, $F_0$ expressivity, speech rate, articulation rate, pause ratio, and mean pause duration. We then define a percentile-based evaluation protocol: extract the same metrics from an S2S output waveform, compare them to the closest matched human reference stratum, and report percentile deviations or 5th-95th percentile out-of-regime flags. On held-out human rows, pooled references over-flag state-conditioned $F_0$ expressivity and rhythm, while matched references return flag rates closer to the nominal 10% and make deviation direction interpretable. These outputs serve as behavioral plausibility checks that complement, rather than replace, perceptual and user-centered evaluation.

AI.tldr: Proposes a percentile-based evaluation protocol for speech-to-speech agents using matched reference strata from 4000+ hours of dyadic conversation, showing that condition-matched norms yield better-calibrated flag rates than pooled statistics for prosodic and rhythmic features.
AI.motivation: Current S2S evaluation lacks interpretable, speech-native measures for conversational prosody and rhythm. Pooled human statistics are poorly calibrated because prosodic features (F0, rate, pausing) shift systematically with speaker traits and interaction state, leading to over-flagging of context-appropriate variation.
AI.method: Using the Seamless Interaction dataset (4000+ hours of dyadic English conversation), the authors construct matched reference regimes stratified by speaker traits and conversational state. They extract six metrics — F0 mean, F0 expressivity, speech rate, articulation rate, pause ratio, and mean pause duration — then define a percentile-based protocol: compare S2S output metrics to the closest matched human reference stratum, reporting percentile deviations and 5th–95th percentile out-of-regime flags.
AI.result: On held-out human data, pooled references over-flag state-conditioned F0 expressivity and rhythm, while matched references achieve flag rates closer to the nominal 10% and yield directionally interpretable deviations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework functions as a behavioral plausibility check that complements perceptual and user-centered evaluation, offering better-calibrated, interpretable diagnostics for prosodic and rhythmic aspects of S2S output.

title: OpenLife: Toward Open-World Artificial Life with Autonomous LLM Agents
summary: Artificial life has explored life-like behavior on many computational substrates, but mostly in researcher-designed closed worlds. We argue that large language model (LLM) agents, with persistent memory, tool use, network access, and payment, now make it possible to move artificial life into the open social, technical, and economic world, a paradigm we call open-world Artificial Life (open-world ALIFE). Our proof-of-concept, OpenLife, surrounds a stateless LLM not with a single "smart agent" but with a society of asynchronous processes: memory, perception, evaluation, and a budget-based metabolism that makes persistence normative. With no fixed objective available, experience is appraised by open-vocabulary LLM judgment rather than scalar reward, and memory is rewired by meaning rather than frequency. Running six such agents in the open world for about twelve weeks and counting, we report the life-like dynamics that emerge: a shift from reactive to spontaneous activity, individuation into distinct agents, emergent social structure, and a first self-earned external income. We do not claim OpenLife has realized artificial life, but that open-world ALIFE is now a viable experimental paradigm and a concrete platform for studying what might cautiously be called living AI.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "open-world ALIFE," a paradigm where LLM agents with persistent memory, tools, and budgets operate autonomously in real-world environments. A proof-of-concept called OpenLife ran six agents for ~12 weeks, demonstrating emergent life-like dynamics including spontaneous activity, individuation, social structure, and self-earned income.
AI.motivation: Traditional artificial life research operates in researcher-designed, closed-world simulations. The authors argue that modern LLM agents—now capable of persistent memory, API/tool use, network access, and financial transactions—enable a shift to open-world settings where life-like behavior can emerge in genuine social, technical, and economic environments rather than constrained sandboxes.
AI.method: The OpenLife system surrounds a stateless LLM with a society of asynchronous processes: memory (rewired by semantic meaning rather than frequency), perception, evaluation via open-vocabulary LLM judgment (no scalar reward), and a budget-based metabolism that enforces persistence as normative. Six agents were deployed in the open world for approximately twelve weeks.
AI.result: Emergent life-like dynamics included: (1) a shift from purely reactive to spontaneous, self-initiated activity; (2) individuation into distinct agent personalities/behaviors; (3) emergent social structures among agents; and (4) the first instance of an agent earning external income independently.
AI.conclusion: The authors do not claim to have fully realized artificial life, but assert that open-world ALIFE is now a viable experimental paradigm and a concrete platform for studying what might cautiously be termed "living AI."

title: Multistage Defer Trees for Hybrid Interpretability: If at First You Can't Succeed, Tree Again
summary: Recent work has shown that well-optimized individual decision trees can match complex black box models in some settings, primarily in noisy domains. For the remaining settings, however, complex ensembled compositions of trees often achieve higher accuracy at the cost of interpretability, leaving practitioners with difficult modeling decisions along an accuracy-interpretability tradeoff. Ideally, we would like to classify as much of the data as possible with one or a small number of trees, achieving interpretability for most samples while maintaining state-of-the-art accuracy. We introduce Multistage Defer Trees: a sequence of sparse decision trees that each make predictions for most samples, while deferring a small proportion to the next tree in the sequence or, ultimately, to a black box. We demonstrate that we can train this model class to match the performance of complex tree-based ensembles while routing most samples through only one or a small number of sparse decision trees. We discuss a range of techniques for training these models while maintaining simplicity. Our method expands the accuracy--interpretability frontier in settings where single-tree methods remain insufficient, demonstrating that even when complex models are necessary, they need not be fully opaque.

AI.tldr: Introduces Multistage Defer Trees — a sequence of sparse decision trees that classify most samples through few trees while deferring hard cases to later trees or a black box, achieving complex ensemble-level accuracy with substantially greater interpretability.
AI.motivation: Single decision trees are interpretable but often insufficiently accurate; tree ensembles (e.g., random forests, gradient boosting) achieve state-of-the-art accuracy but are opaque. Practitioners face an accuracy-interpretability tradeoff. The authors aim to classify most samples using only one or a few sparse trees while preserving high accuracy, expanding the Pareto frontier.
AI.method: Multistage Defer Trees: a cascade of sparse decision trees where each tree predicts for most samples and defers a small fraction to the next tree or ultimately to a black-box model. Multiple training techniques are proposed to maintain tree sparsity and simplicity throughout the sequence.
AI.result: The model matches the predictive performance of complex tree-based ensembles while routing the majority of samples through only one or a small number of sparse decision trees.
AI.conclusion: The method expands the accuracy-interpretability frontier in regimes where single-tree approaches are insufficient, showing that even when complex models are necessary, they need not be entirely opaque — interpretability can be preserved for most predictions.

title: Digital signature schemes based on code equivalence and syndrome decoding from restricted errors
summary: Digital signature schemes are an important cryptographic tool to ensure data authenticity and integrity in many applications that must be resilient to attacks, including those facilitated by quantum computers. We consider the two digital signature schemes based on error-correcting codes that are second-round candidates in NIST's call for Additional Signature Schemes, which is part of the Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization Process. Specifically, we provide an overview of the Codes and Restricted Objects Signature Scheme (CROSS) and the Linear Equivalence Signature Scheme (LESS). We describe their underlying problems of syndrome decoding from restricted errors and code equivalence. We review sigma protocols and how they can be transformed into digital signature schemes via the Fiat-Shamir transform. Finally, we explain how this procedure yields code-based digital signatures believed to be post-quantum secure.

AI.tldr: Survey of two NIST PQC second-round code-based signature schemes (CROSS and LESS), explaining their underlying hard problems (syndrome decoding from restricted errors, code equivalence), the sigma protocol framework, and how the Fiat-Shamir transform yields post-quantum secure digital signatures.
AI.motivation: Digital signatures must remain secure against quantum adversaries. Post-quantum cryptography standardization (NIST) requires rigorous evaluation of candidate schemes. Code-based signatures like CROSS and LESS, both second-round candidates in NIST's Additional Signature Schemes call, need clear exposition of their foundations to assess their security and viability.
AI.method: The paper provides an expository overview. It describes the hard problems underlying CROSS (syndrome decoding with restricted errors) and LESS (linear/code equivalence). It reviews sigma protocols — three-move public-coin honest-verifier zero-knowledge proofs of knowledge — and details how the Fiat-Shamir transform (replacing the verifier's random challenge with a hash output) converts them into non-interactive digital signature schemes in the random oracle model.
AI.result: The paper synthesizes how CROSS and LESS instantiate the sigma-protocol-with-Fiat-Shamir paradigm using code-based hardness assumptions. CROSS relies on the hardness of decoding syndromes when error vectors are restricted to a specific set (restricted errors). LESS relies on the hardness of testing linear equivalence of two codes. Both constructions yield signatures believed post-quantum secure.
AI.conclusion: Code-based cryptography, leveraging problems like syndrome decoding with restricted errors and code equivalence, provides a viable foundation for post-quantum digital signatures. The sigma protocol plus Fiat-Shamir paradigm successfully transforms these hard problems into practical signature schemes (CROSS, LESS).

title: ScratchWorld: Evaluating If World Models Compute Executable Consequences
summary: World-model evaluations often score a predicted future by overlap with a target state or observation. In sparse-change worlds, this can turn copied persistent state into apparent accuracy. We introduce ScratchWorld, an offline diagnostic benchmark that treats Scratch projects as executable worlds and uses a pinned Scratch VM to produce replay-verified transitions, hidden variables, causal traces, and counterfactual outcomes. ScratchWorld evaluates next-state prediction, long-horizon tracking, causal event attribution, and counterfactual prediction; each replay-verified target can be presented under raw-program, structured-state, natural-language, or rendered input modalities, and our experiments use the structured-state condition. Its primary state metric is value-aware changed-field $F_1$, which gives credit only for the changed field and its executed value. In a 659-example release, seven prompted language/reasoning models reach at most 13.8% value-aware changed-field $F_1$ in a state-only partial-observation stress test. A same-instance copy diagnostic makes the overlap confound concrete: copying the input state reaches 98.0% implied full-state field accuracy and 0.0% changed-field $F_1$, with the largest inflation on real projects. Auxiliary diagnostics separate hidden-state rollout drift, intervention sensitivity, causal attribution, and perturbation robustness. Across these settings, models often react to actions or interventions without following the executable rule that determines the changed value.

AI.tldr: ScratchWorld is a benchmark that evaluates world models using executable Scratch projects, introducing a changed-field F1 metric that penalizes trivially copying persistent state. In experiments, seven prompted models achieve at most 13.8% on this metric, while a copy baseline scores 98% on traditional accuracy but 0% on changed-field F1, exposing a fundamental evaluation confound in sparse-change environments.
AI.motivation: Standard world-model evaluations measure prediction quality by overlap with target states, but in environments where most state remains unchanged between steps (sparse-change worlds), models can achieve high accuracy simply by copying the input forward without modeling dynamics. This creates a misleading confound: apparent predictive ability that reflects persistence rather than genuine causal understanding of how actions change the world.
AI.method: The authors introduce ScratchWorld, an offline diagnostic benchmark built on Scratch projects executed through a pinned Scratch VM. The VM produces replay-verified transitions with hidden variables, causal traces, and counterfactual outcomes. The benchmark evaluates four capabilities: next-state prediction, long-horizon tracking, causal event attribution, and counterfactual prediction. The key innovation is the value-aware changed-field F1 metric, which only credits correct prediction of the specific field that changed and its executed value. A same-instance copy diagnostic and auxiliary diagnostics (hidden-state rollout drift, intervention sensitivity, causal attribution, perturbation robustness) systematically isolate failure modes.
AI.result: Seven prompted language/reasoning models achieve at most 13.8% value-aware changed-field F1 on a state-only partial-observation stress test across 659 examples. The copy diagnostic starkly reveals the confound: copying the input state yields 98.0% implied full-state field accuracy but 0.0% changed-field F1, with inflation being largest on real projects. Auxiliary diagnostics show models frequently react to actions or interventions without following the executable rules that determine changed values, indicating shallow pattern matching rather than rule-based dynamics modeling.
AI.conclusion: Current language and reasoning models fail to model the executable dynamics of Scratch programs when evaluated with a metric that isolates changed-state prediction. The widespread overlap-based evaluation in world-model research systematically overestimates model capabilities in sparse-change settings. ScratchWorld provides a rigorous diagnostic framework and the changed-field F1 metric offers a more honest signal for progress in learning executable world dynamics.

title: Estimating Supply Incrementality in Two-sided Marketplaces: A Causal Machine Learning Approach
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the KDD 2025 Workshop on Causal Inference and Machine Learning in Practice (not presented)
summary: In two-sided marketplaces with heterogeneous products, it is important to understand the causal relationship between additional supply and marketplace outcomes, such as the total quantity transacted or transaction value in the marketplace. This paper studies a causal machine learning approach to estimating this relationship across product segments. We use the Airbnb marketplace as an example, focusing on the impact of additional listing supply on total bookings, but the methodology applies to other two-sided marketplaces. Our approach combines double/debiased machine learning with a hierarchical Bayesian framework that leverages pre-existing knowledge as priors. We construct tractable and informative features for the model by leveraging measures of product segment similarity from the geospatial literature. We find that such a model provides plausible estimates of the marketplace returns to additional supply and strong out of sample performance.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a causal machine learning method combining double/debiased ML with a hierarchical Bayesian framework to estimate the returns to additional supply across product segments in two-sided marketplaces, demonstrated on Airbnb data with geospatial similarity features, yielding plausible estimates and strong out-of-sample performance.
AI.motivation: Two-sided marketplaces with heterogeneous products need to understand how adding supply causally affects transaction outcomes (e.g., bookings, revenue) across different product segments. Traditional methods struggle with confounding and limited data in fine-grained segments, motivating a principled causal ML approach that leverages prior knowledge.
AI.method: The approach integrates double/debiased machine learning (DML) for causal estimation with a hierarchical Bayesian framework that incorporates pre-existing knowledge as priors. Geospatial similarity measures are used to construct tractable, informative features. The hierarchical structure shares statistical strength across product segments, while DML addresses confounding using flexible ML nuisance models.
AI.result: The model produces plausible estimates of marketplace returns to additional listing supply and demonstrates strong out-of-sample predictive performance when applied to Airbnb data.
AI.conclusion: Combining DML with hierarchical Bayesian modeling offers an effective framework for estimating heterogeneous causal effects of supply in two-sided marketplaces, particularly when augmented with domain-informed similarity features, and generalizes beyond the Airbnb context to other two-sided platforms.

title: Hybrid Topological Data Analysis and LSTM Networks for Enhanced Network Intrusion Detection Using CIC-IDS2017 Dataset
summary: Network intrusion detection systems (NIDS) are crucial in cybersecurity infrastructure, needing advanced techniques to detect hostile activity in network traffic. This research introduces a hybrid approach that combines Topological Data Analysis (TDA) with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to improve anomaly detection in network security. Our multi-layered design combines TDA's persistent homology with LSTM networks to capture topological characteristics of network traffic patterns and simulate temporal sequences. We assessed our methodology using the CIC-IDS2017 dataset, which includes over 2.8 million labelled flows, 77 network variables, and 14 attack categories that reflect modern threat landscapes such as DDoS, brute force, web attacks, penetration, and botnet activities. Integrating Betti curves and persistence diagrams with deep learning architectures enhances feature extraction performance. Our hybrid TDA+LSTM model has an AUC of 1.000 and F1-score of 1.000, with 5-fold cross-validation producing a mean AUC of 1.000 $\pm$ 0.000 and mean F1 of 0.999 $\pm$ 0.001. An ablation research demonstrates the complimentary contributions of topological (F1=0.990) and temporal characteristics (F1=1.000). Comparative research shows that the suggested strategy beats TDA+Random Forest (F1=0.994) and Isolation Forest (F1=0.835) baselines in several attack categories.

AI.tldr: A hybrid Network Intrusion Detection System combining Topological Data Analysis (persistent homology) with LSTM networks achieves near-perfect detection (AUC=1.000, F1=1.000) on the CIC-IDS2017 dataset across 14 attack categories, outperforming TDA+Random Forest and Isolation Forest baselines.
AI.motivation: NIDS are critical for cybersecurity but require advanced techniques to detect diverse and evolving hostile network activities. The authors aim to improve anomaly detection by capturing both topological structures and temporal dynamics in network traffic, which traditional methods often fail to jointly model.
AI.method: A multi-layered hybrid architecture integrating: (1) Topological Data Analysis via persistent homology to extract topological signatures (Betti curves, persistence diagrams) from network traffic; (2) LSTM networks to model temporal sequences.
