AI.method: FORA (Function-space Orthogonal Residual Adaptation) estimates per-layer principal directions Q from input-activation covariance using label-free calibration inputs. It forms a right projector P_Q = I - QQ^T to bar updates from capability-relevant function directions, combined with a left projector P_U from weight SVD. The update rule: ΔW = P_U M P_Q + U_2 D_δ V_2^T, where the first term is a high-capacity branch blocked from reading capability directions, and the second is a narrow spectral channel for controlled plasticity. This extends to LoRA-style parameter-efficient adaptation via M → (α/r)BA.
AI.result: Across three settings on Qwen3-1.7B — learning COGS/GSM8K while preserving translation, and learning translation while preserving math — FORA consistently outperforms weight-space projection and standard regularization in capability preservation, with only a small new-task trade-off in the math-preservation setting. A controlled ablation confirms the advantage stems from projecting onto capability-derived (activation) directions rather than weight-derived directions.
AI.conclusion: Function-space projection via activation covariance provides a more faithful characterization of LLM capabilities than weight-space geometry, enabling better preservation during fine-tuning. FORA demonstrates this with consistent improvements and minimal new-task degradation.

title: Probing Memorization of Tabular In-Context Learning
comment: Accepted at 2nd ICML Workshop on Foundation Models for Structured Data, 2026
summary: Large tabular models (LTMs), i.e., tabular foundation models leveraging in-context learning (ICL), achieve state-of-the-art performance on tabular tasks. While LLMs are known to unintentionally memorize training data, the memorization dynamics of LTMs remain largely unexplored. We investigate the potential for parametric memorization in tabular ICL. We introduce ICLMEM, a probing framework designed to separate context-based predictions from parametric memorization. Our zero-information multiple-choice context strips away valid contextual patterns to force the model to fall back on its parametric memory. Our controlled fine-tuning setup establishes membership ground truth and accounts for common pitfalls, e.g., distribution shift, feature contamination, base-rate fallacy, and the pre-trained base model acts as reference to calibrate for sample difficulty. Our controlled evaluation on a leading real-world-trained LTM detects moderate memorization signals in 8 out of 10 tasks ($\text{AUC}$ up to $0.67$ and TPR at $1\%$ FPR $>0.1$). Notably, memorization signals are strongest for low-cardinality and binary tasks. However, they largely vanish under realistic training conditions. Our findings show LTM memorization signals under specific circumstances (single-task fine-tuning with fixed samples across many epochs and small query size). To protect sensitive data, appropriate measures must be taken, which we discuss.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ICLMEM, a framework to detect parametric memorization in large tabular models (LTMs). Using controlled fine-tuning and zero-information prompts, it finds moderate memorization signals under specific conditions (single-task, many epochs, small query size), but these signals largely vanish under realistic training regimes.
AI.motivation: While LLM memorization is well-studied, the memorization dynamics of large tabular models (LTMs) using in-context learning remain unexplored. Understanding whether LTMs memorize training data parametrically is critical for privacy and data protection in sensitive tabular domains.
AI.method: The authors propose ICLMEM, a probing framework with: (1) zero-information multiple-choice contexts that strip away valid patterns, forcing the model to rely on parametric memory; (2) a controlled fine-tuning setup establishing membership ground truth; and (3) calibration against a pre-trained base model to account for sample difficulty, distribution shift, feature contamination, and base-rate fallacy.
AI.result: On a leading real-world-trained LTM, moderate memorization signals were detected in 8 out of 10 tasks (AUC up to 0.67, TPR at 1% FPR > 0.1). Memorization was strongest for low-cardinality and binary tasks. However, signals largely disappear under realistic training conditions (multi-task, fewer epochs, larger query sizes).
AI.conclusion: LTM parametric memorization occurs under narrow conditions — specifically single-task fine-tuning with fixed samples across many epochs and small query sizes. Under realistic training, the risk is low, but appropriate protective measures should still be adopted when handling sensitive data.

title: Gated Multi-Graph Fusion via Graph Attention Networks for Alzheimer's Disease Detection
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables, and accepted in interspeech 2026 conference
summary: Spontaneous speech is a vital non-invasive biomarker for Alzheimer's Disease (AD), yet many systems overlook non-linear structural disruptions and clinical heterogeneity in pathological language. We propose a Multi-View Gated Graph Attention Network that transcribes audio via Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) to construct semantic, dependency, and co-occurrence graphs, characterizing speech through a "content-structure-flow" framework. Notably, the co-occurrence graph leverages Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) from a normative corpus to quantify narrative logic and linguistic deviation. To address symptomatic diversity, an adaptive gated fusion mechanism dynamically integrates these views. Evaluated on the ADReSSo dataset, our model achieves 90.00% accuracy. Ablation results confirm that the PMI-based graph and heterogeneity-aware gating are essential for robust classification across diverse clinical populations. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/opeacc/AD.

AI.tldr: A Multi-View Gated Graph Attention Network that constructs semantic, dependency, and PMI-based co-occurrence graphs from transcribed speech achieves 90.00% accuracy for Alzheimer's Disease classification on ADReSSo, with the PMI graph and adaptive gating proving essential for handling clinical heterogeneity.
AI.motivation: Existing speech-based AD detection systems overlook two key challenges: (1) non-linear structural disruptions in pathological language that go beyond simple lexical or acoustic features, and (2) clinical heterogeneity—symptomatic diversity across patients that makes one-size-fits-all models unreliable. The authors aim to capture rich linguistic structure while adaptively weighting different linguistic views per patient.
AI.method: A three-pronged approach: first, spontaneous speech is transcribed via ASR. Then three graph views are constructed—(1) a semantic graph capturing meaning relations, (2) a dependency graph encoding syntactic structure, and (3) a co-occurrence graph using Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) derived from a normative corpus to quantify narrative logic and linguistic deviation. These graphs are processed through a Multi-View Gated Graph Attention Network, where an adaptive gated fusion mechanism dynamically integrates the three views to account for symptomatic diversity across patients.
AI.result: The model achieves 90.00% classification accuracy on the ADReSSo dataset. Ablation studies confirm that both the PMI-based co-occurrence graph and the heterogeneity-aware gating mechanism are critical components for maintaining robust performance across diverse clinical populations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed "content-structure-flow" framework, powered by PMI-informed co-occurrence graphs and adaptive multi-view fusion, provides a robust, clinically-aware approach to AD detection from spontaneous speech. The public release of source code facilitates reproducibility and further research.

title: ClawArena-Team: Benchmarking Subagent Orchestration and Dynamic Workflows in Language-Model Agents
summary: Production large language-model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed not as lone problem-solvers but as managers: a main model creates specialized subagents, delegates work, and orchestrates their parallel, asynchronous returns through dynamic workflows. Whether one model can actually run such a team is largely unmeasured: existing benchmarks score a policy's own task-solving or a fixed multi-agent system's emergent behavior, but none isolate the management ability of the single LLM acting as leader. We introduce ClawArena-Team, a benchmark of 41 multi-turn, multimodal, multi-directory scenarios spanning 258 evaluation rounds and 72 staged updates that measures this management ability. The main agent is deliberately constrained: it natively perceives only text and directly accesses only part of the workspace. It commands a fixed, locally served subagent pool, so score differences reflect management skill, not raw capability. All scoring is execution-based with no LLM judge: an overall score -- the Subagent-Management Score (SMS) -- multiplies task correctness by a least-privilege and modality-routing factor. Across twelve proprietary, community-hosted, and self-hosted models, experiments show that the management bottleneck is privilege granting rather than perception (no model exceeds 50% workspace-permission precision); that cost and management quality are decoupled (API cost spans over 100 times while the overall score spans under 4 times, with the cheapest open models on the Pareto frontier); and that most leaderboard scores cluster within a 9.9-point band while orchestration behaviors diverge by more than an order of magnitude. Code and data will be released.

AI.tldr: ClawArena-Team is a benchmark that isolates and measures a single LLM's ability to act as a manager — delegating tasks to subagents via dynamic workflows — using 41 multimodal, multi-directory scenarios with execution-based scoring that reveals management bottlenecks (privilege granting, not perception) and decouples cost from management quality.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM benchmarks evaluate either a model's solo task-solving ability or emergent behavior in fixed multi-agent systems, but none isolate the management skill of a single LLM acting as a leader orchestrating subagents. With production LLM agents increasingly deployed as managers, this capability gap needs measurement.
AI.method: The benchmark comprises 41 multi-turn, multimodal, multi-directory scenarios with 258 evaluation rounds and 72 staged updates. The main agent is text-only with partial workspace access and commands a fixed, locally served subagent pool. Scoring uses a Subagent-Management Score (SMS) that multiplies task correctness by a least-privilege and modality-routing factor. All scoring is execution-based with no LLM judge. Twelve models (proprietary, community-hosted, and self-hosted) are evaluated.
AI.result: (1) The management bottleneck is privilege granting, not perception — no model exceeds 50% workspace-permission precision. (2) Cost and management quality are decoupled: API cost spans >100× while overall score spans <4×, with the cheapest open models on the Pareto frontier. (3) Leaderboard scores cluster within a 9.9-point band, yet orchestration behaviors diverge by more than an order of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: LLM management ability is a distinct and measurable capability orthogonal to raw model power. Privilege granting — not perception — is the critical bottleneck, and strong management performance is achievable with inexpensive open models, suggesting that architectural design of agent orchestration may matter more than scaling model size or cost.

title: Explaining Machine Learning and Memorization with Statistical Mechanics
comment: PhD thesis defended on January 15, 2026. Supervisor: Daniele Tantari. Committee: Elena Agliari, Aurelien Decelle, Daniele Tantari, Fosca Gianotti, Fabrizio Lillo
summary: Artificial neural networks (NNs) and machine learning (ML) algorithms are poorly understood from a theoretical perspective, which makes it difficult to fully realize their potential and overcome their weaknesses. For instance, ML algorithms train NN weights by moving them along a low-dimensional subspace of their allowed values, but this implicitly low-dimensional learning structure is not properly exploited to improve training because its nature is not well understood. Moreover, trained NNs are easily confused by pervasive adversarial attacks whose theoretical underpinnings are still unclear. This thesis aims to improve our theoretical understanding of NNs and ML, with a particular focus on adversarial attacks and implicitly low-dimensional learning. For this purpose, we use mathematical tools from statistical mechanics to study different types of NNs and ways in which they can fit the data. In particular, we study two classes of models that fit the data with various degrees of learning and memorization: dense associative memory (DAM) and restricted Boltzmann machines (RBM). In the process, we investigate connections between different versions of these models that are useful to make analytical investigations more efficient.

AI.tldr: This thesis leverages statistical mechanics to theoretically analyze neural networks and machine learning, focusing on adversarial attacks and implicitly low-dimensional learning. It studies dense associative memory (DAM) and restricted Boltzmann machines (RBM) to understand how NNs fit data through varying degrees of learning versus memorization.
AI.motivation: Neural networks and ML algorithms lack robust theoretical foundations. Two key open problems motivate this work: (1) training implicitly operates in a low-dimensional subspace, but this structure is poorly understood and therefore not exploited; (2) adversarial attacks easily fool trained NNs, yet their theoretical underpinnings remain unclear. Addressing these gaps could unlock NN potential and remediate weaknesses.
AI.method: The author applies mathematical tools from statistical mechanics to analytically study two model classes — dense associative memory (DAM) and restricted Boltzmann machines (RBM) — which exhibit different degrees of learning and memorization when fitting data. The thesis also investigates interconnections between different versions of these models to streamline analytical investigations.
AI.result: The abstract does not disclose specific quantitative results; it signals that the thesis yields improved theoretical insights into adversarial attacks and low-dimensional learning dynamics through the statistical-mechanical analysis of DAM and RBM models, including more efficient analytical approaches via cross-model connections.
AI.conclusion: A statistical-mechanics framework applied to DAMs and RBMs provides a pathway toward better theoretical understanding of neural network behavior, particularly regarding adversarial vulnerability and the low-dimensional nature of gradient-based learning.

title: Robust Text Watermarking for Large Language Models via Dual Semantic Embeddings
summary: This work presents Dual-Embedding Watermarking (DEW), a semantic watermarking scheme for large language models (LLMs) that leverages contextual and token-level embeddings to enhance robustness against paraphrasing and translation. DEW utilizes a signal-processing methodology, applying algebraic vector-space operations to \mbox{token and context embeddings to derive a watermark signal that degrades gracefully under semantic shifts. The method obfuscates the watermark by projecting embedding vectors through pseudo-random matrices seeded with a secret key. Relevant distributions derived from the underlying algebra are evaluated and employed for statistical testing and benchmarking of DEW. Experimental results across multiple LLMs indicate that DEW improves post-paraphrase detection while maintaining competitive text quality, and remains detectable after translation, even when prior semantic watermarks degrade significantly. These findings position DEW as a practical and robust solution for safeguarding LLM-generated text and addressing critical issues in responsible AI deployment.

AI.tldr: DEW is a semantic watermarking scheme for LLMs that operates on both token and context embeddings using algebraic vector-space operations. It enhances robustness against paraphrasing and translation attacks while maintaining text quality, outperforming prior semantic watermarks in post-paraphrase and post-translation detection.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM watermarking methods lack robustness against semantic-preserving transformations like paraphrasing and translation, which can easily strip or degrade watermarks. A more resilient watermark is needed to reliably attribute LLM-generated text and support responsible AI deployment in real-world scenarios where text may be modified.
AI.method: DEW applies algebraic vector-space operations to both token-level and contextual embeddings to derive a watermark signal. The watermark is obfuscated via pseudo-random projection matrices keyed with a secret key. Statistical tests based on derived algebraic distributions are used for watermark detection. The signal is designed to degrade gracefully under semantic shifts rather than being destroyed entirely.
AI.result: DEW improves post-paraphrase detection accuracy across multiple LLMs compared to prior methods while preserving competitive text quality. Crucially, DEW remains reliably detectable after machine translation, whereas previous semantic watermarks degrade significantly under the same conditions.
AI.conclusion: DEW represents a practical and robust watermarking solution for LLM-generated text, effectively addressing vulnerabilities to paraphrasing and translation. Its dual-embedding, signal-processing-based approach positions it as a strong candidate for real-world responsible AI applications.

title: Can LLMs Imagine Moral Alternatives Beyond Binary Dilemmas?
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as moral advisors and agents, they need to address dilemmas between two competing values. However, existing research on LLMs with moral dilemmas overlooks a central aspect of human moral cognition: the ability to imagine alternatives that move beyond the given options. We introduce MoralAltDataset, a dataset of 307 moral dilemmas spanning narrative Advisor dilemmas and AI-facing Agent dilemmas, each augmented with compromise and reframed alternatives. We first examine whether humans and LLMs shift their judgments when such alternatives are introduced. Across 15 LLMs, we find that compromise alternatives are often preferred over either original option, substantially reshaping moral choice. We then evaluate the quality of LLM-generated alternatives against human-authored ones using pairwise preference and expert-based criteria. Results show that LLM-generated alternatives are often preferred and better satisfy fine-grained structural and ethical criteria, while revealing trade-offs between structural quality and practical feasibility.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MoralAltDataset, a dataset of 307 moral dilemmas augmented with compromise and reframed alternatives, and evaluates how 15 LLMs respond to such alternatives. LLMs often prefer compromise alternatives over original options, and LLM-generated alternatives are frequently preferred over human-authored ones in pairwise comparisons.
AI.motivation: Existing research on LLMs and moral dilemmas overlooks the human cognitive ability to imagine alternatives beyond given binary options. The paper aims to fill this gap by studying how LLMs handle compromise and reframed alternatives in moral decision-making.
AI.method: The authors built MoralAltDataset (307 dilemmas with Advisor and Agent scenarios, each with compromise and reframed alternatives). They tested 15 LLMs to see if judgments shift when alternatives are introduced. They then evaluated LLM-generated alternatives against human-authored ones using pairwise preference judgments and expert-based structural/ethical criteria.
AI.result: Compromise alternatives are often preferred over original options, significantly reshaping moral choice. LLM-generated alternatives are often preferred over human-authored ones and better satisfy fine-grained structural and ethical criteria, though trade-offs exist between structural quality and practical feasibility.
AI.conclusion: LLMs exhibit a strong inclination toward compromise alternatives when available, and can generate high-quality moral alternatives that rival or exceed human-authored ones. This highlights the importance of incorporating alternative imagination into LLM moral reasoning research.

title: HealthAgentBench: A Unified Benchmark Suite of Realistic Agentic Healthcare Environments for Challenging Frontier AI Agents
summary: As AI agents become increasingly capable of complex, long-horizon reasoning, rigorous and holistic evaluation is essential for measuring progress toward real-world healthcare applications. We introduce HealthAgentBench, a suite of 54 agentic healthcare tasks across 7 categories each with its unique environment. The benchmark suite spans diverse workflows throughout the patient journey and a broad range of modalities. Each task is designed to replicate an end-to-end clinical workflow: given minimal instructions, an agent must explore raw healthcare data, operate within a complex environment, and execute multi-step solutions that go beyond naive prompting. A final task success rate is reported to provide a single, interpretable metric for HealthAgentBench overall performance for each agent. Evaluating frontier agents on HealthAgentBench, we find that overall task success rate remains low, underscoring the difficulty of the suite. The strongest and the most cost effective agent, Codex GPT-5.5, achieves only approximately 42% success rate. Beyond aggregate performance, HealthAgentBench reveals nuanced strengths and weaknesses across task categories. Frontier agents show promise in automatically developing research modeling pipelines over EHR data, but medical imaging remains especially challenging, particularly for Claude Code models, while Codex GPT-5.5 shows emerging capability. Tasks that combine large search spaces with compositional reasoning requirements remain difficult for all current agents. Together, these results suggest that HealthAgentBench provides a challenging and realistic benchmark with substantial room for future progress. We release our benchmark at https://github.com/microsoft/HealthAgentBench.

AI.tldr: HealthAgentBench is a benchmark of 54 healthcare agent tasks across 7 categories, evaluating AI agents on end-to-end clinical workflows. Frontier agents struggle, with the best (Codex GPT-5.5) achieving only ~42% success rate. Medical imaging and compositional reasoning tasks prove especially hard.
AI.motivation: As AI agents advance toward complex, long-horizon reasoning, there is a lack of rigorous, holistic benchmarks for evaluating their real-world healthcare capabilities. Existing evaluations may not capture end-to-end clinical workflows that require exploration, environmental interaction, and multi-step reasoning beyond simple prompting.
AI.method: The authors introduce HealthAgentBench, a suite of 54 agentic healthcare tasks across 7 categories, each with a unique environment. Tasks span diverse patient-journey workflows and modalities. Each task provides minimal instructions; an agent must explore raw healthcare data, operate in a complex environment, and execute multi-step solutions. Performance is measured by a single final task success rate.
AI.result: Overall success rates are low. Codex GPT-5.5, the strongest and most cost-effective agent, reaches ~42%. Frontier agents perform relatively better on EHR-based research modeling pipelines but struggle with medical imaging (especially Claude Code). Tasks requiring large search spaces plus compositional reasoning remain unsolved across all agents.
AI.conclusion: HealthAgentBench presents a challenging, realistic benchmark with substantial room for progress. It reveals nuanced strengths and weaknesses across task categories, highlighting that current frontier agents are far from reliably handling complex healthcare workflows. The benchmark is publicly released.

title: Visualizing High-Dimensional Graph Embeddings via Informed Multi-View Projections
summary: Graphs are commonly visualized in 2D, where humans readily interpret spatial relationships, yet such layouts often distort higher-dimensional structure. We propose to embed graphs in high-dimensional space and search for informative 2D viewpoints that optimize aesthetic and readability metrics (e.g., edge crossings and angular resolution), enabled by a novel differentiable surrogate for edge crossings. Numerical experiments show that these viewpoints consistently outperform standard 2D layouts, and can even surpass methods explicitly designed to optimize these metrics. We further introduce DataFly, an interactive system for exploring multiple candidate viewpoints through seamless navigation. A usability study demonstrates that our approach reveals structural patterns that remain hidden in conventional 2D visualizations.

AI.tldr: Proposes embedding graphs in high-dimensional space and optimizing 2D viewpoints via a differentiable edge-crossing surrogate; demonstrates superior layout quality and introduces DataFly for interactive exploration.
AI.motivation: Standard 2D graph layouts distort higher-dimensional structure, and existing methods for optimizing aesthetic/readability metrics like edge crossings are limited. The authors aim to leverage high-dimensional embeddings to find better 2D projections.
AI.method: Graphs are embedded in high-dimensional space, then informative 2D viewpoints are searched by optimizing aesthetic and readability metrics (edge crossings, angular resolution). A key contribution is a novel differentiable surrogate for edge crossings, enabling gradient-based optimization. The DataFly interactive system supports navigating multiple candidate viewpoints.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show the optimized viewpoints consistently outperform standard 2D layouts and can surpass methods explicitly designed to optimize these metrics. A usability study demonstrates that DataFly reveals structural patterns hidden in conventional 2D visualizations.
AI.conclusion: High-dimensional embedding combined with differentiable metric optimization produces superior graph layouts. The approach, paired with the DataFly interaction system, enables discovery of structural patterns invisible in traditional 2D layouts.

title: Probing Stylistic Appropriation using Large Language Models: An Evaluation Framework for Copyright Infringement under EU Law
summary: Large language models (LLM) trained on web-scale corpora generate output that may infringe copyright, yet existing technical safeguards focus narrowly on verbatim memorisation. EU copyright doctrine applies a broader standards: substantial similarity, which extends to stylistic choices, narrative structure, and creative elaboration. This mismatch between what current methods detect and what the law protects leaves a significant compliance gap. We introduce PSALM, an LLM-as-a-judge framework that operationalises EU copyright doctrine through ten evaluators assessing computational overlap, stylistic dimensions (writing style, narrative voice), content dimensions (character, plot, scene, world building), and statutory exceptions (parody, pastiche, quotation, scènes à faire). Applying PSALM to Llama~3.2 models fine-tuned on translated historical Dutch literary works, we find that: 1) instruction-tuned models exhibit non-trivial baseline stylistic similarity prior to corpus exposure; 2) fine-tuning induces systematic stylistic appropriation across all infringement-relevant dimensions, extending beyond verbatim memorisation to abstract narrative patterns; 3) Negative Preference Optimisation unlearning substantially reduces similarity but leaves detectable residual stylistic patterns. These findings indicate that safeguards targeting literal copying alone are insufficient to mitigate broader copyright risks. PSALM provides infrastructure for auditable, legally informed compliance evaluation, though the relationship between automated similarity scores and infringement determinations requires validation by legal experts. This work bridges qualitative legal standards and quantitative technical measurement, exposing fundamental tensions between generative AI and EU intellectual property law.

AI.tldr: PSALM is an LLM-as-a-judge framework that operationalizes EU copyright doctrine through ten evaluators assessing computational, stylistic, content, and statutory exception dimensions. Applied to Llama 3.2 models fine-tuned on Dutch literary works, it reveals that fine-tuning induces systematic stylistic appropriation beyond verbatim memorization, and that Negative Preference Optimization unlearning reduces but does not eliminate residual stylistic patterns, exposing a compliance gap between technical safeguards and legal standards.
AI.motivation: Existing technical safeguards for copyright in LLMs focus narrowly on verbatim memorization, but EU copyright doctrine applies a broader "substantial similarity" standard encompassing stylistic choices, narrative structure, and creative elaboration. This mismatch creates a significant compliance gap between what current methods detect and what the law actually protects.
AI.method: PSALM (LLM-as-a-judge framework) with ten evaluators organized into four categories: computational overlap, stylistic dimensions (writing style, narrative voice), content dimensions (character, plot, scene, world building), and statutory exceptions (parody, pastiche, quotation, scènes à faire). Deployed on Llama 3.2 models fine-tuned on translated historical Dutch literary works.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) instruction-tuned models show non-trivial baseline stylistic similarity even before corpus exposure; (2) fine-tuning induces systematic stylistic appropriation across all infringement-relevant dimensions, extending beyond verbatim memorization to abstract narrative patterns; (3) Negative Preference Optimization unlearning substantially reduces similarity but leaves detectable residual stylistic patterns.
AI.conclusion: Safeguards targeting only literal copying are insufficient for broader copyright risks. PSALM provides auditable, legally informed compliance evaluation infrastructure, though validation by legal experts is needed for the relationship between automated scores and infringement determinations. The work bridges qualitative legal standards and quantitative measurement, exposing tensions between generative AI and EU IP law.

title: AI-Assisted Discovery of Convex Relaxations via Dual Agents
summary: Recent work shows that LLM agents can improve sharp-constant inequalities by searching for extremal constructions, which yield upper bounds. We address the complementary side: a lower bound holds for every admissible function and follows from a convex relaxation of the nonconvex problem, with tighter relaxations giving stronger bounds. We instantiate the autoresearch paradigm to discover such relaxations: a coding agent proposes valid tightening constraints, a theory agent verifies each one and searches for counterexamples, and every reported bound is certified by an explicit dual-feasible point checked in rigorous interval arithmetic. On two optimization constants studied by \citet{tao2025alphaevolve} - the first autocorrelation inequality ($C_{6.2}$) and the Erdős minimum-overlap constant ($C_{6.5}$) - we improve the certified lower bounds from $1.28$ to $1.2937$ and from $0.379005$ to $0.37912$, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an autoresearch paradigm for discovering convex relaxations that yield certified lower bounds for optimization constants. A coding agent proposes tightening constraints, a theory agent verifies them and searches for counterexamples, and bounds are certified via dual-feasible points in rigorous interval arithmetic. The method improves lower bounds on two constants from Tao (2025): the first autocorrelation inequality constant from 1.28 to 1.2937, and the Erdős minimum-overlap constant from 0.379005 to 0.37912.
AI.motivation: Prior work (Tao 2025) used LLM agents to find extremal constructions yielding upper bounds for sharp-constant inequalities. This paper addresses the complementary direction: deriving stronger certified lower bounds. Lower bounds hold for all admissible functions and arise from convex relaxations of nonconvex problems. The challenge is automatically discovering tighter relaxations to push these bounds upward.
AI.method: The authors propose an autoresearch paradigm with two cooperating agents: (1) a coding agent that proposes valid tightening constraints to strengthen the convex relaxation, and (2) a theory agent that verifies each proposed constraint and searches for counterexamples. Every reported bound is certified by an explicit dual-feasible point, checked using rigorous interval arithmetic to guarantee correctness.
AI.result: On two optimization constants from Tao (2025): (1) the first autocorrelation inequality constant C₆.₂ improved from certified lower bound 1.28 to 1.2937; (2) the Erdős minimum-overlap constant C₆.₅ improved from 0.379005 to 0.37912. Both improvements are numerically modest but rigorously certified.
AI.conclusion: The autoresearch paradigm successfully discovers tighter convex relaxations for sharp-constant inequalities, producing machine-verifiable, dual-certified lower bounds. This complements the upper-bound extremal search approach and points toward fully automated discovery of both bounds for optimization constants.

title: Can Tabular In-Context Learners Generalize to Biomolecular Property Prediction?
summary: Predicting biomolecular properties from limited labeled data is a central bottleneck in protein engineering and small-molecule design. As strong pretrained encoders now supply rich fixed-length representations, the difficulty has shifted from representation learning to building a data-efficient predictor for the few-shot regime. Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN3 and TabICL are unlikely candidates for this role: they are in-context learners pretrained on synthetic tables drawn from random causal graphs, a generative prior with no obvious correspondence to the processes that produce protein sequences or molecular graphs. That this tabular, causal inductive bias should transfer to biomolecular data at all is unintuitive, yet we find it does. Treating each method as a predictor-representation pair, we evaluate across two domains. Over a fixed ESMC representation, tabular in-context learning is consistently competitive for protein fitness regression on ProteinGym and a diverse esterase dataset. For small-molecule classification with ECFP/RDKit descriptors, no single pairing dominates across TDC ADMET, MoleculeNet, FS-Mol, and DrugOOD; representation choice becomes a primary determinant, as expected when the predictor's own prior is indifferent to molecular structure. We conclude that tabular foundation models are strong performers on biomolecular prediction tasks, but that their performance depends strongly on the sequence or molecular representation used.

AI.tldr: Tabular foundation models (TabPFN3, TabICL) pretrained on random causal graphs unexpectedly perform competitively on biomolecular prediction tasks in the few-shot regime, but their success is strongly contingent on the quality of the upstream sequence or molecular representation used.
AI.motivation: Scarcity of labeled biomolecular data limits predictive modeling in protein engineering and drug design. While pretrained encoders now provide rich fixed representations, efficient few-shot predictors remain a bottleneck. The authors investigate whether tabular foundation models—despite their causally-synthetic pretraining prior—can serve as effective data-efficient predictors for biomolecular tasks.
AI.method: The authors treat each approach as a predictor–representation pair and benchmark across two domains: (1) protein fitness regression using a fixed ESMC representation on ProteinGym and an esterase dataset; (2) small-molecule classification using ECFP/RDKit descriptors on TDC ADMET, MoleculeNet, FS-Mol, and DrugOOD. Tabular in-context learners (TabPFN3, TabICL) are compared against other predictor–representation combinations.
AI.result: For protein fitness regression with fixed ESMC representations, tabular in-context learning is consistently competitive. For small-molecule classification, no single predictor–representation pairing dominates across all benchmarks; representation choice emerges as the primary performance determinant, consistent with the predictor's prior being indifferent to molecular structure.
AI.conclusion: Tabular foundation models are strong performers on biomolecular few-shot prediction tasks, but their effectiveness is highly dependent on the representation. The unexpected transfer of a causal-tabular inductive prior to biomolecular data suggests new avenues for few-shot learning in protein and small-molecule domains.

title: When the Database Fails: Prompting LLM Dialogue Agents for Safe Recovery in Task-Oriented Dialogue
summary: Large language models used in task-oriented dialogue often produce fluent but unsafe responses when backend database calls fail, return empty results, or surface mismatched information, inventing venues, confirmations, or booking details not grounded in the database. We study a lightweight prompting-based recovery approach that improves robustness without retraining or additional model calls. We compare three response strategies, including a guided recovery prompt conditioned on structured database status, across six open-weight model families (DeepSeek-R1, Gemma-2, Llama-3, Mistral, Phi-3, and Qwen-2.5) and four database conditions: empty result, wrong-domain retrieval, API error, and clean retrieval. Using fault-injected benchmarks built on two structurally different datasets, MultiWOZ 2.2 (5 domains) and SGD (20 domains), we find that naive agents hallucinate on 30.5% of failure turns on MultiWOZ and 20.9% on SGD. Our Guided-Retry strategy reduces hallucination by 50% on MultiWOZ (30.5 to 15.3%) and by 42% on SGD (20.9 to 12.2%) without retraining. However, residual hallucination remains substantial (6-37% across models), with wrong-domain failures the hardest case. Results are consistent across both datasets and all six model families, and human annotation shows substantial agreement while supporting the validity of the automatic commitment-safety metric.

AI.tldr: LLMs in task-oriented dialogue hallucinate responses when backend database calls fail. A lightweight Guided-Retry prompting strategy reduces hallucination by ~42-50% without retraining, but residual errors persist, especially for wrong-domain failures.
AI.motivation: Task-oriented dialogue LLMs frequently produce fluent but factually incorrect (hallucinated) responses when backend database calls fail, return empty results, or retrieve mismatched information. Existing solutions often require retraining or additional model calls, motivating a lightweight, prompting-only recovery approach.
AI.method: The authors compare three response strategies, centered on a Guided-Retry prompt conditioned on structured database status. They evaluate six open-weight model families (DeepSeek-R1, Gemma-2, Llama-3, Mistral, Phi-3, Qwen-2.5) across four database conditions: empty result, wrong-domain retrieval, API error, and clean retrieval. Fault-injected benchmarks are built on MultiWOZ 2.2 (5 domains) and SGD (20 domains) datasets. Automatic evaluation uses a commitment-safety metric validated by human annotation.
AI.result: Naive agents hallucinate on 30.5% of failure turns (MultiWOZ) and 20.9% (SGD). Guided-Retry reduces hallucination by 50% on MultiWOZ (to 15.3%) and 42% on SGD (to 12.2%). Residual hallucination remains substantial (6–37% across models), with wrong-domain failures being the hardest case. Results are consistent across all six model families and both datasets. Human annotation shows substantial agreement with the automatic metric.
AI.conclusion: Prompting-based recovery with structured database status (Guided-Retry) significantly and consistently reduces hallucination across diverse models and datasets without retraining. However, non-trivial residual errors remain, particularly for wrong-domain failures, highlighting an open challenge for robust task-oriented dialogue systems.

title: Agentic RAG-VLM: Affordance-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Self-Reflective Planning for Robotic Grasping
summary: Generalizable robotic grasping in cluttered environments is essential for deploying manipulators in unstructured human spaces, yet existing VLM-based methods rely on visual similarity for object matching, neglecting physical affordances such as handle graspability and material fragility, and operate open-loop without spatial reasoning or failure recovery, limiting their effectiveness when objects are densely packed or physically diverse. We present Agentic RAG-VLM, a unified framework that bridges VLM-based semantic understanding and physically grounded grasp execution by integrating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with vision-language models (VLMs) and agentic self-reflective planning. Agentic RAG-VLM introduces three tightly coupled components: (1) a Hierarchical Affordance-Aware RAG (HAA-RAG) that encodes four-dimensional affordance descriptors, including type, material, fragility, and graspable region, and retrieves strategies by functional affordance compatibility rather than visual appearance; (2) a Scene Graph Constraint Reasoner that constructs spatial relationship graphs from VLM perception and translates proximity, occlusion, and support constraints into concrete grasp parameter adjustments; and (3) an Agentic Self-Reflective Pipeline with a 14-type failure taxonomy and three-level adaptive retry for closed-loop grasp refinement. Evaluated on a 12-task benchmark spanning single-grasp, interactive, and long-horizon scenarios with 360 trials per configuration, Agentic RAG-VLM achieves 78.3 percent overall success, a 53.3 percentage-point absolute gain over VLM-only baselines, demonstrating that affordance-aware retrieval, scene graph reasoning, and agentic recovery are jointly essential for robust manipulation.

AI.tldr: Agentic RAG-VLM combines retrieval-augmented generation with vision-language models and agentic self-reflective planning to enable physically grounded robotic grasping. It introduces affordance-aware retrieval, scene graph constraint reasoning, and a closed-loop failure recovery pipeline, achieving 78.3% success on a 12-task benchmark — a 53.3 percentage-point gain over VLM-only baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing VLM-based robotic grasping methods rely on visual similarity for object matching and operate in an open-loop manner without spatial reasoning or failure recovery. They neglect physical affordances such as handle graspability and material fragility, leading to poor performance in cluttered, physically diverse environments typical of unstructured human spaces.
AI.method: The framework comprises three tightly coupled components: (1) Hierarchical Affordance-Aware RAG (HAA-RAG) that encodes four-dimensional affordance descriptors (type, material, fragility, graspable region) and retrieves strategies by functional affordance compatibility; (2) a Scene Graph Constraint Reasoner that constructs spatial relationship graphs from VLM perception and translates proximity, occlusion, and support constraints into grasp parameter adjustments; and (3) an Agentic Self-Reflective Pipeline featuring a 14-type failure taxonomy with three-level adaptive retry for closed-loop refinement.
AI.result: Evaluated on a 12-task benchmark covering single-grasp, interactive, and long-horizon scenarios with 360 trials per configuration, Agentic RAG-VLM achieved 78.3% overall success, representing a 53.3 percentage-point absolute improvement over VLM-only baselines.
AI.conclusion: Affordance-aware retrieval, scene graph reasoning, and agentic failure recovery are jointly essential for robust robotic manipulation in cluttered environments. The results validate that bridging semantic VLM understanding with physically grounded execution significantly enhances generalizable grasping.

title: A Bayesian Filtering Approach for Learning Lagrangian Dynamics from Noisy Measurements
summary: This paper proposes a Bayesian filtering-based approach for learning the dynamics of a physical system from partial, noisy measurements. We model the system dynamics using a Lagrangian mechanics formulation. As in Lagrangian neural networks (LNNs), we parameterize the kinetic and potential energies with neural networks. The unknown external forces in the Lagrangian formulation are modeled as white Gaussian noise. The corresponding Euler--Lagrange equations then yield a continuous-time stochastic state-space model (SSM) that describes the system dynamics. The neural network parameters and system states are then jointly learned via a maximum-likelihood method using Gaussian-approximation-based Bayesian filters. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated on pendulum and Duffing oscillator examples, and its performance is compared with conventional LNNs and with approximate Bayesian filters using known system models.

AI.tldr: A Bayesian filtering framework is proposed for learning Lagrangian dynamics from partial, noisy observations, where kinetic/potential energies are parameterized by neural networks, external forces are modeled as white Gaussian noise, and joint state-parameter estimation is performed via Gaussian-approximate maximum-likelihood filtering.
AI.motivation: Conventional Lagrangian neural networks (LNNs) learn deterministic dynamics from clean, full-state observations and cannot handle partial, noisy measurements or explicitly account for stochastic external disturbances. This limits their applicability to real-world physical systems where sensor noise and incomplete observations are ubiquitous.
AI.method: The authors formulate system dynamics using Lagrangian mechanics with neural-network-parameterized kinetic and potential energies. Unknown external forces are treated as white Gaussian noise, yielding a continuous-time stochastic state-space model via the Euler-Lagrange equations. Neural network parameters and latent system states are jointly estimated using a maximum-likelihood approach based on Gaussian-approximation Bayesian filters (e.g., extended/unscented Kalman filters).
AI.result: The proposed method is validated on pendulum and Duffing oscillator examples, demonstrating effective learning of system dynamics from partial, noisy data.
AI.conclusion: The Bayesian filtering-based approach successfully extends LNNs to handle partial, noisy measurements and stochastic disturbances, outperforming conventional LNNs and matching the performance of approximate Bayesian filters that assume known system models.

title: LOPA: Enhancing Spoken Language Assessment via Latent Ordinal Prototype Alignment
summary: Fueled by increasing model scale and multimodal inputs, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for Spoken Language Assessment (SLA). While effective, this paradigm often overlooks the intrinsic ordinal structure of language acquisition. This paper works around the necessity of large-scale MLLMs by introducing Latent Ordinal Prototype Alignment (LOPA) for SLA, a prototype-based regularizer that enforces an ordinal geometric prior directly on the latent space. Coupled with Semantic-Anchored Layer Routing (SALR), which adaptively harvests multi-depth representations from a frozen Whisper encoder, our framework achieves an RMSE of 0.361. This performance rivals billion-parameter systems without the need for LLM-based fine-tuning. Further analysis reveals that SALR's synergy with LOPA offers interpretable, criterion-aligned preferences, thereby supporting an efficient and ordinal-aware modeling alternative to current scaling-centric models for SLA.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes LOPA (Latent Ordinal Prototype Alignment), a prototype-based regularizer enforcing ordinal structure on latent space, combined with SALR (Semantic-Anchored Layer Routing) for adaptive multi-depth feature extraction from a frozen Whisper encoder. Together, they achieve RMSE 0.361 on Spoken Language Assessment, rivaling billion-parameter MLLMs without LLM fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Current MLLM-based SLA approaches overlook the intrinsic ordinal structure of language acquisition (e.g., proficiency levels are ordered) and rely on massive model scale. The authors aim to provide an efficient, ordinal-aware alternative that captures this ordinal prior without requiring large-scale LLMs.
AI.method: Two key components: (1) LOPA — a prototype-based regularization that imposes an ordinal geometric prior on the latent space, aligning representations with ordered prototypes reflecting acquisition levels; (2) SALR — a routing mechanism that adaptively harvests multi-depth representations from a frozen Whisper encoder, using semantic anchors to select relevant layers. The framework avoids LLM fine-tuning entirely.
AI.result: The combined LOPA + SALR framework achieves an RMSE of 0.361 on SLA benchmarks, matching the performance of billion-parameter MLLM systems. SALR also provides interpretable, criterion-aligned layer preferences, demonstrating meaningful synergy with the ordinal prior.
AI.conclusion: Ordinal-aware modeling via prototype-based regularization and adaptive multi-depth feature harvesting offers a compelling, parameter-efficient alternative to scaling-centric MLLM approaches for Spoken Language Assessment, with the added benefit of interpretability.

title: Towards Inclusive Mobility Modeling: Characterizing and Evaluating Elderly Trajectory Patterns in Urban Systems
summary: The rapid advance of smart cities increasingly depends on trajectory data mining, yet underrepresented demographic groups, particularly the elderly, are often sparsely represented in public mobility datasets. This underrepresentation can introduce systematic bias into mobility modeling and downstream urban planning. Using the 2016-2020 Jersey City subset of the Citi Bike System Data, this study quantitatively examines how the absence of underrepresented subgroups' mobility signatures affects mobility modeling, using synthetic trajectory generation as a case study. The analysis reveals that elderly riders exhibit a structurally distinct mobility signature, including localized activity spaces (958 m vs. 1,189 m for young riders), lower mobility entropy (1.82 vs. 4.15), and asymmetric off-peak temporal patterns. To demonstrate that relying on majority-dominated training data yields biased synthetic outcomes, we further evaluate both a first-order Markov chain and a Qwen3-4B model fine-tuned with QLoRA across three demographic training settings: the full population, young riders only, and elderly riders only. Results show that models trained on majority-dominated populations systematically misrepresent elderly mobility behavior, particularly for spatial mobility metrics. The Markov model trained on the full population overestimates elderly step length by 4.5% and dwell time by 8.9%, whereas the elderly-specific model achieves substantially lower errors across most metrics. Comparisons between the Markov and LLM-based frameworks further show that higher-capability models do not necessarily improve subgroup-level fidelity under limited demographic data. These findings underscore the importance of demographic representation in mobility modeling and its downstream applications for underrepresented populations.

AI.tldr: Underrepresented elderly riders in bikeshare data exhibit distinct mobility patterns; models trained on majority-dominated populations systematically misrepresent elderly mobility, and higher-capability models do not necessarily improve subgroup fidelity under limited demographic data.
AI.motivation: Underrepresented demographic groups (especially the elderly) in public mobility datasets can introduce systematic bias into mobility modeling and downstream urban planning. The study aims to quantify how this underrepresentation affects synthetic trajectory generation.
AI.method: Using the 2016-2020 Jersey City Citi Bike dataset, the authors: (1) quantitatively characterize elderly vs. young rider mobility signatures (activity space, mobility entropy, temporal patterns); (2) train first-order Markov chain and Qwen3-4B (QLoRA fine-tuned) models under three demographic settings (full population, young-only, elderly-only); and (3) evaluate fidelity across spatial-temporal metrics.
AI.result: Elderly riders show localized activity spaces (958m vs 1,189m), lower entropy (1.82 vs 4.15), and asymmetric off-peak patterns. Full-population Markov models overestimate elderly step length by 4.5% and dwell time by 8.9%. Elderly-specific models achieve lower errors. LLM-based models did not improve subgroup-level fidelity over the Markov baseline under limited data.
AI.conclusion: Demographic representation matters critically in mobility modeling. Training on majority-dominated data yields biased synthetic outcomes for underrepresented subgroups, and model capacity alone cannot compensate for demographic data imbalance.

title: PPT-Eval: A Benchmark for Computer-Use Agents on PowerPoint Tasks
comment: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea. PMLR 306, 2026
summary: Creating and editing slides is a rich, multimodal activity that is ubiquitous in professional and educational settings, making it an ideal testbed for real-world computer-use agents. Microsoft PowerPoint is among the most widely adopted and feature-rich environments for presentation creation. We introduce PPT-Eval, a benchmark of 120 PowerPoint tasks across 12 files that cover both content creation and presentation editing scenarios, organized by difficulty. A central challenge in this domain is evaluation: tasks are complex, multimodal, and often admit many valid solutions. Moreover, today's agents frequently make only partial progress, which binary success metrics fail to capture. To address this, we design a robust evaluation framework to help create task-specific rubrics for PowerPoint tasks, taking inspiration from and building on past works for rubric-based evaluation. These rubrics award partial credit for intermediate steps, penalize unnecessary changes and poor aesthetics, and provide natural language feedback. This nuanced approach proves highly effective, achieving a Kendall's τ-b correlation of 0.77 with human judgments. We find that existing frontier agents still struggle with solving PowerPoint tasks, with strong models like Claude-4.5-Opus achieving only a 45% success rate and an average partial score of 57%. The benchmark is located at: https://microsoft.github.io/ppteval.

AI.tldr: PPT-Eval is a benchmark of 120 PowerPoint tasks across 12 files that evaluates multimodal agents on slide creation and editing. It introduces a rubric-based evaluation framework that awards partial credit and achieves 0.77 Kendall's τ-b correlation with human judgments. Frontier models like Claude-4.5-Opus reach only 45% success rate.
AI.motivation: Slide creation/editing is a ubiquitous, multimodal real-world activity ideal for testing computer-use agents, but existing evaluation metrics are binary and fail to capture partial progress. A robust, nuanced evaluation framework is needed to assess agent performance on complex PowerPoint tasks where many valid solutions exist.
AI.method: The authors construct PPT-Eval, a benchmark of 120 PowerPoint tasks across 12 files spanning content creation and editing, organized by difficulty. They design a task-specific rubric-based evaluation framework inspired by prior work, awarding partial credit for intermediate steps, penalizing unnecessary changes and poor aesthetics, and providing natural language feedback. Human judgment correlation is measured via Kendall's τ-b.
AI.result: The rubric-based evaluation achieves a Kendall's τ-b correlation of 0.77 with human judgments, validating its effectiveness. Frontier agents struggle: Claude-4.5-Opus achieves only 45% success rate and an average partial score of 57%, indicating significant room for improvement.
AI.conclusion: PPT-Eval provides a challenging, ecologically valid benchmark for multimodal computer-use agents, and the rubric-based evaluation framework offers a reliable, human-aligned alternative to binary success metrics for complex, multi-solution tasks.

title: BlockPilot: Instance-Adaptive Policy Learning for Diffusion-based Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates inference by using a lightweight draft model to generate candidate tokens in parallel, and are then verified by the target model, enabling lossless acceleration. Recently, diffusion-based speculative decoding further improves parallelism by generating multiple tokens per forward pass via block-level diffusion, achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance. However, existing methods adopt a fixed inference block size and assume a uniform optimal decoding strategy across all inputs. In this paper, we show that this assumption is suboptimal, as the optimal block size varies across samples and plays a critical role in speculative decoding performance. Moreover, these values exhibit a clear local structure, concentrating around the training block size, which reduces the problem to a low-dimensional and structured decision space. Based on these insights, we propose BlockPilot, a sample-adaptive policy that predicts the optimal block size from the prefilling representation. Specifically, we formulate block size selection as a lightweight policy learning problem and propose an instance-adaptive decision mechanism that predicts the optimal block size based on the representation of the prefilling stage. The prediction is performed only once after prefilling, allowing for seamless integration. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method is plug-and-play, introduces minimal overhead, and consistently improves efficiency, achieving an acceptance length of 5.92 and a 4.20$\times$ speedup on Qwen3-4B under temperature $T=1$.

AI.tldr: BlockPilot proposes a sample-adaptive policy that predicts the optimal block size for diffusion-based speculative decoding, showing that a fixed block size is suboptimal and that optimal values vary per sample but cluster around the training block size, achieving improved efficiency with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based speculative decoding methods use a fixed inference block size, assuming a uniform optimal strategy across all inputs. The authors demonstrate this is suboptimal — optimal block size varies significantly across samples and critically affects performance.
AI.method: BlockPilot formulates block size selection as a lightweight policy learning problem. It uses an instance-adaptive decision mechanism that predicts the optimal block size from the prefilling stage representation, requiring only a single prediction after prefilling. The approach exploits the observation that optimal block sizes exhibit local structure around the training block size, reducing the decision space to a low-dimensional, structured problem.
AI.result: BlockPilot achieves an acceptance length of 5.92 and a 4.20× speedup on Qwen3-4B at temperature T=1, with minimal overhead and plug-and-play integration.
AI.conclusion: Sample-adaptive block size selection consistently improves speculative decoding efficiency. The plug-and-play nature and low overhead make BlockPilot a practical enhancement over fixed-size approaches.

title: Long-term Traffic Simulation via Structured Autoregressive Modeling
summary: Interactive traffic simulation is a vital world model for autonomous driving. A central challenge in long-horizon simulation is modeling sustained multi-agent interactions, which is further exacerbated by dynamic token cardinality as agents continuously enter and exit the scene. In this work, we propose that the solution lies in the synergy between the architectural inductive biases and statistical priors of large-scale sequence models, e.g., Large Language Models (LLMs). Our probing experiments reveal that the transferability of attention mechanisms and the distributional consistency between motion tokens and natural language enable small-scale, heavily frozen LLMs to rapidly adapt to traffic modeling. Building on this insight, we introduce RosettaSim, a unified framework that projects scene topology, agent states, and spawning intents into a structured autoregressive stream with variable length, achieving both strong short-term accuracy and stable long-horizon simulation fidelity. Furthermore, evaluating extended rollouts presents yet another hurdle, as one-to-one agent correspondence inevitably fades over time. To address this, we introduce Retrieval-based Traffic Evaluation (RTE), which retrieves semantically similar real-world scenarios as context-aware reference anchors. Experiments on the Waymo Open Sim Agent Challenge (WOSAC) demonstrate that RosettaSim achieves state-of-the-art performance in both short- and long-term simulation. Furthermore, RTE exhibits a stronger correlation with standard metrics ($r=0.83$) than existing approaches ($r=0.74$), indicating improved alignment with long-horizon simulation fidelity.

AI.tldr: RosettaSim leverages frozen LLMs with structured autoregressive streams for long-horizon multi-agent traffic simulation, and introduces Retrieval-based Traffic Evaluation (RTE) for improved fidelity assessment, achieving SOTA on WOSAC.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon interactive traffic simulation faces two key challenges: (1) modeling sustained multi-agent interactions with dynamic token cardinality as agents enter/exit, and (2) evaluating extended rollouts where one-to-one agent correspondence degrades over time. Existing approaches struggle with both.
AI.method: RosettaSim projects scene topology, agent states, and spawning intents into a structured, variable-length autoregressive stream. It adopts small-scale, heavily frozen LLMs, exploiting the transferability of attention mechanisms and distributional consistency between motion tokens and natural language. For evaluation, RTE retrieves semantically similar real-world scenarios as context-aware reference anchors, replacing fading one-to-one agent correspondence.
AI.result: RosettaSim achieves state-of-the-art on both short- and long-term simulation in WOSAC. RTE shows stronger correlation with standard metrics (r=0.83) compared to existing approaches (r=0.74), indicating better alignment with long-horizon simulation fidelity.
AI.conclusion: The synergy between LLM architectural inductive biases and statistical priors enables effective traffic modeling with frozen small-scale LLMs. Combined with RTE for robust evaluation, this unified framework advances long-horizon interactive traffic simulation for autonomous driving.

title: ComplianceGate: Classifier-Gated Multi-Tier LLM Routing for Inference in Regulated Industries
summary: Large language models deployed in regulated industries operate under two constraints: compliance enforcement and cost efficiency. Personally identifiable information (PII) in user queries can reach model endpoints before the system determines whether that data should leave its jurisdictional boundary. Serving all queries through a single large model consumes full GPU capacity regardless of query complexity while offering no mechanism for geographic routing. Mixture-of-Experts architectures do not address this routing occurs between expert layers within the model after data has already arrived at the endpoint, with all experts loaded in memory regardless of query complexity. We propose a classifier-gated routing architecture that enforces compliance by design. A trained encoder classifier sits before any decoder inference, evaluating each query for complexity and data sensitivity, then routing it to an appropriately sized dense model in the appropriate geographic location. PII-containing queries route to local endpoints before any LLM computation begins, making data residency violations structurally impossible. Simple queries reach small, fast models at a fraction of the cost. Our evaluation on 600 queries demonstrates 39% median latency reduction, 33-52% cost savings depending on query distribution, and generation throughput of 122-200 tokens/second versus 50-64 for the baseline. The encoder classifier achieves 99.2% accuracy with near-perfect PII recall at 7ms inference overhead, establishing pre-inference classification as a practical path to compliance-by-design LLM deployment.

AI.tldr: A paper proposing a classifier-gated routing architecture for LLM deployment that enforces data compliance (PII containment) and reduces cost by classifying queries before inference and routing them to appropriately sized models in the correct geographic region. Achieves 39% latency reduction, 33-52% cost savings, and 99.2% classification accuracy with 7ms overhead.
AI.motivation: Regulated industries face two constraints: compliance enforcement (PII must not leave jurisdictional boundaries) and cost efficiency (using large models for all queries wastes GPU capacity). Existing Mixture-of-Experts architectures fail because routing occurs internally after data reaches the endpoint, and all experts remain loaded regardless of query complexity. A structural solution is needed that prevents data residency violations before any LLM computation begins.
AI.method: A classifier-gated routing architecture: a trained encoder classifier sits before any decoder inference, evaluating each query for complexity and data sensitivity (PII detection), then routes it to an appropriately sized dense model in the appropriate geographic location. PII-containing queries are routed to local endpoints before LLM computation starts. Simple queries go to small, fast models; complex queries go to larger models.
AI.result: Evaluation on 600 queries: 39% median latency reduction, 33-52% cost savings (distribution-dependent), generation throughput of 122-200 tokens/second vs. 50-64 baseline. Encoder classifier achieves 99.2% accuracy with near-perfect PII recall at only 7ms inference overhead.
AI.conclusion: Pre-inference classification via an encoder classifier is a practical path to compliance-by-design LLM deployment, structurally eliminating data residency violations while simultaneously improving latency and cost efficiency.

title: Linguistic Bias Mitigation for Spoofing Detection via Gradient Reversal and A Variational Information Bottleneck
summary: Rapid advancements in generative speech technology have compromised the reliability of voice biometrics. While current spoofing detectors excel when assessed under in-domain conditions, generalisation to out-of-domain settings is often poor. We show that this can be due to linguistic bias. A reliance on linguistic cues observed in training data can then compromise robustness to cross-data. We propose a linguistic-invariant spoofing detection framework utilizing teacher-student adversarial learning. The linguistic-aware teacher model, pre-trained on linguistic content of an external dataset, guides the student detector via gradient reversal to minimize the linguistic information. To prevent the inadvertent removal of non-linguistic cues, we incorporate a Variational Information Bottleneck to enable suppression of principal cues. Across nine DF Arena datasets, our method achieves up to a 36.2% relative reduction in the EER compare to the baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a linguistic-invariant spoofing detection framework using teacher-student adversarial learning with a Variational Information Bottleneck to suppress linguistic cues in training data, achieving up to 36.2% relative reduction in EER across nine DF Arena datasets.
AI.motivation: Current voice spoofing detectors generalize poorly to out-of-domain settings due to linguistic bias — models inadvertently rely on linguistic cues present in training data rather than genuine spoofing artifacts, compromising cross-data robustness.
AI.method: A teacher-student adversarial learning framework: (1) a linguistic-aware teacher model pre-trained on linguistic content guides a student detector; (2) gradient reversal is used to minimize linguistic information in the student's representations; (3) a Variational Information Bottleneck (VIB) is incorporated to preserve non-linguistic cues while suppressing principal linguistic ones.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves up to a 36.2% relative reduction in Equal Error Rate (EER) compared to the baseline across nine DF Arena datasets.
AI.conclusion: Linguistic-invariant learning via adversarial teacher-student distillation with VIB effectively mitigates linguistic bias, substantially improving cross-dataset generalization in voice anti-spoofing.

title: Thinking Before Retrieving: Robust Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval via Strategic Planning and Self-Criticism
summary: Composed image retrieval requires identifying a target image from a gallery by integrating a reference image with a textual modification instruction. In a training-free zero-shot setting, this task relies on constructing a retrieval-oriented textual query within a frozen vision--language embedding space at inference time. Existing approaches predominantly rely on a single-pass generation strategy that fuses the reference context and modification text into a unified description. This strategy makes it difficult to detect or correct semantic distortions and omissions during generation. Consequently, the preservation of reference attributes and the integration of textual requirements interfere with each other, which degrades retrieval precision. To address these challenges, we introduce PEC-CIR, a training-free framework that structures query construction as a multi-stage reasoning pipeline. The framework operates through a Planner--Executor--Critic architecture where the Planner extracts explicit constraints, the Executor generates multiple candidate target descriptions, and the Critic evaluates these candidates based on constraint compliance. By reframing query construction as a staged inference process instead of a single-pass output, PEC-CIR reduces the propagation of generative errors by explicitly evaluating candidate queries before retrieval, thereby improving retrieval stability.

AI.tldr: PEC-CIR proposes a training-free, multi-stage reasoning framework (Planner–Executor–Critic) for composed image retrieval that improves retrieval precision by decomposing query construction into explicit constraint extraction, candidate generation, and constraint-compliance evaluation, rather than relying on error-prone single-pass generation.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free zero-shot composed image retrieval methods use single-pass generation to fuse reference image context and modification text into a unified query, causing semantic distortions and omissions to go undetected. This leads to interference between preserving reference attributes and integrating textual requirements, degrading retrieval precision.
AI.method: PEC-CIR introduces a Planner–Executor–Critic pipeline operating in a frozen vision–language embedding space. The Planner extracts explicit constraints from the reference image and modification text. The Executor generates multiple candidate target descriptions. The Critic evaluates each candidate against the extracted constraints, and the best-scoring candidate is used for the final retrieval query.
AI.result: By reframing query construction as staged inference with explicit candidate evaluation, PEC-CIR reduces generative error propagation and improves retrieval stability compared to single-pass baselines, all without any training.
AI.conclusion: Multi-stage reasoning with a Planner–Executor–Critic architecture effectively addresses the error-propagation weaknesses of single-pass query generation in zero-shot composed image retrieval, yielding more reliable retrieval without requiring task-specific training.

title: AETDICE: Unified Framework and Offline Optimization for Nonlinear Multi-Objective RL
summary: Optimizing nonlinear preferences in multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) is essential for capturing complex trade-offs like risk aversion or fairness. However, such non-linearity has historically bifurcated nonlinear MORL objectives into two distinct paradigms: Scalarized Expected Return (SER) and Expected Scalarized Return (ESR). While SER requires global-level optimization and ESR requires non-Markovian policies, leading to fragmented optimization strategies, we bridge this divide through the Aggregation-Expectation-Transformation (AET) framework. By unifying both criteria through a tripartite decomposition of scalarization, AET provides a principled foundation for general nonlinear MORL. Building on this framework, we propose AETDICE, a tractable offline RL algorithm for AET objectives. By utilizing DICE-style density-ratio estimation in an augmented state space, AETDICE enables sample-based optimization from static datasets. Our framework resolves long-standing barriers and captures respective trade-offs induced by AET framework, which existing methods fail to address.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Aggregation-Expectation-Transformation (AET) framework that unifies the two historically separate paradigms in nonlinear multi-objective RL — Scalarized Expected Return (SER) and Expected Scalarized Return (ESR) — and introduces AETDICE, a practical offline RL algorithm based on DICE-style density-ratio estimation for optimizing AET objectives from static datasets.
AI.motivation: Nonlinear preferences in MORL (e.g., risk aversion, fairness) create a fundamental divide: SER requires global-level optimization while ESR demands non-Markovian policies, resulting in fragmented, incompatible optimization strategies. A unified framework is needed to bridge this gap and enable general nonlinear MORL.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Aggregation-Expectation-Transformation (AET) framework, which decomposes scalarization into three sequential stages — aggregation, expectation, and transformation — thereby subsuming both SER and ESR under a single principled formulation. Building on this, they develop AETDICE, an offline RL algorithm that employs DICE-style density-ratio estimation in an augmented state space to perform sample-based optimization from static datasets.
AI.result: AETDICE successfully captures the respective trade-offs induced by the AET framework that existing methods cannot address, resolving the long-standing incompatibility between SER and ESR optimization approaches.
AI.conclusion: The AET framework provides a unified theoretical foundation for general nonlinear MORL, and AETDICE demonstrates its practical tractability in offline settings, overcoming barriers that have historically fragmented the field.

title: Clinically Structured Rank-Gated LoRA for Cross-Benchmark Medical Question Answering
summary: Medical multiple-choice question answering requires parameter-efficient adaptation across heterogeneous knowledge domains and reasoning operations. A medication question, a diagnostic decision, a public-health item, and a nursing-action item may require different low-rank updates, while some recall items should preserve the base model's representation with only mild adapter intervention. We propose BiRG-LoRA, a single-adapter rank-gated LoRA method for medical question answering. BiRG-LoRA keeps one LoRA module per target layer but makes its rank dimension input-conditioned: for each question, a biaxial gate combines hidden semantic evidence with specialty/profession priors, clinical-operation priors, and their interaction to select a sparse top-$k$ subset of rank atoms. A scalar injection coefficient further controls the strength of the selected adapter update. Under a matched Qwen3-8B CMB-source protocol, BiRG-LoRA achieves the highest four-benchmark macro-average accuracy among trainable PEFT baselines and matched routing controls: 69.31% averaged over CMB, CMExam, MedQA, and MedMCQA. It improves over MoELoRA by 0.89 percentage points while using 28.1% fewer trainable parameters; a paired, benchmark-stratified bootstrap over final predictions gives a 95% confidence interval of [0.42, 1.37] for this macro-average gain. Basic controls show that BiRG-LoRA also improves over vanilla LoRA r16 and active-rank-matched LoRA r4 by 0.83 macro points, and an evaluation-time weak-axis perturbation check suggests that performance is not brittle to moderate tag noise. The results support a bounded claim: clinically structured rank allocation improves cross-benchmark medical QA under a matched single-seed protocol, while training-seed variance remains future work.

AI.tldr: BiRG-LoRA introduces input-conditioned, biaxial-gated sparse rank selection within a single LoRA adapter, achieving state-of-the-art cross-benchmark medical QA accuracy with 28.1% fewer parameters than MoELoRA.
AI.motivation: Medical QA spans heterogeneous knowledge domains (medication, diagnosis, public health, nursing) and reasoning types; uniform low-rank adaptation is suboptimal because different question categories benefit from different adapter capacities. Some factual recall items need minimal intervention, while complex clinical reasoning items need stronger adaptation. Existing PEFT methods lack fine-grained, input-conditional control over adapter rank allocation.
AI.method: BiRG-LoRA deploys a single LoRA module per target layer with an input-conditioned rank dimension. A biaxial gate fuses hidden semantic evidence from the input with specialty/profession priors, clinical-operation priors, and their interaction to select a sparse top-k subset of rank atoms. A scalar injection coefficient further modulates the adapter update strength. Evaluated under a matched Qwen3-8B CMB-source protocol on four benchmarks: CMB, CMExam, MedQA, and MedMCQA.
AI.result: BiRG-LoRA achieves 69.31% macro-average accuracy across four benchmarks, outperforming MoELoRA by 0.89 points (95% CI: [0.42, 1.37]) with 28.1% fewer trainable parameters. It also surpasses vanilla LoRA r16 and active-rank-matched LoRA r4 by 0.83 macro points. An evaluation-time weak-axis perturbation check shows robustness to moderate tag noise.
AI.conclusion: Clinically structured rank allocation improves cross-benchmark medical QA performance under a matched single-seed protocol. Training-seed variance remains unaddressed and is left for future work.

title: Agentic-Ideation: Sample Efficient Agentic Trajectories Synthesis for Scientific Ideation Agents
summary: Ideation plays a pivotal role in scientific discovery. Recent LLM, especially AI Scientist systems, show promising potential for automated ideation. However, existing approaches predominantly rely on pre-defined agentic workflows. This constraint severely limits the flexibility required to navigate the vast search space of scientific literature and the complex action space of research reasoning. Recently, training Agentic LLMs has emerged as a promising direction, offering flexible reasoning frameworks and the capability for autonomous tool utilization.
