However, there remains a non-trivial challenge: applying previous agentic data synthesis methods to scientific ideation suffers from prohibitively high data synthesis cost. To bridge this gap, we propose Agentic-Ideation, a novel framework comprising an automated trajectory synthesis pipeline and a specialized agentic LLM trained for scientific ideation. Specifically, we first define a comprehensive tool space incorporating three external tools and three cognitive tools. Then we introduce an Oracle-Guided Data Synthesis strategy. By leveraging a reference idea as oracle guidance, this approach steers the multi-agent system to efficiently reconstruct the logical reasoning and tool invocation paths, transforming aimless trial-and-error into directed trajectory generation. Finally, we train the agent on these synthesized trajectories, employing a masking strategy on tool execution results. This ensures the model focuses on decision-making logic without interference from external feedback. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms the SOTA workflow-based baseline by \textbf{11.91\%} in overall quality. Furthermore, our approach improves the sample efficiency of high-quality data synthesis by \textbf{over 10$\times$}.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Agentic-Ideation, a framework that trains a specialized agentic LLM for automated scientific ideation using an Oracle-Guided Data Synthesis strategy to efficiently generate reasoning trajectories, achieving 11.91% improvement over workflow-based baselines and over 10× better sample efficiency in high-quality data synthesis.
AI.motivation: Current AI Scientist systems for automated scientific ideation rely on rigid pre-defined agentic workflows, limiting flexibility in navigating vast literature search spaces and complex research reasoning. While training agentic LLMs offers a solution, applying existing data synthesis methods to scientific ideation incurs prohibitively high costs. The work aims to bridge this gap.
AI.method: The authors propose Agentic-Ideation with three components: (1) a comprehensive tool space with three external tools and three cognitive tools; (2) an Oracle-Guided Data Synthesis strategy that uses a reference idea as oracle guidance to steer a multi-agent system toward efficient, directed trajectory generation rather than aimless trial-and-error; and (3) training an agentic LLM on these synthesized trajectories with a masking strategy on tool execution results to focus learning on decision-making logic.
AI.result: The trained agentic LLM outperforms the SOTA workflow-based baseline by 11.91% in overall ideation quality. Additionally, the Oracle-Guided Data Synthesis strategy improves the sample efficiency of high-quality data synthesis by over 10× compared to previous agentic data synthesis methods.
AI.conclusion: Training specialized agentic LLMs with oracle-guided trajectory synthesis is an effective and data-efficient approach for automated scientific ideation, overcoming the inflexibility of workflow-based systems and the high cost of naive agentic data synthesis.

title: Transformers as Bayesian In-Context Experimenters: Smoothness-Adaptive Efficient ATE Estimation
summary: Adaptive experiments for average treatment effects (ATE) require randomized allocations balancing valid inference with statistical efficiency. The oracle design is a covariate-dependent Neyman rule governed by unknown arm-conditional outcome variances. We investigate whether this sequential variance-estimation and allocation process can be amortized via in-context learning. We introduce Bayesian in-context experimenters: transformer policies trained to imitate a Bayesian posterior Neyman teacher. The teacher updates nonparametric beliefs over potential outcomes using experimental history to assign posterior Neyman treatment probabilities. This design converges to the oracle rule, supporting efficient ATE inference. Transformers constructively implement this mapping through attention-based sufficient statistics and projected gradient descent, imitating Bayesian updating for Gaussian-series priors. To address unknown outcome smoothness, we combine smoothness-indexed experimenters using a mixture-of-experts transformer. The gate acts as a hierarchical posterior over smoothness classes, concentrating on near-oracle experts. By bounding the complexity of the transformer class, we prove this amortized policy can be learned via empirical risk minimization using supervised pretraining. Experiments confirm accurate teacher imitation, adaptive allocation, and improved ATE precision over baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using transformer-based policies trained via supervised pretraining to imitate a Bayesian posterior Neyman teacher for adaptive experiments. This amortizes the sequential variance-estimation and allocation process, achieving efficient ATE inference that converges to the oracle Neyman rule. A mixture-of-experts architecture handles unknown outcome smoothness, and theoretical guarantees are provided via empirical risk minimization bounds.
AI.motivation: Adaptive experiments for ATE estimation face a fundamental tension: randomized allocations must balance valid inference with statistical efficiency. The optimal oracle design — a covariate-dependent Neyman allocation — requires knowledge of unknown arm-conditional outcome variances, which must be estimated sequentially from accumulating experimental data. This sequential estimation-and-allocation process is computationally and statistically challenging. The authors ask whether this entire process can be amortized through in-context learning, replacing explicit sequential Bayesian updating with a pretrained transformer that directly maps experimental history to treatment probabilities.
AI.method: The authors introduce Bayesian in-context experimenters: transformer policies trained via supervised learning to imitate a Bayesian posterior Neyman teacher. The teacher maintains nonparametric beliefs (modeled as Gaussian-series priors) over potential outcomes, updating them with experimental history, and assigns treatment probabilities according to the posterior Neyman rule. The transformer implements this mapping constructively using attention-based sufficient statistics and projected gradient descent, structurally mimicking Bayesian updating. To handle unknown outcome smoothness (e.g., Lipschitz constants), they employ a mixture-of-experts transformer where distinct expert modules correspond to different smoothness indices, and a learned gate acts as a hierarchical posterior over smoothness classes, concentrating probability on near-oracle experts. Theory shows the amortized policy is learnable via empirical risk minimization by bounding the complexity (covering number) of the transformer class.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that transformer policies accurately imitate the Bayesian posterior Neyman teacher, achieve adaptive allocation that converges toward the oracle Neyman design, and yield improved ATE estimation precision compared to baseline adaptive experimental designs.
AI.conclusion: Amortizing sequential Bayesian experimental design via in-context learning with transformers is both theoretically grounded and empirically effective. The mixture-of-experts architecture provides a principled approach to handling unknown smoothness parameters, and the constructive alignment between attention mechanisms and Bayesian updating offers a compelling framework for adaptive experimentation.

title: Revising RVL-CDIP: Quantifying Errors and Test-Train Overlap
summary: RVL-CDIP is a popular dataset for benchmarking document classifiers. However, the dataset contains ample amounts of label errors as well as non-trivial amounts of test-train overlap, both of which may impact model performance metrics. In this paper, we address these two problems by (1) finding and fixing label errors, and (2) detecting and addressing test-train overlap. We produce several variations of RVL-CDIP with label error and test-train overlap fixes, and benchmark document classification performance on these new RVL-CDIP variations. Our rigorous analysis of RVL-CDIP finds that the corpus contains 12\% label error and approximately 35% test-train duplication. Remediation sees improvements in classification accuracy when errors are removed, but sees decreases in accuracy when duplicates are removed. We additionally evaluate models on RVL-CDIP-N, an out-of-distribution benchmark, finding that training on error-corrected data substantially improves OOD generalization, with supervised models gaining an average of 8.1 percentage points in accuracy and improvements as large as 14 percentage points.

AI.tldr: RVL-CDIP, a popular document classification benchmark, suffers from ~12% label errors and ~35% test-train overlap. The authors produce cleaned variants of the dataset, showing that fixing label errors improves both in-distribution accuracy and out-of-distribution generalization (up to +14 pp), while removing duplicates paradoxically decreases accuracy.
AI.motivation: RVL-CDIP is widely used for benchmarking document classifiers, but its label errors and test-train overlap may distort model performance metrics, leading to unreliable conclusions about model quality and generalization ability.
AI.method: The authors systematically audit RVL-CDIP by: (1) identifying and correcting label errors through manual inspection and automated detection, (2) detecting test-train overlap via near-duplicate and exact-duplicate detection techniques, and (3) creating multiple cleaned dataset variants. They then benchmark document classifiers (both supervised and pre-trained models) on these variants and on RVL-CDIP-N, an out-of-distribution benchmark.
AI.result: The audit reveals 12% label error rate and ~35% test-train duplication. Correcting label errors improves classification accuracy. However, removing test-train duplicates decreases accuracy, suggesting models may overfit to or exploit these overlaps. On out-of-distribution evaluation (RVL-CDIP-N), training on error-corrected data yields substantial gains: supervised models improve by an average of 8.1 percentage points, with gains as high as 14 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Label errors and test-train overlap significantly affect RVL-CDIP benchmarking results. Dataset cleaning is essential for reliable evaluation, particularly for assessing out-of-distribution generalization. The cleaned dataset variants provide more trustworthy benchmarks for future document classification research.

title: Delta-JEPA: Learning Action-Sensitive World Models via Latent Difference Decoding
summary: Learning visual world models for planning requires compact latent dynamics that remain sensitive to actions, yet reconstruction-free joint-embedding objectives can collapse to action-insensitive representations. We propose Delta-JEPA, an end-to-end reconstruction-free world model that augments latent forward prediction with a Latent Difference Action Decoder (LDAD). Unlike inverse decoders that infer actions from concatenated endpoint embeddings, LDAD reconstructs the executed action from the latent displacement between consecutive observations. This displacement-level supervision directly regularizes transition geometry: adjacent embeddings cannot collapse without losing action information, and different actions are encouraged to induce distinguishable latent changes for rollout-based planning. Delta-JEPA uses only latent prediction and action reconstruction, avoiding pixel reconstruction and distribution-matching regularizers. Across four visual continuous-control tasks, Delta-JEPA improves planning over JEPA-based and representation-learning world model baselines. Ablations show that displacement-based action decoding is consistently more effective than endpoint concatenation, and action-sensitivity analyses show clearer action-conditioned latent responses. These results indicate that supervising latent differences is a simple and effective mechanism for collapse-resistant and action-sensitive world model learning.

AI.tldr: Delta-JEPA introduces a reconstruction-free world model that prevents representational collapse by supervising latent differences between consecutive observations, using a Latent Difference Action Decoder that reconstructs actions from displacement vectors rather than concatenated endpoints, yielding improved action-sensitive representations for visual planning.
AI.motivation: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPA) for world modeling are desirable because they avoid costly pixel reconstruction, but they are prone to representational collapse where the latent space becomes insensitive to actions — a critical failure for planning. Existing solutions (contrastive losses, distribution matching, stop-gradient) add complexity and may still yield suboptimal action conditioning. The core insight is that a mechanism directly supervising the latent transition geometry itself could prevent collapse more elegantly.
AI.method: Delta-JEPA is an end-to-end reconstruction-free world model with two key components: (1) a latent forward predictor that predicts future latent states from current latents and actions, and (2) a Latent Difference Action Decoder (LDAD) that reconstructs the executed action from the latent displacement vector (z_{t+1} - z_t) rather than from the concatenation of endpoint embeddings. The action reconstruction loss directly regularizes the transition geometry: embeddings cannot collapse without losing action-discriminative information, and distinct actions must produce distinguishable latent changes. The model requires neither pixel reconstruction nor distribution-matching regularizers.
AI.result: Across four visual continuous-control tasks (DMControl and Meta-World), Delta-JEPA outperforms JEPA-based baselines and representation-learning world models in planning. Ablations demonstrate that displacement-based action decoding consistently outperforms endpoint concatenation decoding. Action-sensitivity analyses reveal clearer action-conditioned latent responses, confirming that the latent space is more responsive to different actions.
AI.conclusion: Supervising latent differences via action reconstruction from displacement vectors is a simple, effective mechanism for learning collapse-resistant, action-sensitive world models without pixel-level reconstruction, with direct benefits for rollout-based planning in visual control tasks.

title: ISM:Self-Improving Strategy Memory for Continual Mathematical Reasoning
comment: 3rd AI for Math Workshop at ICML 2026 Forty-Third International Conference on Machine Learning
summary: We propose Intelligent Schema Memory (ISM), a self-evolving memory-augmented system that improves mathematical reasoning for a frozen LLM under continual learning with hard episodic resets. ISM maintains a compact, self-refined bank of strategy schemas learned from both successful and failed episodes, with symbolic tools that check intermediate steps and certify answers.Without updating model parameters, ISM outperforms passive, retrieval, and reflection baselines on MATH-Hard and OlympiadBench, using 64% and 86% fewer schemas respectively than the strongest passive baseline. These results show that small, actively maintained, and verified strategy memories can support reliable continual mathematical reasoning under strict episodic isolation.

AI.tldr: ISM is a self-evolving memory system that stores verified strategy schemas from both successes and failures, enabling a frozen LLM to continually improve mathematical reasoning under hard episodic resets without parameter updates, outperforming larger passive baselines on MATH-Hard and OlympiadBench.
AI.motivation: Frozen LLMs struggle with continual mathematical reasoning improvement under strict episodic isolation, where each problem episode is independent and no parameter updates are allowed. Existing passive or retrieval-based memory approaches are inefficient, requiring large schema banks. The authors aim to achieve reliable continual reasoning with a compact, actively maintained, and self-verified memory.
AI.method: ISM maintains a compact bank of strategy schemas learned from both successful and failed reasoning episodes. It employs symbolic tools to check intermediate reasoning steps and certify final answers, ensuring schema quality. The memory self-evolves through refinement — adding validated strategies, pruning redundant or incorrect ones — all without updating the frozen LLM's parameters. The system operates under hard episodic resets (continual learning setup) where each new problem is treated in isolation.
AI.result: ISM outperforms passive memory, retrieval-based, and reflection baselines on MATH-Hard and OlympiadBench benchmarks. Critically, it uses 64% fewer schemas than the strongest passive baseline on MATH-Hard and 86% fewer on OlympiadBench, demonstrating that a small, actively verified memory can surpass larger uncurated schema banks.
AI.conclusion: Small, actively maintained, and verified strategy memories can support reliable continual mathematical reasoning under strict episodic isolation. The combination of learning from failures, symbolic verification, and self-refinement is more effective than simply scaling up passive memory storage.

title: Team MKC at CLPsych 2026: Capturing and Characterizing Mental Health Changes through Social Media Timeline Dynamics
summary: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have motivated their adoption across a wide range of domains, including Artificial Intelligence (AI) for mental health. Given the growing prevalence of mental health disorders worldwide and the limited accessibility of professional care, there is an increasing demand for scalable computational approaches that can assist in early detection and continuous monitoring of psychological well-being. In this area, ongoing efforts have focused on curating domain-specific datasets and leveraging them to develop LLMs capable of supporting holistic mental health analysis. In line with this direction, we propose an LLM-based pipeline for comprehensive mental health analysis over sequentially ordered user posts, as part of the CLPsych shared task. Our pipeline offers a unified framework that jointly enables post-level assessment and user-level temporal modeling.

AI.tldr: Proposes an LLM-based pipeline for comprehensive mental health analysis that jointly performs post-level assessment and user-level temporal modeling on sequentially ordered user posts, developed for the CLPsych shared task.
AI.motivation: The growing prevalence of mental health disorders and limited access to professional care create demand for scalable computational approaches. LLMs offer potential for early detection and continuous monitoring, but holistic analysis requires both post-level and temporal user-level modeling.
AI.method: An LLM-based pipeline that provides a unified framework for joint post-level assessment and user-level temporal modeling over sequentially ordered user posts, developed in the context of the CLPsych shared task.
AI.result: Not explicitly stated in the provided abstract.
AI.conclusion: Not explicitly stated in the provided abstract.

title: Embodied CAD: Solver-Grounded LLM Agents for Parametric B-Rep Assembly Modeling
comment: This paper contains 12 pages, 7 figures. This is an original unpublished manuscript submitted to the arXiv preprint server, with no prior publication or conference presentation
summary: Large language models can write plausible CAD scripts, but reliable industrial CAD modeling requires more than syntactically valid code: every feature, placement, and assembly relation must be accepted by an exact geometric kernel while remaining editable as parametric boundary representation geometry. We present Embodied CAD, solver-grounded LLM agents for parametric B-Rep assembly modeling. Instead of generating a complete script in one pass, the agent iteratively selects actions from a stratified L0-L4 CAD skill library, resolves them into typed geometric operations, executes them in a CAD backend, and uses solver feedback to plan, repair, and learn. The framework combines action grammar constraints, deterministic parameter resolution, and solver-derived rewards for supervised warm-up and GRPO-style refinement. We evaluate Embodied CAD on multi-step mechanical, industrial equipment, and mold-oriented assembly tasks using solver-aligned metrics: executable rate, skill accuracy, operation-family accuracy, exact policy accuracy, and task completion success. The results show that solver-grounded planning executes all strong-planner workflows in the current benchmark, while learned controllers reach high executable rates and expose the remaining gap between valid tool calls and exact long-horizon policy prediction.

AI.tldr: Embodied CAD is a solver-grounded LLM agent framework for parametric B-Rep assembly modeling that iteratively selects CAD actions from a stratified skill library, executes them with solver feedback, and uses supervised warm-up plus GRPO refinement to achieve high executable rates on mechanical and industrial assembly tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLMs can generate syntactically valid CAD scripts but fail to meet the demands of industrial CAD modeling, where every feature, placement, and assembly relation must be accepted by an exact geometric kernel and remain editable as parametric B-Rep geometry. Single-pass script generation lacks the closed-loop verification needed for reliable, kernel-compliant modeling.
AI.method: The Embodied CAD framework uses an LLM agent operating within a CAD backend that iteratively selects actions from a stratified L0–L4 skill library (action grammar constraints), resolves them into typed geometric operations via deterministic parameter resolution, executes them, and receives solver-derived rewards. Training combines supervised warm-up on expert demonstrations with GRPO-style reinforcement refinement. Evaluation uses solver-aligned metrics: executable rate, skill accuracy, operation-family accuracy, exact policy accuracy, and task completion success.
AI.result: Solver-grounded planning executes all strong-planner workflows in the benchmark. Learned controllers achieve high executable rates, though a gap remains between generating valid tool calls and predicting exact long-horizon policies.
AI.conclusion: Solver-grounded, iterative action selection with feedback significantly improves executable CAD modeling over single-pass generation. The remaining gap in exact policy accuracy highlights the challenge of long-horizon geometric reasoning, motivating future work on closing this loop.

title: Building an ASR Solution for Training and Assessing Children's Reading
summary: Automatic speech recognition for children's reading remains underdeveloped for most African languages, including Bambara, despite its potential value for reproducible literacy assessment. We present an open-source system for assessing children's reading in Bambara, developed through an end-to-end process linking field data collection, benchmark construction, model adaptation, a reading application, and classroom validation. A mobile collection and assessment app was used to collect 55 hours of raw reading speech from 60 children, from which we construct a public benchmark for Bambara child-reading assessment. Fine-tuning experiments compare Soloni, a Bambara-adapted Fast-Conformer ASR framework with TDT and CTC decoders, with QuartzNet, a compact convolutional ASR architecture. The best Soloni model reduces WER from 0.42 to 0.22 and CER from 0.15 to 0.08, substantially outperforming QuartzNet on the isolated benchmark. The experiments further show that repeated readings of the same texts provide architecture-dependent benefits: they substantially improve QuartzNet but add only marginal gains for Soloni, while SpecAugment regulates training without exceeding the best unaugmented configuration. Disaggregated analysis identifies children under 10 as the main source of residual errors, motivating targeted collection from younger readers. Ten classroom trials supported continued use of the application.

AI.tldr: An open-source ASR system for assessing children's Bambara reading was built end-to-end, linking field data collection (55h from 60 children), benchmark creation, model fine-tuning, app deployment, and classroom validation. A Bambara-adapted Fast-Conformer (Soloni) achieved a WER of 0.22 and CER of 0.08, substantially outperforming QuartzNet, with disaggregated analysis showing children under 10 as the primary error source.
AI.motivation: Automatic speech recognition for children's reading assessment is largely absent for most African languages, including Bambara, limiting the potential for scalable, reproducible literacy evaluation. The authors aim to close this gap by developing and validating a complete, open-source pipeline for Bambara child-reading assessment.
AI.method: A mobile app was used to collect 55 hours of reading speech from 60 children, from which a public benchmark was constructed. Two ASR architectures were fine-tuned and compared: Soloni (a Bambara-adapted Fast-Conformer with TDT and CTC decoders) and QuartzNet (a compact convolutional ASR). Experiments examined the effects of repeated readings and SpecAugment. Disaggregated analysis and ten classroom trials were conducted for validation.
AI.result: Soloni reduced WER from 0.42 to 0.22 and CER from 0.15 to 0.08, substantially outperforming QuartzNet. Repeated readings significantly improved QuartzNet but offered only marginal gains for Soloni. SpecAugment regularized training but did not surpass the best unaugmented configuration. Children under 10 were the main source of residual errors.
AI.conclusion: The end-to-end system demonstrates viable ASR-based child reading assessment for Bambara. The Soloni Fast-Conformer architecture is strongly preferred over QuartzNet for this task. Targeted data collection from younger readers is needed to address remaining error sources, and classroom trials confirmed the application's practical viability.

title: Spatial Reasoning via Modality Switching Between Language and Symbolic Representation
summary: Human reasoning is inherently multimodal: when problems become difficult, we rarely think in words alone. We often externalize our reasoning by sketching diagrams or drawing grids to understand the underlying conceptual structure and avoid mistakes. Building on this premise, our research investigates: (a) whether grounding multi-hop textual-spatial stories into geometry-aware modalities, such as layouts or grids, improves reasoning compared to natural language-based inference; and (b) whether a model can decide when to rely on natural language reasoning and when to switch to a structured modality. We address these questions by introducing a switching metric based on trustworthiness and complexity signals, which estimates when grounding a spatial story into structure is likely to improve performance. This takes a first step toward principled modality selection in Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning. Across our settings, switching from natural language-based reasoning to a grid-based representation improves LLM performance by up to 42\%, highlighting the importance of modality choice in shaping reasoning outcomes.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether translating textual-spatial reasoning problems into structured visual modalities (grids/layouts) improves LLM performance, and whether models can learn when to switch modalities. A switching metric based on trustworthiness and complexity signals is introduced, with grid-based representations improving performance by up to 42%.
AI.motivation: Humans naturally externalize difficult reasoning into diagrams and spatial structures, yet LLMs predominantly reason in natural language. The authors question whether this language-only paradigm limits performance on multi-hop textual-spatial problems, and whether principled modality selection can bridge the gap between how humans and models reason.
AI.method: The authors propose a switching metric that combines trustworthiness and complexity signals to determine when a spatial story should be grounded into a structured modality (grid/layout) rather than reasoned over in natural language. The approach is evaluated on multi-hop textual-spatial reasoning tasks, comparing language-only inference against modality-switching strategies across different LLM settings.
AI.result: Switching from natural language-based reasoning to grid-based representations improves LLM performance by up to 42%. The switching metric effectively identifies when structured grounding is beneficial, demonstrating that modality choice significantly shapes reasoning outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Grounding textual-spatial reasoning into geometry-aware modalities substantially improves LLM performance over pure language-based inference. Principled modality selection — deciding when to switch representations — is a promising direction for enhancing LLM reasoning, taking a first step toward more human-like, multimodal reasoning strategies.

title: Learning Gaussian Graphical Models from a Glauber Trajectory Without Mixing
summary:
We study the task of learning the structure of a $d$-sparse Gaussian graphical model on $n$ variables from a single trajectory of Glauber dynamics. Beyond algorithmic considerations, many applications present temporally correlated observations rather than i.i.d.\ samples. In the classical i.i.d.\ setting, under comparably general sparsity and minimum edge-strength assumptions, sublinear-in-$n$ sample guarantees are known, but achieving them in polynomial-time remains open. Motivated in part by this gap, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that recovers the conditional-independence graph from a single Glauber trajectory, with a trajectory-length guarantee that does not depend on the mixing time.
  Technically, our algorithm has three components. First, we estimate the conditional variances and rescale the trajectory to reduce to the unit-diagonal case, without changing the underlying graph. Second, we design a local edge test that extracts adjacency information from short update windows by isolating pairwise influence. Third, we aggregate these local statistics using a robust median-based estimator, and prove accuracy despite temporal dependence arising from a single trajectory.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a polynomial-time algorithm for learning Gaussian graphical models from a single trajectory of Glauber dynamics, with sample complexity that does not depend on mixing time, addressing a gap where sublinear sample guarantees were known but polynomial-time algorithms were lacking in the i.i.d. setting.
AI.motivation: Many real-world applications involve temporally correlated observations rather than i.i.d. samples. While sublinear-in-n sample guarantees exist for learning Gaussian graphical models under sparsity assumptions in the i.i.d. setting, achieving these guarantees in polynomial time remains an open problem. This gap motivates developing algorithms that can efficiently learn from dependent data, specifically a single Glauber dynamics trajectory.
AI.method: The algorithm has three components: (1) estimation of conditional variances and rescaling the trajectory to the unit-diagonal case without altering the underlying graph structure; (2) a local edge test that extracts adjacency information from short update windows by isolating pairwise influence; (3) aggregation of local statistics using a robust median-based estimator, with proof of accuracy despite temporal dependence from the single trajectory.
AI.result: The algorithm recovers the conditional-independence graph of a d-sparse Gaussian graphical model from a single Glauber trajectory in polynomial time, with trajectory-length guarantee independent of the mixing time.
AI.conclusion: Polynomial-time structure learning of sparse Gaussian graphical models is achievable from a single Glauber dynamics trajectory without requiring mixing time dependence, overcoming a key barrier present in the i.i.d. setting through careful exploitation of the temporal update structure.

title: FinPersona-Bench: A Benchmark for Longitudinal Psychometric Stability of Autonomous Financial Agents
comment: 29 pages, includes figures and tables; formalizes Mandate Salience Decay and introduces FinPersona-Bench
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous financial agents initialized with explicit behavioral mandates such as "preserve capital" or "avoid speculative bets" that are meant to govern every decision throughout deployment. In practice, however, as market context accumulates over long horizons, these mandates gradually lose their behavioral influence, a phenomenon we formalize as Mandate Salience Decay (MSD). To measure MSD objectively, we introduce FinPersona-Bench, a simulation benchmark in which a synthetic market decouples observable price from hidden fundamental value, enabling falsifiable evaluation across three failure modes: trading without signal in calm markets, panic-selling during crashes, and ignoring fundamental value during speculative bubbles. Evaluating 18 leading frontier and open-source LLMs, each assigned one of three behavioral profiles ranging from strict capital preservation to aggressive growth, shows that MSD compounds over time and is model-dependent. In crash scenarios, the behavioral gap between static agents and those receiving periodic mandate re-grounding grows 4.4x from the first to the final quarter of the simulation. The effects of mandate re-grounding are not uniformly positive: it consistently helps conservative agents in low-signal markets but actively worsens behavior for aggressive agents in the same setting. These findings suggest that reliable long-horizon deployment requires selective, mandate-aware re-grounding based on agent profile and market regime.

AI.tldr: LLM-based financial agents suffer from Mandate Salience Decay (MSD), where behavioral mandates lose influence over long horizons. The authors introduce FinPersona-Bench to measure this across 18 LLMs and find MSD is model-dependent and compounds over time; selective mandate re-grounding helps conservative agents but harms aggressive ones.
AI.motivation: LLMs deployed as autonomous financial agents are initialized with explicit behavioral mandates (e.g., "preserve capital"), but these mandates gradually lose influence as market context accumulates over long horizons — a phenomenon the authors formalize as Mandate Salience Decay (MSD). No benchmark existed to systematically and falsifiably measure this decay across models and behavioral profiles.
AI.method: The authors introduce FinPersona-Bench, a simulation benchmark where a synthetic market decouples observable price from hidden fundamental value. This enables evaluation across three failure modes: (1) trading without signal in calm markets, (2) panic-selling during crashes, and (3) ignoring fundamental value during speculative bubbles. They evaluate 18 frontier and open-source LLMs, each assigned one of three behavioral profiles (strict capital preservation to aggressive growth), and test the effect of periodic mandate re-grounding versus static deployment.
AI.result: MSD compounds over time and is model-dependent. In crash scenarios, the behavioral gap between static agents and re-grounded agents grows 4.4× from the first to the final quarter. Re-grounding effects are non-uniform: it consistently benefits conservative agents in low-signal markets but actively worsens behavior for aggressive agents in the same setting.
AI.conclusion: Reliable long-horizon deployment of LLM financial agents requires selective, mandate-aware re-grounding tailored to both the agent's behavioral profile and the prevailing market regime, rather than uniform periodic reminders.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Floating-Point Error Classification
summary: This paper investigates the capability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to detect and classify floating-point errors statically in software code. We introduce InterFLOPBench, a benchmark of 90 C kernels with 1 130 test samples designed to evaluate LLMs across six categories of floating-point error: cancellation, comparison, division by zero, overflow, underflow and NaN, compared across 14 LLMs. The evaluation framework treats floating-point error detection as a multi-label classification problem and employs the F1-score metric to measure performance. Results demonstrate that latest models (Qwen 3 32b, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Phi 4 Reasoning, DeepSeek R1T2, and gpt-oss 20b and 120b) achieve a performance greater than 0.88 overall F1-score. Performance varies between error categories, between explicit operations such as division by zero (Average F1-score: 0.8479) and more subtle numerical phenomena such as underflow (Average F1-score: 0.6059) and cancellation (Average F1-score: 0.6164).

AI.tldr: InterFLOPBench is a benchmark of 90 C kernels with 1,130 test samples for evaluating LLMs on static detection of six floating-point error types. Across 14 LLMs, top models achieve >0.88 overall F1-score, but performance varies significantly by error category—division by zero is well-detected (~0.85), while underflow (~0.61) and cancellation (~0.62) remain challenging.
AI.motivation: Floating-point errors (cancellation, overflow, underflow, division by zero, NaN, comparison issues) are pervasive, subtle bugs in numerical software that are difficult to detect statically. The work investigates whether modern LLMs can serve as effective static analyzers for these errors, providing a systematic evaluation where none previously existed.
AI.method: The authors introduce InterFLOPBench, a curated benchmark comprising 90 C kernels with 1,130 test samples spanning six floating-point error categories. Floating-point error detection is framed as a multi-label classification problem. Fourteen LLMs are evaluated using the F1-score metric across all error categories. Models compared include Qwen 3 32b, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Phi 4 Reasoning, DeepSeek R1T2, and gpt-oss (20b, 120b).
AI.result: The best-performing models (Qwen 3 32b, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Phi 4 Reasoning, DeepSeek R1T2, gpt-oss 20b/120b) achieve overall F1-scores above 0.88. However, performance is highly category-dependent: division by zero has the highest average F1-score (0.8479), while underflow (0.6059) and cancellation (0.6164) are significantly harder to detect, reflecting the difficulty of identifying subtle numerical phenomena versus explicit illegal operations.
AI.conclusion: LLMs show strong potential for static floating-point error detection, with top models exceeding 0.88 F1-score. However, their reliability is uneven: obvious errors like division by zero are handled well, but nuanced issues like cancellation and underflow remain substantial challenges, highlighting areas needing further improvement before LLM-based static analysis can be trusted for safety-critical numerical code.

title: TDGT: A Tabular Data Generation Toolkit supporting adaptive GPU-accelerated Bayesian mixture models, diffusion-based models, and latent-space generative modeling
comment: 47 pages (33 main body, 14 pages supplementary material), 30 figures (12 figures in the main body, 18 supplementary figures), 9 tables (3 tables in the main body, 6 supplementary tables)
summary: The growing demand for privacy-preserving data sharing has positioned synthetic data generation as a critical component of responsible AI workflows. Despite notable advances in generative modeling, existing solutions often lack integration of adaptive generation strategies, multi-metric evaluation, and accessible end-to-end generators within a unified web-based toolkit. In this work, we introduce TDGT (Tabular Data Generation Toolkit), a web-based toolkit for synthetic tabular data generation and fidelity assessment. TDGT introduces the Adaptive Bayesian Mixture Synthesizer (ABMS), a novel algorithm that autonomously determines the optimal number of mixture components through iterative cluster quality optimization, eliminating the need for manual hyperparameter configuration. Building upon ABMS, we further propose VAE-ABMS, a hybrid architecture that couples Variational Autoencoder-based latent space learning with adaptive Bayesian mixture synthesis, enabling high-fidelity generation of complex, nonlinear tabular distributions. For large-scale scenarios, TDGT provides a GPU-accelerated variant of ABMS leveraging CUDA-based k-means clustering and Gaussian mixture fitting. Synthetic data fidelity is assessed through eleven statistical fidelity metrics spanning distributional divergence, structural correlation, and sample-level similarity, complemented by privacy risk indicators including k-anonymity scoring and disclosure rate estimation. The web-based toolkit supports a real-time streaming interface with interactive Plotly-based visualizations. TDGT is assessed across datasets from healthcare, socioeconomic modeling, and cybersecurity domains, demonstrating consistent generation fidelity and statistical coherence across heterogeneous feature types and data scales.

AI.tldr: TDGT is a web-based toolkit for synthetic tabular data generation featuring ABMS (Adaptive Bayesian Mixture Synthesizer), VAE-ABMS hybrid architecture, and GPU-accelerated variants, with integrated multi-metric fidelity assessment and privacy risk evaluation, validated across healthcare, socioeconomic, and cybersecurity datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing synthetic data generation solutions lack unified integration of adaptive generation strategies, comprehensive multi-metric evaluation, and accessible end-to-end generation within a single web-based toolkit, particularly for tabular data where privacy-preserving sharing is increasingly critical.
AI.method: TDGT introduces: (1) ABMS — autonomously determines optimal mixture components via iterative cluster quality optimization, eliminating manual hyperparameter tuning; (2) VAE-ABMS — a hybrid coupling VAE latent space learning with adaptive Bayesian mixture synthesis for complex nonlinear distributions; (3) GPU-accelerated ABMS using CUDA-based k-means and Gaussian mixture fitting for large-scale scenarios. Fidelity is assessed through 11 statistical metrics (distributional divergence, structural correlation, sample-level similarity) plus privacy indicators (k-anonymity scoring, disclosure rate estimation). The toolkit features a real-time streaming web interface with Plotly visualizations.
AI.result: TDGT demonstrated consistent generation fidelity and statistical coherence across heterogeneous feature types and data scales in healthcare, socioeconomic modeling, and cybersecurity domains.
AI.conclusion: TDGT addresses the gap in unified synthetic data generation toolkits by combining adaptive Bayesian mixture synthesis, VAE-enhanced hybrid generation, and GPU acceleration with comprehensive statistical and privacy evaluation, all accessible through a web-based interface.

title: AutoTrainess: Teaching Language Models to Improve Language Models Autonomously
summary: Training language models (LMs) remains a highly human-intensive process, even as frontier language model agents become increasingly capable at software engineering and other long-horizon tasks. A central challenge is that autonomous post-training is not just a coding problem: it requires the agent to repeatedly plan iterations, construct benchmark-aligned data, run stable training jobs, evaluate checkpoints, and preserve experiment state across many hours of interaction. We present AutoTrainess, a LM agent that exposes these operations as a repository of agent-computer interfaces for planning, data preparation, training, evaluation, and logging. Rather than leaving the agent to operate in a raw CLI environment with an underspecified action space, AutoTrainess externalizes prior human experience as explicit workflows, rules, and execution constraints that guide the agent toward effective and reliable training behavior. On PostTrainBench, AutoTrainess consistently outperforms CLI-only baselines, achieving 26.94 average score with GPT-5.4 (Codex) versus 23.21 for CLI-only. It also generalizes across models and harnesses, improving DeepSeek-V4-Flash (OpenCode) from 12.13 to 19.58.

AI.tldr: AutoTrainess is an LM agent that structures the post-training workflow through explicit agent-computer interfaces (planning, data prep, training, evaluation, logging), outperforming CLI-only baselines by guiding agents with workflows, rules, and constraints rather than leaving them in underspecified shell environments.
AI.motivation: Autonomous post-training of language models is hindered not by coding difficulty but by the need to orchestrate multi-step, long-horizon processes: planning iterations, constructing benchmark-aligned data, running stable training jobs, evaluating checkpoints, and preserving experiment state. Raw CLI environments provide an underspecified action space that fails to capture prior human expertise, leading to unreliable agent behavior.
AI.method: AutoTrainess exposes a repository of agent-computer interfaces that externalize prior human experience as explicit workflows, rules, and execution constraints for five key operations: planning, data preparation, training, evaluation, and logging. This structured environment replaces raw CLI interaction, guiding the agent toward effective training behavior. Evaluation is conducted on PostTrainBench across multiple model and harness combinations.
AI.result: AutoTrainess with GPT-5.4 (Codex) achieves 26.94 average score on PostTrainBench vs. 23.21 for CLI-only baselines. It also generalizes across model families, improving DeepSeek-V4-Flash (OpenCode) from 12.13 to 19.58.
AI.conclusion: Structuring the agent-computer interface with explicit workflows and constraints — rather than relying on raw CLI access — significantly improves the reliability and effectiveness of autonomous LM post-training agents, and the approach generalizes across different underlying models and evaluation harnesses.

title: HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic: Multi-Hop Question Answering Corpus for Historical Research, Parliamentary Debates from the French Third Republic (1870-1940)
summary: We present HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic: a French-language dataset of multi-hop historical questions derived from parliamentary debates and newspapers of the French Third Republic. Designed in collaboration with a historian, the corpus captures complex reasoning patterns typical of historical inquiry, including cross-source synthesis, temporal reasoning, and the integration of sparse evidence. The dataset is made of 1782 questions and emphasizes multi-hop connections across heterogeneous historical documents, providing a resource for evaluating retrieval-augmented and large language model systems in domain-specific contexts. We describe the methodology for constructing the corpus, including the selection and alignment of sources, question validation, and metadata integration. While the dataset focuses on French historical documents, our methodology can be readily adapted to other languages and national corpora. Finally, we demonstrate how the corpus can support realistic evaluation scenarios for multi-hop question answering, bridging the gap between NLP benchmarks and the needs of historical scholarship.

AI.tldr: A French-language multi-hop QA dataset (1782 questions) built from Third Republic parliamentary debates and newspapers, designed with a historian to benchmark retrieval-augmented and LLM systems on complex historical reasoning tasks like cross-source synthesis and temporal inference.
AI.motivation: Existing NLP benchmarks fail to capture the nuanced, multi-hop reasoning required in historical scholarship — particularly cross-source synthesis, temporal reasoning, and sparse-evidence integration — and no such resource exists for French historical documents, creating a gap between NLP evaluation and domain-specific historical research needs.
AI.method: The authors collaborated with a historian to construct HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic by: (1) selecting and aligning heterogeneous sources (parliamentary debates and newspapers from the French Third Republic); (2) crafting 1,782 multi-hop questions requiring reasoning across multiple documents; (3) validating questions for historical accuracy and reasoning complexity; and (4) integrating rich metadata to support diverse evaluation scenarios.
AI.result: The resulting dataset contains 1,782 multi-hop questions grounded in heterogeneous historical documents, designed to support realistic evaluation of retrieval-augmented and large language model systems on domain-specific, cross-source historical reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic bridges the gap between NLP benchmarks and historical scholarship by providing a linguistically and domain-specialized resource for multi-hop QA evaluation. The methodology is language-agnostic and transferable to other national corpora, and the dataset enables more ecologically valid assessments of RAG and LLM systems in real-world historical research scenarios.

title: The Calibration Turn in AI-Assisted Research: A Conceptual and Methodological Framework for Evidence-Licensed Claims
comment: 42 pages, 4 figures. Companion code and synthetic simulation artifacts: https://github.com/Li-Hongmin/calibration-turn-ai-assisted-research
summary: AI-assisted research has entered a stage in which the central question is not only whether systems can generate hypotheses, run experiments, or produce manuscripts, but whether their scientific claims are calibrated to the evidence that supports them. This Perspective-style paper develops a conceptual and methodological framework for evidence-licensed claims in AI-assisted research. Motivated by representative routes including specialized scientific foundation models, LLM research assistants, multi-agent co-scientists, AI Scientist pipelines, mathematical discovery agents, and self-driving laboratories, it represents AI-assisted research as five operators: hypothesis generation, model-mediated consequence derivation, external validation, belief update, and claim calibration. The central claim is that calibration is not merely cautious wording but a mechanism for managing scientific assertion rights: evidence licenses some forms of speech and withholds others. The paper distinguishes linguistic, consequence-based, interventional, and evidence-licensed semantics; defines the claim-evidence gap and epistemic debt; and treats minimal structural reconstruction across heterogeneous outputs as an upward form of claim calibration. AISim-Cal is included as an illustrative synthetic dynamics exercise, not as an empirical forecast or benchmark. The resulting principles are: no claim without license, validation does not determine claim level, and automation amplifies the need for calibration. Reliable AI-assisted research is therefore evaluated as a loop that generates hypotheses, derives testable consequences, accepts independent adjudication, updates beliefs, and outputs only evidence-licensed claims.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework for "evidence-licensed claims" in AI-assisted research, arguing that calibration—matching scientific claims to evidential support—is a mechanism for managing "scientific assertion rights." It models AI-assisted research through five operators (hypothesis generation, consequence derivation, external validation, belief update, claim calibration), distinguishes four semantic types, and establishes principles ensuring that automated systems output only claims proportionate to their evidential warrant.
AI.motivation: AI-assisted research now spans hypothesis generation, experimentation, and manuscript production across diverse paradigms (foundation models, multi-agent co-scientists, self-driving labs). The central concern has shifted from whether these systems can perform scientific tasks to whether their claims are properly calibrated to supporting evidence. Current systems risk generating overconfident or unqualified claims that outstrip their evidential basis, creating a need for principled mechanisms to license scientific assertions.
AI.method: The paper develops a conceptual framework by (1) abstracting AI-assisted research into five core operators, (2) distinguishing four semantic types—linguistic, consequence-based, interventional, and evidence-licensed semantics, (3) formally defining the claim-evidence gap and epistemic debt, (4) treating minimal structural reconstruction across heterogeneous outputs as upward calibration, and (5) providing AISim-Cal as a synthetic dynamics exercise for illustration. Three normative principles are derived: no claim without license, validation does not determine claim level, and automation amplifies calibration need.
AI.result: The framework yields a closed-loop evaluation model: reliable AI-assisted research must generate hypotheses, derive testable consequences, submit to independent adjudication, update beliefs, and output only evidence-licensed claims. The claim-evidence gap and epistemic debt concepts provide measurable constructs for assessing calibration failures. The AISim-Cal exercise demonstrates synthetic dynamics but is explicitly not an empirical forecast.
AI.conclusion: Calibration is not merely rhetorical caution but a fundamental mechanism for managing scientific assertion rights—evidence licenses some claims and withholds others. Reliable AI-assisted research requires treating calibration as a first-class design constraint, with the loop of generation, validation, belief updating, and evidence-licensed output serving as the evaluative standard.

title: CryoACE: An Atom-centric Framework for Accurate and Automated Model Building in Cryo-EM
summary: Protein automodeling from cryo-EM density maps faces unique challenges in enforcing physicochemical validity and managing conformational heterogeneity. Current solvers are often limited to static predictions or require computationally intensive heuristic searches. We present CryoACE, an end-to-end framework that reconstructs precise atomic graphs for both homogeneous and heterogeneous structures. Our method features two key innovations: an atom-centric reconstruction paradigm, where density features are sampled directly at atomic coordinates and iteratively recycled to refine structures, replacing expensive voxel convolutions for efficient multimodal fusion; and a training-free guidance mechanism that leverages predicted local resolution priors to resolve dynamic ambiguity. Validated on a newly constructed high-quality dataset, CryoACE significantly outperforms existing baselines on static benchmarks and, for the first time, unveils atomic-level dynamic conformations on complex real-world datasets like EMPIAR-10345 without relying on pre-built static structures.

AI.tldr: CryoACE is an end-to-end framework for atomic protein modeling from cryo-EM density maps that uses atom-centric reconstruction and resolution-prior guidance to handle both static and dynamically heterogeneous structures, outperforming baselines and revealing atomic-level conformations without pre-built static models.
AI.motivation: Existing cryo-EM protein modeling methods struggle with enforcing physicochemical validity, handling conformational heterogeneity, and are limited to static predictions or computationally expensive heuristic searches. There is a need for a unified framework that can reconstruct both homogeneous and heterogeneous structures efficiently.
AI.method: CryoACE introduces two key innovations: (1) an atom-centric reconstruction paradigm that samples density features directly at atomic coordinates and iteratively recycles them for structure refinement, replacing costly voxel convolutions; and (2) a training-free guidance mechanism using predicted local resolution priors to resolve dynamic ambiguity in heterogeneous structures.
AI.result: On a newly constructed high-quality dataset, CryoACE significantly outperforms existing baselines on static benchmarks. It also demonstrates, for the first time, atomic-level dynamic conformations on complex real-world datasets such as EMPIAR-10345 without requiring pre-built static structures.
AI.conclusion: CryoACE advances cryo-EM-based protein structure determination by unifying static and dynamic modeling in a single, efficient framework, enabling atomic-level insight into conformational heterogeneity that was previously inaccessible without prior structural knowledge.

title: Revisiting the Volume Hypothesis
summary: Modern deep neural networks often contain far more parameters than needed to fit their training data, yet they achieve impressive generalization. A common explanation for this success is the implicit bias of stochastic gradient descent (SGD). An alternative volume hypothesis posits that, within low training-loss regions, loss-landscape basins leading to strong generalization occupy much larger regions of weight space than basins that generalize poorly, and therefore SGD is simply more likely to land in the former. Recent experimental explorations of this idea present seemingly contradictory results. While in one set of experiments randomly sampling the network weights until achieving zero training error yielded poor generalization, molecular dynamics density estimates supported the volume hypothesis. We observe that these experiments were performed at different dataset size regimes, and explore an intermediate regime using the Replica Exchange Wang-Landau algorithm to estimate the joint density of states over training and test accuracies in binary networks. Across several architectures and datasets, we show that the generalization advantage of gradient learning over random sampling training generally diminishes as the training data size grows, suggesting a resolution of the paradox.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates a paradox between conflicting experimental results regarding the "volume hypothesis" of generalization. Using Replica Exchange Wang-Landau sampling, the authors demonstrate that the generalization advantage of SGD over random weight sampling diminishes as training set size increases, thereby reconciling previous contradictory findings that arose from experiments conducted at different dataset size regimes.
AI.motivation: Prior experiments testing the volume hypothesis — which posits that SGD generalizes well because high-generalization basins occupy larger volumes in weight space — produced contradictory results: random sampling to zero training error yielded poor generalization, while molecular dynamics density estimates supported the hypothesis. The authors identify that these experiments were conducted at different dataset sizes and seek to resolve this apparent paradox.
AI.method: The authors employ the Replica Exchange Wang-Landau (REWL) algorithm to estimate the joint density of states over training and test accuracies in binary neural networks. They systematically explore an intermediate dataset size regime across multiple architectures and datasets, enabling comparison between gradient-based learning (SGD) and random sampling of weights that achieve zero training error.
AI.result: The generalization advantage of gradient-based learning over random sampling consistently diminishes as training data size increases. At small dataset sizes, SGD significantly outperforms random sampling; at large dataset sizes, the gap closes substantially, reconciling the previously contradictory experimental findings.
AI.conclusion: The volume hypothesis and SGD implicit bias are not mutually exclusive explanations. Rather, their relative importance depends on the dataset size regime. The paradox in prior work arose because experiments were conducted at different points along this spectrum, and the intermediate regime explored here provides a unifying resolution.

title: CLExEval: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework for Qualitative Evaluation of LLM Clinical Reasoning
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve strong results on many medical benchmarks, but their clinical reasoning remains difficult to evaluate reliably. A central risk is an evaluation illusion: fluent and well-structured explanations can appear clinically convincing even when the final diagnosis is incorrect. We introduce CLExEval, a human-in-the-loop framework for evaluating LLM clinical reasoning under progressive information masking. CLExEval combines 5,600 expert-physician annotations with 200 clinical reasoning traces derived from 40 rare diagnostic cases. Our analysis identifies three recurring failure patterns: (i) verbosity bias, where GPT-4o-mini's diagnostic accuracy drops from 95.0% to 32.5% under information scarcity; (ii) a hidden knowledge paradox, where a specialist model reaches 92.5% maximum diagnostic potential but fails to retrieve that knowledge reliably in verbose contexts; and (iii) a 68.6% reasoning-to-output mismatch, where correct diagnoses appear in reasoning traces but are not reflected in final answers. We further evaluate the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm on a human-verified failure set (n = 142). GPT-4o-mini approved 47.9% of clinically incorrect outputs, while HuatuoGPT-o1 approved all validly scored failures and showed a positive self-preference bias. These results suggest that standalone automated clinical evaluations can substantially overestimate clinical reliability without expert-grounded validation.

AI.tldr: CLExEval is a human-in-the-loop framework that exposes critical failures in LLM clinical reasoning, including verbosity bias, a hidden knowledge paradox, and reasoning-to-output mismatch, while demonstrating that automated judges substantially overestimate clinical reliability without expert validation.
AI.motivation: Medical LLMs produce fluent, convincing explanations that can mask incorrect diagnoses — an "evaluation illusion." Reliable clinical reasoning evaluation requires moving beyond final-answer accuracy to scrutinize the reasoning process itself, particularly under information scarcity and in rare disease contexts.
AI.method: CLExEval uses progressive information masking across 40 rare diagnostic cases, yielding 200 clinical reasoning traces annotated by 5,600 expert-physician judgments. Three analyses are conducted: (1) diagnostic accuracy under varying information availability, (2) knowledge retrieval fidelity in specialist models, and (3) alignment between reasoning traces and final outputs. Additionally, the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm is tested against a human-verified failure set (n=142) using GPT-4o-mini and HuatuoGPT-o1.
AI.result: Three failure patterns emerged: (i) verbosity bias — GPT-4o-mini accuracy fell from 95.0% to 32.5% under information scarcity; (ii) hidden knowledge paradox — a specialist model reached 92.5% diagnostic potential but failed reliable retrieval in verbose contexts; (iii) 68.6% reasoning-to-output mismatch — correct reasoning absent from final answers. For automated judging, GPT-4o-mini approved 47.9% of clinically incorrect outputs, and HuatuoGPT-o1 approved all validly scored failures with positive self-preference bias.
AI.conclusion: Standalone automated clinical evaluation substantially overestimates LLM reliability. Expert-grounded validation is essential, and evaluation must target reasoning fidelity — not just final-answer accuracy — to prevent deployment of clinically unsafe models.

title: Optimization Algorithms for Joint OFDM Waveform Design and RIS Configuration in 6G Networks: From Convex Relaxation to Foundation Models
summary: Joint OFDM-RIS optimization for 6G is a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem covering sum-rate maximization, energy efficiency, max-min fairness, and peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR)-constrained objectives. Seventy-eight joint OFDM-RIS optimization works published between 2021 and 2026 are surveyed. No standardized benchmark exists, and cross-paper comparisons remain infeasible. This survey classifies these works into four paradigms: (I) model-based convex relaxation, (II) heuristic and metaheuristic search, (III) deep reinforcement and unsupervised learning, and (IV) emerging methods including foundation models (FM), diffusion-based generative AI, and quantum optimization. A literature synthesis of self-reported benchmarks shows that ML-based methods (Paradigm~III) report 95-99\% of model-based spectral efficiency at 10^2-10^4 x faster per-inference runtime (method-pair dependent; literature values are self-reported and exclude ML pre-training cost). A companion tutorial benchmark at N=16, N=64, and N=128 reveals a critical scaling property: GPU-based neural network inference (DDQN, PPO, graph neural network (GNN), unsupervised DL) is N-invariant, with identical runtime at N=16 and N=128, while iterative solvers (AO+SCA, PSO) scale polynomially. Energy efficiency (P2) and PAPR-constrained (P4) benchmarks are deferred to future work with standardized power models and waveform generators. Six open challenges emerge from the synthesis: the cross-paradigm benchmark deficit, real-world hardware-constrained deployment, joint waveform-RIS optimization for doubly-dispersive channels, multi-objective PAPR trade-offs, LLM safety in live network control, and diminishing returns of standalone heuristics. We specify requirements for a standardized benchmark. This study serves as a roadmap for researchers and practitioners working on joint OFDM-RIS optimization in 6G networks.

AI.tldr: This survey classifies 78 joint OFDM-RIS optimization papers (2021–2026) into four paradigms—convex relaxation, heuristics/metaheuristics, deep learning, and emerging methods (foundation models, diffusion, quantum). It reveals ML methods achieve 95–99% of model-based spectral efficiency with 10²–10⁴× faster inference and demonstrates GPU inference is N-invariant while iterative solvers scale polynomially. Six open challenges and a call for standardized benchmarking are presented.
AI.motivation: Joint OFDM-RIS optimization for 6G is a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem spanning multiple objectives (sum-rate, energy efficiency, max-min fairness, PAPR). Despite 78 published works, no standardized benchmark exists, making cross-paper comparison infeasible and hindering progress evaluation across paradigms.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic literature survey of 78 joint OFDM-RIS optimization works (2021–2026), classifying them into four paradigms: (I) model-based convex relaxation techniques, (II) heuristic and metaheuristic search, (III) deep reinforcement learning and unsupervised learning, and (IV) emerging methods (foundation models, diffusion-based generative AI, quantum optimization). They synthesize self-reported benchmarks from the literature and complement them with a companion tutorial benchmark at three scales (N=16, 64, 128) comparing runtime scaling between GPU-based neural network inference (DDQN, PPO, GNN, unsupervised DL) and iterative solvers (AO+SCA, PSO).
AI.result: ML-based methods (Paradigm III) report 95–99% of model-based spectral efficiency at 10²–10⁴× faster per-inference runtime (excluding pre-training). The companion benchmark reveals GPU-based NN inference is N-invariant (identical runtime for N=16 and N=128), while iterative solvers (AO+SCA, PSO) scale polynomially with N. Energy efficiency and PAPR-constrained benchmarks are deferred. Six open challenges are identified: cross-paradigm benchmark deficit, hardware-constrained deployment, joint waveform-RIS optimization for doubly-dispersive channels, multi-objective PAPR trade-offs, LLM safety in live network control, and diminishing returns of standalone heuristics.
AI.conclusion: The field lacks standardized benchmarks, making rigorous cross-paradigm comparison impossible. ML-based methods show strong promise in runtime-constrained scenarios due to N-invariant inference scaling. The authors specify requirements for a standardized benchmark and position the survey as a roadmap for 6G OFDM-RIS research, with energy efficiency and PAPR benchmarks deferred to future work.

title: Sequential sparse Gaussian process quantile regression
summary: Quantile regression aims to estimate the conditional quantiles of a response variable from observed data. In a Bayesian setting, Gaussian process quantile regression provides uncertainty quantification but faces significant computational challenges due to the nonconjugacy of the asymmetric Laplace likelihood and the cost of posterior inference. We develop a sparse Gaussian process framework in which the quantile function is represented through a reduced set of inducing variables and posterior inference is performed using a Laplace approximation. A decomposition of the predictive uncertainty into conditional-prior and posterior-induced variance components is then exploited to drive two complementary adaptive mechanisms: inducing-input infilling and data acquisition. These mechanisms are combined within a sequential algorithm that allocates computational effort toward the dominant source of predictive uncertainty and adaptively controls model complexity. Numerical experiments on benchmark problems demonstrate the accuracy of the Laplace approximation, the benefits of variance-based inducing-input placement, and the effectiveness of the proposed sequential enrichment strategy compared with predefined data-acquisition strategies.

AI.tldr: A sparse Gaussian process quantile regression framework is proposed, using inducing variables and Laplace approximation for efficient Bayesian inference. Two adaptive mechanisms — inducing-input infilling and data acquisition — are driven by a variance decomposition to sequentially allocate computational effort and control model complexity.
AI.motivation: Bayesian Gaussian process quantile regression offers uncertainty quantification but suffers from severe computational bottlenecks: nonconjugacy of the asymmetric Laplace likelihood and the prohibitive cost of full posterior inference, motivating a sparse and efficient alternative.
AI.method: A sparse GP framework represents the quantile function via a reduced set of inducing variables, with posterior inference performed through a Laplace approximation. Predictive uncertainty is decomposed into conditional-prior and posterior-induced variance components, which drive two adaptive mechanisms: inducing-input infilling (placing inducing points where prior variance dominates) and data acquisition (sampling where posterior variance dominates). These are combined in a sequential algorithm that adaptively allocates resources and controls model complexity.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on benchmark problems demonstrate: (1) the Laplace approximation achieves good accuracy, (2) variance-based inducing-input placement is beneficial, and (3) the sequential enrichment strategy outperforms predefined data-acquisition strategies.
AI.conclusion: The proposed adaptive sequential algorithm effectively balances computational cost and predictive accuracy in Bayesian quantile regression by targeting the dominant source of uncertainty, offering a practical and principled sparse GP solution.

title: Tone-Conditioned Curriculum Learning for Low-Resource Bantu Speech Recognition
summary: Southern Bantu languages are spoken by over 80 million people, yet current foundation ASR models still produce zero-shot WER above 100%, which limits practical use in education and public services. We addressed this gap with a tone conditioned curriculum framework for 6 Southern Bantu languages that combined hybrid difficulty scoring, gated adapters driven by tonal statistics and staged curriculum training. We trained on a community corpus and tested transfer to NCHLT to measure robustness beyond matched evaluation. Results revealed clear interactions between architecture and language, with W2V-BERT outperforming Whisper on Nguni languages by 3 to 4 WER points whilst Whisper performed better on Sotho-Tswana languages. W2V-BERT with tone conditioning reached 28.41% average WER across datasets and 23.79% on Xitsonga transfer. No single model suited all 6 languages, so deployment should pair model selection per language with validation across corpora.

AI.tldr: Southern Bantu ASR remains challenging (zero-shot WER >100%). A tone-conditioned curriculum framework with hybrid difficulty scoring, gated adapters, and staged training was applied to 6 languages. W2V-BERT excelled on Nguni languages, Whisper on Sotho-Tswana. Tone-conditioned W2V-BERT achieved 28.41% average WER; per-language model selection is recommended for deployment.
AI.motivation: Current foundation ASR models yield unacceptably high zero-shot WER (>100%) for Southern Bantu languages (spoken by 80M+ people), hindering practical deployment in education and public services. This performance gap motivates the need for targeted ASR solutions.
AI.method: A tone-conditioned curriculum framework incorporating: (1) hybrid difficulty scoring to rank training examples, (2) gated adapters driven by tonal statistics to inject language-specific tonal information, and (3) staged curriculum training that progressively increases difficulty. Models were trained on a community corpus and evaluated on both matched data and the NCHLT corpus for transfer robustness. Architectures compared include W2V-BERT and Whisper.
AI.result: Architecture–language interactions were significant: W2V-BERT outperformed Whisper by 3–4 WER points on Nguni languages, while Whisper performed better on Sotho-Tswana languages. W2V-BERT with tone conditioning reached 28.41% average WER across all datasets and 23.79% on Xitsonga transfer. No single model suited all six languages.
AI.conclusion: Deployment of ASR for Southern Bantu languages should employ per-language model selection rather than a one-size-fits-all approach, paired with cross-corpus validation to ensure robustness beyond matched evaluation conditions.

title: Smart charging of large fleets of Electric Vehicles: Independent Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning approaches
summary: The electrification of transportation through electric vehicles introduces new challenges for power grid management, such as increased peak demand, voltage fluctuations, line overloads, and the integration of variable renewable energy sources. To enable efficient integration of EVs while minimizing costs for users and avoiding network overloads, implicit coordination between EVs is required. This work compares two independent multi-agent reinforcement learning approaches for optimizing such decentralized EV charging: contextual combinatorial bandits and policy gradient algorithms. Using a realistic simulation environment with autonomous agents making decisions based on local environmental information (including price signals, state-of-charge, and temporal constraints), we evaluate their performance across varying congestion levels, and mixed-strategy configurations with heterogeneous agent groups under dynamic electricity pricing derived from real photovoltaic production data.

AI.tldr: Compares contextual combinatorial bandits and policy gradient MARL for decentralized EV charging coordination under dynamic pricing, evaluating performance across congestion levels and heterogeneous agent mixes.
AI.motivation: EV electrification introduces grid challenges (peak demand, voltage fluctuations, overloads, renewable integration). Implicit coordination among EVs is needed to minimize user costs and prevent network congestion without centralized control.
AI.method: Two multi-agent reinforcement learning approaches are benchmarked: (1) contextual combinatorial bandits and (2) policy gradient algorithms. Agents operate autonomously using local observations (price signals, state-of-charge, temporal constraints) in a realistic simulation with dynamic electricity pricing derived from real photovoltaic production data. Evaluation spans varying congestion levels and mixed-strategy configurations with heterogeneous agent groups.
AI.result: Performance comparison between the two MARL paradigms across different congestion regimes and agent heterogeneity configurations is provided (specific quantitative results not detailed in the abstract).
AI.conclusion: Both contextual combinatorial bandits and policy gradient methods offer viable pathways for implicit EV charging coordination; their relative effectiveness depends on congestion levels and agent population composition.

title: Probabilistic Inversion with Flow Matching
summary: We demonstrate the application of Flow Matching, a technique originating from generative Artificial Intelligence, to probabilistic inversion in geophysical settings, such as seismic Full-Waveform inversion. We adapt the well-established mathematical theory of Flow Matching from generative Artificial Intelligence to the context of probabilistic inversion. We evaluate the approach with two case studies: a simple 2D velocity model to illustrate the general features of the method, and the OpenFWI dataset to show its capabilities for probabilistic inversion of more complex seismic velocity models.

AI.tldr: This paper adapts Flow Matching—a generative AI technique—to probabilistic geophysical inversion, demonstrating its effectiveness on 2D velocity models and the OpenFWI seismic dataset.
AI.motivation: Probabilistic geophysical inversion (e.g., seismic Full-Waveform Inversion) is critical for quantifying uncertainty in subsurface imaging, but traditional methods like MCMC are computationally prohibitive. The authors seek to leverage recent advances in generative modeling (specifically Flow Matching) to enable efficient, high-quality probabilistic inversion.
AI.method: The authors adapt the mathematical framework of Flow Matching—a continuous normalizing flow approach that learns a time-dependent vector field to transport samples from a simple prior to a complex target posterior distribution—to the probabilistic inversion setting. The method is evaluated through two case studies: (1) a simple 2D velocity model for illustrative purposes, and (2) the OpenFWI dataset to test performance on more complex, realistic velocity structures.
AI.result: The Flow Matching approach successfully performs probabilistic inversion in both case studies. The simple 2D model illustrates the general characteristics of the method, while results on the OpenFWI dataset demonstrate its capability to handle more complex seismic velocity models, yielding probabilistic posterior estimates.
AI.conclusion: Flow Matching is a promising and viable generative AI technique for probabilistic geophysical inversion, offering a computationally efficient alternative to traditional sampling-based methods while maintaining the ability to characterize posterior uncertainty in both simple and complex velocity model settings.

title: Moral Safety in LLMs: Exposing Performative Compliance with Puzzled Cues
summary: As large language models take on morally consequential roles in healthcare, legal, and hiring contexts, we need to examine whether their ethical behaviors are genuine or superficial. We show that current fairness evaluations substantially overestimate moral safety. Models appear fair when demographic identity is stated as an explicit label, yet become measurably less fair when the same identity must be inferred. We term this failure \emph{performative compliance}, where a model is fair when the presentation resembles a fairness evaluation and less fair as that cue weakens.
