We introduce a cue-variation methodology that holds the moral dilemma and the demographic identity fixed and varies only how that identity is conveyed. Hiding the explicit label raises harmful decisions by $+4.4$~pp and changes model safety rankings, and the shift persists when models correctly infer the demographic, ruling out attribution error. We propose the \textbf{Cue Visibility Gap}, a model-agnostic robustness metric that can be added to any existing fairness benchmark to separate genuine from performative moral safety. Fairness evaluations that omit cue variation measure surface compliance, not moral robustness, and should not ground deployment decisions in high-stakes settings.

AI.tldr: Current fairness evaluations overestimate LLM moral safety because models exhibit "performative compliance" — appearing fair when demographic identity is explicitly labeled but becoming significantly less fair when identity must be inferred. The authors propose a cue-variation methodology and the Cue Visibility Gap metric to distinguish genuine moral robustness from superficial compliance.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are deployed in high-stakes morally consequential domains (healthcare, legal, hiring), it is critical to determine whether their ethical behaviors reflect genuine moral reasoning or merely superficial pattern-matching to evaluation formats. Existing fairness benchmarks fail to test this distinction because they present demographic identity as explicit labels, making it impossible to detect models that only behave fairly when the evaluation setup is transparent.
AI.method: The authors introduce a cue-variation methodology: they hold the moral dilemma and demographic identity constant while systematically varying how identity is conveyed (explicit label vs. implicit cues requiring inference). They measure the resulting shift in harmful decisions and propose the Cue Visibility Gap — a model-agnostic robustness metric computed as the difference in fairness performance between explicit-label and implicit-identity conditions. This metric can be integrated into any existing fairness benchmark.
AI.result: Hiding the explicit demographic label increases harmful decisions by +4.4 percentage points and changes model safety rankings. Critically, this disparity persists even when models correctly infer the demographic from implicit cues, ruling out mere attribution error. The findings demonstrate that standard fairness evaluations systematically overestimate moral safety.
AI.conclusion: Fairness evaluations that omit cue variation measure only surface compliance, not genuine moral robustness. Such evaluations should not ground deployment decisions in high-stakes settings. The Cue Visibility Gap offers a practical, model-agnostic tool for separating performative fairness from robust ethical behavior.

title: ReGRPO: Reflection-Augmented Policy Optimization for Tool-Using Agents
summary: Tool-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) can solve multimodal, multi-step tasks by calling external tools, yet they remain fragile in practice. Existing works have two common gaps. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is built mostly on successful trajectories and offers little signal for recovery after tool failures, while sparse trajectory-level RL rewards provide limited guidance on which step failed and how to repair it. We introduce ReGRPO (Reflection-augmented Group Relative Policy Optimization), a framework that learns reflection-guided correction in tool-using agents. ReGRPO starts with a structured reflective data engine: we execute near-miss actions to collect grounded failure observations, then build Reflection-of-Thought triplets (ErrorType, Evidence, FixPlan) paired with corrected actions for warm-start SFT. We then optimize reflection tokens and corrective actions jointly within local trajectories using group-relative advantages, and include a reflection-cost term to reduce unnecessary reflection. Experiments on GTA and GAIA show that, under the same backbone and tool suite, ReGRPO consistently outperforms strong open-source baselines and achieves the best results among the compared open-source controllers. Code and RoT data are available at https://github.com/showlab/ReGRPO.

AI.tldr: ReGRPO introduces a reflection-augmented reinforcement learning framework for tool-using VLMs, using a Reflection-of-Thought data engine to collect failure observations and jointly optimize reflection tokens with corrective actions via group-relative advantages, outperforming open-source baselines on GTA and GAIA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing tool-augmented VLMs trained via SFT on successful trajectories lack recovery signals after tool failures, while sparse trajectory-level RL rewards fail to pinpoint which step failed or how to fix it. Both gaps lead to fragile agents that cannot self-correct effectively.
AI.method: ReGRPO consists of two stages: (1) a structured reflective data engine that executes near-miss actions to collect grounded failure observations and builds Reflection-of-Thought (RoT) triplets — ErrorType, Evidence, FixPlan — paired with corrected actions for warm-start SFT; (2) a Group Relative Policy Optimization stage that jointly optimizes reflection tokens and corrective actions within local trajectories using group-relative advantages, with an added reflection-cost term to suppress unnecessary reflection.
AI.result: Under the same backbone and tool suite, ReGRPO consistently outperforms strong open-source baselines and achieves the best results among compared open-source controllers on both GTA and GAIA benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: ReGRPO demonstrates that structured reflection data combined with group-relative policy optimization enables tool-using VLMs to learn effective self-correction, addressing the fragility problem in multimodal multi-step tool use.

title: Patch-PODiff-ViT: Structured Latent Diffusion with Patchwise POD for Super-Resolution and Uncertainty Quantification
summary: Diffusion models enable probabilistic super-resolution and conditional generation, but pixel-space methods are computationally expensive and learned latent spaces often lack interpretable uncertainty quantification. We introduce Patch-PODiff-ViT, a structured latent diffusion framework in which the latent space is defined by patchwise Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD), a fixed linear orthonormal basis over local patches, rather than learned by a nonlinear autoencoder. This yields low-dimensional, variance-ordered tokens that preserve spatial structure and enable efficient diffusion in a structured low-dimensional latent space with a Vision Transformer. Because the decoder is fixed, linear, and orthonormal, latent coefficient uncertainty can be propagated directly to physical-space predictive variance, enabling analytic propagation of predictive variance through the linear decoder without Monte Carlo estimation in pixel space. Across sea surface temperature, medical imaging, and natural images, the method achieves strong reconstruction with fewer parameters and lower memory, while producing well-calibrated spatial uncertainty that closely matches empirical ensembles.

AI.tldr: Patch-PODiff-ViT uses patchwise Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) as a fixed, linear, orthonormal latent space for diffusion models, enabling interpretable uncertainty quantification via analytic variance propagation through the decoder, achieving efficient reconstruction and well-calibrated spatial uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Pixel-space diffusion models are computationally expensive, and learned latent spaces (e.g., VAE-based) lack interpretable uncertainty quantification. There is a need for a structured latent representation that is low-dimensional, spatially structured, and allows direct propagation of latent uncertainty to physical-space predictive variance without Monte Carlo sampling.
AI.method: The method defines the latent space using patchwise Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD)—a fixed, linear, orthonormal basis computed over local patches—rather than a learned nonlinear autoencoder. This yields variance-ordered tokens preserving spatial structure. Diffusion is performed in this structured low-dimensional latent space using a Vision Transformer (ViT) backbone. Since the decoder is fixed, linear, and orthonormal, predictive variance in pixel space is computed analytically by propagating latent coefficient uncertainty, avoiding Monte Carlo estimation.
AI.result: Across sea surface temperature, medical imaging, and natural image datasets, Patch-PODiff-ViT achieves strong reconstruction quality with fewer parameters and lower memory requirements compared to alternatives. It produces well-calibrated spatial uncertainty maps that closely match empirical ensembles.
AI.conclusion: A fixed orthonormal POD basis as the latent space for diffusion models provides an effective compromise: it retains the efficiency of latent diffusion while enabling principled, analytic uncertainty propagation. The approach generalizes across diverse image domains.

title: Overview of the TalentCLEF 2026: Skill and Job Title Intelligence for Human Capital Management
summary: This paper presents an overview of the second edition of the TalentCLEF challenge, organized as a Lab at the Conference and Labs of the Evaluation Forum (CLEF) 2026. TalentCLEF is an initiative aimed at advancing Natural Language Processing research in Human Capital Management. The second edition of the challenge consisted of two tasks: Task A, contextualized job-person matching, focuses on identifying and ranking the most suitable candidates represented by their resumes for a given job vacancy in English and Spanish. Task B, job-skill matching with skill type classification, addresses retrieving the most relevant skills for a given job title in English and distinguishing between core and contextual skills. TalentCLEF attracted 113 registered teams and received more than 400 submissions in the two tasks, reflecting the growing interest of the research community in shared evaluation benchmarks for Human Capital Management. This paper describes the motivation and organization of the challenge, summarizes the datasets and evaluation settings, and reports the main results obtained by the participating teams.

AI.tldr: Overview of the second TalentCLEF challenge (CLEF 2026), comprising two NLP tasks in Human Capital Management: Task A (contextualized job-person matching across English/Spanish) and Task B (job-skill matching with skill type classification). The challenge drew 113 teams and 400+ submissions, with the paper detailing motivation, datasets, evaluation, and results.
AI.motivation: To advance NLP research in Human Capital Management by providing shared evaluation benchmarks, addressing the gap in standardized tasks for job-person matching and job-skill alignment.
AI.method: The challenge is structured as a CLEF Lab with two tasks: Task A ranks candidates (resumes) for job vacancies using contextualized matching in English and Spanish; Task B retrieves relevant skills for job titles and classifies them as core or contextual. Standardized datasets and evaluation protocols are employed across both tasks.
AI.result: Strong community engagement: 113 registered teams and over 400 submissions across both tasks, indicating significant research interest in HCM benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: TalentCLEF successfully established a growing shared evaluation framework for NLP in Human Capital Management, with broad participation validating the need for such benchmarks.

title: World-Model Collapse as a Phase Transition
summary: Water looks unchanged as it warms, then at a critical point it boils. We ask whether long-horizon language agents show an analogous transition in their implicit world models. In some parameter settings, changing state load by a small amount, or adding a single step of horizon, leaves behavior nearly unchanged; near a critical boundary, the same small change causes a sudden world collapse. We study this effect in a deterministic task family with exact per-step gold state. A large grid search over state cardinality, dependency density, horizon, branching, observation mode, and mutation rate reveals a phase diagram: a solved plateau, a narrow transition band, and a collapse floor. Per-step traces show the mechanism: world-state fidelity fails before action validity, so the agent is not merely choosing a bad action; it is acting from a corrupted world. Stronger models translate the critical boundary but do not remove the qualitative transition. These results make world-model collapse a measurable bottleneck for long-horizon agents.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a phase-transition phenomenon in long-horizon language agents, where a small increase in task complexity (state load or horizon) near a critical boundary causes a sudden "world-model collapse" — a sharp drop in task performance. Through large-scale grid search, the authors map out a phase diagram showing a solved plateau, a narrow transition band, and a collapse floor, identifying world-model fidelity loss (rather than mere bad action selection) as the root mechanism.
AI.motivation: The authors draw an analogy to water's discontinuous phase transition at boiling point, asking whether long-horizon language agents exhibit a similar critical transition in their internal world models. The goal is to understand whether world-model collapse constitutes a fundamental, measurable bottleneck that limits agent performance as task horizon and complexity grow.
AI.method: The study employs a deterministic task family with exact per-step gold state, enabling precise measurement of world-model fidelity. A comprehensive grid search is conducted over six parameters: state cardinality, dependency density, horizon length, branching factor, observation mode, and mutation rate. The resulting data reveals a phase diagram with three distinct regimes. Per-step trace analysis is used to diagnose the causal mechanism, distinguishing between world-state fidelity loss and action validity failure.
AI.result: The grid search reveals a consistent phase diagram across parameter settings: a solved plateau where agents perform reliably, a narrow transition band where small parameter changes trigger abrupt performance collapse, and a collapse floor. Per-step traces demonstrate that world-state fidelity deteriorates before action validity fails, indicating agents act from corrupted internal representations. Stronger models shift the critical boundary but do not eliminate the qualitative phase transition.
AI.conclusion: World-model collapse is a measurable and fundamental bottleneck for long-horizon language agents. The phase-transition behavior is robust across model scales and parameter settings, suggesting it is an inherent limitation rather than a mere artifact of insufficient capability. This positions world-model fidelity as a key metric for evaluating and improving long-horizon agent performance.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Spacecraft Attitude Control During Atmospheric Re-Entry
summary: Deep reinforcement learning has the potential to solve attitude control problems more adaptively, precisely, and robustly by handling nonlinear dynamics, uncertainties, and failure cases more effectively than traditional attitude control approaches. We explore reinforcement learning (RL) for attitude control in spacecraft re-entry. An industry-standard proportional-integral-derivative controller with gain scheduling serves as a strong baseline for model-free RL and hybrid controllers that combine these two approaches. We formalize the application in the RL framework to apply continuous, off-policy RL. State-of-the-art RL achieves comparable performance to traditional control approaches in this domain. However, its out-of-distribution generalization is not sufficient. Hence, we use dynamics randomization to introduce challenging task variations during training and enforce generalization in a predefined operational envelope. Finally, we assess the best obtained RL-based controllers with application-specific metrics to show superior performance in comparison to traditional controllers in the operational envelope, that is, hybrid controllers are able to track the angle of attack better and are more robust under variations of mass, inertia tensor, and flap actuator bandwidth.

AI.tldr: This paper explores reinforcement learning (RL) for spacecraft re-entry attitude control, comparing pure RL and hybrid RL-PID controllers against a gain-scheduled PID baseline. Dynamics randomization improves out-of-distribution generalization, and hybrid controllers ultimately demonstrate superior tracking performance and robustness to variations in mass, inertia, and actuator bandwidth.
AI.motivation: Traditional attitude control methods (e.g., gain-scheduled PID) struggle with nonlinear dynamics, uncertainties, and failure cases. Deep RL offers potential for more adaptive, precise, and robust control, but its out-of-distribution generalization remains a critical weakness that must be addressed for real-world spacecraft re-entry applications.
AI.method: The authors formalize spacecraft re-entry attitude control as a continuous, off-policy RL problem. They benchmark model-free RL and hybrid RL-PID controllers against an industry-standard gain-scheduled PID controller. To address poor out-of-distribution generalization, they employ dynamics randomization — introducing variations in mass, inertia tensor, and flap actuator bandwidth during training — to enforce robustness within a predefined operational envelope.
AI.result: State-of-the-art RL achieves performance comparable to the PID baseline but exhibits insufficient out-of-distribution generalization. Dynamics randomization mitigates this issue. The resulting hybrid RL-based controllers outperform traditional controllers within the operational envelope, particularly in angle-of-attack tracking accuracy and robustness to parameter variations.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid controllers combining RL with traditional PID control, trained with dynamics randomization, surpass purely traditional approaches for spacecraft re-entry attitude control in terms of tracking performance and robustness, making them promising candidates for real-world deployment within defined operational envelopes.

title: Cross-lingual Relation Extraction with Large Language Models: Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, and Fine-Tuned Evaluation on Romanian
summary: Relation extraction (RE) for low-resource languages is typically constrained by the lack of annotated corpora. We investigate the feasibility of cross-lingual RE for Romanian by combining automatic dataset translation with large language model (LLM) inference. We translate the SemEval-2010 Task 8 benchmark from English to Romanian using an LLM-based translation pipeline and evaluate Gemma 4 31B under zero-shot, few-shot, and QLoRA fine-tuned configurations, against four encoder baselines spanning 125M to 560M parameters: XLM- RoBERTa (base and large), Romanian BERT, and RoBERT- large. We assess two task formulations: relation classification with marked entities and end-to-end extraction. Our results show that Romanian incurs a 3 to 5 percentage point (pp) drop relative to English in prompt-only settings, that few-shot prompting provides marginal gains over zero-shot, and that QLoRA fine-tuning improves macro F1-Score by more than 22 percentage points in both languages while reducing the cross-lingual gap from 3.3 to 1.4pp. The encoder baselines come within 1-4pp of QLoRA Gemma on Romanian despite being 50-250 times smaller, with monolingual Romanian BERT at 125M parameters matching multilingual XLM-R at 278M. The case for using a 31B model for single-task RE on Romanian is therefore weak in deployment scenarios where compute matters. We release the translated dataset, evaluation code, and trained models.

AI.tldr: This paper explores cross-lingual relation extraction for Romanian by translating the SemEval-2010 Task 8 benchmark using an LLM pipeline and evaluating Gemma 4 31B against smaller encoder baselines. QLoRA fine-tuning yields large gains and narrows the cross-lingual gap, but a 125M Romanian BERT performs comparably, weakening the case for deploying a 31B model in compute-constrained settings.
AI.motivation: Low-resource languages like Romanian lack annotated corpora for relation extraction. The authors aim to determine whether combining automatic translation with LLM inference is a viable strategy, and whether the computational cost of a 31B model is justified compared to much smaller monolingual or multilingual encoders.
AI.method: The SemEval-2010 Task 8 dataset is translated from English to Romanian using an LLM-based translation pipeline. Gemma 4 31B is evaluated under zero-shot, few-shot, and QLoRA fine-tuned configurations. Two task formulations are assessed: relation classification with marked entities and end-to-end extraction. Four encoder baselines (125M–560M parameters) are compared: XLM-RoBERTa (base/large), Romanian BERT, and RoBERT-large.
AI.result: Romanian sees a 3–5 pp drop vs. English in prompt-only settings. Few-shot prompting yields marginal gains over zero-shot. QLoRA fine-tuning improves macro F1 by over 22 pp in both languages and reduces the cross-lingual gap from 3.3 to 1.4 pp. Encoder baselines come within 1–4 pp of the fine-tuned Gemma model, with 125M Romanian BERT matching 278M XLM-R. The 31B model’s advantage is limited in compute-sensitive deployments.
AI.conclusion: QLoRA fine-tuning of LLMs substantially improves cross-lingual RE and narrows the performance gap. However, small monolingual encoders can rival large multilingual models at a fraction of the cost, making the case for deploying a 31B model for single-task Romanian RE weak when compute resources matter.

title: Wisdom Of The (AI) Crowd: Investigating Artificial Swarm Intelligence In Large Language Models
comment: 18 pages, 0 figures, 6 tables, Accepted at ECIS 2026 (European Conference on Information Systems), Track: General Track, Paper No. ECIS2026-1499
summary: Human swarm intelligence demonstrates remarkable collective accuracy but faces scalability constraints in cost, coordination, and time. We investigate whether large language models (LLMs) can approximate swarm intelligence effects through artificial swarms, addressing a critical gap in understanding AI-based aggregation mechanisms. We conducted a controlled experiment with 960 manually executed prompts across three proprietary models (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.5), testing intra-model sampling and inter-model aggregation on eight estimation tasks. Results reveal consistent error reduction through intra- and inter-model aggregation, with significant error reductions up to 37 percentage points in MAPE across different aggregation strategies. We observed small to large effect sizes for positive correlations (Spearman's $ρ=0.242-0.568$, all $p<0.001$) between relative confidence interval widths and relative estimation errors, suggesting LLMs possess metacognitive awareness when assessing uncertainty. We discuss implications for research and practice, providing actionable insights for deploying LLM swarms in organizational decision-making.

AI.tldr: This paper explores whether LLM "swarms" can replicate human swarm intelligence effects, finding that intra-model sampling and inter-model aggregation consistently reduce estimation errors by up to 37 MAPE points, and that LLMs exhibit metacognitive awareness via correlations between confidence intervals and error.
AI.motivation: Human swarm intelligence achieves high collective accuracy but faces practical limitations in cost, coordination, and time. There is a critical gap in understanding whether LLMs can approximate swarm intelligence through artificial aggregation mechanisms, offering a scalable alternative.
AI.method: A controlled experiment with 960 manually executed prompts across three proprietary models (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.5) on eight estimation tasks. Two strategies tested: (1) intra-model sampling — multiple samples from the same model aggregated; (2) inter-model aggregation — combining outputs across different models. Error reduction measured via MAPE; metacognitive awareness assessed via Spearman correlation between relative confidence interval widths and relative estimation errors.
AI.result: Consistent error reduction through both intra- and inter-model aggregation, with MAPE reductions up to 37 percentage points. Significant positive Spearman correlations (ρ = 0.242–0.568, all p < 0.001) between confidence interval width and estimation error, indicating metacognitive calibration.
AI.conclusion: LLM swarms can effectively approximate human swarm intelligence effects, offering a practical, scalable mechanism for improving estimation accuracy in organizational decision-making. The metacognitive awareness finding has implications for calibrated uncertainty communication in deployed LLM systems.

title: Safe Online Learning via Smooth Safety-Structured Policy Composition
summary: Safe online reinforcement learning requires policies to respect safety constraints while maintaining smooth optimization dynamics. Existing approaches typically rely on either strict safety enforcement via action interventions, which introduce discontinuities in system interaction and learning, or soft safety constraint formulations, which preserve smooth learning but provide limited safety assurance. We propose AutoSafe, a safety-aware policy architecture that integrates structured safety monitoring and intervention directly into the action generation process. This design enables smooth, risk-dependent transitions between performance-driven and safety-preserving behaviors, resulting in continuous online interaction and learning dynamics. Empirical results across a suite of continuous-control benchmarks demonstrate strong safety enforcement without sacrificing learning smoothness. We further validate AutoSafe on a physical cart-pole system, highlighting its practical effectiveness for safe online learning in the real world.

AI.tldr: AutoSafe integrates safety monitoring and intervention directly into the policy's action generation, enabling smooth transitions between performance and safety behaviors while maintaining continuous learning dynamics.
AI.motivation: Existing safe RL methods face a fundamental trade-off: strict safety enforcement (e.g., action interventions) causes discontinuous learning dynamics, while soft constraint formulations offer smooth optimization but weak safety guarantees. A unified approach achieving both is lacking.
AI.method: AutoSafe is a safety-aware policy architecture that embeds structured safety monitoring and intervention mechanisms directly into the action generation process. This design yields risk-dependent, smooth transitions between performance-driven and safety-preserving behaviors, preserving continuous online interaction and learning dynamics.
AI.result: AutoSafe achieves strong safety enforcement without sacrificing learning smoothness across continuous-control benchmarks. It is further validated on a physical cart-pole system, demonstrating real-world practical effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: AutoSafe resolves the discontinuity–safety trade-off in safe RL by architecturally integrating safety into policy action generation, enabling smooth, safe, and performant online learning both in simulation and on physical hardware.

title: Seeing Is Not Sharing: Some Vision-Language Models Overestimate Common Ground in Asymmetric Dialogue
comment: 17 pages, 9 figures, 8 tables; accepted to SIGDIAL 2026
summary: In collaborative dialogue, shared perception does not guarantee shared interpretation. Mutual understanding must be established through interaction. We investigate whether vision-language models (VLMs) can distinguish what could be shared from what has been shared between dialogue participants through grounding. We formulate this as an interpretation-matching task on 13,077 annotated reference expressions from HCRC MapTask dialogues, and evaluate VLMs under systematically controlled manipulations of dialogue context and map-information access. Our results show that providing authentic map images improves overall performance but shifts models toward over-predicting alignment. Textual descriptions of the same map content reproduce this bias, while non-informative images suppress alignment predictions entirely, indicating that the bias is driven by task-relevant map content, not the visual channel. This improvement comes at the cost of degraded accuracy on non-aligned cases. Calibration analysis and reference-chain tracking further suggest that models rely on static referential cues on the maps rather than tracking how grounding unfolds through dialogue history. We observe these patterns most clearly in Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and, to varying degrees, in four additional models from two architecture families. In models that exhibit the bias, map content, whether presented visually or textually, is treated as evidence of mutual understanding, conflating potential with established common ground.

AI.tldr: VLMs conflate shared perceptual context with established common ground; providing map images improves overall grounding performance but introduces over-prediction of alignment by treating map content as evidence of mutual understanding rather than tracking grounding through dialogue history.
AI.motivation: Shared perception (e.g., seeing the same map) does not guarantee shared interpretation in collaborative dialogue. Mutual understanding must be interactively established through grounding. The authors investigate whether VLMs can distinguish between what *could* be shared (potential common ground via shared visual context) and what *has* actually been shared (established common ground via dialogue).
AI.method: The authors formulate an interpretation-matching task using 13,077 annotated reference expressions from the HCRC MapTask corpus. VLMs are evaluated under systematically controlled manipulations of (1) dialogue context and (2) map-information access. Conditions include: authentic map images, textual descriptions of map content, and non-informative images. They further conduct calibration analysis and reference-chain tracking, testing five models from two architecture families (including Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct).
AI.result: Providing authentic map images improves overall performance but shifts models toward over-predicting alignment (i.e., assuming mutual understanding). Textual map descriptions reproduce this bias; non-informative images suppress alignment predictions entirely. This indicates the bias is driven by task-relevant map *content*, not the visual channel. Improvement on aligned cases comes at the cost of degraded accuracy on non-aligned cases. Calibration and reference-chain analyses reveal models rely on static referential cues on maps rather than tracking how grounding unfolds through dialogue history. Patterns are most pronounced in Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and appear to varying degrees across other models.
AI.conclusion: VLMs treat map content—whether visual or textual—as evidence of mutual understanding, conflating potential common ground with established common ground. This represents a fundamental limitation in their ability to model the incremental, interactional nature of grounding in collaborative dialogue.

title: Xiaomi-GUI-0 Technical Report
summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents build on vision-language models to complete user tasks end-to-end in real applications through interface actions such as tapping, swiping, text entry, and navigation. However, existing GUI agents are trained and evaluated largely on offline trajectories, simulated environments, and standardized benchmarks. These differ substantially from real applications in interface layout, interaction logic, and abnormal-state distribution, and cannot faithfully characterize execution stability in real-world use, where account states, permission dialogs, payment authentication, and risk control continually reshape the state distribution and open a persistent gap between benchmark scores and real usability. To close this gap, we propose Xiaomi-GUI-0, a native multimodal GUI agent for real mobile environments, trained and evaluated within a real-device closed loop. At its core is a real-device-dominant hybrid infrastructure, where physical devices are the primary execution environment and sandboxes provide auxiliary support, so that data collection, training, rollout, and evaluation share an execution distribution close to real deployment. We construct multi-source training data spanning high-frequency head tasks, high-generalization data for long-tail intents, and capability-enhancement data for reflection and memory, and introduce an error-driven data flywheel that turns failure trajectories into corrected actions, reflective explanations, and recovery demonstrations. The model is trained through a progressive three-stage pipeline of supervised fine-tuning, step-level reinforcement learning, and agentic reinforcement learning. Evaluated on public benchmarks and our in-house RealMobile, Xiaomi-GUI-0 achieves 72.0% success on RealMobile and 78.9% on AndroidWorld, while substantially improving execution stability and abnormal-state recognition in real-world tasks.

AI.tldr: Xiaomi-GUI-0 is a multimodal GUI agent trained and evaluated in a real-device closed loop, using a hybrid infrastructure of physical devices and sandboxes, multi-source training data, an error-driven data flywheel, and a three-stage training pipeline (SFT, step-level RL, agentic RL). It achieves 72.0% on RealMobile and 78.9% on AndroidWorld, substantially improving real-world execution stability and abnormal-state recognition.
AI.motivation: Existing GUI agents are trained and evaluated on offline trajectories, simulated environments, and standardized benchmarks that differ substantially from real applications in interface layout, interaction logic, and abnormal-state distribution. Real-world factors like account states, permission dialogs, payment authentication, and risk control continually reshape state distributions, creating a persistent gap between benchmark scores and real usability.
AI.method: The authors propose a real-device-dominant hybrid infrastructure where physical devices serve as the primary execution environment and sandboxes provide auxiliary support, ensuring data collection, training, rollout, and evaluation share a distribution close to real deployment. They construct multi-source training data covering high-frequency head tasks, high-generalization data for long-tail intents, and capability-enhancement data for reflection and memory. An error-driven data flywheel converts failure trajectories into corrected actions, reflective explanations, and recovery demonstrations. The model is trained through a progressive three-stage pipeline: supervised fine-tuning, step-level reinforcement learning, and agentic reinforcement learning.
AI.result: Xiaomi-GUI-0 achieves 72.0% success on the in-house RealMobile benchmark and 78.9% on AndroidWorld, with substantially improved execution stability and abnormal-state recognition in real-world tasks compared to prior GUI agents.
AI.conclusion: Closing the sim-to-real gap for GUI agents requires training and evaluation within a real-device closed loop. The combination of a real-device-dominant hybrid infrastructure, multi-source training data, error-driven data flywheel, and progressive multi-stage training effectively bridges the gap between benchmark scores and real-world usability.

title: Expected Gain-based Escalation in Vertical Federated Learning
summary: Collaborative inference can improve predictive performance by integrating complementary information across agents, but applying collaborative fusion to every sample can incur unnecessary communication and computational overhead. This trade-off is particularly relevant in vertical federated learning (VFL), where clients observe different views of the same sample and fusion typically requires transmitting intermediate representations to a server. We study selective escalation in a two-round VFL inference protocol, in which a low-cost first round produces a prediction from client posteriors and a second embedding-fusion round is invoked only when it is expected to improve the final decision. We formulate routing as expected-gain score estimation: a sample is escalated when a predicted improvement in correctness justifies the additional communication. The proposed analytical score combines a calibrated pooled posterior with classwise reliability estimates of the VFL model, both obtained from held-out calibration data, yielding an interpretable router that requires no separately trained routing network. Experiments on multi-view classification benchmarks, including controlled test--time view degradation settings, show that the proposed router improves the communication-accuracy trade-off over confidence-, learned-gain-, and deferral-based baselines.

AI.tldr: A selective escalation mechanism for two-round vertical federated learning (VFL) inference that uses an analytical expected-gain score — combining calibrated pooled posteriors with classwise reliability estimates — to decide when embedding fusion is worthwhile, improving communication-accuracy trade-offs without training a separate routing network.
AI.motivation: Collaborative inference via embedding fusion in VFL improves accuracy but incurs communication/computation costs for every sample. The authors seek to reduce this overhead by selectively escalating only samples where fusion is expected to yield a net improvement, avoiding unnecessary transmission of intermediate representations.
AI.method: A two-round VFL inference protocol: Round 1 aggregates client posteriors (low-cost); Round 2 performs full embedding fusion (high-cost). A router decides escalation per sample using an analytical expected-gain score that combines (1) a calibrated pooled posterior and (2) classwise reliability estimates of the VFL model, both derived from held-out calibration data. No separate routing network is trained.
AI.result: The proposed router outperforms confidence-based, learned-gain, and deferral-based baselines on multi-view classification benchmarks, including settings with controlled test-time view degradation, demonstrating superior communication-accuracy trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: Analytical expected-gain scoring with calibration yields an effective, interpretable selective escalation strategy for VFL, reducing communication cost while preserving accuracy gains from collaborative fusion.

title: Adapting Foundation ASR Models to Dysarthric Speech: A Case Study
summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems often perform poorly in dysarthric speech, limiting their usefulness to affected speakers in everyday communication. This paper presents a personalized ASR system for a dysarthric speaker, built by adapting a foundation ASR model to speaker-specific data. Using the TEQST tool, we collected 92 hours of read speech and later added 8.8 hours of user corrections gathered through a deployed mobile application. Starting from Whisper, fine-tuning reduced word error rate to 15.8% with only 1.4 hours of adaptation data, reached 10.7% with 22.5 hours, and achieved the best result of 9.7% when using all available data including the corrections. Using LoRA adaptation and/or Qwen3-ASR as foundation model performed worse in this setting. The results show that personalized fine-tuning can make foundation ASR models substantially more effective for dysarthric speech and suitable for practical deployment.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning a Whisper foundation model with 92+ hours of dysarthric speaker data reduced WER to 9.7%, demonstrating that personalized adaptation enables practical ASR deployment for dysarthric speech.
AI.motivation: ASR systems perform poorly on dysarthric speech, limiting accessibility for affected individuals. The paper addresses the need for personalized, practically deployable ASR solutions tailored to individual dysarthric speakers.
AI.method: A personalized ASR system was built by collecting 92 hours of read speech from a single dysarthric speaker using the TEQST tool, plus 8.8 hours of user corrections via a mobile app. The Whisper foundation model was fine-tuned with varying amounts of adaptation data. Additional experiments tested LoRA adaptation and Qwen3-ASR as an alternative foundation model.
AI.result: Fine-tuning Whisper achieved WER of 15.8% with 1.4 hours, 10.7% with 22.5 hours, and 9.7% with all data including corrections. LoRA adaptation and Qwen3-ASR both underperformed relative to full fine-tuning of Whisper.
AI.conclusion: Personalized fine-tuning of foundation ASR models yields substantial WER reductions for dysarthric speech and is viable for real-world deployment. Full fine-tuning of Whisper outperformed parameter-efficient (LoRA) and alternative model (Qwen3-ASR) approaches in this single-speaker setting.

title: Learning to Select, Not Relearn: Hard-Routed Mixtures of Reasoning LoRAs
summary: Composing independently trained LoRA adapters into a single large language model is useful for multi-domain adaptation, especially when the original training data cannot be shared. A common approach is to use MoE-style routing over LoRA experts, but for frozen pretrained adapters, soft weighted combinations can change the unit-scale additive update under which each LoRA module was originally trained. We propose \textbf{Hard-Routed MoR-LoRA}, a two-stage framework for composing frozen reasoning LoRA experts through unit-scale hard selection. First, domain-specific LoRA adapters are trained independently using reinforcement learning from verifiable feedback to obtain reasoning experts. Then, all experts are frozen, reasoning traces are distilled from them, and only a lightweight shared router together with a small attention LoRA is trained for integration. The router selects exactly one expert per token using hard top-1 routing, while a straight-through estimator enables gradient-based training. Experiments across five benchmarks, multiple model scales, and additional model families show that Hard-Routed MoR-LoRA preserves expert behavior while requiring substantially fewer trainable parameters than soft-routing mixture baselines. Our analysis further shows that normalized soft mixtures often concentrate most routing mass on a single expert, suggesting that hard unit-scale routing provides a simple and efficient abstraction for frozen LoRA expert composition.

AI.tldr: Hard-Routed MoR-LoRA proposes a two-stage framework for composing independently trained, frozen LoRA reasoning experts using hard top-1 token-level routing, preserving the unit-scale additive structure of each adapter while requiring fewer trainable parameters than soft-routing MoE baselines.
AI.motivation: Composing independently trained LoRA adapters is valuable for multi-domain LLM adaptation when original training data cannot be shared. Existing MoE-style soft routing over frozen LoRA experts can distort the unit-scale additive updates under which each adapter was originally trained, potentially degrading expert behavior. The authors seek a composition method that respects the original training conditions of each expert.
AI.method: A two-stage framework: (1) Domain-specific LoRA adapters are independently trained via reinforcement learning from verifiable feedback to produce reasoning experts. (2) All experts are frozen; reasoning traces are distilled from them; only a lightweight shared router plus a small attention LoRA is trained. The router uses hard top-1 selection (exactly one expert per token) with a straight-through estimator to enable gradient-based training.
AI.result: Experiments across five benchmarks, multiple model scales, and additional model families demonstrate that Hard-Routed MoR-LoRA preserves expert behavior while using substantially fewer trainable parameters than soft-routing mixture baselines. Analysis reveals that normalized soft mixtures often concentrate routing mass on a single expert anyway, supporting the sufficiency of hard routing.
AI.conclusion: Hard unit-scale routing with top-1 expert selection offers a simple, efficient, and effective abstraction for composing frozen LoRA reasoning experts, avoiding the distortion introduced by soft weighted combinations while matching or exceeding soft-routing performance with fewer parameters.

title: Dualformer: Efficient Feature Extractor for Complex-valued Blind Communication Signal Analysis
summary: Designing effective feature extractors is critical for blind signal analysis tasks such as automatic modulation recognition (AMR), signal scheme recognition (SSR), and \color{black} signal structure parsing (SSP). In this work, we propose dual-channel neural network (DualNN) that efficiently exploits complex-valued signals through parameter sharing across IQ channels. Unlike traditional real-valued or complex-valued models, DualNN is a groundbreaking framework which shares the network parameters for processing the real and imaginary parts of the complex-valued signals, and is theoretically shown to reduce generalization error while preserving expressive capacity. Specifically, we propose a novel Transformer-based architecture to implement DualNN, called Dualformer. The Dualformer segments input signals into patch-level tokens and captures multi-granularity features, enabling robust performance across diverse signal analysis tasks. Furthermore, we conduct extensive experiments comparing Dualformer with three Transformer-based baselines and four conventional DL-based approaches. Results demonstrate consistent performance improvements on AMR, SSR, and SSP tasks. Besides, the modular design of DualNN allows it to generalize well to blind signal processing tasks such as blind source separation and low-SNR spectrum sensing. This work paves the way for a broader application of DualNN architectures in unsupervised and weakly supervised complex-valued signal analysis scenarios.

AI.tldr: A Dual-Channel Neural Network (DualNN) framework is proposed that shares parameters across IQ channels for processing complex-valued signals, with a Transformer-based implementation called Dualformer. It achieves consistent improvements on AMR, SSR, and SSP tasks and generalizes to blind source separation and spectrum sensing.
AI.motivation: Designing effective feature extractors for blind signal analysis tasks (AMR, SSR, SSP) is challenging, and existing real-valued or complex-valued models have limitations. There is a need for a framework that efficiently exploits complex-valued signals while reducing generalization error without sacrificing expressive capacity.
AI.method: The authors propose DualNN, a dual-channel neural network that shares parameters between the real (I) and imaginary (Q) channels of complex-valued signals, theoretically shown to reduce generalization error while preserving expressiveness. A Transformer-based architecture, Dualformer, is introduced to implement DualNN, which segments input signals into patch-level tokens and captures multi-granularity features for robust multi-task performance.
AI.result: Extensive experiments comparing Dualformer against three Transformer-based baselines and four conventional DL-based methods show consistent performance improvements across AMR, SSR, and SSP tasks. The modular design also demonstrates effective generalization to blind source separation and low-SNR spectrum sensing.
AI.conclusion: DualNN, particularly its Dualformer implementation, is a promising framework for complex-valued signal analysis. Its parameter-sharing design and modularity enable strong performance and broad applicability, paving the way for future use in unsupervised and weakly supervised scenarios.

title: STEB: Style Text Embedding Benchmark
summary: While semantic embeddings are rigorously evaluated on the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark, the evaluation of style embeddings remains fragmented, with each work relying on their own set of tasks and datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Style Text Embedding Benchmark, a comprehensive open-source benchmark intended to standardize the evaluation of style embeddings. STEB encompasses 96 datasets across 7 languages, spanning applications such as authorship verification, authorship retrieval, AI-text detection, probing of linguistic features, and others. We find that semantic embeddings consistently fail in stylistic tasks, and that there is no style embedding that is universally superior across all tasks evaluated. We open-source the STEB code base at: https://github.com/rrivera1849/STEB.

AI.tldr: STEB introduces a standardized, multilingual benchmark for evaluating style embeddings across 96 datasets and 7 languages, revealing that semantic embeddings fail on stylistic tasks and no single style embedding excels universally.
AI.motivation: Style embedding evaluation is currently fragmented — each work uses its own ad-hoc tasks and datasets — unlike semantic embeddings which benefit from the standardized MTEB. This lack of standardization hinders fair comparison and progress in style representation learning.
AI.method: The authors construct STEB, a comprehensive open-source benchmark comprising 96 datasets spanning 7 languages. It covers diverse style-centric applications: authorship verification, authorship retrieval, AI-text detection, and linguistic feature probing. They evaluate both semantic embeddings (e.g., from sentence transformers) and existing style embeddings across this unified suite.
AI.result: Two key findings: (1) semantic embeddings consistently underperform on stylistic tasks, confirming they do not capture style well; (2) no single style embedding dominates across all tasks — performance is task-dependent, and there is no universal style representation.
AI.conclusion: STEB fills a critical gap by providing a standardized evaluation framework for style embeddings, analogous to MTEB for semantics. The results underscore the need for continued research into more robust and generalizable style representations, and the open-source release aims to facilitate future work.

title: BP-TTA: Balanced and Prototype-Guided Test-Time Adaptation in Dynamic Scenarios
summary: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) enables models trained on a source domain to adapt online to unlabeled test data under distribution shifts. While recent TTA methods have moved beyond static settings and begun to consider continual domain shifts, they primarily address distribution drift and fail to account for class imbalance in dynamic scenarios. In real-world test-time streams, class imbalance and continual domain shifts often occur at the same time and interact with each other. In this paper, we propose a novel Balanced and Prototype-Guided Test-Time Adaptation (BP-TTA) method, which combines batch-balanced sampling with prototype-guided adaptation to handle the class imbalance and continual domain shift problems. BP-TTA constructs balanced adaptation batches by integrating current samples with high-confidence historical instances, effectively mitigating bias toward dominant classes and stabilizing online updates. Meanwhile, BP-TTA maintains evolving class prototypes during inference and leverages prototype similarity as a constraint for model adaptation, thereby improving the reliability of pseudo-labels and enhancing the stability of online updates under persistent domain shifts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BP-TTA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art TTA methods in dynamic test-time streaming settings.

AI.tldr: BP-TTA addresses simultaneous class imbalance and continual domain shifts in test-time adaptation by combining batch-balanced sampling from historical high-confidence instances with prototype-guided adaptation, outperforming existing methods in dynamic streaming settings.
AI.motivation: Existing TTA methods handle continual domain shifts but overlook class imbalance. In real-world test-time streams, both distribution drift and class imbalance co-occur and interact, degrading adaptation performance. This gap motivates a unified solution.
AI.method: BP-TTA integrates two mechanisms: (1) batch-balanced sampling that combines current test samples with high-confidence historical instances to construct balanced mini-batches, mitigating dominant-class bias; (2) prototype-guided adaptation that maintains evolving class prototypes during inference and uses prototype similarity as a regularization constraint to improve pseudo-label reliability and stabilize updates under persistent domain shifts.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show BP-TTA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art TTA methods in dynamic test-time streaming settings where both class imbalance and continual domain shifts are present.
AI.conclusion: BP-TTA effectively tackles the practical challenge of simultaneous class imbalance and continual domain shifts in online test-time adaptation, demonstrating that balanced sampling coupled with prototype guidance yields more robust and stable adaptation in realistic streaming scenarios.

title: Calibrating the Evaluator: Does Probability Calibration Mitigate Preference Coupling in LLM Agent Feedback Loops?
summary: When large language model (LLM) agents adapt their behavior through evaluator feedback, systematic evaluator biases propagate into the agent's learned strategy distribution - a phenomenon termed evaluator preference coupling. Prior work has documented this coupling and established a diagnostic framework (EPC) to measure it, but has not investigated whether calibration techniques can mitigate the effect. We present the first study of evaluator calibration as mitigation: applying probability calibration to the evaluator's pairwise judgments to reduce spurious preference propagation. In a controlled within-subjects experiment (N=5) comparing standard binary TTRL (win/loss) with confidence-calibrated TTRL (probability-weighted updates) using DeepSeek-V4-Pro as executor and GLM5.2 as evaluator, we find that calibration reduces the coupling coefficient gamma by 20-49% and Jensen-Shannon divergence by 45-67%. A symmetric-LR control confirms the effect is not due to reduced update asymmetry. We release the calibrated TTRL protocol and recommend it as a lightweight mitigation for LLM-as-judge deployment pipelines.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates probability calibration of LLM evaluators as a mitigation for evaluator preference coupling, finding that calibrated TTRL reduces coupling coefficient γ by 20–49% and JS divergence by 45–67% compared to standard binary win/loss updates.
AI.motivation: When LLM agents learn from evaluator feedback, systematic biases in the evaluator propagate into the agent's learned strategy distribution—a phenomenon called evaluator preference coupling. Prior work (EPC framework) only diagnosed this problem but did not explore mitigation techniques. The authors aim to fill this gap by testing whether calibrating the evaluator's confidence scores can reduce spurious preference propagation.
AI.method: A controlled within-subjects experiment (N=5) was conducted using DeepSeek-V4-Pro as the executor agent and GLM5.2 as the evaluator. Two conditions were compared: (1) standard binary TTRL using win/loss signals, and (2) confidence-calibrated TTRL using probability-weighted updates. A symmetric-LR control condition was included to rule out reduced update asymmetry as a confound. The primary metrics were the coupling coefficient γ and Jensen-Shannon divergence.
AI.result: Probability calibration reduced the coupling coefficient γ by 20–49% and Jensen-Shannon divergence by 45–67%. The symmetric-LR control confirmed that these improvements were not merely artifacts of reduced update asymmetry.
AI.conclusion: Evaluator probability calibration is a lightweight, effective mitigation for evaluator preference coupling. The authors release the calibrated TTRL protocol and recommend it for LLM-as-judge deployment pipelines.

title: CHERRY: Compressed Hierarchical Experts with Recurrent Representational Yield
comment: 33 pages, 3 figures, 28 tables. Preprint. Figures are native TikZ/pgfplots. Evaluation is loss-based; downstream benchmarks (KMMLU, HAERAE, KoBEST, MMLU) and selection-control ablations (random-15%, top-loss-15%) to appear in a future version
summary:
We study three complementary techniques for training compute-efficient language models.
  (1) Selective supervision and per-token efficiency. Selective Ground Truth Token Training (SGT) concentrates supervision on the ~15% of output tokens that carry semantic payload. Through positive gradient coupling in position-shared transformer weights -- a token-level instance of auxiliary-task transfer -- the remaining 85% of unsupervised tokens still improve substantially, giving a 4.5x per-supervised-token efficiency (at the step-100 eval optimum, ~67% of the full-sequence loss reduction is recovered from 15% of the supervision). We prove that this improvement on unsupervised tokens is guaranteed whenever the gradient coupling coefficient gamma-bar = 0.72 is positive (Theorem 1), and show the effect is a property of natural-language structure: it collapses on shuffled text.
  (2) Depth compression with recurrent recovery. A 48-layer, 1B-parameter transformer is compressed to 6 layers (227M) by averaging adjacent layers and restored through learned recurrent unrolling. With 34 effective recurrent layers it reaches a held-out loss of 2.934, within measurement noise of a 566M dense model at 2.926 -- a 2.5x reduction in parameters.
  (3) Fusion of compressed experts. Assembling several compressed models as a Mixture of Efficient Experts (MoEE) with multi-token prediction improves over each single expert at comparable active parameters: a 2-expert MoEE reaches loss 2.789 versus 2.926 for the best single compressed model.
  We validate these techniques on CHERRY-1.8B, a Korean foundation model whose every trainable parameter derives from our own training runs. We are explicit throughout about the scope of the evidence (one model family, Korean data, loss-based metrics) and about which claims are established versus prospective.

AI.tldr: Presents three complementary techniques for compute-efficient LLM training: (1) Selective Ground Truth Token Training (SGT) that supervises only semantically rich tokens with formal gradient coupling guarantees, (2) depth compression via layer averaging with recurrent unrolling recovery, and (3) Mixture of Efficient Experts (MoEE) fusing compressed models. Validated on a 1.8B Korean foundation model (CHERRY-1.8B).
AI.motivation: Training large language models is computationally expensive. The authors seek methods to improve training efficiency — reducing supervision needs, model depth/parameters, and leveraging model ensembles — while maintaining competitive loss performance.
AI.method: Three techniques: (1) SGT: supervise only ~15% of output tokens that carry semantic content; prove via Theorem 1 that unsupervised tokens improve when gradient coupling coefficient γ̄ > 0 (measured at 0.72), with the effect disappearing on shuffled text. (2) Depth compression: average adjacent layers of a 48-layer 1B model into 6 layers (227M), then restore expressivity via learned recurrent unrolling (34 effective layers). (3) MoEE: fuse multiple compressed models as a mixture of experts with multi-token prediction.
AI.result: SGT achieves 4.5× per-supervised-token efficiency (~67% loss reduction from 15% supervision). Compressed model reaches held-out loss 2.934 vs. 2.926 for a 566M dense model (2.5× parameter reduction). 2-expert MoEE reaches loss 2.789 vs. 2.926 for best single compressed model.
AI.conclusion: The three techniques are complementary and effective on the CHERRY-1.8B Korean model. Authors are explicit about scope limitations (single model family, Korean data, loss metrics) and distinguish established vs. prospective claims.

title: Ask the World Before Acting: Budgeted Environment Probing for World-Model Calibration
summary: Long-horizon language agents do not only choose actions; they carry a private model of the world from one decision to the next. When that model drifts, a later failure can be decided before the failing action is ever taken. We study a direct repair mechanism: before committing to the next task action, an agent may ask the environment about one belief field and write the answer back into its world model. This makes environment interaction a scarce calibration resource, not merely a way to advance the task. We introduce \method, a budgeted probing operator for structured belief tables. The useful probes are not the same everywhere. Procedural beliefs, such as tool dependencies, can often be repaired by targeted checks, but those checks spend steps that the task may need. Spatial beliefs, such as object locations and graph edges, rely more on structural cues; the agent's own confidence can be a poor guide when the world changes off-screen. A type-stratified analysis formalizes this probe-action frontier, and controlled experiments show that mid-planning environment evidence reduces terminal world-model error when the probe policy follows the structure of the task.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a budgeted probing mechanism that lets long-horizon language agents repair their world model mid-planning by querying the environment, framing environment interaction as a scarce calibration resource rather than purely task advancement.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon language agents maintain a private world model across decisions. When this model drifts from reality, downstream failures become inevitable before the erroneous action is even taken. The problem is that agents lack a principled mechanism to detect and repair belief drift mid-task without wasting scarce interaction steps.
AI.method: The authors propose a budgeted probing operator for structured belief tables. The method distinguishes between procedural beliefs (e.g., tool dependencies), which benefit from targeted checks, and spatial beliefs (e.g., object locations, graph edges), which rely on structural cues. A type-stratified analysis formalizes the probe-action frontier, and the probing policy is guided by task structure rather than naive agent confidence.
AI.result: Controlled experiments demonstrate that mid-planning environment evidence reduces terminal world-model error when the probe policy follows task structure. Naive confidence-based probing is unreliable for spatial beliefs when the world changes off-screen.
AI.conclusion: Environment interaction should be treated as a calibration resource. Structured, budgeted probing aligned with task structure is more effective than undirected or confidence-based approaches for maintaining world-model fidelity in long-horizon language agents.

title: Resolving superposition in AI for interpretability and cross-modal alignment in patient-neuronal images
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures (plus 14 in appendix), 1 table, NeurIPS 2026 preprint
summary: Artificial intelligence is transforming our capability to solve biological challenges. In dimensionality bottleneck regimes exacerbated by high-dimensional biological data, Neural networks force distinct concepts into the lower dimensions known as superposition. Although this superposition is widely known to hinder interpretability, its impact on corrupting the geometry of latent spaces remains critically overlooked. Here, we utilized sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on over 100,000 multiplexed images of patient-derived Parkinson's disease and healthy neurons to resolve superposition. This approach bypasses the mathematical non-uniqueness of feature attribution by shifting to interpretable latent representation analysis. We theoretically and empirically demonstrate that superposition contaminates representational metric spaces, and thereby SAEs successfully recover geometric fidelity. By treating these geometrically purified representations as single-cell state vectors, we adapted single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data analysis methodologies directly to the image domain. Finally, we introduce GW-map, utilizing Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport to align these image representations with authentic scRNA-seq data \emph{de novo}. This coupling reconstructs hierarchical neuronal pathology pathways such as Calcium-AIS scaffold, without reference spatial transcriptomics, establishing a scalable foundation for spatial biology. Code is available at https://github.com/jijihihi/Bio_superposition

AI.tldr: The paper shows that superposition in neural networks corrupts latent space geometry in biological imaging. Using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on Parkinson's disease neuron images, the authors recover geometric fidelity, adapt scRNA-seq analysis methods to images, and introduce GW-map (Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport) to align image representations with scRNA-seq data de novo, reconstructing neuronal pathology pathways without reference spatial transcriptomics.
AI.motivation: Neural networks trained on high-dimensional biological data suffer from the dimensionality bottleneck, forcing distinct concepts into lower-dimensional representations via superposition. While superposition is known to harm interpretability, its corruption of latent space geometry—critical for downstream representational analyses—has been overlooked. This work aims to resolve superposition and restore geometric fidelity to enable meaningful single-cell analyses in image-based spatial biology.
AI.method: The authors employ sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on over 100,000 multiplexed images of patient-derived Parkinson's disease and healthy neurons to disentangle superposed representations. They theoretically and empirically demonstrate geometric corruption from superposition and recovery via SAEs. The geometrically purified representations are then treated as single-cell state vectors, enabling direct adaptation of scRNA-seq data analysis methodologies to the image domain. Finally, they introduce GW-map, which leverages Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport to align these image representations with authentic scRNA-seq data de novo, without requiring reference spatial transcriptomics.
AI.result: SAEs successfully recover geometric fidelity in representational metric spaces previously contaminated by superposition. The approach enables scRNA-seq-style analyses directly on image-derived single-cell state vectors. GW-map reconstructs hierarchical neuronal pathology pathways (e.g., Calcium-AIS scaffold) solely from image-scRNA-seq alignment, without spatial transcriptomics references, establishing a scalable foundation for spatial biology.
AI.conclusion: Superposition corrupts latent space geometry in biological neural network representations—a problem SAEs can resolve. By recovering geometric fidelity, image-based representations become amenable to scRNA-seq analytical frameworks. GW-map enables de novo alignment with transcriptomic data, reconstructing disease-relevant pathways and offering a scalable paradigm for spatial biology that bypasses the need for reference spatial transcriptomics datasets.

title: Explicit Fuzzy Logic in the Feed-Forward Layer: Self-Forgetting Quantifiers Discover Legible Grammatical-Licensing Detectors
summary: A transformer's feed-forward (FFN) sublayer materializes the distinctions attention gathers, yet gives no account of what it computes. In a parameter-neutral replacement, each hidden unit is an explicit fuzzy set operation on sigmoid-bounded [0,1] memberships: intersection A*B and set-difference A*(1-B), the latter a bounded positive negation ("A but not B") that gated/bilinear units lack -- a negation-capable FFN (NC-FFN). On N-bit parity they are the most parameter-efficient reasoning basis at shallow depth; at scale (125M, OpenWebText) NC-FFN ties the GELU baseline's perplexity, every unit carrying explicit logical form. Two limits share one cause: two-operand logic localizes to layer 0 and erodes under training, and the one robust grammatical deficit concentrates in licensing and quantifiers, beyond within-token operators. We resolve both with a small block of sequence quantifiers: a soft existential and a soft proportion, each with a per-unit learned forgetting rate from a sticky init. This recovers the deficit at epoch one (halving the wider epoch-two gap), modestly leads on LAMBADA, and makes the FFN legible: the structure now holds and migrates into depth; the decay un-learns its stickiness (median half-life ~1.5 tokens; zero latch units); and at the semantic layers the units read, without dictionary learning, as grammatical licensing detectors: each fires on a licensor (a comparative, a passive participle, a negative-polarity item) and carries its memory forward to predict the licensed word (than, by, nor). This legibility is localized and free only up to a partition (a fully Boolean FFN diverges in training), but the result is a parameter-neutral, language-model-quality transformer with a readable, interpretable-by-construction grammatical mechanism -- an account not just of what a feed-forward layer represents but how it licenses.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NC-FFN, a feed-forward network where hidden units compute explicit fuzzy set operations (intersection and set-difference) on [0,1]-bounded memberships. While parameter-efficient and interpretable, it suffers from logical erosion during training and a grammatical deficit in licensing/quantifiers. Adding soft sequence quantifiers (existential and proportion) with learned forgetting rates resolves these issues, yielding a transformer with a readable grammatical licensing mechanism.
AI.motivation: Standard transformer FFN sublayers lack interpretability — they offer no account of what they compute. The authors aim to replace FFN hidden units with explicit, interpretable logical operations while maintaining language model quality, making the feed-forward layer's computations legible rather than opaque.
AI.method: Each FFN hidden unit becomes a fuzzy set operation on sigmoid-bounded [0,1] memberships: intersection (A*B) and set-difference (A*(1-B), i.e., "A but not B"). This is contrasted against gated/bilinear units which lack negation. Then, a small block of soft sequence quantifiers is added: a soft existential and a soft proportion, each with a per-unit learned forgetting rate initialized with a "sticky" bias. The full model is evaluated at 125M scale on OpenWebText.
AI.result: NC-FFN ties GELU baseline perplexity at 125M scale. However, two-operand logic localizes to layer 0 and erodes under training, and a grammatical deficit appears in licensing/quantifiers. The sequence quantifier addition recovers this deficit at epoch one, modestly leads on LAMBADA, and yields interpretable units: decay stabilizes at ~1.5 token half-life, and units function as grammatical licensing detectors (firing on licensors like comparatives, passive participles, NPI items, and projecting to licensed words). A fully Boolean FFN diverges in training.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates a parameter-neutral, language-model-quality transformer with an interpretable-by-construction grammatical mechanism in its FFN layers. The NC-FFN with sequence quantifiers provides an account not merely of what the FFN represents, but how it performs grammatical licensing — making the feed-forward sublayer legible without sacrificing performance.

title: CDR-Bench: Evaluating Faithful Execution of Compositional, Order-Sensitive Data Refinement Recipes
comment: 29 pages, 20 figures. Corresponding authors: Daoyuan Chen and Yi R. Fung
summary: Data refinement involves executing multi-step recipes over evolving text states, where both composition and execution order of processing operators determine the outcome. While existing benchmarks either isolate text editing or entangle it with code and tool execution, it remains unclear whether LLMs can directly and faithfully execute these compositional, order-sensitive data refinement recipes. To fill this gap, we introduce CDR-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark featuring 3,462 high-quality tasks spanning four real-world data refinement domains and 29 distinct operators. Our benchmark evaluates models across atomic, order-agnostic, and order-sensitive settings, leveraging deterministic reference outputs to enable exact evaluation. Experiments on 10+ state-of-the-art LLMs reveal consistent failure patterns: performance degrades sharply in compositional settings, and order-sensitive recipe success collapses. These findings underline that current LLMs lack the procedural faithfulness required for reliable compositional data refinement.

AI.tldr: CDR-Bench is a benchmark of 3,462 tasks across four domains and 29 operators for evaluating LLMs on compositional, order-sensitive data refinement. Experiments on 10+ LLMs reveal that performance collapses in compositional and order-sensitive settings, showing current models lack procedural faithfulness for reliable multi-step text transformation.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks either isolate text editing or conflate it with code/tool execution, leaving a gap in understanding whether LLMs can faithfully execute compositional, order-sensitive data refinement recipes directly. The authors aim to systematically assess this capability.
AI.method: The authors construct CDR-Bench, a benchmark with 3,462 tasks across four real-world data refinement domains and 29 distinct operators. Tasks are structured in atomic, order-agnostic, and order-sensitive settings, using deterministic reference outputs for exact-match evaluation. They test 10+ state-of-the-art LLMs across these settings.
AI.result: LLM performance degrades sharply in compositional settings compared to atomic ones. Order-sensitive recipe execution success collapses, revealing consistent failure patterns across all tested models. These results hold across diverse model families and scales.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs lack the procedural faithfulness needed for reliable compositional data refinement. The benchmark serves as a diagnostic tool, and the findings highlight a fundamental limitation in LLMs' ability to follow ordered, multi-step transformation instructions.

title: Mixture-of-Control: State-Aware Fine-Tuning for Transformer-based Models
comment: ICML 2026 Workshop on Connecting Low-rank Representations in AI, CoLoRAI, 26 pages, 12 figures, 5 tables
summary: State-based fine-tuning has emerged as a compelling alternative to weight-based adaptation for transformers, updating lightweight controls into states rather than model weights, offering substantial memory savings while retaining parameter efficiency. However, most existing state-based methods typically apply only per-block control updates, which limits inter-block information exchange and restricts representational adaptation. Meanwhile, prior mechanisms that enable cross-block communication often introduce considerable computational overhead, reducing their practicality for efficient fine-tuning. We introduce Mixture-of-Control (MoC), a lightweight fine-tuning framework that adaptively integrates local and global control signals to enhance representation learning. MoC treats block-wise control states as experts in a sparse mixture-of-experts process, enabling efficient communication across transformer blocks. Empirical results across diverse transformer-based benchmarks demonstrate that MoC outperforms state-based methods while maintaining a comparable memory and computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: MoC introduces a sparse mixture-of-experts framework that treats per-block control states as experts, enabling efficient cross-block communication for state-based transformer fine-tuning, outperforming existing state-based methods with comparable efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing state-based fine-tuning methods apply per-block control updates only, limiting inter-block information exchange and representational capacity. Prior cross-block mechanisms introduce excessive computational overhead, making them impractical for efficient fine-tuning.
AI.method: MoC treats block-wise control states as experts within a sparse mixture-of-experts process, adaptively integrating local and global control signals to enable efficient communication across transformer blocks.
AI.result: MoC outperforms existing state-based fine-tuning methods across diverse transformer-based benchmarks while maintaining comparable memory and computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: MoC successfully bridges the gap between per-block control limitations and cross-block communication overhead, offering a practical and performant state-based fine-tuning solution for transformers.

title: Theory of Mind and Persuasion Beyond Conversation: Assessing the Capacity of LLMs to Induce Belief States via Planning and Action
summary: Theory of Mind (ToM) benchmarks for Large Language Models (LLMs) typically rely on passive question-answering formats, but the deployment of LLMs in increasingly agentic and autonomous forms demands new evaluations. In this paper we evaluate an agent's ability to induce specific belief states in other agents by taking actions rather than using conversational persuasion, a capability we call Non-Conversational Planning ToM (NCP-ToM). NCP-ToM is likely to be essential for many agent use-cases, including within user-assistant interactions and pedagogical contexts, but may also present manipulation or misinformation risks. Using a novel framework, NCP-ExploreToM, we subvert the conventional task structure by providing models with a set of belief state goals and requiring them to move objects or direct characters into rooms to achieve their goals. We evaluated six frontier models, including GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro and the Claude 4 series, and a cohort of human participants, across 600 task instances. GPT-5 was successful on approximately 80% of tasks in the agentic setting, and was the only model to outperform human participants on our task, but was still less robust than humans across contexts. We additionally found that all models, like humans, performed better on tasks inducing true belief states than false belief states, which is a positive signal for alignment efforts. These findings highlight emerging social-reasoning capabilities in LLMs for non-conversational task completion and underscore the necessity of agentic evaluations for understanding the safety and alignment of autonomous social agents.

AI.tldr: Introduces Non-Conversational Planning Theory of Mind (NCP-ToM), evaluating LLMs' ability to induce belief states in other agents through physical actions rather than dialogue. Using the NCP-ExploreToM framework across 600 tasks, GPT-5 achieved ~80% success and was the only model surpassing humans, though all models (like humans) performed better on true-belief than false-belief tasks, with positive alignment implications.
AI.motivation: Existing ToM benchmarks rely on passive Q&A formats, which fail to capture the demands of increasingly agentic and autonomous LLM deployments. The authors argue that a new capability — inducing specific belief states through actions rather than conversation — is essential for real-world agent use-cases (e.g., user-assistant interaction, pedagogy) and carries both utility and manipulation/misinformation risks.
