AI.motivation: Classical deep learning assumes overfitting risk with increased capacity, but QML suffers instead from "quantum underfitting" — the expressivity-trainability paradox where the vast Hilbert space that promises quantum advantage mathematically causes Barren Plateaus, rendering models untrainable at scale. The field needs a rigorous framework to resolve this architectural bottleneck.
AI.method: Synthesizes Dynamical Lie Algebra (DLA) theory and Geometric QML to establish a mathematical framework linking the algebraic dimension of circuit generators to optimization dynamics. Empirically validates on a non-linear binary classification task, comparing unstructured PQCs against symmetry-preserving architectures that embed group-theoretic geometric priors to restrict DLA growth to polynomial regime.
AI.result: Unstructured architectures achieve near-perfect training accuracy through unscalable parameterization (quantum overfitting). Embedding geometric priors via restricted DLA dimension acts as a structural regularizer, sacrificing raw memorization capacity but yielding scalable, gradient-rich training landscapes with guaranteed trainability.
AI.conclusion: A "Trainability-by-Design" paradigm is proposed: restricting DLA growth to polynomial regime through symmetry-preserving geometric priors offers a robust, scalable roadmap for practical quantum neural networks, resolving the expressivity-trainability paradox.

title: ACE: Pluggable Adaptive Context Elasticizer across Agents
summary: The increasing complexity of agentic tasks has led to rapidly growing trajectory lengths, which poses significant challenges for large language model (LLM) based agents with fixed context windows. Existing context management techniques, such as truncation and summarization, suffer from inherent inflexibility and irreversibility: once information is discarded or compressed, it cannot be recovered even when it becomes critically relevant in later decision steps. To address these limitations, we propose the Adaptive Context Elasticizer (ACE), a plug-and-play module that elastically orchestrates historical step information into the agent's context at each decision step. ACE maintains a lossless message maintenance layer that stores both raw messages and compressed abstractions for each historical step, while a context orchestration layer adaptively assigns each step an elastic type as raw, abstract, or drop, at every decision step based on the current task state. This reversible design ensures that the main LLM always receives a compact yet information-rich context. We adapt ACE to four diverse agent frameworks, including ReAct, DeepAgent, WebThinker, and MiroFlow, without training or architectural modifications. Experiments show that ACE consistently outperforms truncation and summarization baselines, and brings consistent performance gains across all four agent frameworks.

AI.tldr: ACE is a plug-and-play module that elastically manages agent context by maintaining lossless storage of both raw and compressed historical steps, adaptively selecting raw/abstract/drop representations per step at each decision point, enabling reversible context orchestration without training or architectural changes.
AI.motivation: Agentic tasks produce increasingly long trajectories that exceed LLM context windows. Existing solutions (truncation, summarization) are inflexible and irreversible—once information is lost, it cannot be recovered when needed later, leading to suboptimal decisions.
AI.method: ACE consists of two layers: (1) a lossless message maintenance layer storing both raw messages and compressed abstractions for each historical step; (2) a context orchestration layer that dynamically assigns each historical step an elastic type (raw, abstract, or drop) at every decision step based on current task state. This reversible design lets the main LLM receive a compact yet information-rich context, allowing previously compressed or dropped information to be recovered when critically relevant.
AI.result: ACE was adapted to four diverse agent frameworks—ReAct, DeepAgent, WebThinker, and MiroFlow—without training or architectural modifications. It consistently outperformed truncation and summarization baselines, delivering consistent performance gains across all four frameworks.
AI.conclusion: ACE provides a flexible, reversible, and training-free solution for context management in LLM-based agents, effectively addressing the tension between context window limits and the need for long-horizon information retention.

title: Introduction to Stochastic Differential Equations for Generative Machine Learning: A Variational Perspective
summary: The use of ordinary and stochastic differential equations has led to substantial progress in generative machine learning with applications to, for example, image, video and biomolecule generation. This paper provides a self-contained and informal introduction to the differential equations, the probabilistic framework for using them in generative modeling and the Fokker--Planck equation that governs the temporal evolution of the marginal distribution of the stochastic variables of the differential equations. The variational lower bound on the log-likelihood (the evidence lower bound, ELBO) is derived and used as a general starting point for a discussion of diffusion models, score matching, and flow matching. All of these approaches may be viewed as specific parameterizations of the most general variational approach. A one-dimensional density modeling problem is used as a simple example to compare different parameterizations.

AI.tldr: A self-contained tutorial introducing the differential equation framework for generative modeling, covering SDEs, the Fokker–Planck equation, and the ELBO, with diffusion models, score matching, and flow matching unified as parameterizations of a general variational approach.
AI.motivation: Generative modeling based on ordinary and stochastic differential equations has achieved significant empirical success across diverse domains (images, video, biomolecules), yet the underlying theory can be opaque. The authors aim to provide an accessible, informal, and unified exposition that demystifies the mathematical foundations and reveals how seemingly distinct approaches share a common variational framework.
AI.method: The paper presents a pedagogical synthesis: it introduces ODEs/SDEs, the probabilistic framework for generative modeling, and the Fokker–Planck equation governing marginal distribution evolution. The evidence lower bound (ELBO) is derived as a variational lower bound on log-likelihood, serving as the unifying starting point. Diffusion models, score matching, and flow matching are then each shown to be specific parameterizations of this general variational objective. A one-dimensional density modeling example is used throughout for concrete illustration and comparison.
AI.result: The paper does not report novel empirical results; rather, it demonstrates conceptual unification: diffusion models, score matching, and flow matching are all shown to be particular parameterizations of the same variational bound. The 1D example provides an intuitive comparison of how each parameterization behaves.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion models, score matching, and flow matching should not be viewed as fundamentally distinct paradigms but as different parameterizations within a single variational framework rooted in SDEs and the Fokker–Planck equation. The ELBO serves as the common theoretical backbone connecting them.

title: Which Tokens Matter? Adaptive Token Selection for RLVR with the Relative Surprisal Index
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a powerful tool for propelling Large Language Models (LLMs) beyond imitation-based training towards more robust reasoning capabilities. Among existing approaches, RL with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a pivotal paradigm for advancing LLM reasoning. Despite its empirical success, recent studies have offered different insights. One line of inquiry advocates prioritizing high-entropy token positions during training, while another perspective cautions against allowing low-probability tokens to dominate gradient updates. Notably, although high-entropy tokens are usually correlated with low probability, both paradigms empirically yield substantial performance gains. In this work, we argue that evaluating sampled-token probability or entropy in isolation is insufficient to capture the policy optimization dynamics. To resolve this tension, we introduce the Relative Surprisal Index (RSI), a principled, information-theoretic metric that naturally couples the token's entropy with the probability of the selected token. We show that, under mild conditions, RSI is related to the local ratio between the first-order variations of the logit-gradient norm and predictive entropy under a selected-logit perturbation. Building on RSI, we propose RSI Selection (RSI-S), an entropy-adaptive token filtering method that retains tokens within a stable RSI interval. RSI-S successfully reconciles previous contradictory paradigms and filters out both redundant low-surprisal tokens and unstable high-surprisal tail tokens. Empirical evaluations show that RSI-S achieves higher avg@32 accuracy across different model scales (Qwen2.5-1.5B, 3B, and 7B) on AIME and AMC benchmarks: RSI-S improves avg@32 accuracy by 2--3 percentage points over GRPO. Overall, RSI offers a promising perspective for RLVR improvement.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Relative Surprisal Index (RSI), an information-theoretic metric coupling token entropy with token probability, and proposes RSI Selection (RSI-S), an entropy-adaptive token filtering method that reconciles conflicting RLVR paradigms — achieving 2–3 pp avg@32 improvement over GRPO on AIME and AMC benchmarks across Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B/7B models.
AI.motivation: Two conflicting paradigms exist in RLVR for LLM reasoning: one advocates prioritizing high-entropy token positions, while the other warns against letting low-probability tokens dominate gradients. Both yield empirical gains, yet evaluating token probability or entropy in isolation fails to capture the full policy optimization dynamics. This tension motivates a unified, principled metric.
AI.method: The authors propose the Relative Surprisal Index (RSI), an information-theoretic metric that couples a token's predictive entropy with the probability of the selected token. Under mild conditions, RSI is shown to relate to the local ratio between first-order variations of the logit-gradient norm and predictive entropy under a selected-logit perturbation. Building on RSI, they introduce RSI Selection (RSI-S), an entropy-adaptive token filtering strategy that retains only tokens whose RSI falls within a stable interval, thereby filtering both low-surprisal (redundant) and high-surprisal (unstable tail) tokens.
AI.result: RSI-S achieves 2–3 percentage points higher avg@32 accuracy over GRPO on AIME and AMC benchmarks across three model scales (Qwen2.5-1.5B, 3B, 7B).
AI.conclusion: The Relative Surprisal Index provides a principled, unified perspective that reconciles previously contradictory RLVR paradigms. RSI-S offers a promising direction for improving RL-based reasoning in LLMs.

title: Robustness of neural networks to random noise perturbations of their inputs
summary: We investigate the problem of the robustness of a trained neural network to the perturbation of its input values. More specifically, we examine the interplay between the accuracy of the network, as measured by the mean squared error, and robustness. Accordingly, we present a robustness measure, which, with high probability, suggests an upper bound on the mean squared error of the network, with respect to an input data set, for a given perturbation of the input values of the network. The measure we propose is both simple and efficient to compute, treating the neural network as a black box. We provide experimental results on several real-world data sets showing the efficacy of the proposed method. We also introduce the concept of robustness curves, which allows us to further analyse robustness within and between data sets.

AI.tldr: Proposes a simple, black-box robustness measure for neural networks that probabilistically bounds MSE under input perturbation, and introduces robustness curves for cross-dataset analysis.
AI.motivation: To formalize and quantify the relationship between neural network accuracy (MSE) and robustness to input perturbations, providing a practical tool for assessing network vulnerability without requiring white-box access.
AI.method: A black-box robustness measure derived with probabilistic guarantees that upper-bounds the expected MSE under input perturbation. The method requires only network outputs, avoiding internal gradient or architecture inspection. Robustness curves are introduced as an analytical tool for comparing robustness across different datasets.
AI.result: Experimental validation on multiple real-world datasets demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed robustness measure and the utility of robustness curves for analyzing robustness patterns within and across datasets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed measure offers an efficient, probabilistically sound way to assess neural network robustness as a black box, and robustness curves provide a meaningful framework for comparative robustness analysis.

title: Scientific Explanations in Health Sciences: Causality, Trust, and Epistemic Adequacy
summary: Medical Artificial Intelligence (AI) is widely expected to transform clinical practice, yet the decision-making processes of many Machine Learning (ML) models remain opaque. Explainability has been advanced as a partial remedy to clarify why AI generates predictions, particularly in high-stakes contexts. Despite ongoing efforts, debates on what constitutes an adequate medical explanation remain unsettled. Yet, explanation has long been a central topic of inquiry in the philosophy of science and medicine. The insights developed in these fields, however, have been largely overlooked in contemporary explainable AI (XAI) research, leaving its foundational assumptions insufficiently examined. To address this gap, this paper develops a critical review at the intersection of philosophy of science and XAI. It examines prevailing accounts of what counts as an explanation in the health sciences and assesses their adequacy for informing XAI in medicine, arguing that they provide necessary conditions for a philosophically grounded approach to explainability in this domain. Building on this foundational philosophical literature, the discussion identifies three central axes of analysis: the role of causality in medical reasoning, the epistemic and relational dimensions of medical trust, and the criteria of explanatory adequacy as shaped by the pragmatic needs of diverse stakeholders. By integrating philosophical analysis with current developments in medical AI, the paper outlines principles for designing XAI systems that offer explanations that are not only epistemically robust but also aligned with the epistemic and practical requirements of clinical decision-making, shaping ongoing debates in medical XAI toward underexplored conceptual foundations.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that contemporary medical XAI research neglects philosophy of science insights about explanation. It reviews philosophical accounts of explanatory adequacy, identifies three key axes (causality, trust, pragmatic stakeholder needs), and proposes principles for building epistemically robust, clinically aligned XAI systems.
AI.motivation: Medical AI models are increasingly deployed in clinical settings, but their opacity undermines trust and safe adoption. Existing XAI approaches lack rigorous conceptual foundations because they overlook decades of philosophical scholarship on what constitutes an adequate explanation in science and medicine. The paper aims to bridge this gap.
AI.method: This is a critical review paper operating at the intersection of philosophy of science and XAI. It surveys philosophical accounts of explanation in the health sciences, evaluates their relevance to medical XAI, and synthesizes three conceptual axes for analysis: causality, epistemic/relational trust, and pragmatic explanatory adequacy.
AI.result: The analysis yields three foundational axes: (1) causality is central to medical reasoning and XAI must engage with causal rather than merely correlational accounts; (2) trust in medical AI has both epistemic and relational dimensions that explanations must address; (3) explanatory adequacy is context-dependent, shaped by the pragmatic needs of diverse stakeholders (clinicians, patients, developers, regulators).
AI.conclusion: Medical XAI needs philosophically grounded reorientation. The paper outlines design principles ensuring explanations are epistemically robust and practically aligned with clinical decision-making, steering the field toward underexplored conceptual foundations rather than solely technical fixes.

title: Evil Spectra: How Optimisers can Amplify or Suppress Emergent Misalignment
summary: Emergent misalignment (EM) is a recently discovered phenomenon in LLMs where fine-tuning on a narrow misaligned task, such as writing insecure code, leads to broadly misaligned behaviour on unrelated prompts. Previous work has noted that the severity of EM is highly sensitive to training choices; however, we still lack a systematic characterisation of this sensitivity. We perform a sweep over several Qwen3 models, optimisers, datasets, and batch sizes, and find that the choice of optimiser has the largest effect, producing a 7x spread in misalignment rate. Surprisingly, model size has a negligible effect within the Qwen3 family. An additional sweep over 12 models from three families using Adam confirms that model scale (1B-235B) and family have negligible effects for that optimiser. Analysing the loss-alignment relationship on Qwen3-8B, we find that final log training loss is a strong predictor of alignment, and that stratifying by optimiser captures nearly all the residual variance. Training dynamics reveal that each optimiser follows a different trajectory through loss-alignment space, and that after significant training, the optimiser becomes more important than training loss as a predictor of alignment. Muon, the adaptive optimiser that preserves alignment the best, implicitly regularises for a more uniform distribution of singular values of the LoRA adapter. We evaluate this insight by training with an additional loss term that incentivises a flatter singular value spectrum, and find that this substantially recovers alignment for the more EM-prone adaptive optimisers (Adam and Lion), with negligible cost to training loss. These results identify optimiser choice as a key factor in EM severity, but show that spectral regularisation can substantially mitigate the effects of EM-prone optimisers.

AI.tldr: Optimizer choice dominates emergent misalignment severity in LLMs (7x spread), while model scale has negligible effect. Spectral regularization of LoRA adapter singular values can substantially recover alignment for EM-prone optimizers like Adam and Lion.
AI.motivation: Emergent misalignment (EM) severity is known to be sensitive to training choices, but no systematic characterization of this sensitivity exists. The authors aim to identify which hyperparameters and training factors most influence EM, and to understand the underlying mechanisms.
AI.method: Systematic sweeps over Qwen3 models (varying optimizers, datasets, batch sizes), followed by broader sweeps over 12 models from 3 families (1B-235B) using Adam. Loss-alignment relationship analysis on Qwen3-8B, training dynamics trajectory analysis, and singular value spectrum analysis of LoRA adapters. An additional spectral regularization loss term is introduced to incentivize flatter singular value distributions.
AI.result: Optimizer choice produces a 7x spread in misalignment rate — the largest effect among all factors tested. Model size and family have negligible effects under Adam. Final log training loss strongly predicts alignment; stratifying by optimizer captures nearly all residual variance. Training dynamics show each optimizer follows distinct loss-alignment trajectories. Muon preserves alignment best by implicitly regularizing for a more uniform singular value distribution of the LoRA adapter. Adding spectral regularization substantially recovers alignment for Adam and Lion with negligible training loss cost.
AI.conclusion: Optimizer choice is the dominant factor in EM severity. Spectral regularization of LoRA adapter singular values offers a practical mitigation strategy, enabling the use of EM-prone adaptive optimizers without sacrificing alignment.

title: Think in English, Answer in Korean: Efficient Adaptation of Multilingual Tool-Using Agents
summary: We present LuckyStar 111B, a 111B-parameter hybrid reasoning model developed through a collaboration between Cohere and LG CNS for Korean-English enterprise agents under practical memory and serving constraints. The model trains from Cohere's fully post-trained Command A model rather than a new pretraining run, and uses preamble conditioning to switch between concise non-reasoning behavior and longer tool-oriented reasoning. We study four choices for scaling tool-using agents efficiently: multilingual supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for multi-step tool-use tasks, language-consistency rewards for Korean user-facing responses, and 4-bit quantization for single-GPU serving. The adapted model improves mathematical reasoning, function calling, and agentic natural-language-to-SQL (NL2SQL) performance while preserving general Korean and English instruction-following quality. These results provide a practical recipe and failure-mode analysis for adapting post-trained multilingual models to verifiable agentic workflows under memory-constrained deployment.

AI.tldr: LuckyStar 111B is a 111B-parameter hybrid reasoning model for Korean-English enterprise agents, adapted from Cohere's Command A via supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, with 4-bit quantization enabling single-GPU deployment. It improves math reasoning, function calling, and NL2SQL while maintaining general instruction-following quality.
AI.motivation: Enterprise deployment of large models faces two key constraints: (1) models must handle both quick, concise responses and multi-step tool-using reasoning within a single system, and (2) serving must fit within practical memory limits (single GPU). Additionally, adapting an existing post-trained model to Korean-English bilingual enterprise agent workflows — rather than training from scratch — is underexplored.
AI.method: The authors adapt Cohere's fully post-trained Command A model using: (1) multilingual supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for Korean-English agent tasks; (2) reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards on multi-step tool-use trajectories; (3) language-consistency rewards to ensure Korean responses stay in Korean; and (4) preamble conditioning — a mechanism that switches model behavior between concise non-reasoning mode and extended tool-oriented reasoning mode based on a prepended control token. The final model is served via 4-bit quantization for single-GPU deployment.
AI.result: LuckyStar 111B shows improved performance on mathematical reasoning, function calling, and agentic NL2SQL benchmarks compared to the base Command A model, while preserving general Korean and English instruction-following capabilities. The paper also provides failure-mode analysis of the adapted model.
AI.conclusion: Post-trained multilingual models can be effectively adapted to verifiable, tool-using agentic workflows under strict deployment constraints using a combination of multilingual SFT, verifiable-reward RL, language-consistency rewards, and quantization. This offers a practical, cost-efficient recipe for enterprise agent deployment without requiring a costly new pretraining run.

title: Calibration, Not Compilation: Detecting and Repairing Misspecified Probabilistic Programs Written by Language Models
summary: Language models increasingly write probabilistic programs (in NumPyro, Stan, or Pyro), but a program that compiles, runs, and passes every unit test can still be \emph{statistically} wrong -- a Gaussian likelihood for heavy-tailed data, a Poisson for over-dispersed counts, an invalid prior support, or a pathological parameterization. The right verifier is therefore not a test suite but the Bayesian workflow itself: posterior predictive checks, simulation-based calibration, sampler diagnostics ($\hat R$, divergences, ESS), and held-out predictive density. We study this calibration oracle along three axes. \textbf{Detection:} on a benchmark of $14$ misspecification types across $10$ model families ($200$ instances), it flags the bug with AUC $0.97$ ($88\%$ at $2\%$ FPR \emph{when handed the correct reference program, an upper bound}) -- and a fully \emph{reference-free} version that uses no correct program reaches $62$--$78\%$ (the upper figure from a small automated model search), versus $0\%$ for a unit-test oracle. \textbf{Repair:} used as feedback in an LLM repair loop across fifteen models, calibration significantly outperforms unit-test feedback -- which is itself \emph{significantly worse than no feedback at all}, a passing test inducing false confidence that suppresses repair -- and improves over no feedback on strong-but-unsaturated models (GPT-5.1 $33{\to}92\%$, Claude $75{\to}100\%$; paired McNemar, $n{=}228$). \textbf{Reality:} on programs LLMs write from scratch for neutral briefs, $15$--$47\%$ of runnable ones are statistically misspecified (unit tests catch none), and calibration-guided repair significantly beats LLM-as-judge review, a Bayesian-workflow checklist, and data-summary self-debug. Across all three, the lesson is the same: for probabilistic programs, correctness is calibration, not compilation.

AI.tldr: Language models that generate probabilistic programs (e.g., in NumPyro, Stan, Pyro) can produce statistically wrong code that passes all unit tests. This paper shows that Bayesian workflow diagnostics — posterior predictive checks, simulation-based calibration, sampler diagnostics — serve as an effective "calibration oracle" for detecting, repairing, and preventing statistical misspecifications, outperforming unit testing and other review methods across all three axes.
AI.motivation: Probabilistic programs present a unique verification challenge: a program can compile, run, and pass unit tests while being statistically misspecified (e.g., wrong likelihood family, invalid prior support, poor parameterization). Standard test suites are blind to such errors. The authors argue that the Bayesian workflow itself — posterior predictive checks, simulation-based calibration, R-hat, divergences, ESS — is the correct verification mechanism, and they systematically evaluate its effectiveness as both a detection and repair signal for LLM-generated probabilistic code.
AI.method: The paper studies a "calibration oracle" along three axes: (1) Detection: benchmarking 14 misspecification types across 10 model families (200 instances), measuring AUC and detection rate at low false-positive rates, comparing a reference-based version (with access to a correct program) against a fully reference-free version using automated model search, with a unit-test oracle as baseline. (2) Repair: using calibration feedback in an LLM repair loop across 15 models, comparing against unit-test feedback and no-feedback baselines, evaluated via paired McNemar tests (n=228) with models including GPT-5.1 and Claude. (3) Reality: evaluating statistical misspecification rates in programs LLMs write from scratch for neutral briefs, then comparing calibration-guided repair against LLM-as-judge review, a Bayesian-workflow checklist, and data-summary self-debug.
AI.result: Detection: The calibration oracle flags bugs with AUC 0.97 (88% detection at 2% FPR) when given a correct reference program (upper bound). The reference-free version achieves 62–78% detection. Unit-test oracle achieves 0%. Repair: Calibration feedback significantly outperforms unit-test feedback, which is significantly worse than no feedback (passing tests induce false confidence). Calibration improves repair on strong models: GPT-5.1 from 33% to 92%, Claude from 75% to 100%. Reality: 15–47% of runnable LLM-written programs are statistically misspecified (unit tests catch none). Calibration-guided repair significantly beats all alternative review methods.
AI.conclusion: For probabilistic programs, correctness is calibration, not compilation. The Bayesian workflow's diagnostic suite — not unit tests — is the appropriate verification oracle, and it serves effectively as both a detection mechanism and a repair signal for LLM-generated statistical code.

title: FARS: A Fully Automated Research System Deployed at Scale
summary: Recent automated research systems show that language-model agents can generate hypotheses, run experiments, and write complete manuscripts, but most evidence still comes from selected examples, human-framed topics, or a few pre-defined research tasks. We present FARS (Fully Automated Research System), a fully automated AI-for-AI research system designed to operate across research topics at scale. FARS autonomously generates and advances projects through ideation, planning, experimentation, and writing, using stage-specific agents coordinated through a shared workspace that records proposals, code, logs, results, and manuscripts. In its first public deployment, FARS produced 166 complete research papers spanning 67 fine-grained AI/ML topics while preserving intermediate artifacts as an auditable corpus rather than a curated set of successes. We evaluate this corpus with 282 structured reviews from volunteer reviewers covering 140 papers, including overall ratings, sub-scores, integrity checks, and LLM-use disclosure. The reviews indicate that FARS can produce review-worthy and occasionally strong AI/ML research artifacts in a large-scale public deployment, while also exposing recurring failure modes in narrow experimental scope, methodological limitations, and integrity issues.

AI.tldr: FARS is a fully automated AI research system that generated 166 complete papers across 67 AI/ML topics, evaluated via 282 volunteer reviews, demonstrating that LLM agents can produce review-worthy research at scale while revealing recurring failure modes.
AI.motivation: Prior automated research systems rely on cherry-picked examples, human-curated topics, or narrow task definitions. There is a need to assess whether fully automated research can operate at scale across diverse topics without human pre-selection, and to systematically characterize both capabilities and failure modes.
AI.method: FARS employs a multi-stage agent architecture with specialized agents for ideation, planning, experimentation, and writing. These agents coordinate through a shared workspace that preserves all intermediate artifacts (proposals, code, logs, results, manuscripts). The system was deployed publicly to autonomously generate end-to-end research projects without human topic framing or pre-selection.
AI.result: The deployment yielded 166 complete papers across 67 fine-grained AI/ML topics. A volunteer review process collected 282 structured reviews on 140 papers, covering overall ratings, sub-scores, integrity checks, and LLM-use disclosure. Results indicate review-worthy and occasionally strong artifacts, but also recurring failures in experimental scope, methodology, and integrity.
AI.conclusion: Fully automated AI-for-AI research at scale is feasible and can produce artifacts meriting peer review, but the uncurated corpus reveals systematic weaknesses that temper claims of autonomous scientific discovery and highlight areas needing improvement.

title: ECHO: Prune to act, trace to learn with selective turn memory in agentic RL
summary: Long-horizon language agents must repeatedly interact with tools, accumulate evidence, and make decisions under bounded context windows. Existing context-management methods make such rollouts feasible by truncating distant history, folding past turns into summaries, or selecting compact memory states. However, these breakthroughs introduce two coupled limitations. First, as the number of turns grows, historical observations are progressively removed or collapsed into compressed states, making it harder for the policy to reuse fine-grained evidence. Second, once the original turns are no longer source-addressable, outcome-based RL loses an explicit path for aligning policy updates with the evidence that supported a successful final answer. To this end, we propose ECHO, a selective turn-memory framework that jointly addresses history collapse and traceable learning through source-indexed reconstruction. Specifically, ECHO compresses each completed environment turn into a compact memory record, reconstructs bounded policy contexts by selecting from these records, and reuses the selected source indices to route positive outcome credit to the evidence and selection actions that support successful answers. On BrowseComp-Plus, ECHO reaches 43.4% held-out accuracy, outperforming GRPO (28.9%) and the rolling-summary baseline SUPO (36.1%), while using fewer turns and lower trajectory volume than SUPO (Figure 1). Additionally, the trained policy improves zero-shot generalization across multi-objective QA, code generation, and deep information-seeking benchmarks on both dense and MoE backbones.

AI.tldr: ECHO is a selective turn-memory framework for long-horizon language agents that compresses environment turns into compact records with source indices, enabling both context reconstruction and traceable credit assignment for RL. It achieves 43.4% accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus, outperforming GRPO and SUPO baselines while using fewer turns.
AI.motivation: Existing context-management methods (truncation, summarization, state compression) introduce two coupled problems: (1) fine-grained historical evidence gets lost through progressive removal/compression as turns accumulate, and (2) outcome-based RL loses explicit traceability to the original evidence that supported correct answers, making credit assignment opaque.
AI.method: ECHO uses source-indexed reconstruction: each completed environment turn is compressed into a compact memory record while preserving its source index. During policy execution, bounded contexts are reconstructed by selecting relevant records. During RL training, positive outcome credit is routed back to the evidence and selection actions using the preserved source indices, enabling traceable learning.
AI.result: On BrowseComp-Plus, ECHO achieves 43.4% held-out accuracy vs. GRPO (28.9%) and rolling-summary baseline SUPO (36.1%), with fewer turns and lower trajectory volume. The trained policy also demonstrates improved zero-shot generalization on multi-objective QA, code generation, and deep information-seeking benchmarks across both dense and MoE backbones.
AI.conclusion: ECHO jointly addresses history collapse and traceable learning through source-indexed memory reconstruction, yielding both stronger task performance and better data efficiency than prior context-management approaches for long-horizon language agents.

title: Arena-T2I Hard: Benchmarking and Improving Faithfulness with Dependency-Aware Checklist
summary: Faithfulness -- how precisely a generated image aligns with its prompt -- is increasingly central to the real-world utility of text-to-image (T2I) models. Existing faithfulness benchmarks, however, rely on simple atomic instructions, on which top-tier systems already achieve near-perfect scores. As T2I models enter creative workflows, users issue multi-faceted requests combining intricate spatial relationships, stylistic constraints, and complex text rendering. In this setting, a single binary VLM-judge score no longer captures which specific constraints the model fails to satisfy. We introduce Arena-T2I Hard, a 310-prompt stress benchmark drawn from real arena T2I logs, with approximately 30 decomposed yes/no constraints per prompt spanning six categories, including text rendering. The strongest closed-source system we evaluate reaches 0.855 with a 33~pp performance gap across 11 systems, demonstrating substantial discriminative power. Moreover, high public-arena rankings fail to predict faithfulness, confirming that holistic Bradley-Terry (BT) preference scores prioritize aesthetics over fine-grained prompt adherence. We propose a dependency-aware checklist reward that decomposes each prompt into a DAG of yes/no questions and zeroes descendants of failed parents, turning faithfulness into a per-constraint training signal. Combined with a BT aesthetic reward via group-decoupled normalization (GDPO), which standardizes each reward within its rollout group so neither collapses, the recipe attains a strictly better faithfulness-aesthetics trade-off on SD3.5-Medium and FLUX.1-dev under MMRB2 pairwise comparisons than every single-reward, naive weighted-sum, or 4-reward BT-ensemble baseline.

AI.tldr: Arena-T2I Hard introduces a challenging faithfulness benchmark with per-constraint evaluation, reveals that arena rankings favor aesthetics over prompt adherence, and proposes a dependency-aware checklist reward combined with group-decoupled normalization (GDPO) to achieve a better faithfulness-aesthetics trade-off.
AI.motivation: Existing T2I faithfulness benchmarks rely on simple atomic instructions where top models score near-perfectly. Real-world creative workflows involve multi-faceted prompts with spatial relations, stylistic constraints, and text rendering — a single binary VLM-judge score cannot pinpoint which specific constraints fail. Additionally, public arena rankings (Bradley-Terry) conflate aesthetics with faithfulness.
AI.method: 1) Arena-T2I Hard: a 310-prompt benchmark from real arena logs, with ~30 decomposed yes/no constraints per prompt across 6 categories. 2) Dependency-aware checklist reward: decomposes each prompt into a DAG of yes/no questions; failing a parent zeroes out descendants, yielding per-constraint training signals. 3) GDPO (Group-Decoupled normalization): standardizes checklist and BT aesthetic rewards within each rollout group so neither collapses, enabling multi-objective optimization.
AI.result: The strongest closed-source system reaches only 0.855 on Arena-T2I Hard with a 33pp performance gap across 11 systems. High public-arena rankings fail to predict faithfulness. The proposed GDPO recipe attains a strictly better faithfulness-aesthetics trade-off on SD3.5-Medium and FLUX.1-dev under MMRB2 pairwise comparisons than all baselines (single-reward, naive weighted-sum, 4-reward BT-ensemble).
AI.conclusion: Faithfulness must be evaluated at per-constraint granularity rather than holistic scores. The dependency-aware checklist reward plus GDPO provides an effective training approach that simultaneously improves faithfulness and aesthetics without the trade-off collapse seen in naive multi-reward methods.

title: Improving Certified Robustness via Adversarial Distillation
summary: Certified training aims to produce models whose predictions can be formally verified against adversarial perturbations, typically by optimising upper bounds on the worst-case loss over an allowed perturbation set. For neural networks, certified training methods based purely on tight relaxation bounds produce networks that are amenable to certification, but sacrifice standard accuracy. Conversely, adversarial training often yields stronger empirical robustness and standard accuracy, but the resulting models are generally difficult to certify with neural network verifiers. Recently, the literature has shown that better standard-certified accuracy trade-offs can be achieved by combining adversarial training objectives with loose over-approximations based on Interval Bound Propagation (IBP), effectively interpolating between lower and upper bounds of the worst-case loss. Building on this, we introduce AD-CERT, a certified training objective that combines adversarial distillation with an IBP upper bound. We show that distilling adversarial information over the logit space from an empirically robust teacher provides an effective lower bound surrogate for certified training, with AD-CERT achieving state-of-the-art certified performance on several robustness benchmarks. Furthermore, in a unified setup, distilling adversarial information at the logit-level is shown to improve certified accuracy over a robust feature-space distillation objective by up to 5.40 percentage points.

AI.tldr: AD-CERT combines adversarial distillation with IBP-based certified training, using logit-level distillation from an empirically robust teacher as a lower bound surrogate, achieving state-of-the-art certified robustness while improving over feature-space distillation by up to 5.40%.
AI.motivation: Certified training via tight bounds sacrifices standard accuracy; adversarial training yields better empirical robustness but is hard to certify. Prior work improved trade-offs by interpolating between loose IBP upper bounds and adversarial objectives. AD-CERT aims to push this further by incorporating adversarial distillation as a stronger lower bound surrogate.
AI.method: AD-CERT is a certified training objective that integrates adversarial distillation with an IBP upper bound. Specifically, logit-level adversarial information is distilled from an empirically robust teacher model. This distillation serves as an effective surrogate for the lower bound in the worst-case loss optimization, effectively interpolating between the adversarial teacher's guidance (lower bound) and the IBP-based over-approximation (upper bound).
AI.result: AD-CERT achieves state-of-the-art certified robustness across multiple benchmarks. In a unified experimental setup, logit-level adversarial distillation improves certified accuracy by up to 5.40 percentage points compared to a robust feature-space distillation objective.
AI.conclusion: Distilling adversarial knowledge at the logit level from an empirically robust teacher provides a highly effective lower bound surrogate for certified training, enabling AD-CERT to set new state-of-the-art results on certified robustness benchmarks while maintaining favorable standard-certified accuracy trade-offs.

title: A Self-Evolving Agentic System for Automated Generation and Execution of Biological Protocols
summary: Autonomous wet-lab experimentation requires more than plausible protocol text: biological intent, quantitative procedures, device constraints and experimental feedback must remain aligned from protocol and SOP design to code and physical execution. We developed ProtoPilot, a self-evolving multi-agent system, together with an expert-grounded benchmark and evaluation framework for testing this conversion as an experimental automation problem. The framework spans 294 synthetic-biology and molecular-biology tasks derived from 98 gold-standard protocols, wet-lab expert rubrics, device-level validity gates and real experimental tests. ProtoPilot incorporates layer-wise verifiability, multi-agent orchestration and a runtime-updated skill library to generate protocols, expand SOPs, synthesize SDK-compliant code and revise workflows from wet-lab feedback. It achieved a Top@3 expert-preference rate of 90.2%, an overall protocol-to-code gate pass rate of 89.5% and an Opentrons pass rate of 88.24%, compared with 32.35% for OpenTrons-AI. Wet-lab validation produced interpretable readouts, Sanger-confirmed products and feedback-corrected PCA-assembled DNA targets, establishing a verifiable route to autonomous experimentation. Together, these results show that the evaluation framework captures execution-relevant requirements for autonomous wet-lab automation, and that ProtoPilot can meet them by converting protocol and code generation into validated execution and feedback-guided revision.

AI.tldr: ProtoPilot is a self-evolving multi-agent system for autonomous wet-lab experimentation that converts protocols into validated, executable code with feedback-guided revision. Tested on 294 tasks from 98 protocols, it achieved 90.2% expert-preference rate and 88.24% Opentrons pass rate, far surpassing OpenTrons-AI (32.35%), with wet-lab validation confirming interpretable readouts and Sanger-confirmed products.
AI.motivation: Autonomous wet-lab experimentation demands more than plausible protocol text — it requires tight alignment across biological intent, quantitative procedures, device constraints, and experimental feedback from design through physical execution. Existing systems fail to maintain this alignment, particularly when converting protocols into device-executable code while incorporating real wet-lab feedback for revision.
AI.method: The authors developed three components: (1) ProtoPilot, a self-evolving multi-agent system with layer-wise verifiability, multi-agent orchestration, and a runtime-updated skill library for protocol generation, SOP expansion, SDK code synthesis, and feedback-driven workflow revision; (2) an expert-grounded benchmark comprising 294 synthetic-biology and molecular-biology tasks from 98 gold-standard protocols; and (3) an evaluation framework with wet-lab expert rubrics, device-level validity gates, and real experimental tests. Wet-lab validation included PCA-assembled DNA targets with Sanger sequencing confirmation.
AI.result: ProtoPilot achieved a Top@3 expert-preference rate of 90.2%, a protocol-to-code gate pass rate of 89.5%, and an Opentrons pass rate of 88.24%, dramatically outperforming OpenTrons-AI at 32.35%. Wet-lab validation produced interpretable readouts, Sanger-confirmed products, and feedback-corrected PCA-assembled DNA targets.
AI.conclusion: The evaluation framework effectively captures execution-relevant requirements for autonomous wet-lab automation, and ProtoPilot successfully converts protocol and code generation into validated execution with feedback-guided revision, establishing a verifiable route to autonomous experimentation.

title: When to Truncate a Feature Ranking: A Residual-Overlap Stopping Rule for Subset Selection
summary:
Feature rankings are widely used in supervised feature selection because they are simple, scalable and easy to interpret. Variables are first ranked by a relevance score, and a subset is then obtained by retaining the top-ranked variables. Although the first stage has been extensively studied, the second is often governed by an arbitrary cardinality, an empirical threshold or cross-validation, without a direct interpretation. This raises a basic question: given a feature ranking, when is there enough accumulated class-separation evidence to stop selecting features?
  This paper develops a distributional framework for transforming supervised feature rankings into class-independent subsets through an explicit risk-calibrated stopping rule. For each variable and each pair of classes, marginal separation is measured by the Bhattacharyya coefficient between the corresponding class-conditional distributions. The proposed method selects a single global subset shared by all classes by retaining the shortest prefix of a ranking whose residual product overlap falls below a prescribed threshold for every relevant class contrast. We derive binary and multiclass Bayes-risk bounds for the labelled product marginal problem, and obtain prior-dependent and prior-free calibrations of the residual-overlap threshold from a target all-pairs risk level.
  An empirical comparison on high-dimensional genomic datasets illustrates that the rule can reduce tens of thousands of variables to a few dozen while maintaining predictive performance statistically comparable to the all-features baseline. As the stopping rule only requires one-dimensional marginal overlap estimates and scans a precomputed ranking, it is well suited to very high-dimensional settings where exhaustive subset search is infeasible and interpretable truncation of feature rankings is essential.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a distributional framework with a risk-calibrated stopping rule that transforms supervised feature rankings into class-independent feature subsets by accumulating marginal separation evidence until residual overlap falls below a threshold, eliminating the need for arbitrary cardinality choices.
AI.motivation: Feature ranking methods lack a principled, interpretable stopping criterion for determining how many top-ranked features to retain; the second stage is typically governed by arbitrary cardinality, empirical thresholds, or cross-validation without direct statistical interpretation.
AI.method: The method uses the Bhattacharyya coefficient to measure marginal class separation between class-conditional distributions for each variable and class pair. It selects the shortest prefix of a ranking whose residual product overlap falls below a prescribed threshold for every relevant class contrast. Bayes-risk bounds (binary and multiclass) are derived, and both prior-dependent and prior-free calibrations of the residual-overlap threshold are obtained from a target all-pairs risk level.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on high-dimensional genomic datasets shows the rule reduces tens of thousands of variables to a few dozen while maintaining predictive performance statistically comparable to the all-features baseline.
AI.conclusion: The stopping rule is well-suited to very high-dimensional settings because it only requires one-dimensional marginal overlap estimates and scans a precomputed ranking, making it practical where exhaustive subset search is infeasible and interpretable truncation is essential.

title: Evo-PI: Aligning Medical Reasoning via Evolving Principle-Guided Supervision
summary: Despite recent progress, the reasoning capabilities of large multimodal language models (MLLMs) remain fundamentally constrained by static supervision, where fixed prompts, rules, or reward models provide non-adaptive guidance throughout training. Such static signals are often sufficient to enforce output formats, but fail to shape the underlying reasoning process, leading to brittle generalization and performance saturation in complex decision-making tasks. We propose Evo-PI, a principle-centric learning framework that treats reasoning principles as explicit, language-based supervision signals that can be generated, evaluated, and iteratively evolved. Instead of relying on fixed rewards, Evo-PI enables a co-evolutionary loop in which principles guide model reasoning, while model behaviors in turn refine the principles that supervise them. This dynamic alignment mechanism allows supervision to progressively adapt to the model's reasoning deficiencies. We instantiate Evo-PI in medical visual question answering as a high-stakes testbed requiring structured visual-textual reasoning. Across eight benchmarks and multiple model backbones, Evo-PI consistently improves reasoning accuracy, achieving gains of up to 24.6%. Our results suggest that evolving principle-guided supervision offers a scalable and general paradigm for training expert-aligned reasoning in MLLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/zhengxianda/Evo_PI.

AI.tldr: Evo-PI proposes a principle-centric learning framework where reasoning principles are iteratively evolved alongside model training, replacing static supervision with dynamic, adaptive guidance. Tested on medical VQA, it achieves up to 24.6% reasoning accuracy gains across eight benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current MLLMs rely on static supervision (fixed prompts, rules, rewards) that only enforce output formats but fail to shape reasoning processes, leading to brittle generalization and performance saturation in complex tasks requiring structured reasoning.
AI.method: Evo-PI establishes a co-evolutionary loop where (1) explicit, language-based reasoning principles are generated to guide model reasoning, and (2) model behaviors are analyzed to identify reasoning deficiencies, which in turn refine the supervising principles. This creates progressively adaptive supervision without fixed rewards.
AI.result: A consistent improvement in reasoning accuracy across eight medical visual question answering benchmarks and multiple model backbones, with gains reaching up to 24.6%.
AI.conclusion: Evolving principle-guided supervision provides a scalable, general paradigm for training MLLMs toward expert-aligned reasoning, particularly in high-stakes domains like medical VQA.

title: Diffusing Blame: Task-Dependent Credit Assignment in Biologically Plausible Dual-Stream Networks
summary: Biological neural circuits obey Dale's principle: each neuron's synapses are uniformly excitatory or inhibitory. Artificial networks that respect this constraint must coordinate separate excitatory and inhibitory populations, fundamentally changing how credit is assigned during learning. Several biologically plausible learning rules avoid backpropagation's weight transport requirement, but it has been difficult to achieve strong performance under Dale's principle beyond MNIST. Error Diffusion (ED) was originally proposed in a dual-stream excitatory/inhibitory architecture, where learning is driven by routing global error signals to all layers without transporting transposed forward weights or relying on random feedback matrices. Whether such a rule can scale under Dale's principle across both supervised classification and reinforcement learning remains unknown. Here, we introduce modulo error routing to extend Error Diffusion beyond binary classification, and show that a dual-stream excitatory/inhibitory architecture trained with this method achieves 96.7% on MNIST and establishes a 61.7% baseline on CIFAR-10, demonstrating that representation learning is possible even when strictly enforcing Dale's principle. For the classification setting, we introduce three domain-specific innovations: layer-specific sigmoid widths, batch-centered class error signals, and asymmetric initialization, and ablation analysis reveals that their relative importance reverses between MNIST and CIFAR-10, exposing task-dependent credit-assignment bottlenecks invisible to single-benchmark evaluation. In reinforcement learning, we integrate ED with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and evaluate it on continuous-control tasks in Google Brax and on Craftax, an open-ended exploration task. We show that ED-PPO achieves competitive performance relative to Direct Feedback Alignment, a backpropagation-free baseline.

AI.tldr: Error Diffusion (ED) is extended via modulo error routing to handle multi-class classification under Dale's principle, achieving 96.7% on MNIST and 61.7% on CIFAR-10 with a dual-stream excitatory/inhibitory architecture. Three innovations (layer-specific sigmoid widths, batch-centered error signals, asymmetric initialization) are introduced and ablated. ED is also integrated with PPO for continuous control and exploration tasks, showing competitive performance against Direct Feedback Alignment.
AI.motivation: Biological neural circuits adhere to Dale's principle (neurons are uniformly excitatory or inhibitory), which fundamentally alters credit assignment. Existing biologically plausible learning rules that respect this constraint have struggled to scale beyond MNIST. Error Diffusion was originally proposed for dual-stream architectures but its scalability under Dale's principle across both classification and RL remains unknown.
AI.method: The authors introduce modulo error routing to generalize Error Diffusion beyond binary classification. Three domain-specific innovations are proposed: (1) layer-specific sigmoid widths, (2) batch-centered class error signals, and (3) asymmetric initialization. ED is also integrated with Proximal Policy Optimization (ED-PPO) for reinforcement learning tasks.
AI.result: The dual-stream ED architecture achieves 96.7% test accuracy on MNIST and 61.7% on CIFAR-10. Ablation studies reveal that the relative importance of the three proposed innovations reverses between MNIST and CIFAR-10. ED-PPO achieves competitive performance against Direct Feedback Alignment on Brax continuous-control tasks and Craftax exploration tasks.
AI.conclusion: Error Diffusion can scale beyond binary classification under strict Dale's principle, achieving non-trivial representation learning on CIFAR-10. Task-dependent credit-assignment bottlenecks are exposed by cross-benchmark ablation. The method also shows promise in reinforcement learning, broadening the scope of biologically plausible learning rules.

title: RAISE: LLM-based Automated Heuristic Design with Robust Adversary Instance Search
summary: Automated Heuristic Design (AHD) with Large Language Models (LLMs) has shown remarkable progress in discovering high-quality heuristics. However, existing LLM-based AHD methods optimize heuristics for a fixed training instance set and may fail catastrophically when deployed under real-world distributional shifts. We propose Robust Adversary Instance Search (RAISE), a framework that integrates constrained worst-case instance search within a principled neighborhood of the training distribution into the LLM-based evolutionary search loop. RAISE treats robust AHD as a constrained adversarial instance search problem: the outer loop evolves heuristics via LLM operators, while an LLM-free inner loop efficiently identifies hard instances within an epsilon-ball around the training instance set using a basis distribution parameterization with boundary projection. Comprehensive experiments on Online Bin Packing (OBP), Online Job Shop Scheduling (OJSP), and Online Vehicle Routing (OVRP) across five distribution families demonstrate that existing LLM-based AHD methods degrade by up to 19 times under distribution shift, while RAISE consistently maintains strong performance across all tested distributions and problem scales

AI.tldr: RAISE is a framework that improves the robustness of LLM-based Automated Heuristic Design by integrating constrained adversarial instance search into the evolutionary loop, enabling heuristics to maintain performance under real-world distribution shifts where existing methods degrade by up to 19x.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based AHD methods optimize heuristics on a fixed training instance set and fail catastrophically when deployed under distributional shifts. This brittleness limits real-world applicability where such shifts are common.
AI.method: RAISE frames robust AHD as a constrained adversarial instance search problem. An outer loop evolves heuristics using LLM operators (crossover, mutation), while an LLM-free inner loop efficiently identifies hard instances within an epsilon-ball around the training set using basis distribution parameterization with boundary projection. The inner loop provides adversarial instances to stress-test candidate heuristics during evolution.
AI.result: Experiments on Online Bin Packing (OBP), Online Job Shop Scheduling (OJSP), and Online Vehicle Routing (OVRP) across five distribution families show existing LLM-based AHD methods degrade by up to 19x under distribution shift, while RAISE consistently maintains strong performance across all tested distributions and problem scales.
AI.conclusion: RAISE effectively addresses the distributional robustness gap in LLM-based AHD, producing heuristics that generalize reliably across diverse real-world conditions without catastrophic failure.

title: Nonlinearity-Aware LoRA: Structured Gate Adaptation under Low-Rank Constraints
summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is commonly viewed as an update-space approximation to full fine-tuning, yet this view is incomplete for self-gated Transformer feed-forward networks. In gated FFNs, a low-rank residual can change not only projected features but also the nonlinear selection weights that determine which channels contribute to the output. We formalize this effect as selection misalignment and connect it to the local effective homogeneity of self-gated activations. This motivates a nonlinearity-aware principle for parameter-efficient fine-tuning: low-rank updates should allocate capacity to gate channels whose nonlinear states remain responsive and should shape the temporal evolution of selection. We propose NA-LoRA, a training-only method with two lightweight mechanisms: a derivative-based temporal-importance mask for gate-related LoRA updates and an activation-specific step-scaling rule when a meaningful coarse effective-homogeneity partition is available. NA-LoRA adds no auxiliary loss and incurs no inference-time overhead. Experiments on language-model fine-tuning and vision-language transfer benchmarks show that NA-LoRA consistently improves over vanilla LoRA and is competitive with or better than strong PEFT variants.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a fundamental limitation of LoRA when applied to gated feed-forward networks (e.g., in Transformers): low-rank updates inadvertently distort the gating mechanism, causing "selection misalignment." The authors propose NA-LoRA, a training-only method that uses derivative-based temporal-importance masking and activation-specific step-scaling to address this, improving performance without inference overhead.
AI.motivation: Standard LoRA is treated as a low-rank approximation in the update space, but this view overlooks a critical effect in self-gated FFNs (e.g., SwiGLU, GELU): a low-rank residual modifies not only the projected features but also the nonlinear gating weights that perform channel selection. This introduces "selection misalignment," where the gate's channel-selection behavior diverges from what full fine-tuning would produce, degrading the effectiveness of parameter-efficient adaptation.
AI.method: The authors propose NA-LoRA (Nonlinearity-Aware LoRA), a training-only method with two mechanisms: (1) a derivative-based temporal-importance mask that allocates LoRA capacity preferentially to gate channels whose nonlinear states remain responsive (i.e., with non-vanishing gradients), and (2) an activation-specific step-scaling rule that adjusts update magnitudes based on coarse effective-homogeneity partitions of the activation function. No auxiliary loss is added, and both mechanisms are discarded at inference.
AI.result: Experiments on language-model fine-tuning and vision-language transfer benchmarks demonstrate that NA-LoRA consistently outperforms vanilla LoRA and is competitive with or surpasses strong PEFT variants, all while adding zero inference-time overhead and no auxiliary loss.
AI.conclusion: The selection-misalignment problem reveals that LoRA's standard formulation is suboptimal for gated FFNs. By making low-rank adaptation nonlinearity-aware—focusing capacity on responsive gate channels and respecting the activation's local effective homogeneity—NA-LoRA achieves better performance without sacrificing the simplicity and inference efficiency of LoRA.

title: Large Databases Need Small, Open-Weight Language Models
summary: Language model systems built around proprietary APIs often operate on a token-based cost model. This becomes prohibitively expensive in the context of large databases, where LM-enhanced relational operators can incur costs exceeding $10,000 for a single set of experiments, hindering thorough research and practical deployment. In this paper, we demonstrate that quantized, open-weight models running locally on just 16GB of VRAM can match or exceed the accuracy of closed-source counterparts at lower latency and a fraction of the price, challenging the prevailing assumption that closed-source LM APIs are necessary for effective LM-database integration. We present and analyze the key system optimizations required to efficiently deploy these open-weight models within an LM-DB system. By integrating these local models into the BlendSQL v0.1.0 framework, we demonstrate a 390x reduction in overall costs and 3.8x reduction in latency compared to a proprietary LM API. We make our code available at https://github.com/CapitalOne-Research/play-by-the-type-rules/tree/main/sembench.

AI.tldr: Open-weight, quantized language models running locally on consumer-grade hardware (16GB VRAM) can match or exceed proprietary API-based models for LM-database integration, achieving 390x cost reduction and 3.8x latency improvement.
AI.motivation: Token-based pricing of proprietary LM APIs makes LM-enhanced relational operators prohibitively expensive on large databases (exceeding $10,000 per experiment set), creating barriers to both research and practical deployment of LM-DB systems.
AI.method: The authors integrate quantized, open-weight models into the BlendSQL v0.1.0 framework and analyze the key system optimizations needed for efficient local deployment of these models within an LM-DB system.
AI.result: Local open-weight models on 16GB VRAM match or exceed closed-source accuracy with lower latency. In BlendSQL, this yields a 390x reduction in overall costs and a 3.8x reduction in latency compared to proprietary LM APIs.
AI.conclusion: The prevailing assumption that closed-source LM APIs are necessary for effective LM-database integration is false. Quantized open-weight models offer a viable, cost-effective alternative without sacrificing accuracy or performance.

title: FedXDS: Leveraging Model Attribution Methods to counteract Data Heterogeneity in Federated Learning
summary: Explainable AI (XAI) methods have demonstrated significant success in recent years at identifying relevant features in input data that drive deep learning model decisions, enhancing interpretability for users. However, the potential of XAI beyond providing model transparency has remained largely unexplored in adjacent machine learning domains. In this paper, we show for the first time how XAI can be utilized in the context of federated learning. Specifically, while federated learning enables collaborative model training without raw data sharing, it suffers from performance degradation when client data distributions exhibit statistical heterogeneity. We introduce FedXDS (Federated Learning via XAI-guided Data Sharing), the first approach to utilize feature attribution techniques to identify precisely which data elements should be selectively shared between clients to mitigate heterogeneity. By employing propagation-based attribution, our method identifies task-relevant features through a single backward pass, enabling selective data sharing that aligns client contributions. To protect sensitive information, we incorporate metric privacy techniques that provide formal privacy guarantees while preserving utility. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach consistently achieves higher accuracy and faster convergence compared to existing methods across varying client numbers and heterogeneity settings. We provide theoretical privacy guarantees and empirically demonstrate robustness against both membership inference and feature inversion attacks. Code is available at https://github.com/MaxH1996/FedXDS.

AI.tldr: FedXDS is the first method to leverage XAI feature attribution in federated learning, using propagation-based attribution to identify task-relevant features for selective data sharing between clients, with metric privacy guarantees to mitigate statistical heterogeneity while protecting sensitive information.
AI.motivation: Federated learning suffers from performance degradation due to statistical heterogeneity (non-IID data distributions) across clients. While XAI has proven effective for model interpretability, its potential beyond transparency remains unexplored. The authors aim to bridge this gap by harnessing XAI to address the heterogeneity challenge in federated learning.
AI.method: FedXDS uses propagation-based feature attribution (e.g., Layer-wise Relevance Propagation or similar) to identify task-relevant features via a single backward pass. These attributions guide selective sharing of data elements between clients, aligning their contributions to mitigate heterogeneity. Metric privacy techniques are incorporated to provide formal privacy guarantees on shared data, protecting against membership inference and feature inversion attacks.
AI.result: FedXDS consistently achieves higher accuracy and faster convergence compared to existing methods across varying numbers of clients and heterogeneity settings. Empirical evaluations also demonstrate robustness against membership inference and feature inversion attacks, supported by theoretical privacy guarantees.
AI.conclusion: XAI techniques can be effectively repurposed beyond interpretability to address core challenges in federated learning. Selective data sharing guided by feature attribution, combined with formal privacy protections, offers a promising direction for mitigating statistical heterogeneity in collaborative training scenarios.

title: Creating Intelligence: A Computational Foundation for AGI
summary: This work introduces a new computational theory of mind grounded in set theory and hyperdimensional computing. Whereas traditional neural networks rely on continuous weights and matrix multiplication, this framework works with sparse binary data. It represents information as discrete sets, directly modeling biological neural population codes. I demonstrate that associative memory emerges naturally from network topologies featuring a combinatorially expanded hidden layer. Learning is driven by topological plasticity rather than scalar weight adjustments. This architecture unifies auto-associative and hetero-associative learning under a single core algorithm: information retrieval via subset pattern matching and exact nearest-neighbor search. Operating with constant-time complexity, these mechanisms bridge perceptual data (sparse distributed representations) and symbols (sparse holographic representations) without continuous bottlenecks. Mapping this framework to neuroanatomy, I propose that both the cerebellum and the neocortex implement variants of this algorithm, making subset pattern matching the fundamental engine of cognition. Because it relies on discrete logic rather than matrix arithmetic, this algorithm translates directly into in-memory hardware. This opens a new route toward synthetic intelligence with human-level energy efficiency.

AI.tldr: A computational theory of mind based on set theory and hyperdimensional computing that uses sparse binary sets instead of continuous weights, enabling associative memory via subset pattern matching with constant-time complexity, mapping to both cerebellum and neocortex, and offering a path to energy-efficient synthetic intelligence.
AI.motivation: Traditional neural networks rely on continuous weights and matrix multiplication, which are biologically implausible and computationally inefficient. The author seeks a framework that directly models biological neural population codes using discrete, sparse representations, unifying learning mechanisms and bridging perceptual data with symbolic reasoning without continuous bottlenecks.
AI.method: The framework represents information as discrete sparse binary sets within hyperdimensional spaces, employing network topologies with a combinatorially expanded hidden layer. Learning occurs via topological plasticity (not scalar weight adjustments). Both auto-associative and hetero-associative learning are unified under a single algorithm: subset pattern matching and exact nearest-neighbor search, operating in constant time. The architecture maps to neuroanatomical structures (cerebellum and neocortex) and leverages in-memory hardware via discrete logic.
AI.result: Associative memory emerges naturally from the combinatorially expanded hidden layer topology. The framework achieves constant-time information retrieval, bridges sparse distributed representations (perceptual) and sparse holographic representations (symbolic), and translates directly to in-memory hardware implementations.
AI.conclusion: Subset pattern matching is proposed as the fundamental engine of cognition, implemented by both the cerebellum and neocortex. The discrete-logic foundation bypasses matrix arithmetic, opening a route toward synthetic intelligence with human-level energy efficiency.

title: Addressing Over-Refusal in LLMs with Competing Rewards
summary: Safety training on language models often induces over-refusal: improved safety on harmful prompts at the cost of increased refusal on harmless ones. Though this trade-off can be mitigated by training models with reinforcement learning (RL) to reason before answering, it does not remove the underlying problem that reasoning can often be a "rubber stamp" for a predetermined response. In this paper, we address the safety-refusal trade-off by rethinking how models are trained to reason about safety. Our key insight is that unsafe reasoning can itself serve as a useful exploratory signal. Rather than preemptively blocking harmful thoughts, we encourage the model to sufficiently explore unsafe reasoning but produce a safe response. The harmful exploration improves the model's ability to distinguish harmful from harmless prompts by resolving ambiguity, allowing it to remain safe while complying only when appropriate. We cast this as an adversarial optimization problem in which a reasoning player explores strategies for producing an unsafe response and an answer player ensures that the final output is safe. We train a single model with dense rewards to play both roles within one chain-of-thought, across different segments. To achieve this, we find that process rewards are crucial for stable optimization of competing objectives. Our resulting model SEAR deliberately engages in harmful reasoning as exploration while reliably flipping back to a safe answer. We demonstrate that this behavior helps mitigate over-refusal and defend against attacks that directly manipulate the reasoning to be harmful.

AI.tldr: SEAR addresses the safety-refusal trade-off in LLMs by training models to deliberately explore unsafe reasoning before producing safe responses, using adversarial optimization with process rewards across chain-of-thought segments.
AI.motivation: Safety training induces over-refusal, and RL-based reasoning approaches often serve as a "rubber stamp" for predetermined responses rather than genuinely resolving ambiguity. The core problem is that models lack the ability to explore harmful reasoning as a discriminative signal.
AI.method: SEAR frames the problem as adversarial optimization between two players within a single chain-of-thought: a "reasoning player" that explores unsafe reasoning strategies, and an "answer player" that ensures a safe final output. Both roles are trained in one model using dense process rewards to stabilize the competing objectives across different CoT segments.
AI.result: SEAR deliberately engages in harmful reasoning as exploration while reliably flipping back to safe answers, effectively mitigating over-refusal and defending against attacks that manipulate reasoning toward harmful outputs.
AI.conclusion: Encouraging controlled exploration of unsafe reasoning, rather than blocking it preemptively, improves the model's ability to distinguish harmful from harmless prompts, resolving the safety-refusal trade-off more effectively than prior approaches.

title: Adaptive Cluster-First Route-Second Decomposition for Industrial-Scale Vehicle Routing
summary: Large-scale capacitated vehicle routing problems (CVRPs) are commonly addressed using cluster-first route-second (CFRS) approaches that split a routing instance into smaller, computationally tractable subproblems. Existing splitting methods typically rely on fixed partitioning rules, predefined optimization objectives, or learned policies, which may perform inconsistently across instances exhibiting different spatial, demand, and operational characteristics. In this work, we propose an adaptive CFRS system that formulates a decomposition procedure as an iterative decision-making process. Motivated by the recent success of large language models (LLMs) in reasoning and tool selection, the system employs an LLM as a high-level decision maker that analyzes the evolving decomposition state and selectively applies further clustering, balancing, and refinement operators. The proposed algorithm jointly partitions customers and vehicles, enabling capacity-aware clustering while adapting partitioning decisions to the characteristics of each problem. We evaluate the approach on synthetic and benchmark-derived CVRP instances containing up to 500,000 customers. Experimental results demonstrate competitive performance on benchmark-scale instances while exhibiting improved scalability and robust routing quality on substantially larger problems. These results highlight the potential of adaptive, LLM-guided decision support as a practical approach for industrial-scale vehicle routing and large-scale logistics planning.

AI.tldr: A cluster-first route-second CVRP framework that uses an LLM as a high-level decision maker to adaptively select clustering, balancing, and refinement operators based on evolving decomposition state, demonstrating scalability to 500,000 customers.
AI.motivation: Existing CFRS methods for large-scale CVRPs rely on fixed partitioning rules, predefined objectives, or learned policies that perform inconsistently across heterogeneous instances with varying spatial, demand, and operational characteristics. There is a need for an adaptive decomposition approach that can tailor its strategy to each problem instance.
AI.method: An adaptive CFRS system that frames decomposition as iterative decision-making. An LLM serves as a high-level decision maker that inspects the evolving decomposition state and dynamically selects among clustering, balancing, and refinement operators. The method jointly partitions customers and vehicles for capacity-aware clustering, adapting decisions to instance-specific characteristics. Evaluated on synthetic and benchmark CVRP instances up to 500,000 customers.
AI.result: Competitive performance on benchmark-scale instances; improved scalability and robust routing quality on large-scale problems up to 500,000 customers.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, LLM-guided decision support shows strong potential as a practical approach for industrial-scale vehicle routing and large-scale logistics planning, offering both scalability and instance-adaptive decomposition.

title: Policy Optimization Achieves Data-Dependent Regret Bounds in MDPs with Unknown Transitions
summary: We study policy optimization for online episodic tabular Markov decision processes with unknown transition kernels, aiming for best-of-both-worlds guarantees together with data-dependent regret bounds. Recent work (Dann et al., 2023; Li et al., 2026) has shown that policy optimization can adapt to both adversarial and stochastic losses with first-order, second-order, and path-length bounds, but only under known transitions, leaving open whether such data-dependent guarantees are achievable by policy optimization when the transition kernel is unknown. We resolve this by developing a new algorithm based on optimistic follow-the-regularized-leader that attains these guarantees under unknown transitions. The key ingredient is a new design of optimistic $Q$-function estimators together with a data-dependent transition bonus that controls estimator bias through the loss-prediction error.
