Our analysis further identifies an unavoidable transition-dependent complexity term that captures the intrinsic cost of estimating the transition kernel. As a result, we obtain first-order, second-order, and path-length bounds with the transition-dependent complexity term while simultaneously achieving gap-dependent $\mathrm{polylog}(T)$ regret in the stochastic regime.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves an open problem in reinforcement learning: whether policy optimization under unknown transition kernels can simultaneously achieve best-of-both-worlds guarantees (adaptivity to both adversarial and stochastic losses) with data-dependent regret bounds (first-order, second-order, path-length). The authors propose an optimistic follow-the-regularized-leader algorithm featuring novel optimistic Q-function estimators and a data-dependent transition bonus, achieving these guarantees while incurring an unavoidable transition-dependent complexity term. Gap-dependent polylog(T) regret is also attained in the stochastic regime.
AI.motivation: Prior work (Dann et al., 2023; Li et al., 2026) established that policy optimization can attain first-order, second-order, and path-length regret bounds adapting to both adversarial and stochastic losses, but only under known transition kernels. It remained open whether such data-dependent guarantees are achievable when transitions are unknown. The paper aims to close this gap by designing a policy optimization algorithm that retains these best-of-both-worlds properties under unknown transition dynamics.
AI.method: The authors develop an algorithm based on optimistic follow-the-regularized-leader (OFTRL). Two key technical innovations are: (1) a novel design of optimistic Q-function estimators that incorporate optimism directly into value estimation, and (2) a data-dependent transition bonus that controls estimator bias via the loss-prediction error. The algorithm operates on online episodic tabular MDPs. The analysis decomposes regret into components attributable to optimization error and transition estimation error, identifying an unavoidable transition-dependent complexity term.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves first-order, second-order, and path-length regret bounds under unknown transitions, each augmented by the transition-dependent complexity term. In the stochastic regime, it simultaneously obtains gap-dependent polylog(T) regret. The transition-dependent complexity term is shown to be unavoidable, capturing the intrinsic cost of estimating the unknown transition kernel.
AI.conclusion: Policy optimization can indeed achieve best-of-both-worlds guarantees with data-dependent bounds under unknown transitions, resolving a prior open question. The key enablers are optimistic Q-function estimators and a data-dependent transition bonus. The identified transition-dependent complexity term characterizes the fundamental price of unknown dynamics, and the algorithm matches this lower bound while enjoying logarithmic regret in stochastic settings.

title: An Agentic AI Framework to Accelerate Scientific Discovery in Plant Phenotyping
summary: High-throughput plant phenotyping now generates image derived datasets far faster than scientists can analyze them. At Oak Ridge National Laboratory's Advanced Plant Phenotyping Laboratory (APPL), automated stations image hundreds of plants daily across multiple remote sensing modalities; yet, trait extraction and interpretation remain manual, expert-bound, and strictly post-hoc, making analysis, not acquisition, the binding constraint on discovery. We present an end-to-end agentic AI framework that turns the facility from a data factory into an interactive autonomous, discovery platform, where scientists partner with AI agents to accelerate time to insight. A conversational Co-Scientist Agent translates a scientist's natural-language question into a structured analysis plan, and a headless Compute Agent dispatches Vision Transformer segmentation and trait extraction on the Frontier exascale supercomputer. The two agents run in separate security and resource domains and communicate over a secure, token-authenticated streaming channel, a design that accounts for the federation, data-movement, and provenance realities cloud-native agentic frameworks ignore, ensuring end-to-end provenance is captured for every interaction. The framework turns a days- to weeks-long analysis process into an interactive loop where agents reason over results, recommend next analyses, and respond to follow-up questions in seconds.

AI.tldr: An agentic AI framework transforms a high-throughput plant phenotyping facility into an interactive discovery platform, pairing a conversational Co-Scientist Agent with a Compute Agent on an exascale supercomputer to reduce analysis time from days/weeks to seconds.
AI.motivation: Manual, expert-bound, post-hoc trait extraction and interpretation from image-derived phenotyping datasets is the bottleneck constraining scientific discovery, as image acquisition far outpaces analysis capacity at facilities like ORNL's APPL.
AI.method: A dual-agent architecture: (1) a conversational Co-Scientist Agent that translates natural-language scientific questions into structured analysis plans, and (2) a headless Compute Agent running Vision Transformer-based segmentation and trait extraction on the Frontier exascale supercomputer. The agents operate in separate security/resource domains and communicate over a secure, token-authenticated streaming channel with full provenance capture.
AI.result: The framework reduces a days- to weeks-long manual analysis process into an interactive loop where agents reason over results, recommend follow-up analyses, and respond to queries in seconds.
AI.conclusion: By federating the conversational interface and high-performance compute across secure domains with provenance guarantees, the system addresses real-world deployment challenges that cloud-native agentic frameworks overlook, converting the phenotyping facility from a data factory into an autonomous discovery platform.

title: Bridging the Gap Between Latent and Explicit Reasoning with Looped Transformers
summary: Language models typically reason via explicit chain-of-thought (CoT), generating intermediate steps token-by-token. Latent CoT offers an alternative: it performs multi-step reasoning in the model's hidden states, replacing decoded tokens with continuous representations for greater efficiency. However, existing latent CoT methods underperform explicit CoT beyond 1B parameters, and the gap widens with scale. Looped, or recurrent-depth, Transformers, which reuse their weights to increase computation depth without adding parameters, are a natural fit for latent reasoning. We therefore ask whether looped Transformers can bridge this gap. We answer affirmatively with a simple recipe: a looped padded Transformer that processes K latent blocks in parallel for R iterations, with a cross-entropy loss on each latent position's gold CoT-step token, similar to explicit CoT supervision. We instantiate it as LOTUS (Looped Transformers with parallel supervision on latents). LOTUS is, to our knowledge, the first latent-CoT method to bridge the gap to explicit CoT at the 3B scale, while cutting thought-phase latency by 2.5x-6.9x from compact math expressions to natural language. Projecting LOTUS's post-loop latents through the base LM head recovers the gold reasoning steps and even surfaces alternative valid intermediate steps, evidence that its latent space is interpretable and CoT-aligned. Ablations confirm that both the looped backbone and the parallel supervision on gold CoT tokens are essential.

AI.tldr: LOTUS introduces looped padded Transformers with parallel supervision on latent CoT tokens, bridging the performance gap between latent and explicit chain-of-thought reasoning at the 3B scale while reducing inference latency by 2.5x–6.9x.
AI.motivation: Existing latent chain-of-thought methods underperform explicit CoT beyond 1B parameters, and the performance gap widens with model scale. The authors investigate whether looped (recurrent-depth) Transformers, which reuse weights to increase computation depth without adding parameters, can close this gap.
AI.method: The proposed method, LOTUS (Looped Transformers with parallel supervision on latents), uses a looped padded Transformer that processes K latent blocks in parallel for R iterations. Supervision is applied via cross-entropy loss on each latent position's gold CoT-step token, mirroring explicit CoT supervision. After the looped iterations, projecting the latents through the base LM head recovers reasoning steps.
AI.result: LOTUS is the first latent-CoT method to match explicit CoT performance at the 3B scale. It achieves 2.5x–6.9x reduction in thought-phase latency, spanning compact math expressions to natural language reasoning. The post-loop latent projections recover gold reasoning steps and reveal alternative valid intermediate steps, demonstrating interpretable, CoT-aligned latent space.
AI.conclusion: Both the looped backbone architecture and parallel supervision on gold CoT tokens are essential components. LOTUS establishes that looped Transformers can effectively close the latent-to-explicit CoT performance gap while offering substantial efficiency gains, with the added benefit of an interpretable latent reasoning space.

title: Harnessing Textual Refusal Directions for Multimodal Safety
summary: To improve safety in Large Language Models (LLMs) we can either perform post-training alignment or exploit refusal directions in the activation space. Both strategies are less feasible in Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) as they require unsafe multimodal data, harder to collect than their unimodal counterpart. In this work, we relax this constraint and investigate whether textual refusal directions, extracted directly from the LLM backbone, generalize across modalities (i.e., image, video). Preliminary findings confirm this ability, though effectiveness is conditioned by layer selection, steering strength, and cross-modal alignment, with the latter causing safe multimodal inputs to be spuriously steered toward refusal. Building on this, we introduce Modality-Agnostic Refusal Steering (MARS), a light-weight training-free approach that injects multimodal safety without the need for multimodal safety data. MARS corrects modality misalignment via activation re-centering, adaptively scales steering strength within a geometrically defined trust region, and selects the optimal intervention layer, operating at the first generated token. Evaluated on five SOTA MLLMs across safety, utility, and video jailbreak benchmarks, MARS achieves consistent safety gains while preserving utility. These results reveal that safety-relevant structure is shared across modalities and that textual refusal directions are a powerful and underexplored foundation for multimodal alignment.

AI.tldr: MARS (Modality-Agnostic Refusal Steering) is a training-free method that improves multimodal LLM safety by transferring textual refusal directions from the LLM backbone to visual modalities, using activation re-centering, adaptive steering within a trust region, and optimal layer selection — all without requiring multimodal safety data.
AI.motivation: Existing safety strategies (post-training alignment, activation-space refusal steering) require unsafe multimodal data, which is hard to collect. The authors investigate whether textual refusal directions from the LLM backbone alone can generalize across modalities (image, video), enabling multimodal safety without multimodal safety data.
AI.method: MARS operates via three components: (1) activation re-centering to correct cross-modal misalignment that causes spurious refusal on safe inputs; (2) adaptive steering strength scaling within a geometrically defined trust region to balance safety and utility; and (3) selection of the optimal intervention layer at the first generated token. No training or multimodal safety data is required.
AI.result: Evaluated on five SOTA MLLMs across safety, utility, and video jailbreak benchmarks, MARS achieves consistent safety gains while preserving utility, demonstrating that textual refusal directions effectively transfer across modalities.
AI.conclusion: Safety-relevant representations are shared across modalities in MLLMs. Textual refusal directions, extracted solely from the LLM backbone, serve as a powerful and previously underexplored foundation for multimodal alignment, enabling lightweight, training-free safety interventions.

title: Relational and Sequential Conformal Inference for Energy Time Series over Graphs via Foundation Models
summary: Accurate energy demand forecasting is essential for the reliable operation and planning of modern sustainable energy systems. Spatial-temporal graph neural networks (STGNNs) have recently achieved strong performance in point forecasting by jointly modeling temporal dynamics and relational dependencies across interconnected energy nodes. However, in real-world energy systems, accurate point forecasts alone are insufficient, as operators also require reliable uncertainty estimates to support risk-aware decision-making, grid stability, and operational planning under uncertainty. Conformal prediction provides a principled and model-agnostic framework for uncertainty quantification with statistical coverage guarantees, making it particularly attractive for safety-critical energy applications. However, existing conformal prediction approaches often fail to fully capture the complex spatial-temporal structure of energy systems. To address these limitations, we propose STOIC (Spatial-Temporal Graph Conformal Prediction with In-Context Learning), a novel framework that integrates graph-based forecasting with the zero-shot calibration capabilities of tabular foundation models. STOIC first generates point forecasts using an STGNN and subsequently reformulates spatial-temporal residuals into a tabular representation suitable for in-context learning. Leveraging a tabular foundation model, STOIC calibrates prediction intervals without task-specific retraining, effectively capturing both sequential and relational dependencies. We evaluate STOIC on five diverse benchmarks, including synthetic simulations as well as real-world electricity and district heating networks. Across all datasets, STOIC consistently outperforms existing conformal prediction baselines, delivering more reliable and robust uncertainty estimates for complex graph-structured energy time series.

AI.tldr: STOIC integrates STGNN point forecasts with a tabular foundation model for zero-shot conformal prediction, reformulating spatial-temporal residuals into tabular in-context learning to produce calibrated prediction intervals for energy demand forecasting.
AI.motivation: Energy system operators need both accurate forecasts and reliable uncertainty estimates for risk-aware decision-making. Existing conformal prediction methods fail to capture the full spatial-temporal structure of energy networks, limiting their effectiveness for graph-structured energy time series.
AI.method: STOIC first generates point forecasts via an STGNN, then reformulates spatial-temporal residuals into a tabular representation. A tabular foundation model is used for zero-shot in-context learning to calibrate conformal prediction intervals, capturing both sequential and relational dependencies without task-specific retraining.
AI.result: STOIC consistently outperforms existing conformal prediction baselines across five diverse benchmarks, including synthetic simulations, real-world electricity, and district heating networks, delivering more reliable and robust uncertainty estimates.
AI.conclusion: STOIC provides a principled, model-agnostic uncertainty quantification framework tailored for graph-structured energy time series, bridging the gap between spatial-temporal forecasting and statistically guaranteed prediction intervals via in-context learning.

title: Geometry-Preserving Orthonormal Initialization for Low-Rank Adaptation in RLVR
summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and its variants enable parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models under the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) paradigm. However, their efficacy and behavior under Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) are less well understood. In particular, two structurally initialized LoRA variants, PiSSA and MiLoRA, which outperform standard LoRA under SFT, can underperform standard LoRA under RLVR and may even exhibit training instability. These observations suggest that how to initialize the low-rank matrices in RLVR remains unclear. In this work, we develop a theoretical analysis of LoRA in RLVR, showing that orthonormal initialization achieves the minimal gap between LoRA outcome and that of full fine-tuning. Guided by this insight, we propose geometry-preserving orthonormal initialization for low-rank adaptation in RLVR, leading to two new variants, RLPO and RLMO. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that the proposed orthonormal initialization stabilizes RLVR training and outperforms standard LoRA, contrasting with PiSSA and MiLoRA. Finally, our unified analysis for LoRA initialization also explains why PiSSA and MiLoRA can underperform in RLVR, which may be of independent interest. Code and checkpoints are publicly available at https://github.com/Richard-ZZZ/geometry-preserving-orthonormal-init-rlvr.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals that PiSSA and MiLoRA, which outperform standard LoRA under supervised fine-tuning, can underperform or become unstable under RLVR. The authors prove theoretically that orthonormal initialization minimizes the gap between LoRA and full fine-tuning in RLVR, and propose RLPO and RLMO variants that stabilize training and outperform baselines on math reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Prior work shows PiSSA and MiLoRA (structurally initialized LoRA variants) excel under SFT, but their behavior under RLVR is poorly understood. The authors observed these variants can underperform standard LoRA or exhibit training instability under RLVR, motivating a principled investigation into optimal LoRA initialization for the RLVR setting.
AI.method: The authors develop a theoretical analysis of LoRA under RLVR, proving that orthonormal initialization of the low-rank matrices A and B achieves the minimal gap between LoRA and full fine-tuning outcomes. Guided by this, they propose two geometry-preserving orthonormal initialization variants: RLPO (orthonormal initialization for standard LoRA) and RLMO (orthonormal initialization for MiLoRA-style structured adaptation), and provide a unified framework explaining why PiSSA/MiLoRA underperform in RLVR.
AI.result: Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH) show RLPO and RLMO stabilize RLVR training and outperform standard LoRA, while PiSSA and MiLoRA underperform or exhibit instability. The unified analysis also successfully explains the failure modes of PiSSA and MiLoRA under RLVR.
AI.conclusion: Orthonormal initialization is theoretically optimal for LoRA under RLVR, and the proposed RLPO/RLMO variants provide stable, superior performance. The findings highlight that optimal initialization strategies differ between SFT and RLVR paradigms, and the unified analysis framework may be of independent interest.

title: Self-Study Reconsidered: The Hidden Fragility of Learning from Self-Generated QA
summary: Language models are increasingly taught from synthetic question--answer (QA) supervision: a model generates questions about a document, answers them from the same text, and the resulting pairs are used to fine-tune, distill, or compress knowledge into another model. We show that this generation step is not neutral preprocessing. It is an implicit policy that both selects which evidence becomes training signal and decides how that evidence is answered, and it is fragile at both stages. When choosing what to ask, generators do not scan a document uniformly. Coverage saturates early and concentrates on salient spans, diverse prompts converge on the same regions, and what looks question-worthy is driven by local presentation. As a result, salient artifacts such as poorly cleaned markup can hijack question generation across model families and scales. When answering, the model that produces the supervision tends to obey instruction-like passages embedded in the text. This compliance depends on the intent and surface form of the passage rather than its strictness, and is worst under task conflict, where larger models comply more often. These failure modes arise from choices made during QA generation, so they can be reduced without changing the training loop. Tying each question to a fixed target reduces biased selection, and filtering instruction-like spans before answering lowers mean injection compliance from $88\%$ to $13\%$ in our evaluation while retaining nearly all clean text.

AI.tldr: Synthetic QA generation for language model training introduces systematic biases: question selection over-focuses on salient spans and is hijacked by markup artifacts, while answer generation complies with instruction-like passages in the source text—both failure modes can be mitigated through fixed-target tying and pre-filtering.
AI.motivation: Synthetic QA supervision is widely used for fine-tuning, distillation, and knowledge compression, yet the generation step is treated as neutral preprocessing. The authors argue it is an implicit, fragile policy that can systematically skew what evidence is learned and how it is answered, motivating a rigorous examination of failure modes.
AI.method: The authors analyze QA generation across model families and scales, measuring question coverage uniformity and concentration on salient spans, examining the influence of document presentation (e.g., markup artifacts), and testing answer-generation compliance with instruction-like passages under varying intent, surface form, and task conflict. They propose two interventions: tying each question to a fixed target span (reducing biased selection) and filtering instruction-like passages before answering (lowering injection compliance).
AI.result: Question generation saturates early, concentrates on salient regions, and is vulnerable to artifacts (e.g., poorly cleaned markup) hijacking generation across models. Answering models comply with embedded instruction-like passages at 88% mean injection rate, driven more by intent/surface form than strictness, with larger models complying more under task conflict. The proposed fixes reduce injection compliance from 88% to 13% while retaining nearly all clean text.
AI.conclusion: QA generation is not neutral; it embeds implicit biases in both question selection and answer production. These biases can be substantially reduced through targeted preprocessing (fixed-target tying and instruction filtering) without altering the downstream training loop.

title: Low-dimensional topology of deep neural networks
summary: We study layered models, including feedforward networks, ResNets, and transformers, by limiting each layer to a width of $d = 3$, i.e., $\mathbb{R}^3$ as representation space. This allows us to track how a neural network changes low-dimensional topological invariants through its layers. Just about any topological structure may be simplified or even trivialized by simply increasing dimension; e.g., any knot is equivalent to an unknot in $\mathbb{R}^4$. By restricting to $\mathbb{R}^3$, we not only isolate the effects of activation and depth from that of width, we work in a space that lends itself to easy visualization. We focus on linking number here, deferring other invariants like link groups, Milnor's $\barμ$-invariants, knot types, ambient cobordisms, to a sequel. We provide full proofs and empirical experiments to justify the following insights: When measured by their power to effect changes in linking numbers, the layer-skipping feature in ResNets is as powerful as the attention mechanism in transformers; both ResNets and transformers are strictly more powerful than feedforward neural networks with monotonic activations, which are in turn more powerful than invertible and flow-based models; but replacing monotonic activation with a nonmonotonic one elevates a feedforward network into the same expressivity class as ResNets and transformers. These results suggest that low-dimensional topology can be a useful tool to guide designs of AI architectures. We also generalize our results from $d = 3$ to arbitrary $d > 3$.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes neural network architectures (feedforward, ResNets, transformers) restricted to width d=3 (ℝ³ representation space) to study how layers alter topological invariants, specifically linking numbers. The key finding: ResNets' skip connections and transformers' attention are equally powerful at changing linking numbers, both surpassing standard feedforward nets with monotonic activations; however, nonmonotonic activations elevate feedforward nets to the same expressivity class as ResNets and transformers.
AI.motivation: Increasing dimension can trivially simplify or eliminate topological structures (e.g., any knot unknots in ℝ⁴). By restricting to ℝ³, the authors isolate the effects of depth and activation functions from width, enable easy visualization, and use low-dimensional topology as a lens to compare and understand the expressivity of different neural architectures.
AI.method: The authors restrict each layer of feedforward networks, ResNets, and transformers to a width of d=3, operating in ℝ³. They track how layers transform low-dimensional topological invariants — primarily linking numbers — across architectures. Full proofs are provided alongside empirical experiments. Results are also generalized from d=3 to arbitrary d > 3.
AI.result: (1) ResNet skip connections and transformer attention are equally powerful at effecting changes in linking numbers. (2) Both ResNets and transformers are strictly more powerful than feedforward networks with monotonic activations. (3) Feedforward networks with monotonic activations are more powerful than invertible/flow-based models. (4) Replacing monotonic activations with nonmonotonic ones elevates feedforward networks to the same expressivity class as ResNets and transformers.
AI.conclusion: Low-dimensional topology provides a rigorous and intuitive framework for comparing neural network expressivity. The layer-skipping mechanism (ResNets) and attention mechanism (transformers) are topologically equivalent in power, and nonmonotonicity in activations is a critical factor for expressivity. These insights can guide future AI architecture design.

title: Review Residuals: Update-Conditioned Residual Gating for Transformers
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures. Also on Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21053343 ; Code: https://github.com/SixSigmaEngineer/review-residuals
summary: Residual connections add every sublayer's proposed update with a fixed coefficient of one; the network never evaluates whether an update is reliable before committing it. Drawing on the human-factors principle of independent verification, we introduce Review Residuals, which scale each update by a learned, input-dependent gate conditioned on both the current state and the proposed update: h_l = h_{l-1} + r_l * u_l with r_l = sigmoid(W[RMSNorm(h_{l-1}), RMSNorm(u_l)]). Conditioning the gate on the update is the property that distinguishes it from prior gated and scaled residuals. We report two findings. First, a depth-stability result: a convex (Highway-style) form of the gate reintroduces vanishing gradients and fails to train beyond ~20 layers, whereas the additive, identity-preserving form trains stably at all depths we tested. Second, an emergence-with-scale result: trained from scratch across five sizes (60M-1B parameters, multi-seed), Review Residuals show no advantage at small scale but at 590M significantly outperform both a parameter-matched Highway gate and a parameter-matched standard residual (p<0.05), with a larger advantage at 1B. The benefit grows with model size rather than shrinking.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Review Residuals, a gated residual connection where the update is scaled by a learned, input-dependent gate conditioned on both the current hidden state and the proposed update. This contrasts with standard residuals (fixed coefficient of 1) and prior gated residuals. Key findings: (1) the additive identity-preserving gate form enables stable training at arbitrary depths, unlike Highway-style convex gates which reintroduce vanishing gradients; (2) Review Residuals exhibit emergence with scale—no benefit at small model sizes but statistically significant gains over both Highway gates and standard residuals at 590M parameters and above, with the advantage growing as model size increases.
AI.motivation: Standard residual connections blindly add every sublayer update with a fixed coefficient of 1, without evaluating the update's reliability. This contrasts with human-factors engineering principles of independent verification. The authors aim to introduce a mechanism that allows the network to assess and modulate each update before committing it, potentially improving training dynamics and model quality.
AI.method: The proposed Review Residual computes h_l = h_{l-1} + r_l * u_l, where the gate r_l = sigmoid(W[RMSNorm(h_{l-1}), RMSNorm(u_l)]) is a learned, input-dependent scalar conditioned on both the current state and the proposed update via concatenation of their RMS-normalized representations. This differs from prior gated residuals (e.g., Highway Networks) because the gate explicitly conditions on the update itself. Experiments span five model sizes (60M–1B parameters) with multi-seed training from scratch, comparing against standard residuals and parameter-matched Highway gates.
AI.result: Two principal results: (1) Depth-stability—a convex Highway-style gate formulation reintroduces vanishing gradients and fails beyond ~20 layers, while the additive, identity-preserving Review Residual trains stably at all tested depths. (2) Emergence with scale—Review Residuals show no advantage at small scales (60M) but significantly outperform both Highway gates and standard residuals at 590M parameters (p<0.05), with an even larger advantage at 1B parameters. The benefit grows with model size rather than diminishing.
AI.conclusion: The key design principle is conditioning the gate on the proposed update, which distinguishes Review Residuals from prior gating mechanisms. The additive identity-preserving form is critical for depth scalability. The emergence-with-scale property suggests that learned input-dependent verification of updates becomes increasingly valuable as model capacity grows, making Review Residuals a promising architectural modification for large-scale transformers.

title: PolicyGuard: From Organizational Policies to Neuro-SymbolicCompliance Review Engines
summary: Policy-grounded document review requires determining whether a target document complies with organization-specific policies, guidelines, or playbooks. While large language models can assist with policy interpretation and document analysis, end-to-end prompting leaves the applied policy logic implicit, making compliance decisions difficult to inspect, update, and test. We present PolicyGuard, a neuro-symbolic framework for policy-grounded document compliance review. PolicyGuard converts organizational policy guidance into an executable review engine consisting of typed relational logic rules and atom-level extraction questions. During review, LLMs answer these local questions using retrieved document evidence, and a symbolic evaluator applies the formal rules to detect non-compliance. We instantiate and evaluate PolicyGuard on company-specific NDA compliance review, where contract clauses must be checked against organization-specific negotiation policies. By separating policy formalization, local document interpretation, and symbolic compliance evaluation, PolicyGuard makes document review more explicit, maintainable, and systematically testable.

AI.tldr: PolicyGuard is a neuro-symbolic framework for policy-grounded document compliance review that decomposes the task into: (1) converting organizational policies into executable relational logic rules and atom-level extraction questions, (2) using LLMs to answer local questions from document evidence, and (3) employing a symbolic evaluator to apply formal rules for detecting non-compliance. This separation makes compliance decisions explicit, maintainable, and testable.
AI.motivation: End-to-end prompting of LLMs for policy-grounded document review leaves the applied policy logic implicit, making compliance decisions opaque and difficult to inspect, update, or systematically test. There is a need for a framework that makes the reasoning behind compliance decisions explicit and modular.
AI.method: PolicyGuard, a neuro-symbolic framework consisting of three components: (1) conversion of organizational policy guidance into typed relational logic rules paired with atom-level extraction questions, (2) LLM-based answering of these local extraction questions using retrieved evidence from the target document, and (3) a symbolic evaluator that applies the formal logic rules to the extracted answers to determine compliance or detect non-compliance.
AI.result: The framework was instantiated and evaluated on company-specific NDA (Non-Disclosure Agreement) compliance review, where contract clauses must be checked against organization-specific negotiation policies.
AI.conclusion: By separating policy formalization, local document interpretation, and symbolic compliance evaluation, PolicyGuard makes document review more explicit, maintainable, and systematically testable compared to end-to-end prompting approaches.

title: Signed-Permutation Coordinate Transport for RMSNorm Transformers
summary: Modern LLM workflows move coordinate-indexed objects across checkpoints: steering vectors, sparse autoencoders, top-$k$ neuron sets, attribution lists, and merge alignments. This is only well posed after fixing the model's residual-stream gauge, which we show is architecture-dependent: LayerNorm residual charts have permutation gauge $S_d$ (up to a global sign flip), while RMSNorm charts with generic per-channel gain have signed-permutation gauge $B_d = S_d \ltimes \{\pm 1\}^d$. Permutation-only alignment is therefore symmetry-incomplete for RMSNorm models. We introduce sign-marginalized Hungarian matching and prove a sharp failure mode: with decorrelated coordinates, raw signed-correlation matching has a structural permutation-accuracy ceiling at the positive-sign fraction of the true gauge, which sign-marginalization removes. We then make coordinate-preserving transport, not function-level merging, the primary object: composing saved-checkpoint local $B_d$ gauges along same-base fine-tuning trajectories recovers 91.1% of cross-run coordinates at 1500 steps versus 60.3% for endpoint matching, and the gain is not explained by merely routing through the base. The recovered gauge transfers tools that permutation-only alignment breaks: TinyLlama SAE reconstruction has NMSE 0.004 under $B_d$ versus 1.08 under $S_d$; Qwen sentiment steering preserves 95.8% of its effect versus 17.2%; refusal steering reverses sign under $S_d$; coordinate-preserving merges behave the same way. The same covariance governs stateful training: signed transport of AdamW state preserves the resumed trajectory, while permutation-only state follows a different one from a functionally identical checkpoint. Finally, gauge-sweep audits show index-level interpretability claims are reproducible only relative to an explicit gauge.

AI.tldr: LayerNorm and RMSNorm architectures induce different gauge symmetries (permutation vs. signed-permutation) on residual streams. Permutation-only alignment is symmetry-incomplete for RMSNorm models, causing tool breakage; sign-marginalized Hungarian matching recovers the correct gauge, preserving coordinates, steering effects, optimizer state, and interpretability across checkpoints.
AI.motivation: Modern LLM workflows (steering vectors, SAEs, neuron attribution, model merging) rely on coordinate-indexed objects that are only well-defined after fixing the residual-stream gauge. The authors identify that existing permutation-only alignment methods are symmetry-incomplete for RMSNorm architectures, which dominate current LLMs, leading to systematic failures in cross-checkpoint coordinate transport.
AI.method: The paper formalizes the gauge group: LayerNorm yields permutation group S_d (up to global sign flip), while RMSNorm with per-channel gain yields signed-permutation group B_d = S_d ⋉ {±1}^d. They introduce sign-marginalized Hungarian matching and prove a structural failure mode where raw signed-correlation matching has a permutation-accuracy ceiling at the positive-sign fraction. They propose coordinate-preserving transport by composing local B_d gauges along same-base fine-tuning trajectories, and validate via gauge-sweep audits across multiple downstream tasks.
AI.result: Coordinate-preserving transport along same-base fine-tuning trajectories recovers 91.1% of cross-run coordinates at 1500 steps vs. 60.3% for endpoint matching. Under B_d gauge: TinyLlama SAE reconstruction NMSE = 0.004 (vs. 1.08 under S_d); Qwen sentiment steering preserves 95.8% effect (vs. 17.2%); refusal steering sign flips under S_d. Signed transport of AdamW state preserves the resumed training trajectory, while permutation-only state diverges. Gauge-sweep audits show index-level interpretability claims are reproducible only relative to an explicit gauge.
AI.conclusion: The residual-stream gauge is architecture-dependent and must be explicitly accounted for. For RMSNorm models, the B_d signed-permutation gauge is necessary and sufficient for coordinate-preserving operations. Sign-marginalized matching and trajectory-based gauge transport provide practical algorithms that restore cross-checkpoint compatibility for steering, SAEs, merging, optimizer state, and interpretability.

title: AxDafny: Agentic Verified Code Generation in Dafny
summary: We study agentic code generation in Dafny, where a model must generate both executable code and the proof artifacts for verification. We present AxDafny, a verifier-guided repair framework that iteratively generates implementations, invariants, assertions, and termination arguments. We also introduce LiveCodeBench-Pro-Dafny (LCB-Pro-Dafny), a benchmark of 250 competition-style programming problems translated into Dafny with formal specifications and a verifier-based evaluation harness. On LCB-Pro-Dafny, AxDafny substantially improves verification success over baseline GPT-5.5 performance. On DafnyBench, AxDafny achieves 92.7\% verification success, outperforming the strongest previously reported proof-hint baseline by 6.5 percentage points. Lastly, we show that verification success and runtime test performance measure different aspects of generated code.

AI.tldr: AxDafny is a verifier-guided repair framework that iteratively generates Dafny code along with proof artifacts (invariants, assertions, termination arguments). It achieves 92.7% verification success on DafnyBench (outperforming prior baselines by 6.5pp) and substantially improves over GPT-5.5 on a new benchmark called LCB-Pro-Dafny (250 competition-style problems with formal specs). The paper also demonstrates that verification success and runtime test performance capture distinct aspects of code quality.
AI.motivation: Agentic code generation for verified languages like Dafny requires not only executable code but also proof annotations (invariants, assertions, termination metrics). Existing approaches struggle with this dual requirement, and there is a need for both stronger repair methods and better benchmarks to evaluate verifier-guided code generation.
AI.method: AxDafny is a verifier-guided repair framework that iteratively generates implementations along with required proof artifacts. It uses a feedback loop where the Dafny verifier's output guides subsequent repair attempts. The authors also introduce LCB-Pro-Dafny, a benchmark of 250 competition-style programming problems translated into Dafny, complete with formal specifications and an automated verifier-based evaluation harness.
AI.result: On LCB-Pro-Dafny, AxDafny substantially improves verification success over baseline GPT-5.5. On DafnyBench, AxDafny achieves 92.7% verification success, surpassing the strongest prior proof-hint baseline by 6.5 percentage points. The authors also demonstrate a divergence between verification success rates and traditional runtime test performance, indicating the two metrics measure different aspects of generated code quality.
AI.conclusion: Verifier-guided iterative repair significantly boosts the ability of LLMs to generate formally verified Dafny code. Verification success and runtime test performance are complementary evaluation dimensions, and benchmarks like LCB-Pro-Dafny are needed to properly assess progress in agentic code generation with formal guarantees.

title: Sequential RC-TGAN: Generating Relational Time Series with Spectral Envelope Loss
summary: The generation of synthetic relational databases often involves modeling complex temporal dynamics, such as transaction logs or event sequences. A significant challenge in this domain is the handling of categorical time series (e.g., status codes), where standard encoding methods like one-hot encoding fail to capture intrinsic frequency-domain features such as seasonality and cyclicity. In this paper, we introduce Sequential RC-TGAN (Seq. RC-TGAN), a temporal extension of the RC-TGAN framework, equipped with a novel integrated loss function based on the \textit{Spectral Envelope Theory}. This differentiable loss allows the generator to directly optimize the preservation of latent periodic structures via backpropagation. While spectral envelope theory is inherently designed for categorical sequences, we extend this frequency-domain regularization to continuous time series by employing a Variational Gaussian Mixture Model (VGM) discretization strategy. To establish a mathematically rigorous evaluation standard, we simulate categorical time series governed by a parameter $α$, with exactly known theoretical spectral envelopes. Integrating these dynamic sequences into the child tables of a relational database yields a robust ground-truth benchmark for evaluating the frequency-domain fidelity of our generative framework. Furthermore, we address the lack of robust evaluation standards for relational time series by proposing two new metrics: Spectral Density Divergence and Spectral Envelope Divergence. Experimental results on real-world datasets, as well as our simulated benchmarks, demonstrate that our end-to-end approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art systems in reproducing cyclic patterns and long-term seasonality across both categorical and continuous features.

AI.tldr: Seq. RC-TGAN extends the RC-TGAN framework to handle temporal relational data by introducing a spectral envelope-based loss function that preserves periodic structures in both categorical and continuous time series, validated via novel frequency-domain metrics and simulated ground-truth benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing generative models for synthetic relational databases fail to capture frequency-domain features (seasonality, cyclicity) in categorical time series, and evaluation standards for temporal fidelity in the frequency domain are lacking.
AI.method: The authors propose Sequential RC-TGAN with a differentiable loss based on Spectral Envelope Theory to optimize periodic structure preservation via backpropagation. For continuous time series, they use a Variational Gaussian Mixture Model (VGM) discretization strategy to extend the same frequency-domain regularization. They also construct simulated categorical time series with known theoretical spectral envelopes (parameterized by α) embedded in relational child tables as ground-truth benchmarks, and introduce two new evaluation metrics: Spectral Density Divergence and Spectral Envelope Divergence.
AI.result: Experimental results on both real-world datasets and simulated benchmarks show that Seq. RC-TGAN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art systems in reproducing cyclic patterns and long-term seasonality for both categorical and continuous features.
AI.conclusion: The end-to-end frequency-domain regularization approach effectively captures temporal dynamics that standard methods miss, and the proposed benchmarks and metrics provide a rigorous foundation for evaluating generative models on relational time series.

title: Interface-Aware Neural Newton Preconditioning for Robust Cohesive Zone Model Simulations
summary: Cohesive Zone Models (CZMs) are widely used to simulate interface fracture, delamination, adhesive failure, and fiber--matrix debonding in aerospace composite structures. In implicit quasi-static finite element analyses, cohesive softening may introduce negative interface tangents, solution jumps, and Newton-basin mismatch, so the previous converged state can become a poor initial guess for the next increment. This may lead to stagnation, wrong-branch convergence, or repeated step cuts. Existing remedies, including viscous regularization, path following, dynamic relaxation, and manual Newton--Raphson (NR) modification, either alter the effective response, increase cost, or rely on hand-crafted interface rules. This work proposes an Interface-Aware Neural Newton Preconditioner (IA-NNP) for difficult CZM increments. IA-NNP recasts manual NR modification as rule-based interface lifting and generalizes it into a learned, state-dependent interface correction. The method acts only on active interface variables and preserves the original traction--separation law, residual assembly, tangent evaluation, history update, and dissipation checks. Two realizations are developed: IA-NNP-Init for learned initial-guess lifting and IA-NNP-NL for iteration-level nonlinear right preconditioning. Interface graph features encode opening, traction, tangent, damage/history variables, mode mixity, residuals, and neighboring states. The correction is bounded, confidence-gated, and accepted only through the original CZM Newton solve. A root-equivalence property shows that IA-NNP changes the path to convergence but not the discrete CZM solution set. Tests on horizontal, circular, two-interface, and active-front benchmarks show improved difficult-increment convergence, better branch recovery, and fewer failures than standard NR and manual NR modification, while preserving the force--displacement response.

AI.tldr: IA-NNP is a learned preconditioner for cohesive zone models that improves Newton-Raphson convergence on difficult quasi-static increments by applying state-dependent corrections only to active interface variables, without altering the physical solution.
AI.motivation: CZM simulations in implicit quasi-static FE suffer from convergence failures due to cohesive softening (negative tangents, solution jumps, Newton-basin mismatch). Existing remedies (viscous regularization, path following, dynamic relaxation, manual NR tricks) either distort the physical response, increase computational cost, or require ad-hoc rules. A general, principled approach is needed.
AI.method: IA-NNP reformulates manual NR modification as rule-based interface lifting, then generalizes it into a learned correction operating on active interface DOFs. Two variants: IA-NNP-Init (initial-guess lifting) and IA-NNP-NL (iteration-level nonlinear right preconditioning). Interface graph features encode opening, traction, tangent, damage, mode mixity, residuals, and neighbor states. Corrections are bounded, confidence-gated, and validated through the original CZM Newton solve. A root-equivalence property guarantees the corrected path converges to the same discrete solution.
AI.result: On horizontal, circular, two-interface, and active-front benchmarks, IA-NNP improved difficult-increment convergence, enabled better branch recovery, and reduced failures compared to standard NR and manual NR modification, all while preserving the force-displacement response.
AI.conclusion: IA-NNP offers a robust, physics-preserving convergence aid for CZM quasi-static analysis, outperforming heuristic NR modifications without distorting the traction-separation law.

title: SemRF: A Semantic Reference Frame for Residual-Stream Dynamics in Language Models
summary: Residual-stream analysis asks how language-model computation evolves across depth, but intermediate decoding requires comparable readout coordinates across layers. If embedding anchors and unembedding readout disagree on the chosen span, apparent motion may reflect measurement drift rather than computation. We introduce \emph{Semantic Reference Frames} (SemRF), an anchor-based formalism separating semantic measurement from residual dynamics. A SemRF fixes anchors and measures states against them. Pseudo-inverse tying gives exact synchronization; under restricted bi-invertibility, SemRF yields stable semantic-basis coordinates, distortion bounds, and near-identity changes. With the frame fixed, residual computation becomes a depthwise semantic trajectory. The anchors induce a semantic Voronoi diagram: distance, or evidence such as logits, assigns each layer to a coarse cell, while coordinates retain within-cell motion and margins. We define layerwise steps, contribution profiles, and imbalance diagnostics, then use the Voronoi trace to define a margin-relaxed tube. The canonical trace is the minimum-action path inside this tube; when nonempty with positive quadratic weight, it is unique and obeys a discrete spline equation away from active constraints. Excess action controls step, curvature, and profile mismatch. Low curvature implies piecewise-linear compressibility and local knowledge density: lower trace complexity means fewer semantic knots. Through the parameter-to-trajectory map, this gives a conditional link to parameter efficiency: among admissible settings fitting data, lower-action and lower-complexity traces use fewer semantic degrees of freedom. The guarantees require controlled interface error and small projection residual under explicit tube constraints.

AI.tldr: Introduces Semantic Reference Frames (SemRF), an anchor-based formalism that decouples semantic measurement from residual-stream dynamics in language models. By fixing anchors and using pseudo-inverse tying, SemRF enables stable coordinate systems for tracking semantic trajectories across layers, yielding a Voronoi-based trace framework with minimum-action principles that link trajectory complexity to parameter efficiency.
AI.motivation: Residual-stream analysis of language model computation across layers requires consistent readout coordinates. When embedding anchors and unembedding readout disagree on the semantic span, observed changes may reflect coordinate drift rather than genuine computation. This motivates a formalism that cleanly separates measurement from dynamics.
AI.method: The authors propose Semantic Reference Frames (SemRF): fix semantic anchors, measure all layer states against them using pseudo-inverse tying for exact synchronization. Under restricted bi-invertibility, this yields stable semantic-basis coordinates with distortion bounds. Anchors induce a semantic Voronoi diagram, assigning each layer to coarse cells via distance or logit evidence, while retaining within-cell coordinates. They define the canonical trace as the minimum-action path inside a margin-relaxed tube, which is unique under positive quadratic weight and obeys a discrete spline equation away from active constraints.
AI.result: The framework yields layerwise steps, contribution profiles, and imbalance diagnostics. Low curvature implies piecewise-linear compressibility and local knowledge density — lower trace complexity means fewer semantic knots. Through the parameter-to-trajectory map, lower-action and lower-complexity traces use fewer semantic degrees of freedom among admissible parameter settings. Guarantees require controlled interface error and small projection residual under explicit tube constraints.
AI.conclusion: SemRF provides a principled way to separate measurement from dynamics in residual-stream analysis, enabling rigorous tracking of semantic computation across layers. The minimum-action trace formalism establishes a conditional link between trajectory geometry and parameter efficiency, suggesting that models with simpler semantic trajectories may achieve comparable performance with fewer effective degrees of freedom.

title: Making Sense of Touch from the Child's View for Contrastive Learning
summary: Is the sense of touch a mechanism for human babies' learning of visual concepts? If so, can we quantify its importance, and to what extent do babies rely on their sense of touch for visual learning? To approach these questions in a principled way, we propose a structured coding system for baby-centric touch events, yielding a dataset of 264k two-second clips of touch events coded according to this system. Using this dataset, we pretrain developmentally grounded models that reveal promising insights into the nature of baby learning from touch.

AI.tldr: Proposes a structured coding system for baby-centric touch events, yielding a 264k-clip dataset, and uses it to pretrain models that investigate how touch contributes to infants' visual concept learning.
AI.motivation: Quantify the role and importance of tactile sensation as a mechanism for human babies' learning of visual concepts — a question largely unexplored in a principled, computational manner.
AI.method: Designed a structured coding system for baby-centric touch events; constructed a dataset of 264k two-second video clips of touch events; pretrained developmentally grounded models on this dataset to probe the relationship between touch and visual learning.
AI.result: Pretrained models reveal promising insights into how babies may leverage touch for visual concept acquisition.
AI.conclusion: Touch appears to be a meaningful mechanism for infant visual learning, and structured computational modeling offers a principled way to quantify its contribution.

title: QVal: Cheaply Evaluating Dense Supervision Signals for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures in main text; 48 pages, 6 figures with appendix
summary: LLM agents increasingly act over long horizons, where a single trajectory can contain hundreds or thousands of actions. In these settings, outcome-only rewards provide too sparse guidance, failing to inform the model about the goodness of intermediate actions. Dense supervision methods aim to solve this problem by scoring intermediate steps, from intrinsic confidence to self-distillation and embedding similarities. However, it is common practice to evaluate them by measuring the downstream performance of a training pipeline that integrates them. This is expensive, conflates supervision quality with training engineering confounders, and renders different methodological families requiring distinct training setups incomparable. As a result, dense supervision methods are rarely benchmarked on common ground. We introduce QVal, a training-free testbed for directly evaluating dense supervision signals. Given a state-action pair, QVal measures how well a method's score is Q-aligned: whether it orders actions according to the Q-values of a strong reference-policy. This lets us compare signals before any training run and separate signal quality from other engineering choices. We instantiate QVal as QVal-v1.0, benchmarking 21 dense supervision methods across four diverse environments and seven methodological families, with over 1.2K evaluation experiments across six open-weight model backbones. We find that simple prompting baselines consistently outperform recent dense supervision methods from the literature, and that performance clusters strongly by family. These findings hold across model sizes, environments, and observation modalities. QVal is designed to be easily extensible to new environments and methods, enabling researchers to iterate on dense supervision methods before any training run.

AI.tldr: QVal is a training-free benchmark for evaluating dense supervision signals in LLM agents. It measures "Q-alignment" — how well a method's intermediate action scores match a strong reference policy's Q-values. Benchmarking 21 methods across 4 environments reveals that simple prompting baselines beat recent dense supervision methods, and performance clusters by methodological family.
AI.motivation: Dense supervision methods for long-horizon LLM agents are currently evaluated indirectly through downstream training performance, which is expensive, conﬂated with training engineering confounders, and incompatible across methodological families. There is no common benchmark to directly compare the quality of intermediate supervision signals, hindering progress in the field.
AI.method: The authors propose QVal, a training-free testbed that evaluates dense supervision signals via "Q-alignment": given a state-action pair, it measures whether the method's score orders actions consistently with the Q-values of a strong reference policy. They instantiate QVal-v1.0, benchmarking 21 methods from 7 families across 4 diverse environments using 6 open-weight model backbones, totaling over 1,200 evaluation experiments.
AI.result: Simple prompting baselines consistently outperform recent dense supervision methods from the literature. Performance clusters strongly by methodological family rather than by individual method innovations. These findings are robust across model sizes, environments, and observation modalities.
AI.conclusion: QVal enables direct, training-free comparison of dense supervision signals before committing to expensive training runs, decoupling signal quality from training engineering. The finding that simple prompts beat complex methods suggests the field may be over-engineering solutions, and QVal provides an extensible platform for more principled iteration on dense supervision approaches.

title: Amplifying Membership Signal Through Chained Regeneration
summary: The tendency of large generative models to memorize training data makes sample verification critical for privacy auditing and copyright enforcement. Current membership (MIA) and dataset inference (DI) attacks often rely on one-shot generations, which yield weak signals and limited sensitivity across modalities. Inspired by Model Autophagy Disorder (MAD), we introduce MADreMIA, a model-agnostic framework that enhances white-, gray-, and black-box MIA and DI. Rather than relying on shadow model training -- often infeasible for large generative models -- our framework facilitates scalable inference by leveraging inherent signals through iterative trajectories. This process utilizes chained generations across diverse modalities, where each output serves as the subsequent input, to improve membership evidence at low FPR. We demonstrate that memorized training samples exhibit significantly higher coherence and slower degradation during iterative regeneration than non-member generations. Our results show that MADreMIA provides richer signals across diverse model families and modalities; we present comprehensive evaluations for IARs, diffusion, and language models, alongside preliminary results demonstrating its potential for audio models.

AI.tldr: MADreMIA enhances membership inference and dataset inference attacks on generative models by exploiting iterative self-generation trajectories, where memorized training samples show higher coherence and slower degradation than non-member samples, enabling scalable, model-agnostic auditing without shadow models.
AI.motivation: Current MIA and DI attacks on large generative models rely on one-shot generations that produce weak, modality-limited signals. Additionally, shadow model training—commonly needed for strong attacks—is often computationally infeasible for large models. There is a need for richer, more sensitive membership signals that scale across modalities without auxiliary model training.
AI.method: MADreMIA leverages Model Autophagy Disorder (MAD) dynamics by performing iterative chained generations: each model output becomes the subsequent input, creating a regeneration trajectory. Member samples (memorized training data) exhibit higher coherence and slower degradation across these trajectories compared to non-member samples. The framework works under white-, gray-, and black-box access and is model-agnostic, requiring no shadow model training.
AI.result: MADreMIA provides significantly richer membership signals compared to one-shot attacks across diverse model families and modalities—including image auto-regressive models, diffusion models, and language models. It achieves improved membership evidence at low false positive rates, with preliminary results also shown for audio models.
AI.conclusion: Iterative regeneration trajectories expose a fundamental asymmetry between memorized and non-memorized samples, offering a powerful, scalable, and modality-agnostic mechanism for privacy auditing and copyright enforcement in large generative models without the burden of shadow model training.

title: Radial Suppression Accelerates Algorithmic Generalization: A Geometric Analysis of Delayed Generalization
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, 10 tables. Presented at the Workshop on High-dimensional Learning Dynamics at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: Why do neural networks memorize algorithmic training data long before they generalize? We present a geometric case study demonstrating that, on tasks where generalization requires discovering structured low-dimensional circuits, the memorization-generalization delay is driven by radial inflation of hidden representations under cross-entropy optimization. We formalize a radial-angular decomposition of activation-space dynamics and derive three testable propositions: (i) that penalizing radial inflation induces anisotropic, data-dependent weight regularization; (ii) that it suppresses radial gradient energy below the isotropic random baseline, forcing predominantly angular updates; and (iii) that it biases convergence toward flatter minima. To empirically validate these propositions, we study a single-hyperparameter norm penalty that softly constrains activations to a sqrt(d)-radius hypersphere. On modular arithmetic, this penalty accelerates grokking up to 6x across MLPs and Transformers, and halves training steps for a 10M-parameter nanoGPT on 3-digit addition.

AI.tldr: Neural networks memorize before generalizing due to radial inflation of hidden representations under cross-entropy optimization. A simple norm penalty constraining activations to a hypersphere suppresses radial gradient energy, enforces angular updates, and accelerates grokking up to 6×.
AI.motivation: Understanding why neural networks exhibit a memorization phase before generalization ("grokking") — specifically, why they memorize algorithmic training data long before developing generalizable low-dimensional circuits.
AI.method: The paper develops a radial-angular decomposition of activation-space dynamics under cross-entropy optimization, deriving three propositions: (i) penalizing radial inflation acts as anisotropic data-dependent weight regularization, (ii) it suppresses radial gradient energy below the isotropic random baseline, forcing angular updates, and (iii) it biases convergence toward flatter minima. Empirically, they test a single-hyperparameter norm penalty that softly constrains activations to a √d-radius hypersphere, validated on modular arithmetic (MLPs and Transformers) and a 10M-parameter nanoGPT on 3-digit addition.
AI.result: The activation norm penalty accelerates grokking up to 6× on modular arithmetic tasks across MLPs and Transformers, and halves training steps for a 10M-parameter nanoGPT on 3-digit addition, confirming the theoretical propositions.
AI.conclusion: The memorization-to-generalization delay ("grokking") is geometrically driven by radial inflation of hidden representations. A simple norm penalty that constrains activations suppresses this inflation, forces angular (structured) updates, and reliably accelerates generalization across architectures and scales.

title: Surrogate Fidelity: When Can Open LLMs Explain Closed Ones?
summary: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) requires full access to model internals, yet the APIs for most widely deployed language models at best expose log-probabilities over output tokens. This creates a surrogate problem: when do measurements made on open models allow us to make claims about a closed model? We evaluate surrogate fidelity at the prediction, attribution, and representation levels. For binary classification tasks, log-odds provide an API-compatible scalar readout of the model's representation space, and leave-one-out attributions provide insight into model behavior. Across eleven models spanning four families (Llama, Qwen, GPT, and Gemini), we find that prediction fidelity substantially overstates attribution fidelity: models that agree on what the answer is often disagree on why. We document an access-validity inversion: white-box signals like attention patterns and perturbation magnitudes are highly stable across models but only weakly predictive of causal attributions, which black-box input ablations capture by design. Mechanistic insight does not automatically transfer to closed targets, and prediction-level agreement is insufficient to warrant such transfer. Code and results are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/surrogate.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether mechanistic insights from open-weight models transfer to closed commercial models when only log-probability APIs are available. It finds that prediction agreement substantially overstates attribution agreement — models agree on answers but disagree on reasons. White-box signals like attention patterns are stable across models but poorly predict causal attributions, while black-box input ablations better capture them.
AI.motivation: Mechanistic interpretability requires full access to model internals, but widely deployed commercial models (e.g., GPT-4, Gemini) only expose log-probabilities. This creates a "surrogate problem": can findings from open models be validly claimed for closed models? The paper aims to systematically evaluate the fidelity of surrogate measurements at multiple levels of analysis.
AI.method: The authors evaluate surrogate fidelity at three levels — prediction, attribution, and representation — across 11 models from four families (Llama, Qwen, GPT, Gemini). For binary classification tasks, they use log-odds as an API-compatible scalar readout of representation space, and leave-one-out attributions to probe model behavior. They compare white-box signals (attention patterns, perturbation magnitudes) with black-box input ablations to assess an "access-validity inversion."
AI.result: Key finding: prediction fidelity substantially overstates attribution fidelity — models agreeing on the answer often disagree on the reason. The paper documents an "access-validity inversion": white-box signals like attention patterns and perturbation magnitudes are highly stable across models but only weakly predictive of causal attributions, whereas black-box input ablations capture causal attributions by design. Mechanistic insight does not automatically transfer to closed targets.
AI.conclusion: Prediction-level agreement between open and closed models is insufficient to warrant claims about mechanistic transfer. Researchers should not assume that insights from open-weight models generalize to closed commercial models without validation. The paper provides empirical grounding for the limits of surrogate-based interpretability.

title: CoMet: Context and Multiplicity Decomposition for Multimodal Uncertainty Estimation
summary: Uncertainty estimation has been a long-standing challenge in AI models; it amounts to "knowing what you don't know," and metacognition is notoriously difficult even for humans (cf. the Dunning-Kruger effect). Although it is still far from solved even in simpler classification systems, tackling it in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) is becoming increasingly important. Within MLLMs, uncertainty can stem from any of the diverse sources as well as from their relationships, and further can stem from the unbounded answers in the open-ended setting. To tackle the issues, we propose CoMet, an MLLM uncertainty estimation method by decomposing uncertainty into a context-specific term and a multiplicity-specific term. The former captures ambiguity induced by the given context (e.g., task or prompt), while the latter captures how many plausible answers determined by the context remain compatible with the given input. We train a lightweight post-hoc uncertainty module to estimate these quantities, which enables efficient uncertainty estimation without autoregressive answer generation or repeated sampling. Experiments on various open-ended multimodal benchmarks, hallucination detection, and multiple-choice visual question answering benchmarks show that CoMet consistently improves uncertainty estimation over existing baselines while remaining efficient in practice. Code is available at https://github.com/princetonvisualai/comet_uncertainty

AI.tldr: CoMet decomposes uncertainty in multimodal LLMs into context-specific and multiplicity-specific terms, trained via a lightweight post-hoc module for efficient, sampling-free uncertainty estimation that outperforms baselines across open-ended QA, hallucination detection, and VQA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty estimation ("knowing what you don't know") is fundamentally challenging yet critical for safe deployment of multimodal LLMs. The problem is compounded in MLLMs because uncertainty arises from diverse sources (context ambiguity, prompt variability) and their interactions, plus the unbounded nature of open-ended generation. Existing methods relying on repeated sampling or autoregressive generation are computationally expensive, motivating an efficient, principled alternative.
AI.method: The authors propose CoMet, which decomposes MLLM uncertainty into two components: (1) a context-specific term capturing ambiguity from the task/prompt, and (2) a multiplicity-specific term capturing how many plausible answers consistent with the context remain viable for a given input. A lightweight post-hoc uncertainty module is trained to estimate these quantities directly from internal representations, avoiding the need for autoregressive answer generation or repeated sampling, yielding efficient inference.
AI.result: Experiments across open-ended multimodal benchmarks, hallucination detection tasks, and multiple-choice VQA benchmarks demonstrate that CoMet consistently improves uncertainty estimation over existing baselines while maintaining practical efficiency.
AI.conclusion: CoMet provides a principled, decomposition-based approach to uncertainty estimation in MLLMs that is both more accurate than prior methods and computationally efficient, making it practically viable for real-world deployment. Code is publicly released.

title: FedLAB: Traceable Semantic Codebooks for Federated Multimodal Graph Foundation Learning
summary: Multimodal graph foundation models aim to learn reusable knowledge from graphs enriched with text, images, attributes, and relational topology, thereby supporting diverse graph-centric and modality-centric tasks. In practice, however, such multimodal graphs are often distributed across decentralized clients, where raw contents and local structures cannot be centrally shared due to privacy constraints. This motivates federated multimodal graph foundation learning, which requires not only transferable representation learning but also intrinsic semantic traceability under strict data isolation. Existing methods usually exchange or store knowledge through parameters, prototypes, embeddings, or compact codebooks, which support optimization and transfer but do not explicitly expose how modality evidence, node semantics, and topology context jointly support predictions. To bridge this gap, we propose FedLAB, a traceable semantic codebook framework that organizes multimodal graph knowledge into typed hierarchical codebooks for modality evidence, node semantics, and topology context. FedLAB further refines these trace units through federated semantic barycenter pre-training while keeping raw multimodal contents and graph structures local. Extensive experiments on 10 benchmarks and 6 downstream tasks show that FedLAB improves over state-of-the-art baselines by up to 7.53\%, while preserving a native semantic trace interface.

AI.tldr: FedLAB proposes a federated multimodal graph learning framework that organizes knowledge into typed hierarchical codebooks (modality evidence, node semantics, topology context), enabling traceable semantic predictions without sharing raw data. It achieves up to 7.53% improvement over baselines across 10 benchmarks and 6 tasks.
AI.motivation: Multimodal graphs (with text, images, attributes, topology) are often distributed across decentralized clients under privacy constraints, preventing centralized training. Existing federated methods (parameter/prototype/embedding exchange) support transfer but lack semantic traceability—they cannot explain how modality evidence, node semantics, and topology jointly contribute to predictions. This gap motivates a traceable federated framework.
AI.method: FedLAB introduces typed hierarchical codebooks that separately capture modality evidence, node semantics, and topology context. It employs federated semantic barycenter pre-training to refine these trace units collaboratively across clients while keeping raw multimodal data and graph structures strictly local.
AI.result: Extensive evaluation on 10 benchmarks and 6 downstream tasks demonstrates that FedLAB outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by up to 7.53%, while maintaining a native semantic trace interface for interpretability.
AI.conclusion: FedLAB successfully bridges the gap between federated learning and multimodal graph foundation models by providing both strong transferable representations and intrinsic semantic traceability, all under strict data isolation constraints.

title: TRIAGE: Role-Typed Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Agentic reinforcement learning requires assigning credit to environment-facing actions such as searches, clicks, edits, navigation commands, and object interactions. Standard GRPO uses the final verifier outcome as a uniform advantage over all action tokens. This outcome signal is useful but structurally incomplete: it punishes useful exploration in failed rollouts and reinforces redundant or regressive actions in successful rollouts. We propose TRIAGE, a role-typed credit assignment framework that adds a semantic role axis to outcome credit. A structured judge classifies each segment as decisive progress, useful exploration, no-progress infrastructure, or regression, and a fixed role-conditioned rule maps these labels to bounded segment-level process rewards. This keeps verifier outcomes as the source of optimization direction while correcting the two main blind spots of outcome-only credit. We further show that role-conditioned credit is the optimal segment-level correction expressible from role labels alone -- a projection of the per-segment advantage residual onto the role variable -- so that the fixed role constants reduce advantage estimation error whenever the judge is reliable, and we connect this to lower-variance policy gradients. Across ALFWorld, Search-QA, and WebShop, TRIAGE improves success rates over GRPO for two policy models and outperforms both a scalar judge-derived process reward and an outcome-supervised shared-backbone value baseline. Ablations show that the gain comes from role typing rather than merely adding dense rewards: reliable detection of regression inside successful trajectories is the dominant contributor, while exploration credit provides a consistent secondary gain; on completed ALFWorld and WebShop rollouts, TRIAGE also reduces environment-facing turns by an additional $10.4\%$ and $14.8\%$ relative to GRPO.

AI.tldr: TRIAGE introduces role-typed credit assignment for RL, where a structured judge classifies action segments into four semantic roles (decisive progress, useful exploration, no-progress infrastructure, regression) and applies fixed role-conditioned process rewards. This corrects GRPO's blind spots — penalizing useful exploration in failures and reinforcing redundant actions in successes — yielding improved success rates and trajectory efficiency across ALFWorld, Search-QA, and WebShop.
AI.motivation: Standard GRPO assigns uniform outcome-based advantage to all action tokens, which is structurally incomplete: it punishes useful exploration in failed rollouts (they contributed information but get negative credit) and reinforces regressive or redundant actions in successful rollouts (they get positive credit despite being harmful). The authors aim to correct these two blind spots without abandoning verifier outcomes as the optimization signal.
AI.method: TRIAGE uses a structured judge to classify each trajectory segment into one of four semantic roles: decisive progress, useful exploration, no-progress infrastructure, or regression. Fixed role-conditioned rule maps these labels to bounded segment-level process rewards. The authors prove this role-conditioned credit is the optimal segment-level correction expressible from role labels alone — a projection of the per-segment advantage residual onto the role variable — reducing advantage estimation error when the judge is reliable. This connects to lower-variance policy gradient estimates.
AI.result: Across ALFWorld, Search-QA, and WebShop, TRIAGE improves success rates over GRPO for two policy models. It outperforms both a scalar judge-derived process reward baseline and an outcome-supervised shared-backbone value baseline. Ablations reveal role typing (not merely dense rewards) drives gains: detecting regression inside successful trajectories is the dominant contributor, with exploration credit providing consistent secondary gains. On completed rollouts, TRIAGE reduces environment-facing turns by 10.4% (ALFWorld) and 14.8% (WebShop) relative to GRPO.
AI.conclusion: Role-conditioned credit assignment via TRIAGE effectively addresses the structural deficiencies of uniform outcome-based credit in GRPO. The role-typing approach — particularly regression detection in successful trajectories and exploration credit in failures — yields both higher success rates and more efficient agent behavior, with theoretical grounding as a variance-reducing projection of the advantage residual.

title: AdaJEPA: An Adaptive Latent World Model
summary: Latent world models enable planning from high-dimensional observations by predicting future states in a compact latent space. However, these models are typically kept frozen at test time: when their predictions become inaccurate, planning can fail, especially under test-time distribution shift. To address this, we propose AdaJEPA, an adaptive latent world model that performs test-time adaptation within the closed loop of model predictive control (MPC). After training, AdaJEPA plans and executes the first action chunk, uses the observed next-state transition as a self-supervised adaptation signal, and replans with the updated model. This closed-loop update continuously recalibrates the world model without additional expert demonstrations. Across a range of goal-reaching tasks, AdaJEPA substantially improves planning success with as few as one gradient step per MPC replanning step.

AI.tldr: AdaJEPA is an adaptive latent world model that performs test-time adaptation within the closed loop of model predictive control (MPC). By using observed next-state transitions as self-supervised adaptation signals after executing action chunks, it continuously recalibrates the world model without extra expert demonstrations, substantially improving planning success under distribution shift with minimal gradient steps.
AI.motivation: Standard latent world models are frozen at test time, causing planning failures when predictions become inaccurate under test-time distribution shift. The authors aim to solve this brittleness by enabling the world model to adapt online without requiring additional expert data.
AI.method: AdaJEPA operates in a closed-loop MPC framework: after training, it plans and executes the first action chunk, then uses the observed actual next-state transition as a self-supervised adaptation signal to update the model via gradient steps. Replanning then proceeds with the updated model. This adaptation loop repeats, requiring as few as one gradient step per MPC replanning step.
AI.result: Across a range of goal-reaching tasks, AdaJEPA substantially improves planning success rates compared to frozen models, demonstrating effective recalibration under distribution shift with minimal computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: Test-time adaptation via closed-loop self-supervision makes latent world models significantly more robust to distribution shift, enabling reliable planning without requiring additional expert demonstrations or retraining.
